                                 Preface

TC 3-21.220 provides all Department of Defense airborne personnel with techniques and training guidelines
to maintain an airborne force. This training circular contains basic and advanced training and techniques for
static line parachute training. It is designed to standardize procedures for initial qualification and training of
personnel in their duties and responsibilities in airborne training operations.

The principal audience for TC 3-21.220 is the airborne commander, jumpmaster, assistant jumpmaster,
safety, departure airfield control officer, drop zone support team leader, drop zone safety officer, and all
members of the airborne community. This manual contains the recommended initial training and
qualifications of the personnel designated to occupy these critical positions. Commanders and staffs of Army
headquarters serving as joint task force or multinational headquarters should also refer to applicable joint or
multinational doctrine concerning the range of military operations and joint or multinational forces. Trainers
and educators throughout the Army also use this publication.

Commanders, staffs, and subordinates ensure that their decisions and actions comply with applicable United
States, international, and in some cases host-nation laws and regulations. Commanders at all levels ensure
that their Soldiers operate in accordance with the law of war and the rules of engagement.
(See FM 6-27/MCTP 11-10C.)

TC 3-21.220 uses joint terms where applicable. Selected joint and Army terms and definitions appear in both
the glossary and the text. For definitions shown in the text, the term is italicized and the number of the
proponent publication follows the definition.

The use of a trade name or brand name does not constitute endorsement of the product.

TC 3-21.220 applies to the Active Army, Army National Guard/Army National Guard of the United States,
United States Army Reserve, Department of the Navy, Department of the Air Force, and the United States
Marine Corps, unless otherwise stated.

The proponent for TC 3-21.220 is the United States Army Maneuver Center of Excellence. The preparing
agency for TC 3-21.220 is the Directorate of Training and Doctrine, United States Army Maneuver Center
of Excellence. Send comments and recommendations on DA Form 2028, (Recommended Changes to
Publications and Blank Forms) to Commander, United States Maneuver Center of Excellence and Fort
Benning, ATZK-TDD, 1 Karker Street, Fort Benning, GA 31905-5410; by email to
usarmy.benning.mcoe.mbx.doctrine@mail.mil; or submit an electronic DA Form 2028.

                                                PART ONE

                      BASIC TECHNIQUES

This part provides all the information the instructor needs to prepare students and Soldiers
to participate safely in static line airborne operations.

                                                 Chapter 1

                         Standards and Purpose

    The Airborne Training is conducted at the Maneuver Center of Excellence, Fort Benning Ga,
    and provides the Department of Defense (DOD) with trained paratroopers.

     1-1. The purpose of airborne training is to qualify personnel in the use of the parachute as a means of combat
     deployment. This training also develops leadership, self-confidence, and an aggressive spirit through tough
     mental and physical conditioning.

     1-2. Airborne training initiates and sustains a high standard of proficiency through repetition and time proven
     techniques. Valid results are obtained when the following training standards are employed:

          • Strict discipline.
          • High standards of proficiency on each training apparatus and during each phase of training.
          • Vigorous physical conditioning programs to ensure paratroopers can jump with a minimum risk of

                injury.
          • A strong sense of esprit de corps and camaraderie among paratroopers.
          • Emphasis on developing mental alertness, instantaneous execution of commands, self-confidence,

                and confidence in the equipment.

     1-3. Volunteers must meet the prerequisites listed in the U.S. Army Training Requirements and Resources
     System website.

                                                 Chapter 2

                            Personal Equipment

    This chapter discusses parachute types, parachute donning, and headgear used in Basic
    Airborne Refresher (BAR) Training.

PERSONAL PARACHUTES

     2-1. The T-11 Personnel Parachute System, national stock number (NSN) 1670-01-539-4525 and MC-6
     Personnel Parachute System (NSN: 1670-01-527-7537), are used during static line airborne operations. The
     T-11 Advanced Tactical Parachute System (ATPS) and MC-6 Personnel Parachute System are highly
     portable systems that include the main canopy assembly, the reserve canopy assembly deployment bag, pack
     tray, harness assembly, risers, and universal static line modified (USLM). They can support 400 pounds. The
     T-11 complete system weight is 53 pounds, and the MC-6 complete system weight is 42 pounds. The T-11
     and MC-6 are limited to operation in winds of 13 knots at the surface. The T-11 main canopy is a
     non-steerable canopy. The MC-6 main canopy is a semi-steerable canopy.

T-11 PARACHUTE SYSTEM AND CHARACTERISTICS

     2-2. The T-11 (NSN: 1670-01-535-2233), parachute component parts and characteristics of each part can be
     found in TM 10-1670-326-23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-473-2.

MC-6 MAIN CANOPY

     2-3. The MC-6 parachute component parts and characteristics can be found in TM 10-1670-327-23&P/T.O.
     14D1-2-472-2/NAVSEA SS400-A1-MMO-010.

     2-4. The T-11 reserve parachute component parts and characteristics can be found in TM 10-1670-326-
     23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-473-2 or TM 10-1670-327-23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-472-2/NAVSEA SS400-A1-MMO-010.

T-11 RESERVE PARACHUTE INSERTS

     2-5. The T-11 reserve inserts are used as a mitigating safety factor for jumpmasters and number (No.) 1
     jumpers. The use of T-11 reserve inserts (see figure 2-1 on page 4) with the T-11 reserve parachute are
     mandatory for all primary jumpmasters (PJMs), assistant jumpmasters (AJMs), and the No. 1 jumper
     assisting in pushing a door bundle. Jumpmasters conducting over-the-ramp operations have the T-11 reserve
     parachute inserts. While conducting rotary-wing operations (UH-60 and UH-1), it is recommended that
     jumpers exposed to winds that cross the front of the reserve parachute have the T-11 reserve parachute inserts
     emplaced.

     2-6. All jumpers that have the T-11 reserve parachute inserts receive a final visual inspection of their reserve
     prior to assuming duties at the door or ramp. This visual inspection is performed by a member of the
     jumpmaster team. This inspection shall be given just prior opening the door or ramp. The T-11 reserve inserts
     will not be removed during this inspection. Adjustments to the T-11 reserve ripcord or inserts are not made
     near an open troop door or ramp.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  3

Chapter 2

                                             Figure 2-1. T-11 reserve inserts

T-11 RESERVE SINGLE PIN PARACHUTE

     2-7. The T-11 reserve single pin parachute (see TM 10-1670-347-23&P/TO 14D1-2-474-2/TM 110834A-
     10&P/NAVAIR 13-1670-347-2) is an aero-conical-design reserve parachute used with the T-11 and MC-6
     Parachute System (NSN: 1670-01-535-2248). The T-11 reserve single pin parachute is an emergency-type
     parachute designed to be activated by the jumper if the main parachute malfunctions. Weighing
     approximately 14.8 pounds, the T-11 reserve is 29 feet in diameter and has a combined shelf and service life
     of 15 years. It is repacked every 365 days. Component parts and characteristics can be found in TM-10-1670-
     347-23&P.

CARE OF THE PARACHUTE BEFORE AND AFTER JUMPING

     2-8. Troop parachute assemblies and reserves may be issued in recovery bags to aid handling and prevent
     damage or unintentional opening. Until removed for fitting by jumpers, parachutes and reserves should
     remain in the recovery bags and protected from moisture during storage to prevent mildew. Recovery bags
     are not waterproof and do not provide adequate protection from wet weather or damp ground. Parachutes
     must be stored in weatherproof areas such as adequate storage buildings, trucks, tents, or transport aircraft.
     (For parachute shakeout procedures, see TM 10-1670-326-23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-473-2 for the T-11 series
     parachute, and TM 10-1670-327-23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-472-2/NAVSEA SS400-A1-MMO-010 for the
     MC-6 series parachute.)

     2-9. The parachute is recovered and properly cared for to minimize damage. Upon landing, jumpers activate
     both canopy release assemblies for the T-11 ATPS or one canopy release assembly for an MC-6 series
     parachute. Take off the harness and place the parachute in the recovery bag using the tactical recovery method
     or by executing a series of figure-eight folds with the arms. (See figure 2-2.)

     2-10. The specific actions for the figure-eight fold are as follows:
          • Remove all air items.
                 Place harness in the recovery bag with the smooth side up, leaving the waistband out.
                 Place the released riser or risers underneath the harness.
          • Move to the apex of the canopy, grasp the drogue parachute and deployment sleeve, elongate the
                parachute into the wind to straighten the canopy and suspension lines, and remove all foreign objects
                and debris from the suspension lines and canopy.

4          TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                              Personal Equipment

• Fold the canopy and suspension lines into a series of figure eights using both arms, but do not twist
     the canopy unnecessarily because friction can cause the nylon to fuse.

• Lay the canopy on the top of the harness, ensuring all the parachute and suspension lines are inside
     the kit bag (recovery bag):
      Place the drogue parachute and deployment sleeve on top of the main parachute.
      Close bag fasteners: do not zip the bag because the canopy may become entangled in the zipper
          and damaged.

• Place the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute in the front storage pocket when using the universal
     parachutist recovery bag (UPRB).

  Note. For the T-11 ATPS, it is necessary to activate both canopy release assemblies upon landing.
  Fold the canopy in figure eights by itself and place it in the kit bag (recovery bag) on top of the
  harness.

                                Figure 2-2. Executing figure-eight folds with arms

SHAKEOUT PROCEDURES

     2-11. The parachute must be prepared for repacking once the airborne mission has been accomplished. The
     procedure is called chute shakeout. Suspend the parachute from a rope passed over a ceiling pulley (or from
     pole’s field expedient) high enough to allow the canopy to clear the surface area. (For parachute shakeout
     procedures, see TM 10-1670-326-23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-473-2 for the T-11 series parachute, and
     TM 10-1670-327-23&P for the MC-6 series parachute.)

Chapter 2

DONNING PARACHUTES

     2-12. Two personnel are required when donning parachutes. Using the buddy system to don properly and
     adjust the troop parachute harness provides an additional safety check, prevents delays during jumpmaster
     personnel inspection (JMPI), and provides minimum discomfort to the jumper while aboard the aircraft and
     when receiving the opening shock of the parachute. The buddy-system method provides the best combination
     of speed and accuracy for jumpers to adjust and check each other’s parachutes. One jumper assumes the role
     as No. 1 jumper and the other jumper assumes the role as No. 2 jumper. Two personnel are required when
     donning the parachute. One assumes the jumper role, the other as the buddy to assist in rigging. This reduces
     the possibility of rigging deficiencies and ensures proper fit of the parachute.

T-11 AND MC-6 HARNESS

     2-13. When donning the T-11 or MC-6 parachutes, jumpers must complete the following steps:
          • Step 1—inspect the parachute assembly for visible defects in accordance with TM 10-1670-326-
                23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-473-2 and TM 10-1670-327-23&P/T.O. 14D1-2-472-2/NAVSEA SS400-A1-
                MMO-010.
          • Step 2—placing the parachute on the ground and ensuring the harness assembly is up and the risers
                are facing away, including—
                 Activating the quick release in the waistband and pulling up each of the activating levers on the
                     leg strap ejector snaps, which releases the leg straps.
                 The jumper then activates the quick release in the chest strap.
                 Sizing the parachute harness must be done prior to donning to ensure proper fit and there are
                     two sizing locations:
                 The diagonal backstraps.
                 The left and right main lift webs.
          • The main parachute harness requires pre-adjustment prior to fitting.
          • Adjusting the harness:
                 The diagonal backstraps provide two of the nine points of adjustment on the parachute harness.
                 There are five sizing channels numbered one through five to adjust for the placement of the
                     canopy release assemblies and position of the pack tray.
                 Unsnap the directional snap fastener on the diagonal backstrap retainer and pull it free from the
                     sizing channel.
                 Select the appropriate size and routing the diagonal backstrap retainer takes through the
                     appropriate sizing channel, then through the appropriate diagonal backstrap keep.
                 The jumper secures the directional snap fasteners.

             Notes. The optimum position for the harness is with the canopy release assembles resting at
             approximately name tape level, with the top edge of the pack tray aligned with the jumper’s
             shoulders (not below) and the saddle routed around the meaty portion of the jumper’s thighs (not
             the buttocks).

             Jumpers who are outside of the 5-to-95 height percentile may require an adjustment. For example,
             a jumper’s diagonal backstrap may require a larger sizing channel adjustment of 3 to achieve the
             proper placement of the canopy release assemblies in the pocket of the shoulder.

          • Step 3—jumpers complete donning preparation by arranging the T-11 main, T-11 reserve/T-11
                reserve single pin, and UPRB by—
                 Letting out the excess webbing from all points of adjustment (leg straps, horizontal backstraps,
                     and the chest strap).
                 Positioning the UPRB (recovery bag) and reserve parachute where it is easily accessible to the
                     jumper while donning the parachute harness.

6  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                  Personal Equipment

                                        WARNING

         When the T-11 harness is donned improperly, the results can
         contribute to static line injuries, weak exits, towed jumpers, riser
         burns, poorly executed slips, and difficulty or an inability to
         recover from a drag during wind gusts after landing.

  Notes. The main lift webs provide two of the nine points of adjustment. There are three size
  settings: small, medium, and large.

  To make main lift web size changes, unsnap the snap fastener and expose the tuck tab. Select the
  appropriate size setting. If selecting small or medium, insert the tuck tab into the appropriate tuck
  pocket and remove any slack from the main lift web adjustment strap. If selecting the large setting,
  the main lift web adjustment strap is fully extended with the tuck tab folded in towards the main
  lift web. Secure the snap fastener again. Conduct the same size change on the opposite main lift
  web.

  The tuck pocket for the small setting is located above the chest strap on each main lift web. The
  tuck pocket for the medium setting is located below the chest strap on each main lift web. For the
  large setting, there is no tuck pocket; the main lift web adjustment strap is fully extended with
  slack removed.

  The main lift webs provide the capability to increase their length to accommodate jumpers at the
  5-to-95 height percentile and permit essential items to be worn under the parachute harness.

• Step 4—don the main parachute harness and then both jumpers perform the following steps:
      The No. 1 jumper dons the helmet and assumes a modified high jumper position.
      The No. 2 jumper places the parachute harness over the jumper’s arms with the diagonal
          backstraps resting on the jumper’s shoulders and holds the pack tray high on the jumper’s back.

• Step 5—secure the chest strap. The No. 1 jumper performs step 5, which includes the following
     actions:
      Ensuring that the quick-release webbing retainer is the width of two to three fingers.
      Completing an S-fold or accordion fold and securing the excess webbing in its webbing retainer,
          ensuring that the tabbed ending points towards the chest strap friction adapter.

• Step 6—pulling the ejector snaps and L-shaped ejector snap pads as far forward as possible towards
     the center of the groin while ensuring that the saddle is routed underneath the hamstrings (not the
     buttocks).

  Note. Maintain a modified high jumper position.

      Secure the UPRB.
      Secure the leg straps with the UPRB.
      UPRB: ensure the left leg strap is properly routed through the left leg strap retainer and the right

          leg strap is properly routed through the right leg strap retainer, then complete an S-fold,
          accordion fold, or roll the free running ends of the leg straps into the webbing retainers.
• Step 7—adjust the parachute to the individual jumper and both jumpers perform step 7, which
     includes the following actions:
      The No. 1 jumper secures the D-rings with the thumbs of each hand, then pulls downward,
          pressing against the body, and stands erect.
      After the No. 2 jumper is standing erect, remove all slack from the horizontal backstrap by
          simultaneously pulling up both sides of the horizontal backstraps where they emerge from the
          main lift web.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  7


---

Chapter 2

          • Step 8—continue adjusting parachute to the individual jumper; both jumpers perform step 8, which
                includes the following actions:
                 The No. 1 jumper remains standing erect, releases the D-rings and applies pressure to the
                     horizontal backstrap just above the leg strap ejector snaps until a tight but not uncomfortable
                     adjustment has been made.
                 The No. 2 jumper removes all slack on each side by placing the palm of one hand on top of a
                     diagonal backstrap and pressing while tightening down the free running end with the other.
                 The jumper S-folds, accordion folds, or rolls the free running ends and secures them into the
                     webbing retainers.

          • Step 9—the next jumper dons a parachute:
                 The No. 1 and No. 2 jumpers change positions and repeat steps 1 through 6.
                 When both jumpers have donned their parachute harnesses, they face each other and make a
                     visual inspection.
                 They correct any discrepancies before securing the reserve parachute with all excess webbing
                     stowed in webbing retainers.

             Note. After donning the T-11 harness, the pack tray’s top edge should be aligned with the jumper’s
             shoulder blades for optimum position of the harness. The center point of the leg strap ejector snaps
             and quick-fit V-ring should rest in the jumper’s hip socket.

T-11 RESERVE/T-11 RESERVE SINGLE PIN DONNING

     2-14. Jumpers attach the reserve parachute The No. 2 jumper S-folds by cradling the parachute in their left
     arm with the connector snaps up and the ripcord handle in the palm of their left hand.

             Note. If jumpers are part of the jumpmaster team or pushing a door bundle, jumpers must have the
             T-11 reserve marked with yellow pressure sensitive tape on the top carrying handle. If any other
             jumper has a T-11 reserve marked for jumpmaster, that reserve must not be used, and another must
             be obtained from control and issue. If jumpers are using the T-11 reserve single pin, no yellow
             pressure sensitive tape marks the top carrying handle.

     2-15. The jumpers perform the following steps when donning the T-11 reserve/T-11 reserve single pin
     parachute:

          • Step 1: No. 1 and No. 2 jumpers take the following actions:
                 No. 1 jumpers cradle the reserve parachute in the crook of their left arm with the ripcord handle
                     in the palm of the left hand.
                 No. 2 jumpers remove all twists from the waistband and hand the free running end to No. 1
                     jumpers, being careful not to reintroduce a twist in the waistband.

          • Step 2: Jumpers Nos. 1 and 2 perform step 2 by taking the following actions:
                 No. 1 jumpers pass the waistband through the waistband retainers on the rear of the reserve
                     parachute from right to left.
                 They attach the right connector snap to the right D-ring on the harness, the left connector snap
                     to the left D-ring and ensure that the waistband is below the D-rings.
                 No. 2 jumpers attach the waistband to the waistband adjuster panel (WAP) and grasp the
                     running end of the jumpers’ waistbands in their right hand, placing the left hand on the end of
                     the reserve for leverage.
                 Jumpers pull the slack from the waistband and secure it to the WAP, forming a quick release.

          • Step 3: The Nos. 1 and 2 jumpers change positions and repeat steps 1 through 3:
                 When both jumpers have donned their parachute harnesses and reserve, they face each other
                     and make a visual inspection.
                 They correct any discrepancies and are now ready to jump; however, before jumping from an
                     aircraft, they receive a detailed safety inspection from a jumpmaster.

at all times to prevent accidental activation of the reserve parachute.

                                                 Chapter 3

                       Five Points of Performance

    The five points of performance are specific actions the jumper performs between the time of
    exit from the aircraft and recovery after landing. Each of the points are stressed during jumper
    training and are taught using one or more of the training apparatuses.
    The five points of performance are individual actions that are essential on every parachute
    jump. Failure to perform any one point correctly could result in an injury to the jumper. A
    proper exit, body position, and count are essential to lessen the possibility of a parachute
    malfunction or bodily injury during the deployment and inflation of the parachute.

T-11 POINT 1. PROPER EXIT, CHECK BODY POSITION, AND
COUNT

     3-1. The first point of performance for the T-11 is exiting properly, checking the body position, and counting.
     The duration of the 6,000 count corresponds to the approximate time it takes the main parachute to deploy
     fully when used by a jumper exiting an aircraft flying 125 knots per hour.

     3-2. The following must be trained as an automatic action as jumpers exit the aircraft:
          • Jumpers start the 6,000 count at ONE THOUSAND, snap their feet and knees together, then lock
                knees to the rear, lowering their head and placing their chin firmly against their chest.
          • At the same time, jumpers rotate their elbows firmly into their sides, both hands over the end of the
                reserve parachute with fingers naturally spread.
          • They then bend their body forward at the waist to look over the reserve to see the toes of their boots
                while continuing to count, TWO THOUSAND, THREE THOUSAND, FOUR THOUSAND, FIVE
                THOUSAND, SIX THOUSAND, at normal cadence.
          • Jumpers keep their eyes open and chin on chest to react to situations around them.

                                                WARNINGS

                    Hands must remain over the ends of the reserve parachute with
                    fingers naturally spread. Failure to do so may cause unintentional
                    activation of the reserve parachute while standing in the door or
                    during exit from the aircraft.

                    If no opening shock is felt by jumpers at the end of the 6,000
                    count, they must activate the reserve parachute for a total
                    malfunction.

POINT 2. CHECK CANOPY AND GAIN CANOPY CONTROLS AND
IMMEDIATELY COMPARE YOUR RATE OF DESCENT

     3-3. The second point of performance is to check the canopy and gain canopy control and immediately
     compare your rate of descent. When the jumper finishes the 6,000 count, the jumper feels the parachute open,
     checks the canopy for malfunctions or damage, and controls the parachute. There are two types of
     malfunctions. A total malfunction is the complete failure of the airdrop system to function as designed (see
     AR 59-4/OPNAVINST 4630.24E/AFMAN 13-210 Volume 1/MCO 13480.1E Volume 1). A partial
     malfunction is the failure of an airdrop system to function properly to the point that the load or parachutist is
     subject to damage or injury (see AR 59-4/OPNAVINST 4630.24E/AFMAN 13-210 Volume 1/MCO
     13480.1E Volume 1).

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  11

Chapter 3

     3-4. Jumpers throw their heads back to inspect the entire canopy and the slider to ensure it slides all the way
     down to the riser assemblies. At the same time, they reach up to the elbow-locked position and secure the
     front set of risers in each hand, simultaneously conducting a 360-degree check of the canopy.

TWISTS

     3-5. The main parachute may have twisted suspension lines, risers, or both. This condition may be caused by
     a single action or combination of actions. The most common causes of twisting include the following:

          • The deployment bag spinning before the canopy deploys.
          • The canopy spinning when it comes out of the deployment bag, before it inflates.
          • The jumper tumbling or spinning (caused by improper exit and body position) during the descent.

     3-6. If the suspension lines are twisted and the jumper cannot raise their head enough to check the canopy
     properly, the jumper must compare their rate of descent with that of nearby jumpers.

RATE OF DESCENT

     3-7. If jumpers’ suspension lines are twisted and the descent is the same as other jumpers, they untwist the
     suspension lines by reaching up and grasping a set of risers with each hand, thumbs down, and knuckles to
     the rear. Jumpers pull the risers apart and begin a vigorous bicycling motion. When the last twist comes out,
     jumpers check the canopy and gain control.

     3-8. If the jumper’s main canopy rate of descent is too fast (when compared to nearby jumpers), the jumper
     activates the reserve parachute. (See chapter 4 for more information on activation of the T-11 reserve/single
     pin parachute.)

     3-9. When other jumpers are not close enough to compare rates of descent, the jumper activates the reserve
     parachute.

POINT 3. ALWAYS KEEP A SHARP LOOKOUT, CONSTANTLY
COMPARING RATE OF DESCENT

     3-10. The third point of performance is for the jumper to keep a sharp lookout at all times and constantly
     compare their rate of descent. Avoiding other jumpers during descent is essential to successful airborne
     operations. A successful jump consists of many of the following actions:

          • The three rules of the air include the following:
                 Always look before making a slip.
                 Always slip in the opposite direction to avoid collisions.
                 The lower jumper always has the right of way.

          • Avoiding fellow jumpers all the way to the ground and maintaining a 25-foot separation when
                jumping the T-11 parachute.

          • At the end of the third point of performance, releasing all appropriate equipment tie-downs.

                                                 WARNING

                    During descent, the jumper must watch to avoid collisions and
                    entanglements with other jumpers and to avoid obstacles on the
                    drop zone (DZ). Jumpers must stay 25 feet away from other
                    jumpers.

     3-11. The degree of maneuverability with a T-11 parachute is limited compared to the MC-6. The jumper
     maneuvers the T-11 parachute using slips, which are described and used as follows:

          • Use of slips—the jumper performs a slip to avoid other jumpers, to avoid obstacles on the ground,
                and to prepare to land.

          • Types of slips—the two types of slips are the two-riser and the one-riser.
          • For an effective slip of either type, the jumper must ensure their hands are not placed through or

                behind the risers.

12  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                                Five Points of Performance

          • Slips are executed with the following actions:
                 When slipping, the jumper looks in the direction that the slip is being made.
                 The jumper makes a sharp initial pull using the slip assist loops or slip assist tabs to spill air
                     from the canopy effectively and lets up slowly to prevent spinning or oscillations.
                 A two-riser slip is made by reaching up to the elbow-locked position, grasping a pair of slip
                     assist loops or slip assist tabs on the risers in the desired direction of movement, and pulling
                     them down to the chest.
                 A one-riser slip (left or right front, left or right rear) is made by pulling down one to three
                     full-arm lengths of the one riser nearest the desired direction of movement with a
                     hand-over-hand motion.

COLLISIONS, ENTANGLEMENTS, AND CENTER PANEL STRIKES

     3-12. A collision is the physical impact or contact, however slight, of one jumper or jumper’s equipment with
     that of another jumper where both jumpers separate prior to making contact with the ground. An entanglement
     is the entwining or attachment of a jumper or jumper’s equipment with that of another jumper during descent,
     whether or not the entanglement lasts until the jumpers contact the ground.

     3-13. Jumpers must be alert in the air and warn each other of impending collisions. If a collision cannot be
     avoided by slipping or turning, the jumper attempts to bounce off the other jumper’s suspension lines or
     canopy by spreading their arms and legs just before making contact.

     3-14. If a jumper becomes entangled with one or more suspension lines of another parachute, the jumper
     does one of the following, depending on the type of parachute being used and the incident altitudes:

          • High altitude occurs from aircraft exit throughout full canopy deployment (first point of
                performance).

          • Mid altitude occurs after full canopy deployment throughout descent to the preparation for landing
                altitude designated for the jumped parachute (second, third, and fourth points of performance).

          • Low altitude occurs from the preparation for landing altitude throughout descent to landing
                (fourth point of performance).

CENTER PANEL STRIKE EMERGENCY PROCEDURES

     3-15. (Actions of the higher jumper) if higher jumpers are drifting toward a fellow jumper. Higher jumpers
     look and immediately slip away in the opposite direction of lower jumpers using a one riser diagonal slip:

          • If higher jumpers are drifting over a jumper’s canopy and believe they will land on top of the lower
                jumper’s canopy, before making contact with the canopy, higher jumpers:
                 Begin a vigorous running motion in the direction of the slip.
                 Attempt to stay on their feet, until they are off the lower jumper’s canopy.

          • Continue to slip away until a minimum of 25-feet separation has been achieved.
          • If higher jumpers land on the lower jumper’s canopy and cannot run off:

                 It is vital higher jumpers maintain momentum.
                 This should allow higher jumpers to remain on their feet and attempt to get off the closest edge

                     of the canopy that their momentum allows.
          • If higher jumpers cannot stay on their feet, they should:

                 Employ a crawling technique by reaching as far as possible in the direction of the closest edge
                     of the canopy.

                 Grasp the canopy and continue to pull towards themselves, using the hand-over-hand method
                     until they are free from the lower jumper’s canopy.

          • Once higher jumpers are falling free, the jumpers create a clear and unobstructed path, then activate
                their reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

          • Higher jumpers keep their feet and knees together and are prepared to execute a parachute landing
                fall (PLF).

Chapter 3

                                                 WARNING

                    Attempting to roll off the canopy could wrap the suspension line
                    around the higher jumper’s body, preventing the main canopy
                    from re-inflating and preventing them from deploying the reserve.

     3-16. (Actions of the lower jumper) if the lower jumper finds another jumper on top of their canopy—
          • If there is damage to the canopy or a jumper is on top, compare the rate of descent with fellow
                jumpers.
          • If the lower jumper is falling faster than their fellow jumpers, they immediately activate the reserve
                parachute using the pull drop method.
          • If there is a jumper on top of the lower jumper’s canopy and they are not falling faster than fellow
                jumpers, continue to observe the canopy.
          • If at any time the main parachute begins to deflate, immediately activate the reserve parachute using
                the pull drop method.
          • If the higher jumper slides off the canopy, the lower jumper uses a one-riser diagonal slip in the
                opposite direction to avoid fellow jumpers.

                                                 WARNING

                    When slipping away from fellow jumpers, always use a diagonal
                    slip. If the higher jumper should fall through a corner vent, they
                    should remain where they are and be prepared to conduct a PLF.

     3-17. In the event of an entanglement, the following actions should be taken:
          • If jumpers use the T-11 parachute and become entangled, the higher jumpers climb down to the
                lower jumpers using the hand-under-hand method.
          • Be sure to stay away from the corner vents located on all four corners of the canopy and the bridle
                line on top of the canopy.
          • Should jumpers fall through a vent or become entangled in the bridle line, jumpers should stay where
                they are and be prepared to execute a proper PLF.
          • Once both jumpers are even, they face each other and grasp each other’s left main lift web,
                continuing to observe both canopies and take one of the following actions:
                 If one canopy collapses, neither jumper activates their reserve parachute as one T-11 parachute
                     can safely deliver two combat-equipped jumpers to the ground.
                 If both canopies collapse, both jumpers immediately turn away from each other to create a clear
                     path and activate their reserve parachutes using the pull drop method.
                 Both jumpers discuss which PLF to execute.
                 Both jumpers conduct the same PLF.
                 Neither jumper executes a front PLF.

STEALING AIR

     3-18. A descending parachute causes an area of partial air compression immediately below the canopy, and
     an area of partial vacuum and descending turbulent air above the canopy. This turbulent air extends about
     100 feet above the T-11 canopy.

     3-19. A parachute falling into an area of partial vacuum (from a parachute below) does not capture enough
     air to stay fully inflated. The top parachute may partially collapse and drop below the other jumper’s canopy
     until the force of unaffected air reinflates it. Then this canopy (being lower) steals the air from the canopy
     above, causing the canopy above to partially collapse and the jumper to drop past the lower canopy. This
     leapfrogging continues unless corrective action is taken by the jumper.

14         TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                                Five Points of Performance

     3-20. To move away from the area, the jumper slips away using a one riser slip in the opposite direction,
     providing at least a 25-foot distance between the parachutes. (Both jumpers execute a slip away from each
     other when facing another jumper.) When there is enough distance, the jumper takes one of the actions:

          • The jumper slips vigorously using a one-riser slip to maintain a lateral distance of at least 25 feet
                between the parachutes.

          • When jumpers are 250 feet or less above the ground, they must exercise care to avoid stealing air
                from another parachute, because a deflated canopy is not high enough above the ground to reinflate
                completely.

          • The jumper immediately prepares to land and executes a PLF if this situation occurs.

Point 4. Prepare to Land

     3-21. The fourth point of performance is preparing to land. A proper landing attitude is necessary to lessen
     the risk of injury to jumpers when hitting the ground. (See figure 3-1.) Preparation includes the following:

          • When jumpers commit to the final approach, they should plan to do all slipping approximately 200
                feet above ground level (AGL).

          • At 200 feet AGL, jumpers slip with the T-11 directly into the wind.

                                                 WARNING

                    DO NOT change slips or make any more turns with the parachute
                    unless it is to avoid other jumpers in the air or obstacles on the
                    ground.

                                           Figure 3-1. Landing attitude

3-22. After slipping into the wind on final approach, jumpers take the following actions:
     • Keep a sharp lookout during descent for other jumpers.
     • Lower all equipment at 200 feet AGL while facing directly into the wind.
     • Regain canopy control with both hands once the equipment is released.

3-23. Jumpers take the following actions:
     • Jumpers look below at approximately 200 feet AGL, to ensure there are no fellow jumpers before
          lowering their equipment.
     • They slip into the wind at approximately 200 feet AGL and do the following:

                 If the wind is blowing from the left, the jumper must reach up with both hands and grasp the
                     left set of slip assist loops or slip assist tabs and pull them deep into their chest.

                 If the wind is blowing from the front, the jumper must reach up with both hands and grasp the
                     front set of slip assist loops or slip assist tabs and pull them deep into their chest.

                 If the wind is blowing from the right, the jumper must reach up with both hands and grasp the
                     right set of slip assist loops or slip assist tabs and pull them deep into their chest.

                 If the wind is blowing from the rear, jumpers must reach up with both hands and grasp a rear
                     slip assist loop or slip assist tab and pull one to three full-arm lengths of the one riser deep into
                     their chest.

     3-24. There are three different types of PLFs that can be performed, depending on whether they are executed
     from the front, rear, and the side:

          • The two types of front PLFs are right front and left front:
                 The right front PLF is used if the direction of (wind) drift is to the front and slightly to the right.
                 The left front PLF is used if the direction of drift is to the front and slightly to the left.
                 If the direction of drift is directly to the front, the jumper selects either PLF.

          • The two types of rear PLFs are right rear and left rear:
                 The right rear PLF is used if the direction of (wind) drift is to the front and slightly to the right.
                 The left rear PLF is used if the direction of drift is to the front and slightly to the left.
                 If the direction of drift is directly to the front, the jumper selects either PLF.

          • The two types of side PLFs are right side and left side:
                 The right side PLF is used if the direction of (wind) drift is directly to the right.
                 The left side PLF is used if the direction of drift is directly to the left.

          • After jumpers have slipped into the wind, they assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees
                together, knees slightly bent, elbows tight into their sides, head and eyes on the horizon, and eyes
                open.

OBSTACLES

     3-25. Jumpers slip to avoid obstacles. They take the following emergency procedures if obstacles (trees,
     water, or high-tension wires) cannot be avoided.

TREE LANDING

     3-26. When using the T-11, (see figure 3-2) jumpers take the following actions:
          • They immediately slip away, using a one-riser slip when beginning to drift towards a tree.
          • If jumpers cannot slip away and have lowered the equipment, they look below to ensure there are
                no fellow jumpers below and jettison the equipment, making a mental note of where it lands to be
                recovered at a later time.
          • If jumpers have not lowered the equipment, they keep the equipment on them for extra protection
                while passing through the trees.
          • They assume a good landing attitude at approximately 200 feet AGL.
          • They keep feet and knees together, knees slightly bent, head and eyes on the horizon, eyes open,
                and hands in front of their face with elbows high.
          • They are prepared to execute a PLF if passing through the trees.
          • If jumpers are hung up in the trees and do not feel they can safely lower themselves to the ground,
                they stay where they are and wait for assistance.

                                       Figure 3-2. Tree landing attitude

                                            WARNING

               Make sure the reserve reaches the ground or is close to it before
               continuing with the following actions.

3-27. A jumper takes the following action if becoming hung up in a tree and decides to climb down:
     • Jettisons all unneeded equipment.
     • Ensures that the helmet is maintained.
     • Activates the quick release in the waistband.
     • Applies inward pressure to the ripcord assembly with either hand.
     • Removes the top tuck tab with the opposite hand.
     • Maintains steady inward pressure, and with the opposite hand inserts it behind the ripcord assembly
          and applies inward pressure.
     • Grasps the ripcord handle with the opposite hand and pulls and drops it.
     • Controls the activation of the reserve parachute toward the ground with both hands, ensuring that
          all suspension lines are completely deployed.
     • Disconnects the left connector snap and rotates the reserve parachute down and to the right.
     • Attaches the left connector snap to the triangle link on their right side.
     • Activates the quick release in the chest strap and completely removes the chest strap from the chest
          strap friction adapter.
     • Grasps the main lift web with either hand below the canopy release assembly and with the other
          hand activates the leg strap ejector snaps and climbs down the outside of the reserve parachute.

                                            WARNING

               Extreme care must be taken when climbing down the T-11
               reserve/T-11 reserve single pin parachute suspension lines
               because of the slippery coating applied to the suspension lines.
               When in doubt, stay where you are and wait for assistance.

WATER LANDING

     3-28. As soon as jumpers realize they are going to land in water, they take the following actions:
          • Immediately try to slip away immediately if drifting towards a body of water.
          • Look down to ensure there are no fellow jumpers below them if unable to slip away, and then lower
                and jettison their equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Jettison the helmet, again making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Activate the quick release in the waistband, disconnect the left connector snap, and rotate the reserve
                parachute to the right.
          • Seat themselves well into the saddle and activate the quick release in the chest strap, completely
                removing the chest strap from the chest strap friction adapter.
          • Regain canopy control.
          • Assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together, knees slightly bent, and place hands
                on the leg strap ejector snaps prior to entering the water.
          • Activate both ejector snaps for the leg straps, arch their back, throw their arms above their head, and
                slide out of the parachute harness when the balls of the jumpers’ feet make contact with the water.
          • Swim upwind or upstream away from the canopy.
          • Locate a seam and follow it to the skirt of the canopy if the canopy comes down on top of the
                jumpers.
          • Prepare to execute a PLF if the water is shallow (2 feet or less in depth).

Water Landing Without a Life Preserver

     3-29. Jumpers do the following (in addition to the actions under a water landing, see figure 3-3:
          • Look below themselves to ensure there are no follow jumpers and lower and jettison their
                equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Jettison their helmet, again making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Activate the quick release in their waistband, disconnect the left connector snap, and rotate the
                reserve parachute to the right.
          • Seat themselves well into the saddle and activate the quick release in the chest strap, completely
                removing the chest strap from the chest strap friction adapter.
          • Regain canopy control.
          • Assume a landing attitude prior to entering the water by keeping their feet and knees together, knees
                slightly bent and place their hands on the ejector snaps for the leg straps.
          • Activate both ejector snaps for the leg straps, arch their backs, and throw their arms above their head
                and slide out of the parachute harness when the balls of their feet make contact with the water.
          • Swim upwind or upstream away from the canopy.
          • Locate a seam and follow it to the skirt of the canopy if the canopy comes down on top of jumpers.
          • Prepare to execute a PLF if the water is shallow (2 feet or less in depth).

Water Landing With a Life Preserver

     3-30. When wearing a T-11 parachute harness and jumping with a life preserver (see figure 3-4 on page 20),
     the jumper does the following in addition to the actions mentioned under water landing:

          • While still in the air, the jumper activates the life preserver prior to assuming a landing attitude.
          • If the life preserver fails to inflate, the jumper inflates the life preserver manually by blowing air

                into the inflation valve hose.
          • The jumper looks below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers below, lowers their equipment, and

                jettisons their equipment.
          • The jumper assumes a landing attitude and prepares to do a PLF in the event the water is shallow.
          • Once in the water, the jumper activates both canopy release assemblies by using the hand-to-

                shoulder method, or the hand-to-assist method.
          • The jumper removes the harness and any remaining equipment.

             Note. For more information on life preservers, see chapter 12.

HIGH-TENSION WIRE LANDING

     3-31. Jumpers do the following if unable to avoid high tension lines when landing (see figure 3-5):
          • If jumpers are drifting towards wires, they immediately try to slip away.
          • If jumpers cannot slip away, they look below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers below and
                jettison their equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Jumpers must ensure they maintain their helmet.
          • Jumpers assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together and exaggerating the bend in
                their knees. Jumpers keep eyes open, chin on chest, and their back arched.
          • Jumpers place the palms of their hands high on the inside of the front set of risers.
          • When jumpers make contact with the wires, they begin a hard rocking motion and attempt to pass
                through the wires.
          • Jumpers prepare to do a PLF in the event they pass through the wires.
          • If jumpers are hung up in the wires, they do not attempt to lower themselves to the ground; jumpers
                stay where they are and wait for assistance.

             Note. If the jumper becomes entangled in the wires, they make no attempt to climb down but wait

POINT 5. LAND

     3-32. The fifth point of performance is land. To lessen the possibility of injuries, the jumper is trained to
     absorb the impact of landing by executing a proper PLF. To do this, the following five fleshy portions of the
     body must contact the ground in sequence:

          • Balls of feet.
          • Calf.
          • Thigh.
          • Buttocks.
          • Pull-up muscle.

     3-33. The three basic PLFs are:
          • Front (right or left).
          • Rear (right or left).
          • Side (right or left).

     3-34. The direction of the wind drift dictates the type of fall the jumper makes. The jumper judges the
     direction of drift by looking at the ground before assuming the landing attitude. The jumper prepares to make
     the appropriate PLF after determining the direction of the wind and the type of fall.

FRONT PARACHUTE LANDING FALL

     3-35. The two types of front PLFs are right front PLF and left front PLF:
          • The right front PLF is used if the direction of (wind) drift is to the front and slightly to the right.
          • The left front fall is used if the direction of drift is to the front and slightly to the left.
          • If the direction of drift is directly to the front, the jumper selects either PLF.
          • For a left front PLF, when the balls of the feet hit the ground, the jumper:
                 Places their chin on their chest, tenses the neck muscles, and presses their elbows against the
                     chest.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  21


---

Chapter 3

                 The jumper pushes the right knee into the left knee, exposing the second and third points of
                     contact (calf, thigh) in the direction of drift.

                 The jumper rotates from the waist up, further exposing the four remaining points of contact.
                 The jumper continues to bend at the knees, maintaining pressure with the right knee into the

                     left knee and lays the four remaining points of contact on the ground in sequence.
          • As the PLF is completed in the direction of drift, the jumper maintains tension in the neck to prevent

                their head from striking the ground.
          • The momentum caused by the drift brings the feet around to the right and into the direction of the

                drift.
          • The jumper activates both canopy release assemblies to keep from being dragged after completing

                the PLF.
          • The jumper rotates to the left when executing the right front PLF.

REAR PARACHUTE LANDING FALL

     3-36. The two variations of the rear PLF are right rear PLF and left rear PLF. The jumper determines which
     PLF to make by checking the direction of drift. If the drift is directly to the rear, they select the appropriate
     PLF and take the following actions:

          • The left rear PLF is used if the direction of (wind) drift is to the rear and slightly to the left.
          • For a left rear PLF, when the balls of the feet make contact with the ground, the jumper:

                 Places their chin on their chest, tense their neck muscles, and press their elbows against the
                     chest.

                 The jumper pushes their right knee into their left knee exposing the second, third, and a portion
                     the fourth point of contact (calf, thigh) to the ground.

                 The jumper bends forward at the waist looking between their elbows, down toward the right
                     boot heel, fully exposing the second, third, fourth, and fifth points of contact to the ground.

                 The jumper continues to bend at the knees, maintaining pressure with the right knee into the
                     left knee and lays the four remaining points of contact on the ground in sequence.

          • As the PLF is completed in the direction of drift, jumpers maintain tension in their neck to prevent
                the head from striking the ground.

          • The momentum caused by the drift brings their feet around to the right and into the direction of the
                drift.

          • The jumper activates both canopy release assemblies to keep from being dragged after completing
                the PLF.

          • The right rear PLF is used if the direction of (wind) drift is to the rear and slightly to the right.
          • When executing the right rear PLF, the jumper rotates to the right.

SIDE PARACHUTE LANDING FALL

     3-37. As the balls of the feet make contact with the ground, the jumper begins several actions at the same
     time. As the fall continues, they do the following to complete a left side PLF:

             Note. The right side PLF is like the left side PLF, except the points of contact on the right side of
             the body are used.

          • The jumper places their chin on chest and tenses the neck muscles.
          • The jumper holds the risers in front of their face and presses their elbows against the chest.
          • The jumper pushes their right knee into the left knee, exposing their second and third points of

                contact (calf, thigh) in the direction of drift.
          • The jumper rotates from the waist up, to their right, looking down at the right boot heel exposing

                the fourth and fifth points of contact (buttocks, pull-up muscle) to the ground in the direction of
                drift.
          • The jumper continues to bend at the knees, maintaining pressure with the right knee into the left
                knee and lays the four remaining points of contact on the ground in sequence.
          • As the PLF is completed in the direction of drift, the jumper maintains tension in the neck to prevent
                their head from striking the ground.

          • The momentum caused by the drift brings the feet around to the right and into the direction of drift.
          • The jumper activates both canopy release assemblies to keep from being dragged after completing

                the PLF.

LAND

     3-38. Never attempt to make a stand-up landing. Remain on the ground and activate both canopy release
     assemblies using the hand assist method. The hand assist method consists of the jumper taking the following
     actions:

          • With the thumb and index finger of one hand, the jumper pulls out and down on the safety clip.
          • Forms a fist with the thumb exposed and then inserts the thumb into the cable loop.
          • Turns the head in the opposite direction.
          • With the other hand assisting, pulls out and down on the cable loop.
          • Repeats this process with the opposite canopy release assembly.
          • Activates both canopy release assemblies on the T-11 parachute.

     3-39. Once both canopy release assemblies are activated, the jumper places the weapon into operation and
     removes the parachute harness.

MC-6 POINT 1. PROPER EXIT, BODY CHECK POSITION, AND
COUNT

     3-40. The first point of performance for the MC-6 is to properly exit, check the body position, and count
     which are essential to lessen the possibility of a parachute malfunction or bodily injury during the deployment
     and inflation of the parachute. The duration of the MC-6’s 4,000 count corresponds to the approximate time
     it takes the main parachute to deploy fully when used by a jumper exiting an aircraft flying 125 knots per
     hour. The following must be trained reflex actions as the jumper exits the aircraft:

          • The jumper starts the 4,000 count for the MC-6 at ONE THOUSAND, snaps feet and knees together,
                then locks the knees to the rear, lowers the head, and places the chin firmly against the chest.

          • At the same time, the jumper rotates the elbows firmly into the sides, both hands over the end of the
                reserve parachute with fingers naturally spread.

          • The jumper then bends the body forward at the waist to look over the reserve to see the toes of the
                boots while continuing to count, TWO THOUSAND, THREE THOUSAND, FOUR THOUSAND,
                at normal cadence (jumpers keep their eyes open and chin on chest to react to situations around
                them).

                                                WARNINGS

                    Hand must remain over the ends of the reserve parachute with
                    fingers naturally spread. Failure to do so may cause unintentional
                    activation of the reserve parachute while standing in the door or
                    during exit from the aircraft.

                    If no opening shock is felt by the jumper at the end of the 4,000
                    count, the jumper must activate the reserve parachute for a total
                    malfunction.

Chapter 3

POINT 2. CHECK CANOPY AND GAIN CANOPY CONTROL AND
IMMEDIATELY COMPARE YOUR RATE OF DESCENT

     3-41. The second point of performance is to check the canopy and gain canopy control. When the jumper
     finishes the 4,000 count, the jumper feels the parachute open, checks the canopy for malfunctions or damage,
     and controls the parachute.

     3-42. The jumper throws their head back to inspect the entire canopy and at the same time reaches up and
     secures a toggle in each hand bringing the toggles to eye level, simultaneously conducting a 360-degree check
     of the canopy.

TWISTS

     3-43. The main parachute may have twisted suspension lines, risers, or both. This condition may be caused
     by a single action or combination of actions. The most common causes of twisting include the following:

          • The deployment bag spinning before the canopy deploys.
          • The canopy spinning when it comes out of the deployment bag before it inflates.
          • The jumper tumbling or spinning (caused by improper exit and body position) during the descent.

     3-44. If the suspension lines are twisted and the jumper cannot raise their head enough to check the canopy
     properly, the jumper compares their rate of descent with that of nearby jumpers.

RATE OF DESCENT

     3-45. If the jumper’s suspension lines are twisted and their descent is the same as the other jumpers, the
     jumper untwists their suspension lines by reaching up and grasping a set of risers with each hand, thumbs
     down, knuckles to the rear. The jumper pulls the risers apart and begins a vigorous bicycling motion. When
     the last twist comes out, the jumper checks the canopy and gains control.

     3-46. If the jumper’s main canopy rate of descent is too fast (when compared to nearby jumpers), they activate
     the reserve parachute. (See chapter 6 for more information on activation of the T-11 reserve/single pin
     parachute.)

     3-47. When other jumpers are not close enough to compare rates of descent, the jumper activates the reserve
     parachute.

POINT 3. KEEP A SHARP LOOKOUT AT ALL TIMES, CONSTANTLY
COMPARE YOUR RATE OF DESCENT

     3-48. The third point of performance is for the jumper:
          • To always keep a sharp lookout and constantly compare the rate of descent.
          • To avoid other jumpers during descent which is essential for successful airborne operations.
          • A successful jump consists of many of the following actions, including the following three rules of
                the air:
                 Always look before turning.
                 Always turn in the opposite direction to avoid collisions.
                 The lower jumper always has the right of way.

                                                 CAUTION

                    Avoid fellow jumpers all the way to the ground and maintain a 50-foot
                    separation and at the end of the third point of performance, release all
                    appropriate equipment tie-downs.

24  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026

                                                                                                                Five Points of Performance

                                                WARNINGS

                    During descent, the jumper must watch to avoid collisions and
                    entanglements with other jumpers and to avoid obstacles on the
                    DZ. Jumpers stay 50-feet away from other jumpers.
                    Due to the canopy’s steerability and maneuverability, jumpers
                    should stay at least 50-feet apart in the air to prevent collisions
                    and entanglements.

     3-49. Depending on the wind conditions and their skill, the jumper can steer the parachute to a selected point
     of impact (PI) on the DZ to avoid other jumpers in the air, avoid obstacles on the ground, or use a preferred
     PLF. To control movement and direction of the MC-6, the jumper must know the principles by which the
     canopy operates and the factors that govern its control. The movement of the canopy is controlled by the
     action of the wind and the position of the canopy’s three drive vents relative to wind direction, and the way
     in which the control lines are manipulated.

HOLDING: OPENING AWAY FROM THE WIND AND RUNNING: OPENING WITH THE WIND

     3-50. When the three drive vents are located directly opposite the wind, the thrust of the drive vents are acting
     against the wind. This reduces the effect of wind velocity on the canopy and retards the lateral movement of
     the canopy in the direction of the wind. This technique is called holding.

     3-51. When the three drive vents are located directly with the wind, the thrust of the drive vents combines
     with the thrust of the wind to speed the movement of the canopy in the direction of the wind. This technique
     is called running.

CRABBING OR QUARTERING: OPENING AT AN ANGLE

     3-52. When the three drive vents are at an angle to the wind direction, the force of the wind from one direction
     and the thrust of the orifice at the angle move the canopy in a near right angle direction toward the direction
     of orifice thrust. The direction of movement varies with wind velocity and the angle at which the drive vents
     are pointed. This technique is called crabbing or quartering.

     3-53. Maneuvering while running with, at an angle to, or holding into to the wind, is performed by rotating
     the canopy to the left or right. As the canopy begins to move in the desired direction, the jumper manipulates
     the control line toggles to maintain this direction.

                                                 WARNING

                    Before attempting any maneuvers, jumpers must check around
                    themselves to prevent collisions with other jumpers.

CANOPY MANIPULATION

     3-54. Properly executed maneuvers require correct canopy manipulation to combine the force of the wind
     and the thrust of the canopy drive vents to move the parachute in a given direction. To maneuver the parachute
     to a certain point on the ground or to avoid ground obstacles, the jumper may have to turn and hold into the
     wind, run with the wind, or crab to the left or right while running or holding with the wind.

Turning

     3-55. This is accomplished by pulling down one control line toggle. The farther down the toggle is pulled,
     the faster the turn. Pulling the right toggle causes a right turn. Pulling the left toggle causes a left turn.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  25

Chapter 3

Braking

     3-56. Pulling both toggles at the same time reduces forward speed. This is called braking. There are six
     control input positions that affect the performance of the canopy. Proper application of the braking techniques
     reduces landing impact.

Holding Into the Wind

     3-57. This is done by rotating the MC-6 canopy until the drive vents are on the downwind side. Thereafter,
     the jumper manipulates the control line toggles to retain this position.

Running With the Wind

     3-58. This is accomplished when the jumper rotates the canopy until the drive vents are on the upwind side.
     Thereafter, control line toggles are manipulated as needed to retain the position.

BRAKING

     3-59. The six control input positions that affect canopy braking performance are: no brake, quarter brake,
     half brake, three-quarter brake, full brake, and reverse flight.

     3-60. The no brake position is attained when the jumper has the toggles in line with the top of the advanced
     combat helmet (ACH) or higher, allowing the canopy to achieve a maximum forward speed of 10 knots.

     3-61. The quarter brake position is attained when the jumper has the toggles between eye level and shoulder
     level and it reduces the forward drive of the canopy. The jumper uses this to maneuver the canopy while in
     flight and when preparing to land, given prevailing wind conditions on the DZ. The quarter brake position
     should be utilized during high wind conditions.

     3-62. The half brake position is reached when the jumper has the toggles at chest level, also reducing the
     forward drive of the canopy. The jumper uses this to maneuver the canopy while in flight and when preparing
     to land, given prevailing wind conditions at the DZ. When executing this position, the jumper should have
     their elbows held tightly into their sides, and hands facing forward in line with the top of the reserve
     parachute. Maintaining this body position minimizes the possibility of injury to the jumper’s hands, wrists,
     and arms when executing a PLF. The jumper executes a PLF from this body position and must keep their
     hands and arms inside the area of their body frame.

     3-63. The three-quarter brake position is attained when the jumper has the toggles between chest level and
     above their waistline. This reduces the forward drive of the canopy and is used by the jumper to maneuver
     the canopy while in flight and when preparing to land, given prevailing wind conditions on the DZ. The
     jumper should have their elbows tightly into their sides, and hands facing forward. The inside of the jumper’s
     wrists should rest along the outside edge of the reserve parachute, hands, wrists, and arms when executing a
     PLF. The jumper executes a PLF from this body position and must keep their hands and arms inside the area
     of their body frame. The three-quarter brake position is utilized during low- to no-wind conditions.

     3-64. The full brake position is reached when the jumper has the toggles at waist level. This reduces the
     forward drive of the canopy to its slowest and is used by the jumper to maneuver the canopy while in flight
     and when preparing to land, given prevailing wind conditions on the DZ. The jumper should hold their elbows
     tightly into their side, with the hands facing forward and thumbs touching each other. Maintaining this body
     position minimizes the possibility of injury to the jumper’s hands, wrists, and arms when executing a PLF.
     Jumpers execute a PLF from this body position and must keep their hands and arms inside the area of their
     body frame.

     3-65. The reverse flight position is attained when the jumper pulls the toggles below their waistline, and takes
     the following actions:

          • Jumpers must hold their elbows tightly into their sides with the heel of their wrists resting along the
                front of their thighs.

          • Jumpers must maintain this body position minimizing the possibility of injury to the jumper’s hands,
                wrists, and arms when executing a PLF.

26  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                                Five Points of Performance

          • Jumpers must keep their hands and arms inside the area of their body frame while executing a PLF
                from this body position.

     3-66. When the toggles are pulled below waist level, the canopy briefly becomes unstable. The jumper feels
     the sensation of rocking back and forth as though balancing on a ball. This is a specific design and
     performance characteristic of this canopy allowing an experienced jumper to land on a desired point in a
     rough, unimproved DZ.

     3-67. If the toggles are pulled below waist level and the canopy moves into reverse flight, the jumper must
     not let the toggles go to the no brake position. This causes a surge in forward speed and descent rate causing
     the jumper to impact on the ground with increased force.

     3-68. Avoid holding the toggles below waist level. Doing so can cause the canopy to become somewhat
     unstable and increase landing impact energy by about 20 percent.

             Notes. All toggle manipulation below 200 feet should be soft and slow adjustments on final
             approach. Radical adjustments in forward speed or direction can cause the parachute to oscillate
             and increase the rate of descent resulting in injury to the jumper.

                                                 WARNING

                    Running with the wind just prior to landing can cause injury and
                    must be avoided below 100 feet above the ground.

MANEUVERING WITH AN INVERSION OR BROKEN CONTROL LINE

     3-69. The jumper reverses the maneuvering technique if the canopy has inverted while opening. The jumper
     pulls down on the right control line to turn left and pulls down on the left control line to turn right.

     3-70. During routine parachute jumps, when a jumper experiences one or more broken control lines during
     the parachute’s inflation phase, the canopy can no longer be controlled by the opening and closing of the
     extended gore, and the jumper must use alternate means to control the canopy. If a right or left control line
     is broken, the canopy can still be maneuvered, though more slowly. The jumper reaches high on the right or
     left rear riser and pulls down on the opposite side of the broken control line.

CANOPY MANIPULATION

     3-71. Guiding or turning the MC-6 parachute using riser slips is accomplished by the jumper manipulating
     the risers. The MC-6 utilizes the standard four-riser system: two risers each from both shoulders of the
     jumper. A turn or slip in the desired direction is accomplished by pulling in an appropriate riser. Reaching
     high and pulling in on either rear riser distorts the lower lateral band, pulling it out of alignment in such a
     manner that it forces the air to escape which forces the parachute to rotate or turn.

     3-72. A turn to the right is accomplished by pulling in the right rear riser, and a turn to the left is accomplished
     by pulling in the left rear riser. Slips are also possible by pulling two risers; however, such slips are not
     executed as rapidly as the turning action of the parachute’s one-riser slip. Results in this case cause the
     parachute to glide in the direction of the two-riser slip instead of changing the direction of airflow through
     the orifice. All manipulations need to consider the following:

          • The remaining steering line can also be used to turn (control) the canopy; however, the canopy turns
                left or right depending on the distance the steering line is pulled down.

          • At approximately 100 feet AGL, the jumper must determine the direction of the surface winds prior
                to the fourth point of performance PREPARE TO LAND and turn the canopy into the wind to slow
                the canopy’s ground speed (lateral velocity).

          • To land safely, the jumper releases the toggle and utilizes a two-riser slip less than 12 inches into
                the wind to slow the canopy.

          • Prior to landing, be prepared to execute the appropriate PLF.

Chapter 3

                                                WARNINGS

                    Continuing to utilize one steering line during the fifth point of
                    performance causes the canopy to remain in a turn and does not
                    slow the jumper’s lateral ground speed.

                    All riser slips during the last 200 feet should be gentle and
                    smooth enough to adjust direction only as needed. Pulling down
                    12 inches or more on both rear risers smoothly and quickly
                    reduces forward speed, then increases the jumper’s rate of
                    descent in less than 2 seconds.

MANEUVERING WITH A TANGLED CONTROL LINE

     3-73. The jumper uses the same procedure as with a broken control line if the control line becomes tangled
     in a suspension line.

     3-74. If the control line becomes tangled with the L-bar connector link, the jumper reaches up under the
     affected riser and attempts to untangle the control line from the L-bar connector link. If the jumper is
     unsuccessful in their attempt, the canopy can still be controlled with the unaffected control line.

COLLISIONS AND ENTANGLEMENTS

     3-75. Collision is the physical impact or contact, however slight, of one jumper or jumper’s equipment with
     that of another jumper where both jumpers separate prior to making contact with the ground. An entanglement
     is the entwining or attachment of a jumper or jumper’s equipment with that of another jumper during descent,
     whether the entanglement lasts until the jumpers contact the ground.

     3-76. Jumpers must be alert in the air and warn each other of impending collisions. If a collision cannot be
     avoided by turning away, they should take the following actions:

          • Assume a spread-eagle position.
          • Attempt to bounce off the jumper’s canopy and suspension lines and immediately turn away.

     3-77. If a jumper becomes entangled with one or more suspension lines of another parachute, the jumper
     does the following:

          • Remains where they are.
          • Obtains a clear path.
          • Activates their reserve immediately using the pull drop method.

STEALING AIR

     3-78. A descending parachute causes an area of partial air compression immediately below the canopy, and
     an area of partial vacuum and descending turbulent air above the canopy. This turbulent air extends about
     50 feet above the canopy.

     3-79. A parachute falling into an area of partial vacuum (from a parachute below) does not capture enough
     air to stay fully inflated. The top parachute may partially collapse and drop below the other jumper’s canopy
     until the force of unaffected air reinflates it. Then this canopy (being lower) steals the air from the canopy
     above, causing the canopy above to collapse partially and the jumper to drop past the lower canopy. This
     leapfrogging action continues unless corrective action is taken by the jumper.

     3-80. To move away from the area, the jumper turns in the opposite direction, providing at least a 50-foot
     distance between the parachutes. (Jumpers turn away from each other when facing another jumper.)

     3-81. When 250 feet or less AGL, jumpers must exercise care to avoid stealing air from another parachute,
     because a deflated canopy is not high enough above the ground to reinflate completely. The jumper
     immediately prepares to land and executes a PLF if this situation occurs.
