                                                                                                                Five Points of Performance

POINT 4. PREPARE TO LAND

     3-82. The fourth point of performance is preparing to land. A proper landing attitude is necessary to lessen
     the risk of injury to jumpers when they hit the ground. Preparation includes the following:

          • When jumpers commit to the final approach, they should plan to do all turning at approximately
                250 feet AGL, so the final approach is smooth and the landing soft.

          • At 250 feet AGL, jumpers turn with the MC-6 directly into the wind.
          • The location where they turn over the landing area is based on the wind speed above the landing

                area.
          • After turning into the wind on final approach, jumpers take the following actions:

                                                 CAUTION

                    DO NOT make any more turns with the parachute unless it is to avoid
                    other jumpers in the air or obstacles on the ground.

                 Keep a sharp lookout during descent for other jumpers.
                 Turn into the wind prior to lowering equipment.
                 Bring both toggles in front of their face and transfer control of one toggle to the opposite hand

                     so that both toggles are being controlled by one hand.
                 Use the free hand to lower their combat equipment (CE) while maintaining both toggles in front

                     of the face.
                 Regain canopy control immediately with both hands and continue to keep a sharp lookout for

                     other jumpers once jumpers have lowered their CE.

MC-6 PARACHUTE KEY POINTS

     3-83. When jumping with an MC-6 parachute, the jumper takes the following actions:
          • Determines the direction of drift at approximately 250 feet AGL.
          • Pulls the left toggle down when the wind is blowing from the left and lets up slowly to prevent
                oscillation when facing into the wind.
          • Pulls the right toggle down if the wind is blowing from the right and lets up slowly to prevent
                oscillation when facing into the wind.
          • Pulls either toggle down if the wind is blowing from the rear and lets up slowly to prevent oscillation
                when facing into the wind.
          • Makes minor corrections to remain facing into the wind, if the wind is blowing from the front.
          • Looks below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers.
          • Transfers control of one toggle to the opposite hand at approximately 200 feet AGL so that one hand
                is controlling both toggles.
          • Lowers CE with a free hand.
          • Regains canopy control immediately with both hands.
          • Assumes a proper prepare-to-land attitude by pulling the toggles to the appropriate break position.
          • Keeps feet and knees together, knees slightly bent, elbows rotated in toward the sides, and head and
                eyes on the horizon.

OBSTACLES AND TREE LANDING

     3-84. The jumper turns to avoid obstacles. When using the MC-6, the jumper takes the following precautions
     if obstacles (trees, water, or high-tension wires) cannot be avoided:

          • If a jumper is drifting toward trees, they immediately turn away.
          • If the jumper cannot avoid the trees and has lowered the equipment, the jumper:

                 Looks below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers.
                 Jettisons the equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.
          • If the jumper has not lowered the equipment, the jumper keeps it on to provide extra protection
                while passing through the trees.

          • At approximately 250 feet AGL, the jumper assumes a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees
                together, knees slightly bent, with head and eyes on the horizon.

          • The jumper rotates their hands in front of their face with elbows high when the balls of their feet
                make contact with the trees.

          • The jumper is prepared to execute a PLF if the jumper passes through the trees.

                                                 WARNING

                    Make sure the reserve reaches the ground or is close to it before
                    continuing with the following actions.

     3-85. A jumper takes the following actions if becoming hung up in a tree and decides to climb down:
          • Jettisons all unneeded equipment.
          • Ensures that the helmet is maintained.
          • Activates the quick release in the waistband.
          • Applies inward pressure to the ripcord assembly with either hand.
          • Removes the top tuck tab with the opposite hand.
          • Maintains steady inward pressure and with the opposite hand, inserts it behind the ripcord assembly
                and applies inward pressure.
          • Grasps the ripcord handle with the opposite hand, pulls, and drops the handle.
          • Controls the activation of the reserve parachute toward the ground with both hands, ensuring that
                all suspension lines are completely deployed.
          • Disconnects the left connector snap and rotates the reserve parachute down and to the right.
          • Attaches the left connector snap to the triangle link on their right side.
          • Activates the quick release in the chest strap and completely removes the chest strap from the chest
                strap friction adapter.
          • Grasps the main lift web with either hand below the canopy release assembly and with the other
                hand activates the leg strap ejector snaps and climbs down the outside of the reserve parachute.

                                                 CAUTION

                    Extreme care must be taken when climbing down the T-11 reserve/T-11
                    reserve single pin parachute suspension lines because of the slippery
                    coating applied to the suspension lines. When in doubt, stay where you
                    are and wait for assistance.

WATER LANDING

     3-86. As soon as jumpers realize they are going to land in water, they take the following actions:
          • Immediately try to turn away if drifting towards a body of water.
          • If jumpers cannot turn away, they look below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers underneath, and
                lower and jettison their equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Jettison the helmet, again making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Activate the quick release in the waistband, disconnect the left connector snap, and rotate the reserve
                parachute to the right.
          • Seat themselves well into the saddle and activate the quick release in the chest strap, completely
                removing the chest strap from the chest strap friction adapter.
          • Regain canopy control.
          • Prior to entering the water, jumpers assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together,
                knees slightly bent, and place hands on the leg strap ejector snaps.
          • When the balls of the feet make contact with the water, jumpers—
                 Activate both leg strap ejector snaps.

                 Arch their backs, throw arms above the head, and slide out of the parachute harness.
          • Swim upwind or upstream away from the canopy.
          • Are prepared to execute a PLF if the water is shallow (2 feet or less in depth).

Without a Life Preserver

     3-87. Jumpers do the following (in addition to the actions under water landing) when wearing the
     MC-6 parachute harness and executing a water landing without a life preserver is imminent (see figure 3-3 on
     page 19):

          • Look below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers and lower and jettison their equipment, making a
                mental note of where it lands.

          • Jettison their helmet, again making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Activate the quick release in the waistband, disconnect the left connector snap, and rotate the reserve

                parachute to the right.
          • Seat themselves well into the saddle and activate the quick release in the chest strap, completely

                removing the chest strap from the chest strap friction adapter.
          • Regain canopy control.
          • Prior to entering the water, jumpers assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together,

                knees slightly bent and hands on the ejector snaps for the leg straps.
          • When the balls of the feet make contact with the water, jumpers—

                 Activate both leg strap ejector snaps.
                 Arch their backs, throw arms above the head, and slide out of the parachute harness.
          • Swim upwind or upstream away from the canopy.
          • If the canopy comes down on top of jumpers, they locate a seam and follow it to the skirt of the
                canopy.
          • Are prepared to execute a PLF if the water is shallow (2 feet or less in depth).

With a Life Preserver

     3-88. When wearing an MC-6 parachute harness and jumping with a life preserver (see figure 3-4 on
     page 20), jumpers do the following in addition to the actions mentioned for a water landing:

          • While still in the air, they activate the life preserver prior to assuming a landing attitude.
          • If the life preserver fails to inflate, they inflate the life preserver manually by blowing air into the

                inflation valve hose.
          • Look below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers, lower their equipment, and jettison their

                equipment.
          • Assume a landing attitude and prepare to do a PLF in the event the water is shallow.
          • Once in the water, they activate both canopy release assemblies using procedures previously

                described for recovering from the drag:
                 The hand-to-shoulder method.
                 The hand-to-assist method.

             Note. See chapter 12 for more information on life preservers.

HIGH-TENSION WIRE LANDING

     3-89. Jumpers do the following if unable to avoid high tension lines when landing (see figure 3-5 on page 21):
          • If they drift towards wires, they immediately try to turn away.
          • If they cannot turn away, they look below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers and jettison the
                equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Ensure that they maintain their helmet.
          • Assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together and exaggerating the bend in the
                knees, keeping eyes open, chins on chest, and their backs arched.
          • Place the palms of hands high on the inside of the front set of risers.

          • When jumpers make contact with the wires, they begin a hard rocking motion and attempt to pass
                through the wires.

          • Prepare to do a PLF in the event they pass through the wires.

POINT 5. LAND

     3-90. The fifth point of performance is land. To lessen the possibility of injuries, the jumper is trained to
     absorb the impact of landing by executing a proper PLF. To do this, the following five fleshy portions of the
     body must contact the ground in sequence:

          • Balls of feet.
          • Calf.
          • Thigh.
          • Buttocks.
          • Pull-up muscle.

     3-91. The three basic PLFs are:
          • Front (right or left).
          • Rear (right or left).
          • Side (right or left).

     3-92. The direction of the wind drift dictates the type of fall the jumper makes. The jumper judges the
     direction of drift by looking at the ground before assuming the landing attitude. The jumper prepares to make
     the appropriate PLF after determining the direction of the wind and the type of fall.

FRONT PARACHUTE LANDING FALL

     3-93. The two types of front PLFs are right front PLF and left front PLF. They are used as described:
          • The right front PLF is used if the direction of (wind) drift is to the front and slightly to the right.
          • The left front fall is used if the direction of drift is to the front and slightly to the left.
          • If the direction of drift is directly to the front, the jumper selects either PLF.
          • For a left front PLF, when the balls of the feet make contact with the ground:
                 The jumper places their chin on their chest and tenses the neck muscles, then presses their
                     elbows against the chest.
                 The jumper pushes the right knee into the left knee, exposing the second and third points of
                     contact (calf, thigh) in the direction of drift.
                 The jumper rotates from the waist up, further exposing the four remaining points of contact.
                 The jumper continues to bend at the knees, maintaining pressure with the right knee into the
                     left knee, and lays the four remaining points of contact on the ground in sequence.
          • As the PLF is completed in the direction of drift, the jumper maintains tension in the neck to prevent
                their head from striking the ground:
                 The momentum caused by the drift brings the feet around to the right and into the direction of
                     drift.
                 The jumper activates one canopy release assembly to keep being dragged after completing the
                     PLF and only activates the second canopy release assembly if needed.
                 The jumper rotates to the left when executing the right front PLF.

32  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026

                                                                                                                Five Points of Performance

REAR PARACHUTE LANDING FALL

     3-94. The two variations of the rear PLF are right rear PLF and left rear PLF. The jumper determines which
     PLF to make by checking the direction of drift. If the drift is directly to the rear, the jumper selects the
     appropriate PLF. The jumper determines which rear PLF to make by checking the direction of drift, and takes
     the following actions:

          • For a left rear PLF, when the balls of the feet make contact with the ground:
                 The jumper places their chin on their chest and tenses the neck muscles, then press their elbows
                     against their chest.
                 The jumper pushes their right knee into the left knee, exposing the second, third, and a portion
                     the fourth point of contact (calf, thigh) to the ground.
                 The jumper bends forward at the waist looking between their elbows, down toward the right
                     boot heel, fully exposing the second, third, fourth, and fifth points of contact to the ground.
                 The jumper continues to bend at the knees, maintaining pressure with the right knee into the
                     left knee, and lays the four remaining points of contact on the ground in sequence.

          • As the PLF is completed in the direction of drift, the jumper maintains tension in the neck to prevent
                the head from striking the ground.

          • The momentum caused by the drift brings their feet around to the right and into the direction of drift.
          • The jumper activates one canopy release assembly to keep being dragged after completing the PLF

                and only activates the second canopy release assembly if needed.
          • When executing the right rear PLF, the jumper rotates to the right.

SIDE PARACHUTE LANDING FALL

     3-95. As the balls of the jumper’s feet make contact with the ground, the jumper begins several actions at the
     same time. As the fall continues, they do the following to complete a left side PLF:

             Note. The right side PLF is similar to the left side PLF, except the points of contact on the right
             side of the body are used.

          • The jumper lowers the chin firmly to the chest and tenses the neck muscles.
          • If the jumper is in the no brake, one-fourth brake, or half brake position, the jumper brings hands up

                in front of their head and elbows in front of their chest and continues to grasp the toggles.
          • If the jumper is in the three-fourth brake, full brake, or reverse flight position, they cross their wrists

                by rotating the forearms into the center of their body and hold their elbows into their sides while
                continuing to grasp the toggles.
          • The jumper pushes their right knee into the left knee, exposing the second and third points of contact
                (calf, thigh) in the direction of the drift.
          • The jumper rotates from the waist up, to the right, looking down at the right boot heel exposing the
                fourth and fifth points of contact (buttocks, pull-up muscle) to the ground in the direction of drift.
          • The jumper continues to bend at the knees, maintaining pressure with the right knee into the left
                knee and lays the four remaining points of contact on the ground in sequence.
          • As the PLF is completed in the direction of drift, the jumper maintains tension in their neck to
                prevent their head from striking the ground.
          • The momentum caused by drift brings the jumper’s feet around to the right and into the direction of
                drift.
          • The jumper activates one canopy release assembly to keep being dragged after completing the PLF
                and only activates the second canopy release assembly if needed.

Chapter 3

LAND

     3-96. Never attempt to make a stand-up landing. Remain on the ground and activate one canopy release
     assembly using either the hand-to-shoulder method or the hand assist method. The hand assist method is the
     most preferred, and consists of the jumper taking the following actions:

          • With the thumb and index finger of one hand, pulls out and down on the safety clip.
          • Forms a fist with the thumb exposed and then inserts their thumb into the cable loop.
          • Turns the head in the opposite direction.
          • Then assisting with the other hand, pulls out and down on the cable loop.
          • Repeats this process with the opposite canopy release assembly.
          • Activates one canopy release assembly.

     3-97. Once both canopy release assemblies have been activated, the jumper places their weapon into
     operation and removes the parachute harness.

                                                 Chapter 4

        Reserve Activation and Parachute Malfunctions

    The techniques and procedures described in this chapter are used throughout jumpers’ airborne
    careers. They allow the jumper to demonstrate proficiency in the tasks necessary to react
    appropriately and without hesitation to a parachute malfunction.

T-11 RESERVE/SINGLE PIN ACTIVATION (PULL DROP METHOD)

     4-1. When conducting an airborne operation, a jumper must count to 6,000 with a T-11 ATPS (4,000 with a
     MC-6) series parachute and immediately activate the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute if no opening shock
     is felt using the pull drop method. Jumpers conduct a good check of the main parachute canopy during the
     second point of performance, looking for any damage or irregularities. They also constantly compare the rate
     of descent throughout the entire jump. If at any time they cannot compare the rate of descent, or feel they are
     falling faster than fellow jumpers, they immediately activate the reserve parachute using the pull drop
     method.

     4-2. During instrument meteorological conditions (IMC), if the jumper has any malfunction, or any reason
     to believe they are falling faster than fellow jumpers, they immediately activate the reserve parachute using
     the pull drop method because they cannot compare the rate of descent with fellow jumpers.

     4-3. To activate the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute using the pull drop method, the jumper—
          • Maintains a good, tight body position.
          • Keeps their feet and knees together.
          • Grasps the ripcord handle with either hand.
          • Throws their head back and to the rear.
          • Pulls the ripcord handle and drops it to the ground; the reserve parachute activates.
          • Ensures neither hand is in front of the reserve parachute as it deploys.

     4-4. When descending with only the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute inflated, jumpers control directional
     movement by slipping. When using the T-11 reserve/single pin, the proper landing attitude is obtained by
     reaching up and grasping one riser in the opposite direction of drift; at approximately 200 feet AGL, slip into
     the wind, and prepare to land. Upon landing, jumpers make a quick recovery and collapse the canopy. In
     strong winds, if a quick recovery is impossible, jumpers grasp one suspension line from either suspension
     line group and pull the suspension line toward themselves until the canopy collapses.

PARACHUTE MALFUNCTIONS AND INCIDENTS

     4-5. A malfunction is the failure of an airdrop item to function as it was intended or designed. Some examples
     of malfunctions include but are not limited to—

          • Failure of a main canopy to deploy properly.
          • USLM breaking.
          • Parachute panel or gore blowout.

     4-6. An incident is any action or event that prevented the successful completion of a planned airdrop
     operation. (See AR 59-4/OPNAVINST 4630.24E/AFMAN 13-210 Volume 1/MCO 13480.1E Volume 1 for
     more clarification.) Some examples of incidents include, but are not limited to—

          • Entanglements resulting in reserve parachute deployment.
          • Misrouted static line that resulted in a towed jumper (cutaway or retrieved).

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  35


---

Chapter 4

     4-7. Main parachute malfunctions demand the jumper’s immediate attention. Jumpers must be trained to
     identify parachute malfunctions and to respond instantaneously. Practical exercises involving activation of
     the reserve parachute are incorporated into all phases of the basic airborne course. Each type of malfunction
     is demonstrated in the course so jumpers can see exactly how each type of malfunction looks. There are two
     types of parachute malfunctions:

          • Total.
          • Partial.

TOTAL MALFUNCTIONS

     4-8. A total malfunction is the complete failure of the airdrop system to function as designed (see
     AR 59-4/OPNAVINST 4630.24E/AFMAN 13-210 Volume 1/MCO 13480.1E Volume 1). The failure of the
     parachute to deploy can be caused by a severed static line, a broken snap hook, or a broken anchor line cable.
     The jumper’s failure to hook up also results in the failure of the parachute to deploy. However, these types
     of malfunctions are extremely rare.

     4-9. Although not defined as a total malfunction, a deployed parachute with a ‘cigarette roll’ or ‘streamer’
     provides little or no lift for the jumper. This malfunction must be treated as a total malfunction. The jumper
     immediately activates the reserve using the pull drop method.

                                                 WARNING

                    The towed jumper must remain in a good, tight body position and
                    protect the ripcord handle with both hands. Accidental activation
                    of the reserve while being towed could be fatal.

     4-10. Although not classified as a parachute malfunction, a jumper can be towed behind the aircraft by a
     misrouted USLM or by a piece of equipment that has snagged the aircraft during the jumper’s exit. During
     the 6,000 count with T-11 ATPS or the 4,000 count with MC-6 series parachute, the jumper feels an excessive
     opening shock, and the jumper may be towed. If jumpers are being towed by their USLM and are
     unconscious, they are retrieved back inside the aircraft. If they are conscious, the following actions occur:

          • The jumper maintains a good, tight body position with both hands covering the ripcord handle.
          • An attempt is made to retrieve the jumper inside the aircraft.
          • As the jumper nears the paratroop door, do not reach for retrieval personnel, and continue to protect

                the ripcord handle.
          • If the jumper cannot be retrieved, the USLM is cut.
          • Once jumpers feel themselves falling free from the aircraft, they immediately start—

                 A 6,000 count with the T-11 ATPS.
                 A 4,000 count with MC-6 series parachute.
                 If no opening shock is felt, they activate the reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

     4-11. If the jumper is being towed by an item of equipment, regardless of whether the jumper is conscious or
     unconscious, that item of equipment is cut or jogged free, and the main canopy deploys.

                                                 CAUTION

                    The most important action of a towed jumper is to protect the ripcord
                    handle.

36  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                  Reserve Activation and Parachute Malfunctions

PARTIAL MALFUNCTIONS

     4-12. The seven types of partial malfunctions are—
          • Corner crossover inversion.
          • Hung slider.
          • Sleeve corner vent entanglement.
          • Blown section or holes in the canopy.
          • Broken suspension lines.
          • Delayed opening.
          • Broken control line (MC-6).

     4-13. A corner crossover inversion may occur when a portion of the parachute canopy is blown inward and
     through one of the four corner vents, creating a bubble-like appearance. This type of partial malfunction can
     reduce lifting surface and increase the rate of descent. If a jumper experiences a corner crossover inversion,
     immediately activate the reserve parachute utilizing the pull drop method.

     4-14. A hung slider may be caused by tension knots in the suspension lines or excessive twists in the risers
     or suspension lines, due to a loose body position or a weak exit. During this malfunction, the slider becomes
     stuck or hung, prior to reaching its full terminal position. If the main canopy has a hung slider, the canopy
     does not fully inflate, and the jumper’s rate of descent increases. If a hung slider occurs, immediately activate
     the reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

     4-15. The sleeve corner vent entanglement malfunction may occur with the T-11 ATPS when a delayed or
     slow opening of the parachute canopy allows the 10-foot bridle line assembly and deployment sleeve to pass
     through one of the parachute’s corner vents. In a sleeve corner vent entanglement, the bridle line and sleeve
     become twisted through the corner vent and may become entangled around several suspension lines just
     below the slider, preventing the slider from reaching its full terminal position. In a sleeve corner vent
     entanglement, the canopy is partially inverted or folded under. This reduces the lifting surface and increases
     the rate of descent. If a sleeve corner vent entanglement occurs, the jumper should immediately activate the
     reserve parachute utilizing the pull drop method.

     4-16. A blown section or holes in the canopy malfunction occurs when the excessive strain placed on the
     canopy during inflation is too great and a panel or gore rips or tears, resulting in a hole(s). Regardless of the
     size of the rip or hole, the jumper compares the rate of descent with fellow jumpers. If the jumper is falling
     faster than other jumpers, they immediately activate the reserve parachute using the pull drop method. If the
     jumper is not falling faster, they continue with the five points of performance while constantly comparing
     the rate of descent with other jumpers.

     4-17. The broken suspension lines malfunction occurs when enough suspension lines break, causing the
     jumper’s rate of descent to be greater than fellow jumpers. When this occurs, the jumper immediately
     activates the reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

     4-18. A delayed opening malfunction occurs when the canopy fails to deploy or fully inflates by the end of
     the jumper’s first point of performance. This type of malfunction is caused when the parachute elongates,
     and an obstruction prevents air from entering the parachute’s air channel during the inflation phase of
     deployment. Possible causes of this malfunction include air starvation, a hung slider, and debris restricting
     full canopy opening. This type of malfunction provides limited or no lift capability to the jumper and fails to
     slow the jumper sufficiently to a normal rate of descent. The jumper must immediately activate the reserve
     parachute using the pull drop method.

     4-19. The broken control lines (MC-6) malfunction occurs when one or both control lines break or become
     stuck above the jumper’s reach during the parachute’s deployment sequence. The canopy can no longer be
     controlled by manipulating the extended gore(s) and the jumper must use the rear set of risers to control the
     canopy.

                                                 Chapter 5

                C-130/C-17/C-27J Exiting Procedures

    This chapter discusses the three exiting procedures, alternate door exit procedures (ADEPT)
    option 1, ADEPT option 2, mass exit, and the proper method for jumpers to safely exit the
    C-130, C-17, and the C-27J aircraft. All units must strictly enforce proper exiting procedures
    from fixed-wing aircraft. Exiting procedures are perishable skills, therefore, be well briefed
    and rehearsed prior to any airborne operation. (See chapter 10 for jumpmaster practical work
    inside the aircraft [PWAC].)

ALTERNATE DOOR EXITING PROCEDURES FOR TRAINING

                                                WARNINGS

                    Only one series of parachutes are suspended in the air at any one
                    given time and on one given pass over the DZ. Mixing parachutes
                    that have different opening performance characteristics may lead
                    to hazardous conditions incidents.
                    Do not sacrifice safety for time, complete the full inspection of
                    each jumper’s USLM down to the main curved pin protector flap.
                    If the inspection cannot be completed in time, the pass is aborted.
                    An improperly routed USLM can cause death or serious injury.

                                                 CAUTION

                    Any member of the jumpmaster team can call a NO DROP anytime it is
                    determined something is wrong or unsafe.

     5-1. The ADEPT for training options is used when jumping the T-11 ATPS and MC-6 series parachutes. This
     training safety measure allows the maximum number of jumpers to exit the aircraft with a minimum risk of
     high-altitude entanglements. ADEPT options are as follows:

          • ADEPT option 1—during a single pass, only one stick of jumpers on one side of the aircraft exits
                their paratroop door.

          • ADEPT option 2—during a single pass, one stick of jumpers exits from the PJM’s door, followed
                by a stick of jumpers from the AJM’s door.

          • Mass exit—this exit procedure is used only when jumping the T-11 ATPS. During this type of exit,
                jumpers exit from both doors at the same time with 1-second intervals between jumpers and a
                ½-second between paratroop doors.

                                                 CAUTION

                    No more than 20 jumpers per anchor line cable for a C-130H; no more
                    than 31 per anchor line cable on a C-130-J30 (C-130J); and no more
                    than 27 per anchor line cable (outboard) and 24 per anchor line cable
                    (inboard) for a C-17 Globemaster III. No more than 13 jumpers per
                    anchor line cable for a C-27J.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  39

Chapter 5

C-130/C-17 ALTERNATE DOOR EXIT PROCEDURES OPTION 1
EXITING PROCEDURES

     5-2. During a single pass over the DZ, only one stick of jumpers on one side of the aircraft jumps. After
     issuing the jump command of STAND UP (see chapter 10 for jumpmaster PWAC), only the jumpers for that
     pass stand up. The following jumper actions then occur:

          • On a C-130 series aircraft:
                 The jumpers sitting in the forward outboard portion may stand up on their seats if required,
                     allowing the inboard personnel to stand up, raise seats, and secure them.
                 In the C-17, standing on seats is not required.

          • Once the inboard seating is raised and secured, the outboard personnel in the forward portion of the
                aircraft rise and secure their seats.

          • Immediately after putting the seats up, the jumper must tighten down their appropriate adjustable
                leg straps and secure the excess webbing in the webbing retainer when jumping with CE.

          • The first three jumpers should be positioned one behind the other, with the rest of the stick staggered
                inboard and outboard.

          • When the command HOOK UP is given, the jumpers detach the USL snap hook from the top
                carrying handle of the reserve parachute:
                 Hook up to the appropriate anchor line cable with the opening gate towards the skin of the
                     aircraft.
                 Jumpers form a bight (four in the hand, two below) and do not touch the double sewn portion
                     of the USLM.
                 The first three jumpers extend their static line arms to obtain the proper distance between
                     jumpers and all others hold their (static line) elbow high.

          • The nonstatic-line hand protects the ripcord handle and the jumper’s feet are staggered with the
                outboard foot forward.

          • When the command CHECK STATIC LINES is given, jumpers—
                 Check the USLM from the point of attachment to where it disappears over the top of the
                     shoulder.
                 The jumper behind traces the USLM past the static line slack retainer band and down to the
                     first stow.
                 If the static line slack retainer band that is holding the USLM breaks, the jumper then stows any
                     excess static line in the other static line slack retainer band.
                 The last two jumpers turn towards the skin of the aircraft and the second to last jumper checks
                     the last jumper’s USLM.

          • On the command CHECK EQUIPMENT, each jumper does the following:
                 Traces the rim of the helmet.
                 Traces the chinstrap.
                 Touches and visually inspects the chest strap, both left and right leg straps.
                 Touches and visually inspects to ensure the hook-pile tape lowering line (HPTLL) is secured to
                     the left triangle link and all excess webbing is properly secured in its appropriate webbing
                     retainers when jumping CE.

          • After the jumpmaster completes the door checks, 1-minute, 30-second time warnings (jumpers relay
                announcements), and gives the command of STANDBY—
                 The jumpmaster escorts the No. 1 jumper into door position.
                 The jumpmaster is positioned close enough to the lead edge of the paratroop door to control the
                     flow of jumpers.
                 The jumpmaster is positioned far enough back as to not impede the jumpers’ movement to the
                     paratroop door.

             Note. On a C-17, the jumpmaster does not issue the command of STANDBY until the amber light
             is on.

                                                                                            C-130/C-17/C-27J Exiting Procedures

     • No. 1 jumpers hand their USLM to the safety and should be positioned about 2 feet from the center
          of the jump platform, keeping their feet spread and legs slightly flexed so that their weight is equally
          distributed over both feet to maintain balance.

     • Follow-on jumpers close behind the preceding jumper and keep a position where feet are spread,
          and legs slightly flexed so their weight is equally distributed over both feet to maintain balance.

     • The jumpmaster can control the No. 1 jumper by grasping one of the jumper’s diagonal backstraps
          or according to the unit’s standard operating procedure (SOP).

     • At the command, GO, the No. 1 jumper—
           Moves toward the door and onto the jump platform, focusing on the horizon.
           The jumper pushes off with either foot and vigorously jumps up 6 inches and out 36 inches
                from the jump platform, immediately snapping into a good, tight body position.

       Note. On a C-17, the jumper takes one or two additional steps on the jump platform before pushing
       off with either foot.

     • As each jumper begins to move, they utilize a controlled movement technique (a slow deliberate
          walk) and assume an elbow-locked position with the arm that is controlling the USLM:
           They place the static line control hand so that it is nearly touching the back of the pack tray of
                the jumper in front of them, establishing the proper interval between jumpers.
           They do not place the static line control hand in a position so that it extends past the pack tray
                of the jumper in front of them.

     • When they are about perpendicular to the paratroop door, jumpers take one more step, make
          eye-to-eye contact with the safety, and the safety takes control of the USLM.

     • The jumper immediately returns the static line hand to the end of the reserve parachute, without
          swimming the USLM.

     • The jumper places the palms of their hands (fingers naturally spread) on the ends of the reserve
          parachute with the elbows tight into the sides.

     • The jumper executes a left or right face to the open paratroop door only when the safety has positive
          control of the USLM.

     • The jumper utilizes the controlled movement technique towards the paratroop door and onto the
          jump platform, focusing on the horizon.

     • The jumper pushes off with either foot, vigorously jumps up 6 inches and out 36 inches from the
          aircraft, immediately snapping into a good, tight body position.

5-3. Once the last jumper exits the active door, the safety immediately conducts a clear to the rear for towed
jumpers, gives a thumbs-up to the loadmaster(s), and helps recover deployment bags. During the pass, the
jumpmaster in the inactive door performs outside air safety checks and then observes the actions in the active
door, since (under this option) they do not have any jumpers exiting that door.

       Note. United States Marine Corps (USMC) and United States Navy (USN) utilize one door; the
       other door remains closed and unmanned. Therefore, only one jumpmaster and one safety are
       needed.

5-4. Subsequent passes alternate from door to door until all jumpers have exited. AJMs are the last jumpers
on their side of the aircraft, and PJMs are the last jumpers to exit the aircraft.

                                            WARNING

               To maximize dispersion and minimize simultaneous exits,
               jumpmasters must control the flow of jumpers, ensuring a
               1-second interval between jumpers at their paratrooper door.

           They place the static line control hand so that it is nearly touching the back of the pack tray of
                the jumper in front of them, establishing the proper interval between jumpers.
           They do not place the static line control hand in a position so that it extends past the pack tray
                of the jumper in front of them.

     • When they are about perpendicular to the paratroop door, jumpers take one more step, make
          eye-to-eye contact with the safety, and the safety takes control of the USLM.

     • The jumper immediately returns the static line hand to the end of the reserve parachute, without
          swimming the USLM.

     • The jumper places the palms of their hands (fingers naturally spread) on the ends of the reserve
          parachute with the elbows tight into the sides.

     • The jumper executes a left or right face (90-degree turn) to the open paratroop door only when the
          safety has positive control of the USLM.

     • The jumper utilizes the controlled movement technique onto the jump platform, focusing on the
          horizon.

     • The jumper pushes off with either foot, vigorously jumps up 6 inches and out 36 inches from the
          aircraft, immediately snapping into a good, tight body position.

5-6. Once the last jumper exits the active door, the safety immediately conducts a clear to the rear for towed
jumpers, gives a thumbs-up to the loadmaster(s), and helps recover deployment bags. During the pass, the
jumpmaster in the inactive door performs outside air safety checks and then observes the actions in the active
door, since (under this option) there are not any jumpers exiting this door.

5-7. Subsequent passes alternate from door to door until all jumpers have exited. AJMs are the last jumpers
on their side of the aircraft, and PJMs are the last jumpers to exit the aircraft.

                                            WARNING

               To maximize dispersion and minimize simultaneous exits,
               jumpmasters must control the flow of jumpers ensuring a
               1-second interval between jumpers at the paratrooper door.

C-130/C-17 ADEPT OPTION 2 EXITING PROCEDURES

     5-8. During a single pass over the DZ, one stick of jumpers exits from the PJM’s paratroop door, followed
     by a stick of jumpers from the AJM’s paratroop door. After issuing the jump command of STAND UP
     (see chapter 11 for jumpmaster PWAC) only the jumpers for that pass stand up and the following jumper
     actions occur:

          • On a C-130 series aircraft:
                 The jumpers sitting in the forward outboard portion may stand up on their seats if required to
                     allow the inboard personnel to stand up, raise seats, and secure them.
                 On the C-17, standing on seats is not required.

          • Once the inboard seating is raised and secured, the outboard personnel in the forward portion of the
                aircraft rise and secure seats.

          • Immediately after putting the seats up, the jumper must tighten down their appropriate adjustable
                leg straps and secure the excess webbing in the webbing retainer when jumping CE.

          • The first three jumpers should be positioned one behind the other, with the rest of the stick staggered
                inboard and outboard.

          • When the command of HOOK UP is given—
                 The jumpers detach the USL snap hook from the top carrying handle of the reserve parachute.
                 They hook up to the appropriate anchor line cable with the opening gate towards the skin of the
                     aircraft.
                 Jumpers form a bight (four in the hand, two below) but do not touch the double-sewn portion
                     of the USLM.
                 The first three jumpers extend their static line arms to obtain the proper distance between
                     jumpers, and all others hold their static line elbow high.

          • The nonstatic-line hand protects the ripcord handle and the jumper’s feet are staggered with the
                outboard foot forward.

          • When the command of CHECK STATIC LINES is given—
                 Jumpers check the USLM from the point of attachment to where it disappears over the top of
                     the shoulder.
                 The jumper behind them stows any excess static line in the static line slack retainer band.
                 The last two jumpers turn towards the skin of the aircraft and the second to last jumper checks
                     the last jumper’s USLM.

          • On the command of CHECK EQUIPMENT, each jumper—
                 Traces the rim of the helmet.
                 Traces the chinstrap.
                 Touches and visually inspects the chest strap, and both left and right leg straps.
                 Touches and visually inspects to ensure the HPTLL is secured to the left triangle link and all
                     excess webbing is properly secured in its appropriate webbing retainers when jumping CE.

          • After the jumpmaster completes the door checks, 1-minute, 30-second time warnings (jumpers relay
                announcements), and gives the command of STANDBY:
                 The jumpmaster escorts the No. 1 jumper into door position.
                 The jumpmaster is positioned close enough to the lead edge of the paratroop door to control the
                     flow of jumpers, but far enough back as to not impede the jumpers’ movement to the paratroop
                     door.

                                                 Chapter 6

           Individual Combat Equipment Jump Loads

    Individual equipment and weapons are attached or worn by the jumper in several
    configurations. They can be placed inside containers, exposed, or a mix of the two. Unit SOPs
    do not deny the jumper the ability to conduct the five points of performance or perform
    emergency procedures. To ensure personnel safety, all small arms must be on SAFE with no
    ammunition chambered when jumping.

JUMPER’S LOAD

     6-1. It is a leader’s responsibility to ensure their personnel are highly proficient in the proper rigging of
     individual items of CE and that they maintain their equipment’s serviceability. The airborne commander is
     responsible to ensure that all unit and individual equipment involved are approved for airborne operations in
     compliance with this training circular.

     6-2. Any test involving a new item of equipment or a procedure that causes a change to the normal use of an
     item of equipment is examined by the Airborne and Special Operations Test Directorate. After the Airborne
     and Special Operations Test Directorate has determined that it is technically safe to use the equipment for
     airborne operations, the U.S. Army Jumpmaster School and U.S. Army Advanced Airborne School evaluates
     any changes to jumpmaster procedures based on the test equipment. However, the U.S. Army Infantry School
     (USAIS) is the final approval for all changes to equipment and procedures for static line operations.
     Equipment authorized for airborne operations can be found in TB 43-0001-80, in addition to safety
     confirmations or safety of use messages.

LOAD DISTRIBUTION

     6-3. Unit commanders and jumpmasters must inspect jumpers to ensure weight and distribution of the load
     does not interfere with the jumper’s ability to perform a strong, safe exit from an aircraft, or hinder a jumper’s
     ability to perform emergency procedures.

LOAD CONSIDERATIONS

     6-4. During planning, leaders at all levels must take into consideration that the total jumper-rigged weight
     cannot exceed the maximum parachute load limit of 400 pounds (T-11 ATPS or the MC-6). Determining
     factors should include the following:

          • The individual jumper’s body weight.
          • Weight of the parachute system.
          • Weight of any equipment attached to the jumper.
          • Experience level of the individual jumper.
          • The unit jumper progression program.

     6-5. Commanders should use all the equipment methods of entry available to them (container delivery system
     [CDS], door bundles, and so on) to prevent overloading any individual jumper. During planning, leaders at
     all levels must take into consideration that the static line retrieval system has a maximum weight limit of 400
     pounds. The maximum rigged weight of the parachutist cannot exceed 325 pounds for over-the-ramp
     operations.

             Note. The maximum total jumper weight criteria does not preclude the PJM of their responsibility
             to ensure that all jumpers can safely and effectively exit from an aircraft.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  51

Chapter 6

PROTECTIVE GEAR

     6-6. Helmets must be fitted properly to ensure they stay on the jumper’s head during deployment of their
     parachute and during PLFs. USN and USMC personnel use helmets approved according to their respective
     regulations and approved equipment lists.

     6-7. The ACH is a modular helmet system that provides ballistic, fragmentation, and impact protection.
     (See figure 6-1.) This system is compatible with the current night-vision devices (NVDs), communications
     packages, and chemical defense equipment. The outer rim of the ACH’s helmet shell must be inspected for
     any sharp or protruding edges that may cut or fray a jumper’s USLM upon exiting the aircraft. Sharp or
     protruding edges are taped with pressure-sensitive adhesive cloth. The ACH has the following characteristics:

          • The helmet system provides 9-millimeter (mm) and fragmentation protection within a spectrum of
                environments:
                 Cold down to -40 degrees Fahrenheit.
                 Hot up to 140 degrees Fahrenheit.
                 Salt water; freshwater; petroleum, oils, lubricants; and so forth.

          • The ACH allows maximum sensory awareness for the operator, which includes an unobstructed
                field of view and increased ambient hearing capabilities.

          • The helmet’s retention and suspension system provides unsurpassed balance, stability, and comfort;
                this unique system provides for proper size, fit, and ventilation.

          • The pad suspension system provides superior impact protection throughout all operational
                requirements.

                                         Figure 6-1. Advanced combat helmet

HELMET ASSEMBLY

     6-8. The ACH has a unique, fully adjustable pad suspension system. The only authorized suspension pads
     are those issued or purchased through official USA supply systems. All suspension pads are secured to the
     helmet shell by hook disks. There are two sizes of suspension pads: size 6, which are 3/4-inches, and size 8,
     which are 1/4-inch thick. All seven suspension pads are the same size, do not mix and match suspension pad
     sizes or manufacturers. Serviceable suspension pads are free of any rips or tears that expose the foam padding
     inside the shell. All seven pads are worn with the helmet. (See figure 6-2.)

52  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026

MODIFIED CHINSTRAP ASSEMBLIES

     6-11. Ballistic mounting screws, securing screws and nuts, and conical nuts must be inspected to ensure they
     are not rusted, cracked, or corroded. Mounting hardware does not protrude excessively into the helmet shell.
     They must be tightened down to ensure that neither piece can move freely from the other, and that they secure
     the chinstrap assembly in place. All screws must be routed from outside to inside and cannot damage the
     material of the helmet shell. Replacement parts must match the original hardware provided with the chinstrap
     assembly. Using replacement parts from the ballistic helmet or unauthorized systems may damage the ACH
     and cause a safety hazard to the jumper. Flush-mounted securing screws or nuts or conical nuts are preferred.
     When tightening, the screw does not protrude past the securing screw or nut or conical nut.

     6-12. As worn, the padded portion of the nape pad must be facing toward the jumper’s skin. The retention
     strap must be properly routed through it and secured by the hook-pile tape (HPT). Ballistic nape pads are not
     authorized for airborne operations.

     6-13. All mounting hardware utilized to secure a base plate or head harness to an ACH must be flush mounted
     on the inside of the helmet shell. Replacement hardware for the night-vision goggle (NVG)/enhanced NVG
     base plate (NSN: 5340-01-509-1467) that allow the traditional style base plate to be safe for operations is
     available. This hardware is only used on this style base plate. Prior to any airborne operation, the head harness
     must be thoroughly padded and taped to cover any sharp or protruding edges. (See figure 6-10.) The mount
     and swing arm assembly for the NVG/enhanced NVG is not jumped attached to the head harness.

6-19. Adapters with Peltor headsets and the Ops Core Rail Attached Communications (RAC) system:

6-20. Installation of Peltor headset (not authorized with the integrated head protection system (IHPS):
     • Secure the adapters to the Peltor headset.

          opposite side, ensuring the cable connecting the two earpieces is inside the helmet and does not
          become a snag hazard.

     • Secure a retainer band to the ARC rail on the side or sides that have push-to-talk (PTT) adapter
          cable; the recommended retainer band is the two-inch heavy duty retainer band.
     • S-fold the PTT adapter cable and stow it in the retainer band as seen in figure 6-14 on page 62 and
          note that the cable is folded so the entire cable can be pulled out of the retainer band.

6-21. Installation of RAC headset (not authorized with the integrated head protection system [IHPS]):

          is affixed to the rear HPT provided on the helmet
     • Secure a retainer band to the side of the connecting cable that has the PTT adapter cable; the
          recommended retainer band is the type-1 retainer band.
     • S-fold the PTT cable and secure in the retainer band as seen in figure 6-14 on page 62.

UNIVERSAL PARACHUTIST RECOVERY BAG

     6-32. The UPRB (NSN: 1670-01-645-1731) is designed as a carriage and storage container for military free
     fall and static line parachute systems. It is a replacement system for the aviator kit bags (also called AKBs)

64         TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                    Individual Combat Equipment Jump Loads

and MC-4 kit bags currently used to support parachute recovery operations. The UPRB has approximately
8,000 cubic inches of storage space. The main storage compartment can hold the T-11 main parachute canopy
and an activated reserve canopy. A storage pocket on the outside of the bag is designed for storing a packed
T-11 reserve/single pin parachute or a military free-fall helmet. The design includes shoulder straps and top
carrying handles to facilitate load carriage and leg strap retainers to secure the UPRB under the parachute
harness leg straps. Details include:

     • Material—7.25 nylon cloth (water and abrasion resistant).
     • Color—Foliage green (F-504).
     • Weight—3 pounds.
     • Size—30 inches x 29 inches.

6-33. The UPRB is not waterproof and is not designed to provide protection from wet weather or damp
ground. Parachute assemblies and reserves may be issued in the UPRB to aid handling and to prevent damage
or unintentional opening. Until removed for fitting by parachutists, parachutes and reserves should remain in
the universal parachutist kit bag and be protected from moisture to prevent mildew during storage and
transport. Storing UPRBs in weatherproof areas such as buildings, trucks, tents, or transport aircraft, reduces
the risk of moisture-related damage.

6-34. The UPRB components consist of the following (see figures 6-17 and 6-18 on page 66):

     • 2. Front pocket securing straps.
     • 3. Front pocket.
     • 4. Heavy duty zipper.
     • 5. Snap fasteners.
     • 6. Top compression strap.
     • 7. Top carrying handles.
     • 8. Side carrying handles.
     • 9. Shoulder straps.

    6-35. To fold the UPRB properly—
         • Place it on a flat surface.
         • Invert the UPRB so that the smooth side is out and tuck all webbing and excess webbing that is on
              the inside and zip it closed.
         • Fold one side of UPRB by aligning the binding tape and tucking all excess material to the inside
              and repeat on the opposite side.
         • Fold the bottom by pulling the top layer up and tucking all excess material to the inside:
               Once excess material is tucked, align the top and bottom binding tape.
               Fold the top with zipper by lifting the top layer toward the center and tuck the zipper and snaps
                    to the inside (do not zip the bag completely closed).
         • Pull the bottom corners:
               This allows the binding tape to lay flat.
               Fold the top layer back onto the bottom layer, aligning the binding tape.
         • Flip the UPRB over so that the leg strap retainer is on the bottom.
         • Ensure the smooth side is up and starting from either side, fold one quarter approximately
              4 to 6 inches towards the center (see figure 6-19).
         • Repeat for the opposite side and fold one quarter (approximately 4 to 6 inches) towards the center.

           Figure 6-19. Universal parachutist recovery bag folds

     6-41. The improved outer tactical vest (IOTV) (NSN: 8470-01-551-7648 Large) has a side opening that
     increases soft ballistic coverage and adjusts for better comfort. It also has a quick-release handle for Soldiers

     supervise their jumpers when donning parachutes to ensure that the IOTV is worn properly, reducing further
     strain and fatigue. Jumpers may need to adjust their parachute harnesses to a size larger than they commonly
     wear to accommodate for the size of the body armor.

JUMPMASTER PERSONNEL INSPECTION SEQUENCE FOR THE WAISTBAND EXTENSION

     6-46. The jumper removes their left hand from behind the reserve and inserts their left index finger and
     middle finger from top to bottom into the quick release formed by the waistband, ensuring it is no more than
     three fingers and no less than two fingers tight, and it is not a false quick release. With their left index finger
     and thumb, pinch off the free running end of the waistband where it emerges from the metal adjuster. Trace
     the free running end of the waistband until the fingers fall off the end to ensure the waistband is not cut, torn,
     or frayed, and is easily accessible to the jumper. Continue tracing the waistband extension until making
     contact with the metal adjuster ensuring the waistband extension is not twisted, cut, or frayed, and is not
     misrouted.

     6-47. The jumpmaster ensures the waistband extension is threaded back through both sides of the metal
     adjuster, ensuring a positive locking action. The jumpmaster also makes sure that any excess webbing is
     secured with a retainer band. The jumpmaster uses their left hand to grasp the carrying handle of the reserve
     with their palm facing the reserve and focuses their attention on their right hand and the WAP. With the right
     hand, the jumpmaster traces the WAP back to where it is sewn into the pack tray to ensure that it is not
     twisted, cut, or frayed. While tracing the WAP, the jumpmaster ensures that the waistband is not misrouted
     behind the horizontal backstrap and that it is properly secured to the pack tray by a single box X stitch with
     at least 50 percent of the stitching present. The jumpmaster returns to the normal JMPI sequence.

TACTICAL ASSAULT PANEL

     6-48. The tactical assault panel (NSN: 8465-01-580-0689) has been fielded to replace the current MOLLE
     fighting load carrier. Jumpmasters ensure the tactical assault panel system does not interfere with the jumper
     reacting to any type of emergency. There are two basic rules: First, the reserve parachute rests parallel with
     the jumper’s torso. Second, when the tactical assault panel system is worn, the items of equipment on the
     side of the tactical assault panel system are not resting in front of the horizontal backstrap. To wear the tactical
     assault panel properly for airborne operations the jumper must—

          • Attach the load carrying harness portion of the tactical assault panel to the ammunition pouch
                portion.

          • Don the tactical assault panel system ensuring there are no twists in the harnesses webbing and the
                adjusting buckles are not cracked or broken, then secure them together.

             Note. Any equipment or pouch attached to the front of the tactical assault panel system that
             interferes with the reserve parachute lying parallel to the jumper’s body must be removed.

          • Remove enough slack from the horizontal backstraps of the tactical assault panel system so it rests
                either—
                 High on the jumper’s chest.
                 Low enough so it does not interfere with the reserve parachute resting flat against the jumper’s
                     body.

          • Secure the free running ends inside their appropriate webbing retainers.

     6-49. Proper rigging of the tactical assault panel and parachute harness includes:
          • Ensuring the waistband is not routed through any item of equipment attached to the tactical assault
                panel system.
          • Ensuring the horizontal backstrap is not routed in front of or over the top of any item attached to the
                tactical assault panel system:
                 This prevents the jumper from properly reacting to an emergency landing.
                 This impedes the jumper from getting out of the parachute harness once they have landed.
          • Reducing all slack in the horizontal backstrap following the rule stated above.
          • Tightening the horizontal backstrap so that it is snug against the jumper’s body.

TACTICAL ASSAULT PANEL WITH NETT WARRIOR SYSTEM OR A SIMILAR PLATFORM

     6-50. A rules-based approach is necessary for this type of system because of the various types of load-bearing
     vests authorized for use:

          • Nothing on the tactical assault panel is attached to the parachute harness.
          • The reserve parachute must rest parallel to the jumper’s torso.
          • Four inches of the quick release in the waistband must be exposed from the metal adjuster to ensure

                the jumper can properly activate the quick release.
          • Handheld radios—4-to-6 inches of the quick release in the waistband must be exposed from the

                metal adjuster to ensure the jumper can properly activate the quick release.
          • Antennas can be secured to the radio; however, it cannot extend above the bottom of the canopy

                release assembly.
          • Adapter cables and accessories—all adapter cables, except for the headset, can be connected prior

                to donning the parachute harness:
                 All excess cable is stowed and secured so it does not interfere with the jumper properly exiting

                     the aircraft or becomes a hazard throughout their descent.
                 Each type of tactical assault panel has different capabilities for stowing/securing cables.
                 Jumpmasters must use their best judgement when evaluating the jumper’s tactical assault panel

                     configuration.
          • Once the jumper has completed JMPI, the headset adapter cable can be connected to the PTT device

                to allow leaders to communicate enroute to the DZ (see figure 6-26).
          • Key leaders must disconnect the headset adapter cable and re-secure it to their helmet at the

                20-minute time warning
          • The attachment panel for the radio with end user device—this system requires an attachment panel

                to be attached to the tactical assault panel, so the end user device is accessible to the jumper when
                rigged in the parachute harness (see figure 6-26). See the jump configuration in figure 6-27.

ADVANCED TACTICAL ASSAULT PANEL

     6-51. The advanced tactical assault panel (A-TAP) is an individual load-bearing system designed to provide
     static line parachutists the ability to rig their fighting load under their parachute harness and below their
     waistline. The intent is to remove the Soldier’s fighting load from behind the reserve parachute thereby
     providing better access to the reserve ripcord handle. The A-TAP design is also intended to provide
     parachutists immediate access to their fighting load upon landing:

          • When donning the A-TAP for airborne operations it must be placed into jump configuration as such:
                 The two front quick-release buckles, connecting the suspenders to the panels, must be released
                     and the webbing extended so that the A-TAP sits below the waistline.
                 The center attachment buckle must be undone.

          • Using the buddy system, jumpers don their T-11 ATPS over the A-TAP and when properly worn—
                 The A-TAP is positioned just below the bottom of the pack tray.
                 No portion of the parachute harness (waistband, horizontal back strap, for example) rests on
                     any major accessory item of the A-TAP (ammunition pouches or canteens, for example).
                 The A-TAP does not cover any points of contacts and is not buckled in front (see figure 6-28
                     on page 74 with the A-TAP under T-11 parachute harness).

SOLDIER PLATE CARRIER SYSTEM

     6-52. The Soldier plate carrier system (NSN: 8470-01-592-9480 Large) is designed as a lightweight
     alternative (not a replacement) for the IOTV, the core of the body armor system. It is intended to increase
     mobility and maneuverability by lighting the Soldier’s load when operating on foot in mountainous terrain
     or at high altitude.

     6-53. The Soldier plate carrier system is worn underneath the parachute harness. Accessory items should not
     be worn on the plate carrier during a static line operation.

HARNESS, SINGLE-POINT RELEASE

     6-54. The harness, single-point release (HSPR) (NSN: 1670-01-227-7992) is an H-type design. It is made of
     nylon webbing with friction adapters to secure it around the load, and it has two adjustable D-ring attaching
     straps.

     6-55. To stabilize the pack to the jumper during movement in the aircraft, upon exit, and during the
     deployment phase of the main parachute canopy, two adjustable leg straps are provided to secure the pack to
     the jumper’s right and left legs. The leg straps are equipped with the male portion of the leg strap release
     assembly. The harness has a single-point release handle assembly that simultaneously releases the load and
     leg straps from the jumper and parachute harness. (See figure 6-29.)

       tie-down strap stow pocket. The male portion leg strap release assembly is routed through this
       retainer band when placing the jumper into jumper configuration. This mitigates tripping or snag
       hazards that exist with the adjustable leg strap.

6-56. Inspection criteria include the following:
     • All components are present.
     • Plastic components cannot be cracked or broken.
     • All webbing, straps, and type I, 9/16-inch nylon tape are free of cuts, tears, excessive frays, and dry
          rot.
     • All metallic items are free of rust and corrosion:
           They cannot be cracked or bent.
           All opening gates must have proper spring tension and full range of motion.
     • The release handle cable cannot be kinked, frayed, or corroded.
     • All webbing retainers must be—
           Present and have sufficient elasticity.
           Replaced with a retainer band, if necessary.
     • HPT must be present and have sufficient adhesion.

     6-57. Assembly of the HSPR includes—
          • Laying out the HSPR on a flat surface ensuring that the three color-coded attaching loops are facing
                skyward, and all twists are removed from the equipment retainer straps.
          • Placing the adjustable D-ring attaching straps next to the HSPR, ensuring that the opening gates of
                the snap hooks are facing down:
                 Place the female portion of the leg strap release assembly next to the adjustable D-ring attaching
                     strap.
                 Ensure the three component parts are facing skyward.
          • Routing the release handle assembly from bottom to top through both piles of the release handle
                cross strap:
                 Ensure there are no twists in the release handle lanyard.
                 Secure the release handle lanyard in place utilizing the HPT.
          • Routing—
                 The white attaching loop from bottom to top through the triangle link.
                 The green attaching loop from bottom to top through the white attaching loop.
                 The red attaching loop from bottom to top through the green attaching loop and through the
                     grommet in the female portion leg strap release assembly.
          • Routing the release handle cable through the red attaching loop and into the cable loop retainer:
                 Route the white attaching loop from bottom to top through the triangle link.
                 Route the green attaching loop from bottom to top through the white attaching loop.
                 Route the red attaching loop from bottom to top through the green attaching loop and through
                     the grommet in the female portion leg strap release assembly.
          • Routing the release handle cable through the red attaching loop and into the cable loop retainer:
                 Rotate the HSPR over so that the opening gates of the snap hooks are facing skyward.
                 Remove all twists from the equipment retainer straps.
                 The HSPR is now ready to accommodate a jumpable pack.

ALL-PURPOSE LIGHTWEIGHT INDIVIDUAL CARRYING EQUIPMENT

     6-69. The ALICE pack (NSN: 8465-001-6481) is available in medium and large sizes. The ALICE may be
     rigged with or without a frame; however, it must always be rigged to be lowered. The large ALICE pack can
     sustain loads ranging from a minimum of 35 pounds to a maximum of 95 pounds. The medium ALICE pack
     can sustain loads ranging from 35 pounds to 70 pounds. The ALICE pack should maintain a square
     configuration as much as possible to ensure the HSPR remains tightly secured to it.

     6-70. Any items of equipment that may fall out or come free must be tied down with 1/4-inch cotton webbing
     to the ALICE pack. All fragile or sharp items must be padded and placed inside the main compartment of the
     ALICE pack according to the unit SOP. The outer accessory pouches must be filled with nonfragile items of
     equipment. The lower securing straps are secured by routing them through the V-notch, one complete turn
     around the tubular portion of the ALICE pack frame (through the V-notch twice), to the adjusting buckle on
     the base of the ALICE pack. The only authorized items of equipment that can be rigged under the closing
     flap of the ALICE pack are as follows:

          • A maximum of three light antitank weapons; however, they must be secured together with masking
                tape.

          • The M240B machine gun tripod (M192 lightweight ground mount [LWGM]) separate from the
                spare barrel bag.

          • A M240B machine gun spare barrel bag without tripod.
          • A bedroll or half-improvised litter.
          • Two M3 multirole antiarmor/antipersonnel weapon system (MAAWS) rounds in the short twin

                tubes.
          • Aiming stakes with case.

     6-71. Rigging procedures for the ALICE pack with a frame include the following:
          • Lay out a properly assembled HSPR with the opening gates of the snap hooks facing skyward and
                remove all twists from the equipment retainer straps.

                 Under the tubular portion of the ALICE pack frame and the envelope cushion portion of the
                     ALICE pack.

                 Route it back onto itself, forming a quick release.
          • Adjust the HSPR prior to tightening:
                 Ensure the white attaching loops are centered on the bottom portion of the ALICE pack.
                 Ensure the center outer accessory pouch is between the release handle cross strap and the

                     adjustable cross strap.
                 Tighten the equipment retainer straps by pulling the quick releases in a seesaw motion.
          • Adjust the quick releases so they are two to three fingers in length.
          • S-fold and secure the free running ends, equipment retainer straps with masking tape or retainer
                bands, ensuring the quick release is not secured in the S-folded portion.
          • Remove all slack in the shoulder carrying straps and the excess webbing is then S-folded only and
                secured with masking tape or retainer bands:
                 One of the two, never both.
                 There is no preferred method.
          • Secure the HPTLL in its normal configuration to the X configuration by—
                 Routing the looped end HPTLL from top to bottom or bottom to top under the X configuration.
                 Routing the entire HPTLL through the looped end of the HPTLL, forming a girth hitch.
          • Route the HPTLL over the left shoulder carrying strap and secure it to the tubular portion of the
                ALICE pack frame utilizing two retainer bands:
                 One must be above the horizontal frame support and one below it, with the retainer flap centered

                     between the two retainer bands.
                 The HPTLL should be routed from bottom to top as the ALICE pack is worn by the jumper (see

                     figures 6-48 and 6-49).

6-73. Attaching the ALICE pack to the parachute harness:
     • Attach the snap hooks of the adjustable D-ring attaching straps to the equipment rings on the T-11
          parachute harness.
     • Adjust the length of the adjustable D-ring attaching straps by pulling on the free running ends:
           The base of the ALICE pack frame should be snug against the bottom of the reserve parachute.
           Do not tighten the adjustable D-ring attaching straps so much that the reserve parachute is tilted
                upward.
     • If the ALICE pack is rigged to be jumped and lowered as a single item of equipment, attach the
          ejector snap of the HPTLL to the triangle link with the opening gate facing towards the jumper.
     • If the ALICE pack is rigged to be jumped and lowered as a tandem load—
           Route the ejector snap of the HPTLL between the attachment loop and the main body of the
                MAWC, from front to rear, as worn by the jumper.
           Attach the ejector snap to the triangle link with the opening gate facing the jumper.
