     6-74. After JMPI has been conducted, the jumpmaster routes the adjustable leg straps as follows:
          • Right paratroop door:
                 The left adjustable leg strap is secured around the jumper’s leg and the MAWC, then routed
                     through the retainer band.
                 A retainer band can be used to help secure the adjustable leg strap if using the HSPR.
                 The right adjustable leg strap is not used and remains secured to the ALICE pack.
          • Left paratroop door:
                 The right adjustable leg strap is secured around the jumper’s leg.
                 The left adjustable leg strap is only secured around the MAWC and routed through the retainer
                     band.
                 A retainer band can be used to help secure the adjustable leg strap if using the HSPR.
          • Ensure that enough slack is left in the adjustable leg straps to allow freedom of movement ease of
                seating on board the aircraft.
          • Once the jumpers have been given the command, OUTBOARD/INBOARD PERSONNEL
                STAND UP—
                 They remove the slack in the adjustable leg straps.
                 They then S-fold or roll the excess webbing and secure it in the appropriate webbing retainer.
          • Units are authorized to utilize both adjustable leg straps if directed by the airborne commander.

     6-75. Rigging procedures for the ALICE pack without a frame include the following:
          • Lay out a properly assembled HSPR and place the ALICE pack—
                 On top of it with the center outer accessory pouch resting between the release handle cross strap
                     and the adjustable cross strap.
                 The bottom (as worn) of the ALICE pack should be facing towards the friction adapters.
          • Route the equipment retainer straps under the envelope cushion portion and then cross them in an
                X configuration.
          • Continue routing the equipment retainer straps around the remainder of the load:
                 Secure the equipment retainer straps in the friction adapters and rig the ALICE pack as before.
                 Ensure that a quick release is placed in the equipment retainer straps.
          • To attach the HPTLL—
                 Route the looped end of the HPTLL from bottom to top or top to bottom, under the X
                     configuration formed by the equipment retainer straps.
                 Route the entire HPTLL through the looped end of the HPTLL, forming a tight girth hitch.
          • Girth hitch two retainer bands to the left side of the ALICE pack:
                 One is attached to the horizontal equipment hanger and one to the vertical equipment hanger.
                 Ensure one is above and one is below the horizontal frame support, with the retainer flap
                     centered between the two retainer bands.
                 The HPTLL is routed from bottom to top as the ALICE pack is worn by the jumper.
          • Route the male portion, leg strap release assembly from the point where it is sewn to the equipment
                retainer straps by the most direct route, down the side of the ALICE pack:
                 Secure the male portion to the female portion, leg strap release assembly.
                 Tighten the adjustable leg strap, then S-fold or roll the excess webbing and secure it in the
                     webbing retainer.

MODULAR LIGHTWEIGHT LOAD-CARRYING EQUIPMENT ASSAULT PACK

     6-76. The modular lightweight load-carrying equipment assault pack (MAP) (NSN: 8465-01-580-0981) is
     authorized to be jumped using an HSPR and an HPTLL. The 18-inch attaching straps located inside the MAP
     are not authorized for rigging. The MAP can sustain loads ranging from a minimum of 35 pounds to a
     maximum of 50 pounds. The MAP cannot be jumped in conjunction with the M50 JSGPM. If the M50
     JSGPM must be jumped, it should be placed inside the MAP. The convenience pouch located on the front of
     the MAP must be filled with nonfragile items of equipment. Prior to rigging, all excess webbing must be
     secured with masking tape, retainer bands, or appropriate webbing retainers.

6-77. Rigging procedures for the MAP include:
     • Laying out a properly assembled HSPR with the opening gates of the snap hooks facing skyward
          and removing all twists from the equipment retainer straps.
     • Placing the MAP on top of the HSPR, convenience pouch facing down with the bottom of the MAP
          facing towards the friction adapters.
     • Routing the equipment retainer straps under the top carrying handle staying toward the inside of the
          shoulder carrying straps and then crossing them at the back of the MAP forming an X configuration.
     • Routing the friction adapters under the waist strap at the bottom of the MAP:
           The waist strap must be secured together and tightened.
           The waist strap must have all excess webbing stowed.
     • Securing the equipment retainer straps to their appropriate friction adapters and forming quick
          releases.
     • Before tightening the HSPR, adjust it so that the release handle cross strap is directly above the
          bottom of the convenience pouch, making the following steps easier to accomplish.
     • Tightening the HSPR and forming two-to-three finger quick releases:
           S-fold the excess and secure it with masking tape or retainer bands (one of the two, never both).
           There is no preferred method.
     • Reducing the excess of both shoulder carrying straps:
           S-fold the excess.
           Secure with masking tape or retainer bands.
     • Securing the HPTLL in its normal configuration to the X configuration by—
           Routing the looped end HPTLL from top to bottom or bottom to top under the X configuration.
           Routing the entire HPTLL through the looped end HPTLL, forming a girth hitch.
     • Routing the HPTLL over the left shoulder carrying strap:
           Secure it to the left side of the MAP by girth hitching two retainer bands to the nylon equipment
                hangers.
           The HPTLL should be routed from bottom to top as the ALICE pack is worn by the jumper.
     • Securing the sternum strap in front of the quick releases to hold the shoulder carrying straps in place
          (see figure 6-51).

Figure 6-51. Sternum strap secured on the modular lightweight load-carrying equipment

     6-79. The M7 and M9 aid bags are authorized to be jumped using a HSPR and a HPTLL. The M7 and M9
     can sustain loads ranging from a minimum of 35 pounds to a maximum of 50 pounds. The M7 or the M9
     cannot be jumped in conjunction with the M50 JSGPM. If the M50 JSGPM must be jumped, it should be
     placed inside of the M7. Prior to rigging, all excess webbing must be secured with masking tape, retainer
     bands, or appropriate webbing retainers. Rigging procedures for the M7 and M9 aid bag are as follows:

          • Lay out a properly assembled HSPR with the opening gates of the snap hooks facing skyward and
                remove all twists from the equipment retainer straps.

          • Place the M7 or M9 on top of the HSPR, with the bottom of the M7 or M9 facing towards the friction
                adapters.

          • Route the equipment retainer straps under the top carrying handle and then cross them at the back
                of the M7 or M9 forming an X configuration.

          • Route the friction adapters under the waist strap at the bottom of the M7 or M9; the waist strap must
                be secured together and tightened with all excess webbing stowed.

          • Secure the equipment retainer straps to their appropriate friction adapters and form quick releases.
          • Before tightening the HSPR—

                 Adjust it so that the release handle cross strap is centered.
                 Doing this makes the following steps easier to accomplish.
          • Tighten the HSPR and form two- or three-finger quick releases:
                 S-fold the excess and secure it with masking tape or retainer bands (one of the two, never both).
                 There is no preferred method.
          • Reduce the excess of both shoulder carrying straps, then S-fold the excess and secure with masking
                tape or retainer bands.

     assemblies. The hydration packs are jumped upside down with the bottom resting against the bottom panel
     of the reserve parachute.

     the main compartment. Prior to rigging the hydration packs, all excess webbing should be secured with
     masking tape, retainer bands, or in their respective HPT retainers. The hydration packs may be jumped with
     or without the kidney pad attached. The shoulder carrying straps can be routed as normal with excess webbing
     removed, or they may be placed completely under the comfort pads. (See figure 6-69 on page 100.)

INDIVIDUAL WEAPONS AND WEAPON’S CASES

     6-89. Individual weapons can be jumped with loaded magazines in combat. Blank or live ammunition for
     individual weapons is secured in ammunition pouches and stowed or worn on the jumper. When utilizing the
     MAWC, a magazine can be inserted into the magazine well, ensuring there is no round chambered. The M16
     rifle or the M4 carbine may be rigged exposed when being jumped with certain items of equipment such as
     the COM-201B tactical communications antenna and SMJP. An exposed weapon must be protected to keep
     dirt and debris out during the PLF. It takes time to remove this protection. However, if it is jumped in a
     properly rigged MAWC, the jumper’s weapon is fully protected and can be ready for action immediately
     after landing.

     6-90. To rig the M16 series rifle or M4 carbine exposed, the following must be completed:
          • Fully extend the sling and tape the keepers in place.
          • Pad and tape the muzzle and front sight post of the weapon with one layer of cellulose wadding
                secured by masking tape.
          • Insert a magazine into the weapon, tape it to the receiver, and cover the ejection port cover.
          • Pad and tape the forward assist and the charging handle.
          • Tape the hand guards to prevent loss upon impact when landing.
          • Secure a 12- to 18-inch strand of 1/4-inch cotton webbing by girth, hitching it to the rear sling
                swivel.
          • Route the strand of 1/4-inch cotton webbing on the rear swing swivel—
                 Under the left riser assembly.
                 Through the outermost diagonal backstrap sizing channel above the one being utilized with the
                     diagonal backstrap retainer.
                 Tie the 1/4-inch cotton webbing with a single- or double-looped bowknot (see figure 6-72 on
                     page 102).

     6-91. Inherent hazards of the exposed weapon include:
          • Entanglement of the weapon with another jumper’s parachute if a mid-air collision occurs.
          • Possible injury to the jumper during the PLF.
          • Damage to the weapon during landing, which may cause a failure to fire.

PISTOLS

     6-92. The pistol does not have a loaded magazine inside the magazine well during training operations, and
     there is never a round chambered:

          • The pistol can be jumped inside the MAWC as a tandem load, inside a jumpable pack, or in a leg
                holster.

          • If the pistol is jumped in a MAWC it is jumped as a tandem load (with an M4, M240, for example):
                 The pistol is placed in a holster and secured in two places to the nylon webbing under the foam
                     padded internal divider with 1/4-inch cotton wedding.
                 The secondary load is placed on top of the internal padded divider.

          • If the pistol is jumped inside a jumpable pack the pistol is placed in a holster and tied down.
          • If the pistol is jumped inside a leg holster the jumper must—

                 Be able to secure holster to their belt and leg.
                 Rotate the holster to the front of the jumper’s leg to avoid the jumper landing on it while

                     conducting a side PLF (see figure 6-74 on page 104).
                 Route the pistol (possibly) over the top of the UPRB depending on the jumper’s height

                     (see figure 6-75 on page 104).
          • Ensure a lanyard is present and tied down to the jumper.

     6-93. The M320 GLM comes with a day/night sight (DNS) which may remain attached to the weapon in

          • Padded with one turn of bubble wrap.
          • Secured by masking tape or retainer bands.
          • The DNS must only be removed if the M320 GLM is to be jumped exposed; the M320 GLM can

                be jumped in two different configurations:

       Note. No ammunition is loaded in the chamber of any weapon to include the M320 GLM during

6-94. Rig the M4 with the M320 attached (host-weapon configuration):
     • Collapse the forward pistol grip alongside the barrel into its slimmest configuration and secure it in
          place with masking tape as seen in figure 6-76.
     • Use one strand of masking tape to secure the breech, running laterally from one side of the barrel,
          around the trigger mechanism, and back to the opposite side of the barrel:
           This secures the barrel and breech in its closed position.
           This prevents it from opening during the jump.

                    Figure 6-76. Properly taped M320 grenade launcher module

6-95. Rig the M4 inside the MAWC as normal:
     • When jumping the M320 attached to M4 with a sighting system, it is too large to fit in the adjustable
          nose cone of the MAWC:
           The M4 is placed inside the MAWC.
           An adequate piece of paper board honeycomb (PBHC) must be used to fill the adjustable nose
                cone.
     • To allow the jumper faster access to the weapon system, all strands of masking tape should have a
          tag-end folded over, forming a pull-tab.

6-96. Rig the M320 in a stand-alone configuration:
     • The DNS can be padded with one turn of bubble wrap and placed inside its carrying case, if desired.
     • When it is rigged to be jumped without the carrying case, collapse the buttstock to its shortest
          position.
     • Collapse the forward pistol grip alongside the barrel into its slimmest configuration and secure it in
          place with masking tape.
     • Use one strand of masking tape to secure the breech, running laterally from one side of the barrel,
          around the trigger mechanism, and back to the opposite side of the barrel:
           This secures the barrel and breech in its closed position.
           This prevents shifting during the jump.
     • To allow jumpers faster access to the weapon system, all strands of masking tape should have a
          tag-end folded over, forming a pull-tab.
     • The entire M320 GLM must be then placed inside of the main compartment of the combat load, not
          in any outer accessory pouch or under the nose cone divider of the MAWC.
     • Ensure there is no metal-to-metal contact or contact with any other rigid item of equipment inside
          of the load (such as a radio or ammunition).

       Note. Any second item of equipment placed under the internal padded divider must be secured in
       place using 1/4-inch cotton webbing. This prevents the item of equipment from potentially sliding
       out of the sides of the adjustable nose cone.

OPTIC SIGHTS AND LASERS

     6-98. The decision to jump with optic sights and lasers, either attached or unattached (in the ALICE/MOLLE
     pack or the MAWC), is left up to the airborne or tactical commander based upon assessment of the mission.
     If attached, only the blank firing adapter is padded with a minimum of one turn of bubble wrap and secured
     horizontally and vertically with masking tape.

     6-99. If the optic or laser is removed from the weapon and placed in the ALICE/MOLLE pack or the MAWC,
     it can be padded and taped with one turn of bubble wrap and masking tape vertically and horizontally.
     Variable or thermal scopes must be padded and taped.

MODULAR AIRBORNE WEAPONS CASE

     6-100. The MAWC is a modular, fully adjustable, padded, reinforced design, multipurpose airdrop container
     that can be rigged to a variety of weapons and equipment in a single container, reducing the number of
     modified legacy containers currently fielded. There are two fielded versions of the MAWC: a smaller version
     properly referred to as the MAWC and the second is properly referred to as the large MAWC:

          • MAWC—15-inches wide, 32.5-inches in length in its smallest configuration and extends to 42.5
                inches of useable length.

          • Large MAWC—16-inches wide, 40.5 inches in length in its smallest configuration and extends to
                54 inches of useable length.

     6-101. There are MAWC rigging equipment and limitations:
          • All individual items of CE approved for airdrop can be placed inside the MAWC unless they violate
                the restrictions outlined in this chapter.

106  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

             Individual Combat Equipment Jump Loads

     • Only one primary weapon should be rigged inside the MAWC.
     • There is a maximum weight for loads:

           MAWC—the maximum weight does not exceed 65 pounds in compliance with
                TM 10-8465-236-10.

           Large MAWC—the maximum weight does not exceed 85 pounds in compliance with
                TM 10-8465-236-10.

6-102. Inside the MAWC, variable or thermal scopes must be padded and taped, along with the blank firing
adapter if present. However, all remaining metallic items do not need to be padded and taped if separated by
the foam padded internal divider or inside their carrier.

6-103. When adjusting the nose cone to the minimum length, the first piece of pile tape on the nose cone
must be fully secured to the hook tape on the pack body. For the maximum length, the last piece of pile tape
on the nose cone must be fully secured to the hook tape on the pack body.

       Note. Compression straps and their quick-release buckles must be secured, and all slack removed
       and secured inside their webbing retainers. If compression straps cannot be secured due to the
       bulkiness of the load, it cannot be rigged inside the MAWC or the large MAWC.

6-104.  There are authorized expendables for rigging the MAWC. This includes—
     •
          PBHC which is used to fill the void from the base of the nose cone to the end of the item of
     •    equipment or weapon being placed in the nose cone.

     •    PBHC which is also used to accommodate large weapons, such as the M3 MAAWS where the
          diameter of the tube is too large to reach the base of the nose cone.
     •
          1/4-inch cotton webbing is used to secure second items of equipment to the pouch attachment ladder
          system webbing, so they do not shift inside the pack body.

          Type-1 (short and fat) and type-64 (long and skinny) retainer bands are used to secure the free
          running ends of webbing and tape:
           A type-64 retainer band is girth hitched to the vertical nylon equipment hanger below the lower

               tie-down strap stow pocket.
           This secures the adjustable leg strap.

6-105. Donning of the MAWC for a proper fit to the jumper’s height includes:
     • When properly rigged and secured to the parachute harness, the bottom of the adjustable nose cone
          is not less than 6 inches from the ground.
     • The top of the MAWC rests between the top of the D-ring and the base of the left canopy release
          assembly.
     • Ensure the jumper has good range of motion with their left arm regardless of what paratroop door
          they are exiting.
     • The yellow safety lanyard is secured to the male portion snap fastener that provides the most slack.

6-106. A thorough MAWC inspection is conducted prior to any airborne operation. Inspect the following
items to ensure:

     • An upper tie-down tape is present, constructed of 1/4-inch cotton webbing, and secured to one of
          the tie-down loops at the top of the closing flap.

     • The quick-release buckles are not cracked or broken.
     • The compression straps are not cut or excessively frayed.
     • The slide fastener and tab thong are present.
     • The nose cone securing straps are not cut or excessively frayed and they are properly routed through

          the friction adapters.
     • The pile tape on the nose cone is not excessively worn.
     • The adjusting strap is properly adjusted and secured behind the nylon equipment hangers, properly

          routed through the friction adapter, and the free running end is secured.
     • The bottom two male-portion snap fasteners are present on the pack body so they can be secured to

          the yellow safety lanyard.

          • When using the HSPR, girth hitch a retainer band at the lower horizontal nylon equipment hanger

     6-107. Sizing, rigging, and donning the MAWC to jump as a tandem load with an M4 carbine involves
     several steps. When sizing the MAWC, the following actions are completed:

          • Lay the MAWC out flat with the closing flap facing up and opened.
          • Loosen the securing straps located inside the pack body and release the HPT securing the nose cone

               in place.
          • Lay the foam-padded internal divider down so the rifle butt pocket is facing skyward:

                Place the muzzle of the weapon inside the nose cone and the rifle butt into the rifle butt pocket
                     (ensure the rifle butt stock is extended to at least the three-quarter position).

                Ensure the forward assist is facing skyward.
          • Adjust the nose cone so the muzzle of the weapon is firmly against the base of the nose cone.
          • Remove the weapon and secure the hook tape on the pack body to the pile tape on the nose cone.
          • Ensure the type 8 nylon webbing located above the hook tape is folded back up inside the pack body

               so it does not interfere with properly securing the HPT.
          • When extending the MAWC to its maximum length, fully secure the uppermost strip of pile tape to

               the hook tape.
          • Remove all slack from the securing straps inside the pack body, then place the weapon back inside:

                Muzzle first.
                Rifle butt in the rifle butt pocket.
                The forward assist facing skyward.

            Note. A 30-round magazine may be placed inside the magazine well, but no round is chambered.

          • Secure the closing flap.
          • Utilize the HPT, two snap fasteners, and the slide fastener and tab thong, routing the slide fastener

               and tab thong up until it rests against the upper spring stop.
          • Route the compression strap through the appropriate vertical nylon equipment hanger, secure the

               quick-release buckles of the compression straps, and remove all slack:
                Ensure the excess of the compression straps are rolled or S-folded and secured inside their

                     webbing retainers.
                Use a retainer band or 1-inch-wide masking tape if the webbing retainers are not present.

            Note. The quick-release buckles of both compression straps must be secured.

     6-108. After the jumper dons their main and reserve parachute and the ALICE pack or MOLLE is properly
     secured to the jumper’s parachute harness, fit the MAWC to the jumper. To do this, take the following
     actions:

          • When secured to the jumper, the base of the adjustable nose cone rests no less than 6 inches from
               the ground.

          • The top of the MAWC rests between the top of the D-ring and the base of the left canopy release
               assembly.

          • Ensure the jumper has good range of motion with their left arm regardless of what paratroop door
               they are exiting.

          • The yellow safety lanyard is secured to the male portion snap fastener that provides the most slack.
          • The opening gate must be facing the jumper.
          • An assessment must be conducted and any adjustments necessary must be made to comply with the

               first four actions stated here.
          • If adjustments are needed, release the snap shackle, remove the MAWC, and make the appropriate

               adjustments.

     6-109. Adjusting the MAWC to the height of the jumper involves utilizing the adjusting strap:
          • Do not remove the free running end of the adjusting strap from the friction adapter to make any
               adjustments to its length.

     • Ensure that after the adjustments are made, the adjusting strap is secured inside the horizontal nylon
          equipment hangers, leaving enough free for the snap shackle to reach the left equipment ring
          (approximately 1 to 2 inches).

     • The free running end is secured in one of two ways:
           It is secured underneath the horizontal nylon equipment hangers (not preferred).
           A retainer band can be girth hitched to the horizontal nylon equipment hanger located just above
                the friction adapter.

     • The free running end can then be rolled or S-folded and secured with the retainer band, which is the
          preferred method for securing the excess.

       Note. Prior to rigging the MAWC, a retainer band can be girth-hitched to the horizontal nylon
       equipment hanger just above the friction adapter of the adjusting strap. A retainer band can also
       be girth-hitched to the vertical nylon equipment hanger below the lower tie-down strap stow
       pocket to secure the adjustable leg strap.

6-110. After the MAWC has been properly adjusted to the height of the jumper, re-secure the snap shackle
as the outermost item of equipment on to the left equipment ring in the following manner:

     • Secure the yellow safety lanyard to one of the three male portion snap fasteners:
           Using the top snap fastener is not recommended to ensure proper placement of the MAWC.
           The top of the MAWC must rest between the base of the left canopy release assembly and above
                the left D-ring and the base of the nose cone rests no less than 6 inches from the ground.

     • Utilize the snap fastener that provides the most slack in the yellow safety lanyard.
     • Secure the tab thong by the snap fastener and the upper tie-down tape.
     • Girth hitch the upper tie-down tape to the horizontal backstrap below the excess webbing and above

          the WAP.
     • Route one end of the upper tie-down tape—

           Around the pack body.
           Through the window created in tab thong portion of the slide fastener and tabbed thong.
           Through the vertical nylon equipment hanger on the front of the closing flap.
     • Route the opposite end of the upper tie down tape—
           From back to front through the small cutaway portion of the left equipment ring.
           Secure it to the lead edge of the MAWC with a single- or double-loop bow knot

                (see figure 6-78).

• Route the ejector snap of the HPTLL—
      From front to rear as worn by the jumper.
      Through the attachment loop, and secured to the triangle link or the equipment ring as the
          outermost item of equipment.

M3 MULTIROLE ANTIARMOR/ANTIPERSONNEL WEAPON SYSTEM

     6-113.  Rigging the MAWC to be jumped as a tandem load with the M3 MAAWS:
          •
          •    Due to the size and weight of the M3 MAAWS rigged inside the large MAWC, it is considered a

          •    special item of equipment.

               The following procedures and restrictions are in place to ensure the safe delivery of this item to the

               DZ:
                The jumper is no less than 70 inches in height (5 feet, 10 inches).
                It is only exited from the right paratroop door and is considered one of the 12 special items of

                    equipment allowed on any one aircraft.
                The safety dons the M3 MAAWS on the jumper at the 20-minute time warning and conducts a

                    technical inspection (T.I.) ensuring it is properly rigged to the jumper.
                The M3 MAAWS must be rigged in the large MAWC while the M3 MAAWS may be rigged

                    with an M4.

               Components:
                M3 MAAWS.
                Telescopic sight.
                M4 rifle.
                One 4-inch piece of PBHC.
                HPTLL.

6-114.  Preparation of equipment and rigging procedures:
     •
     •    Inspect the large MAWC to ensure serviceability.
          Lay the MAWC on the ground with the internal padded divider folded over the closing flap and the
     •    adjustable nose cone fully elongated.
     •
     •    Insert one 4-inch by 10-inch piece of PBHC into the adjustable nose cone of the weapons case.
     •
          Place the venturi and muzzle covers on the weapon.
     •
          Remove the telescopic sight and laser and pad with bubble wrap or cellulose wadding.
     •    Either position the telescopic sight package—
     •     Between the front grip and the shoulder pad, or alongside the firing mechanism and secure to

     •         the weapon with two lengths of 1/4-inch cotton webbing.
     •     Place inside the main compartment of the ALICE pack or MOLLE.

          Place the weapon in the case with the muzzle towards the bottom of the case and the front grip flat
          against the case.
          Position the weapon so the carrying handle is against the non-slide fastener side of the case.

          Push the venturi end of the weapon—
           Extending the adjustable nose cone until the weapon end is nearly flush with the top of the

               MAWC.
           There should be four strips of HPT showing on the adjustable nose cone of the weapons case.
          Tighten the securing straps, ensuring the adjustable nose cone does not extend any further.

          Place the M4 in the MAWC with the muzzle pointed down and the pistol grip towards the M3
          MAAWS.

STINGER MISSILE JUMP PACK

6-135. The SMJP is designed to contain one stinger missile. The jump pack consists of a pack body
constructed of 7.25-ounce nylon duck material with 1/4-inch polyester felt material, nylon side securing
straps, a carrying handle, a lowering line extension sling, and a snap shackle and hook with spring opening
gate.

6-136. When the SMJP is rigged with a missile round, it weighs approximately 38 pounds, has a cross section
that varies from 5 to 11 inches and is 67-inches long. It is secured vertically by the snap shackle and hook
with spring opening gate to the left equipment-ring of the parachute harness. To prevent the SMJP from
swaying during the jumper’s exit from the aircraft and/or from the opening shock of the parachute, an upper
and lower attaching strap are provided. The upper attaching strap is routed around the SMJP and behind the
left main lift web directly below the chest strap, while the lower attaching strap is routed through the frame
of the authorized jumpable pack, between the jumper’s legs, and around the SMJP and the jumper’s left leg.

6-137. The HPTLL is used to lower the SMJP and the authorized jumpable pack. Route the HPTLL ejector
snap through the D-ring on the lowering line extension sling on the SMJP, then the ejector snap is attached
to the triangle link on the left side of the parachute harness.

6-138. Upon landing, the jumper can rapidly get to the weapon by pulling the free running ends of the quick
releases on the side securing straps of the SMJP.

QUALIFICATIONS, CURRENCY, AND LIMITATIONS

6-139. To be allowed to jump:
     • The jumper must be at least 5 feet, 8 inches tall.
     • The jumper must have at least 12 static line jumps from high-performance aircraft.
     • The jumper must make two perfect exits from the right paratroop door of the 34-foot tower with an
          SMJP.
     • The jumper must be talked through the five points of performance and lowering procedures, with
          the SMJP, while in the suspended harness.
     • The jumper must make two T-11 daytime jumps from 1,250 feet AGL before they can jump the
          SMJP from 1,000 feet AGL.

6-140. The time requirements include the following:

     • The jumper must jump once every 180 days from a USAF aircraft, with the SMJP.

     • If not, the jumper must go back through the prescribed training requirements/qualifications outlined
          in paragraph 6-138.

     • If it has been more than one year—
           Since the last exit from a USAF aircraft with the SMJP, it is recommended (not required) the
                jumper conduct one daylight jump from 1,250 feet AGL.
           Resume jumping at 1,000 feet AGL.

6-141.  Limitations include:
     •    The SMJP cannot be jumped from the left paratroop door of USAF aircraft due to the size and
          bulkiness of the SMJP.
     •    With the SMJP on the jumper’s left side, it is more likely the jumper could bump the left trail edge
          of the door with the SMJP when exiting the aircraft.
     •    The SMJP cannot be jumped from USA aircraft.
     •    When exiting an A-series container from the right paratroop door, no SMJP is exited on that pass.
     •    The SMJP and the MAWC cannot be jumped at the same time as the jumper’s M16A1/A2 rifle or
          the M4 carbine is jumped exposed.
     •    The SMJP must be jumped from the No. 1 and No. 2 jumper positions.

RIGGING THE STINGER MISSILE JUMP PACK TO THE JUMPER

     6-142.  Padding the Stinger missile includes:
          •
          •    Flipping up the sight assembly of the missile.

          •    Fold the bubble wrap over itself three to four times:
          •     Place the bubble wrap under the sight assembly and flip the sight assembly down onto the

          •         cellulose wadding.
          •     Firmly press down on the sight assembly to make sure the bubble wrap fills the gap between
          •
          •         the sight assembly and the launch tube, and the sight assembly locks in position.
          •     Wrap two to three turns of bubble wrap around the sight assembly and launch tube and secure
          •
          •         it in place with masking tape.
          •
               Wrap bubble wrap around the aft end of the launch tube to ensure the end cap fits snugly to the
          •    launch tube.

               Place the foam shock absorber—
                Onto the forward end of the launch tube in the same fashion.
                Ensuring the ‘lollipop’ on the forward cap is positioned in the cutout portion of the foam shock

                    absorber.

               Tape the foam shock absorbers together using 100-mph tape if available; masking tape
               (1- or 2-inches wide) may be used if the other 100-mph tape is not available.

               Positioning the Stinger missile—the pack body is placed with the felt side of the pack body facing
               up and extend all side securing straps.

               The aft shock absorber (opposite end from the sight assembly) is fitted into the launcher’s aft end
               bridle of the pack body.

               The Stinger missile is positioned in the pack body with the sling facing up.

               Closing the pack body—the pack body is folded around the Stinger missile so the flap with the
               friction adapters is on the outside of the pack body.

               The five side securing straps are routed through the friction adapters using a quick-release fold and
               are loosely tightened down to ensure the pack body is formed around the Stinger missile.

               The five side securing straps should be secured with retainer bands or masking tape, using one of
               the two methods but never both.

               The SMJP is placed up on end so the launcher forward end securing straps are on top:
                The end straps are routed through the friction adapters opposite of each strap.
                The pack is held off the ground and shaken to ensure the non-adjustable end strap bridle is taut.
                The end straps are tightened down all the way.
                A quick-release fold is not used here; they are rolled back on themselves and secured with

                    1/4-inch cotton webbing using a single- or double-looped bow knot.

               The pack body is positioned on the aft shock absorber:
                A 6-inch by 6-inch square block of PBHC is centered and secured across the launcher forward

                    end shock absorber of the Stinger missile, using the launcher forward end securing straps.
                They are routed over the PBHC, through the appropriate friction adapters, and tightened down

                    to form an X over the center of the PBHC.
                The launcher forward end securing straps are secured by rolling them back onto themselves and

                    secured with 1/4-inch cotton webbing using a single or double looped bow knot.
                Jumpers then secure a single piece of 1/4-inch cotton webbing and double it, then form an X

                    configuration over the launcher forward end securing straps and on top of the PBHC.

6-143.  Attaching the SMJP release assembly:

          The jumpmaster is JMPI (in accordance with chapter 9) from the helmet to the weapon:

           Inspect the exposed weapon to ensure it is rigged as previously described.

6-144. Attaching the SMJP to the jumper:

     6-146.  Individual jump procedures:
          •
          •    The SMJP is jumped with a front-mounted authorized jumpable pack.
          •    At the 20-minute time warning, one designated safety attaches the SMJP to the jumper and inspects
               it.
          •
          •    To release the SMJP on the HPTLL, the jumper does the following:
                Looks to see that the area below, left, right, front and rear are clear, at approximately 200 feet

                    AGL, and activates the release handle assembly on the SMJP.
                The carrying handle of the SMJP has a 3-foot piece of 1/4-inch cotton webbing connected to it

                    and to the release handle of the HSPR.

               Once the SMJP is lowered, it pulls the 1/4-inch cotton webbing and activates the release handle on
               the HSPR and lowers the authorized jumpable pack.

               The SMJP is suspended approximately 4-feet below the authorized jumpable pack.

           Note. When jumping a live Stinger missile, the polyurethane shock absorbers and PBHC must be
           in place and securely fastened.

     6-147. Stinger missile components include identification, friend or foe, a battery coolant unit, and a separable
     grip stock. The separable Stinger components (identification, friend or foe, battery coolant unit and separable
     grip stock) are individually wrapped in bubble wrap and packed in the main compartment of the authorized
     jumpable pack. The components must remain in the authorized jumpable pack during the jump.

WEAPONS AND EQUIPMENT CONTAINER SYSTEM

     6-148. The airborne pack (AIRPAC) AJM (NSN: 1670-01-414-2757) is a lightweight nylon equipment pack
     system used to enclose a jump load. The AIRPAC front-mount container can accommodate all size packs,
     radios, and 60-mm mortar with base plate or bipod. The side-mount container can hold one AT4, M4, M24,
     M249, M240B machine gun, and other ancillary equipment.

     6-149. The AIRPAC consists of the front-mount container, the side-mount container, and the parachutist’s
     individual equipment rapid release (PIE/R2) mechanism. Loads in the front-mount container are rigged
     according to the equipment used.

RIGGING JUMPABLE PACKS

     6-150.  Jumpable packs are rigged in the following manner:
          •
          •    Extend all retaining straps outward to their limits (the retainer strap with the circular closing flap is
          •    the top of the container).
          •
          •    Place the container so that the retaining straps face the ground, and the parachute recovery bag faces
          •    up.
          •
          •    Fold the parachute recovery bag so that no portions protrude outside the container limits.

          •    Place the pack on the parachute recovery bag and ensure the circular release rings on the bottom of
               the container are not constrained by the pack.

               The jumpable pack is jumped upside down, with the waist pad against the front of the thighs.

               Bring the right side of the container material up first, then the left side and the bottom flap, and then
               the top flap.

               Place the circular closing flap on top of the pack and open the circular closing flap by pulling the
               tab.

               Bring the left, right, and bottom retaining straps to the center of the circular closing flap and route
               the white grommet securing loop through each grommet of the retaining straps:
                No specific order is required.
                Bring the top flap material up last.
                Place the cotter pin through the white grommet securing loop.

               Tighten all retaining straps, ensuring that the circular closing flap remains centered on the jumpable
               pack:
                Adjust the protective flaps to stow excess fabric.
                Close the circular closing flap using three hook-pile tabs.

• Underhand fold the free running ends of the retaining straps toward the friction adapters and secure
     them under the webbing retainers.

  Note. The circular release rings should be exposed on the top flap of the front-mount container. If
  the rigged pack is above the rings and restricts movement of the rings, the load must be adjusted.

RIGGING RELEASE MECHANISM OF FRONT-MOUNTED CONTAINER

6-151.  To rig the front-mount container release mechanism, use these procedures:
     •
     •    Stand the rigged pack in an upright position with the bottom of the AIRPAC facing the jumper.
     •
     •    Route release handle cables through the cross strap on top of the container and secure the HPT.
     •
          With the attaching strap snap hook facing down and towards the jumper, route the circular ring of
     •    the attaching strap from bottom to top through the circular release ring on top of the container.
          Fold the circular ring of the attaching strap back over and route the red attaching loop through the
          attaching ring on the attaching strap.

          With the cable loop retainer on the female portion of the leg strap release assembly facing up—
           Route the red attaching loop from the bottom to the top through the grommet on the female

               portion of the leg strap release assembly.
           Route the release handle cable through the red attaching loop and then through the cable loop

               retainer.

          Repeat this sequence for the other strap.

RIGGING HOOK-PILE TAPE LOWERING LINE

6-152. HPTLL is rigged by taking the following actions:
     • Select the desired landing orientation of the front-mount container (horizontally or vertically) and
          attach the short bridle to the appropriate triangle link.
     • Route the looped end of the HPTLL through the unsewn portion of the short bridle and form a girth
          hitch.
     • Place a retainer band around the nylon tab located inside the closure flaps:
           Route the HPTLL through the retainer band and stow in the retention pocket.
           Secure the HPT.
     • Attach the ejector snap to the primary short bridle triangle link for transportation.

RIGGING LOAD FOR SIDE-MOUNT CONTAINER

6-153. To rig the load for a side-mount container, the following is required:
     • Place the side-mount container on the ground with the friction adapters facing down and the free
          running ends of the internal securing strap to the right.
     • Position packing material flush with the bottom edge of the fabric flaps and place the weapon on
          the container in the following orientation (see table 6-1).

• Tape and pad exposed or protruding parts (such as sight posts, grip stocks, or bipods) with soft
     material such as bubble wrap or an adequate substitute.

• Center load on the internal securing strap and pull the lower fabric flap over packing material.
• Route the free running end of the internal securing strap through the friction adapter on the lower

     fabric cap.

     6-154.  The AIRPAC is rigged as a tandem load with HPTLL by taking the following actions:
          •

AIRBORNE PACK ATTACHED TO JUMPER

     6-155. The AIRPAC is attached to jumper using the PIE/R2 mechanism as follows:
          • Place the front-mount container attaching straps under the reserve parachute.
          • Attach the front-mount container snap hooks to the equipment rings (same as a single-point release
               system).
          • Attach the HPTLL ejector snap to the left triangle link on the jumper’s harness.

           Note. When using the PIE/R2 mechanism, ensure the harness has a lowering line adapter web or

          and secure the extended bridle under the retention flap on the container.

     • On the PIE/R2 mechanism, route the upper tie-down tape—
           Around the side-mount container.
           Through the D-ring from bottom to top.

LIFE PRESERVERS

     6-156. Jumpers wear life preservers whenever a flight is conducted over water, a water obstacle is on the DZ,
     or the intended DZ is close to a water obstacle (see chapter 28 and appendix C). A water obstacle is any body
     of water (for example, a lake, pond, river, stream, or canal) that has a depth of 4 feet or more, is at least 40-
     feet wide, and is located within 1,000 meters of any edge of the surveyed or tactically assessed DZ. The
     tactical flotation support system (TFSS), B-7, B-5, life preserver unit (LPU) 10/P, and life preserver inflatable
     (NSN: 4220-00-705-8648) are currently certified for use by jumpers. Other life preservers may be used if
     approved by the individual service components. When jumping life preservers, all jumpers must review
     rigging and activating procedures prior to executing the airborne operation.

     6-157. The TFSS-5326 (NSN: 4220-01-524-5318) is a life-saving product designed to be fastened to an
     individual’s waist belt. This product uses two separate flotation bladders located in two separate pouches.
     Each pouch contains a manually operated firing mechanism and a carbon dioxide (CO2) gas cylinder that
     inflates the flotation bladders. (See figure 6-97 on page 130.) The TFSS-5326 is intended for use with the
     T-11 and MC-6 Personnel Parachute Systems.

LIFE PRESERVER UNIT 10/P

     6-160. The LPU 10/P (NSN: 4220-00-850-8655) is a standard USAF CO2 cartridge-activated life preserver
     assembly worn during flights over water, or during airdrops when water obstacles are near (or on) the
     intended DZ. The LPU 10/P has an adjustable harness and underarm inflation bladders. It is designed to keep
     the wearer’s head above water at weights up to 250 pounds for up to 10 minutes. The LPU 10/P must be
     maintained in compliance with the USAF.

     6-161. The LPU 10/P is worn under the parachute harness. The harness is worn so that the inflatable pockets
     are under the jumper’s arms. The manual inflating valves should be completely closed when donning the life
     vest. The shoulder and waist straps are then adjusted to ensure the inflation container is one-hand width
     beneath the armpit and not constrained by the parachute harness.

                                                 WARNING

                    The inflation wings must be one-hand width beneath the jumper’s
                    armpits and clear of the harness straps. If the inflation pockets
                    are too snug under the armpit, or if they are between the harness
                    and the jumper’s body, the jumper can experience severe pain or
                    crushed ribs during inflation.

     6-162. The jumper inflates the LPU 10/P flotation bladders by pulling two toggle cords (at the bottom of the
     vest) which activate the CO2 cartridges that fill the bladders with gas. An alternate provision for inflating the
     vest is by blowing into the manual inflation valve rubber hoses located on the bottom side of the wings.
     Manual inflation should be used only if the CO2 inflation valves fail to operate.

B-7 LIFE PRESERVER

     6-163. The B-7 LPU (NSN: 4220-00-657-2197) is worn under the parachute harness. To fit the B-7 life
     preserver, the jumper places one flotation packet under each arm so the packet flaps face out, and the toggle
     cords hang down and to the front. The shoulder strap should run from front to rear over the left shoulder,
     under the backstrap, then from rear to front over the right shoulder, and be attached to the ring on the right
     flotation packet. Jumpers adjust the shoulder strap so the flotation packets fit snugly against the armpits. The
     jumper then attaches the chest strap to the attachment rings on the left flotation packet, forming a quick
     release.

                                                PART TWO

                  ADVANCED TECHNIQUES

This part discusses key personnel, jumpmaster, safety actions, and the departure airfield
control officer (DACO).

                                                 Chapter 7

                                Key Personnel

    This chapter discusses responsibilities of key personnel, prerequisites, and currency. The initial
    training and follow-on refresher training of key personnel are of major concern to commanders.
    Proper training and supervision ensure that these key personnel follow the correct procedures
    and operational safety measures during airborne operations. Unit commanders certify
    jumpmasters assigned to their units prior to a jumpmaster conducting duties.

    A jumpmaster may remain current after a permanent change of station if they performed
    jumpmaster or AJM duty on a high-performance aircraft within the preceding 180 days of
    signing into a gaining unit. A jumpmaster should ensure that upon arrival at their gaining unit
    and completing reception and integration training, that their next duty is still within 180 days
    of the last duty they performed prior to permanently changing their station. A Memorandum
    for Record signed by the first colonel/O-6 in the Soldier’s chain of command stating that the
    jumpmaster performed above stated duty within 90 days is required. This Memorandum of
    Record and DA Form 1307 (Individual Jump Record) reflecting the same information must go
    forward with the jumpmaster to their next duty station.

    BAR training is conducted to validate that newly assigned jumpers can properly rig their
    individual equipment, properly fit their parachute harness, safely perform their individual tasks
    inside the aircraft, and conduct a proper PLF. Jumpmaster refresher training is conducted to
    validate newly assigned jumpmaster qualified personnel on new equipment training for all unit-
    specific equipment and newly fielded equipment. They also receive training on JMPI, sustained
    airborne training (SAT), DZ control and support criteria, mock door training, and PWAC. This
    training also ensures that unit-specific items of equipment and unit SOPs are covered, and the
    Soldier is familiar with the equipment and SOPs.

COMMANDER’S RESPONSIBILITIES

     7-1. The airborne commander designates the key personnel for each airborne operation. These key personnel
     are the PJMs and AJMs, safety personnel, DACO, drop zone support team leader (DZSTL), drop zone safety
     officer (DZSO), and malfunction officer (MALFO). The jumpmaster, DACO, DZSTL, or DZSO can delegate
     their authority to subordinates, but they cannot delegate their responsibilities:

          • The airborne commander—
                 Should be a jumper but not a member of any jumpmaster team, or serve as DACO, DZSO, or
                     DZSTL.
                 Must be assigned to the command that approved the DD Form 2977 (Deliberate Risk
                     Assessment Worksheet) for the airborne operation being conducted.

          • Each aircraft has a designated PJM, AJM, and safety personnel:
                 The airborne commander gives the designated PJM responsibility for and command authority
                     over all personnel onboard a jump aircraft.
                 PJM, AJM, and safety personnel duties are described in chapters 9, 10, and 11.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  135


---

Chapter 7

          • The DACO:
                 Is located at the departure airfield and has coordination responsibility with the ground liaison
                     officer (also called GLO) and airlift control element (ALCE) or aircrew for the loading of
                     personnel, equipment, and supplies into the aircraft.
                 Provides the jumpmaster with changes to station time and the overall operational plan, current
                     DZ weather, airfield crossing procedures, and the aircraft parking plan.
                 Complete DACO duties are discussed in chapter 8.

          • Each DZ has a DZSO or DZSTL:
                 The DZSO or DZSTL has command authority over the actions and safety of all personnel on
                     the DZ.
                 The DZSO and DZSTL procedures for DZ operations are described in chapters 19, 20, and 21.

          • The MALFO:
                 As a member of the drop zone support team (DZST), the MALFO is located on the DZ where
                     they can best view the airdrop.
                 It is the responsibility of MALFOs to investigate malfunctions promptly and accurately,
                     enlisting as many personnel as needed to watch for malfunctions and assist during the
                     investigation process.
                 The MALFO possesses AR 59-4/OPNAVINST 4630.24E/AFMAN 13-210 Volume 1/MCO
                     13480.1E Volume 1 during jump operations as it describes in detail MALFO duties and
                     responsibilities during any investigation resulting in the partial or total malfunction of personnel
                     airdrops.

KEY PERSONNEL PREREQUISITES

     7-2. The following minimum standards must be met before personnel are allowed to perform PJM, AJM,
     safety, DACO, DZSO, DZSTL, or MALFO duties for personnel and heavy equipment airdrop operations.
     Individuals, who are appointed as PJMs, AJMs, or safety personnel, must have the prerequisites described.
     The following qualifications apply to jumpmasters who are commissioned officers, warrant officers, or
     noncommissioned officers (NCOs):

          • United States Army (USA) and USN: E-5 or above.
          • USMC and United States Air Force (USAF): E-4 or above.

     7-3. Airborne commanders select and certify individuals to perform jumpmaster duties. All jumpmasters
     should complete a formal program of instruction that meets the requirements according to appendix B. Army
     personnel who have graduated from an approved USAIS jumpmaster course may be awarded the additional
     skill identifier 5W. Jumpmaster-qualified personnel, who are not current jumpmasters, must go through
     jumpmaster refresher training prior to conducting any jumpmaster duties. (See appendix B for reception and
     integration requirements.)

     7-4. To be jumpmaster current, the jumpmaster must have either performed jumpmaster or AJM duties within
     the preceding 180 days; or if a senior-rated or master-rated parachutist, performed duty as a safety on military,
     high-performance fixed-wing aircraft utilizing a door or ramp exit within the preceding 180 days; or
     completed a jumpmaster refresher course (see appendix C) in the preceding 180 days and is a current jumper.
     A jumpmaster must be a current and qualified T-11 or MC-6 (or both) jumper to perform jumpmaster duties.

             Notes. Jumpmasters must perform duties every 180 days to maintain currency on T-11 or MC-6
             parachutes.

             For USN and USMC only: if fixed-wing, high-performance aircraft are not available, the
             jumpmaster, AJM, and safety may meet currency requirements using organic rotary-wing or
             nonstandard aircraft.

     7-5. A new graduate of a recognized jumpmaster course must perform safety duties twice before performing
     AJM duties and perform AJM duties twice before performing PJM duties. This is referred to as jumpmaster
     baseline currency. Once a jumpmaster has performed baseline requirements after graduating from a
     recognized course, no further baseline requirements are needed after jumpmaster refresher training.

136  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026

                                                                                                                                  Key Personnel

ROTARY-WING AIRCRAFT/NONSTANDARD AIRCRAFT
PERSONNEL

     7-6. To perform the duties of the PJM on a rotary-wing aircraft or nonstandard aircraft, the jumpmaster must
     first meet the performance duty requirements of the PJM on a fixed-wing. A jumpmaster may conduct
     jumpmaster duties and maintain currency from a rotary-winged or nonstandard aircraft during a 180-day
     period. However, the next jumpmaster duty counted towards currency must be from a fixed-wing,
     high-performance craft within the next 180 days. A jumpmaster cannot maintain currency with two
     consecutive jumpmaster duties from a rotary-winged nonstandard aircraft, as stated in this paragraph.

             Note. This allows all jumpmasters 1 year to execute jumpmaster duties from a fixed-wing,
             high-performance aircraft.

     7-7. Jumpmasters must observe a current jumpmaster in the performance of their duties for a rotary-wing or
     nonstandard aircraft operation (prejump training, mock door training, aircraft inspection, rigging procedures,
     and the actual airdrop operation). The qualifying jumpmaster must then be observed during the performance
     of their duties by a current rotary-wing, aircraft-qualified PJM before being allowed to perform the duties
     listed above unsupervised.

     7-8. In addition to meeting the qualifications listed in paragraphs 7-4 and 7-5, the AJM must have performed
     the duties of a safety officer at least twice. Safety personnel must also meet the qualifications listed in
     paragraph 7-2 and also be a current and qualified jumpmaster to be appointed a safety.

     7-9. To be appointed a DACO, individuals must meet the prerequisites listed in paragraph 7-2, be a current
     and qualified jumpmaster and have performed the duties as an assistant DACO at least once.

     7-10. DZSOs must meet the qualifications listed previously in paragraphs 7-4 and 7-5 and are current and
     qualified jumpmasters or are combat control team (CCT) certified. For ground marking release system
     (GMRS) or verbally initiated release system (VIRS) drops, the DZSO must be a qualified jumpmaster in the
     type of jump being conducted and have assisted a current and qualified DZSO performing their duties during
     an airdrop operation involving personnel or heavy equipment.

     7-11. For USN and USMC operations, the DZSO is an E-4 or above, or DOD Civilian equivalent. USN and
     USMC DZSOs are also—

          • Qualified and current in the operation being conducted (static line or free fall).
          • Completed a DZSO course of instruction using Naval Special Warfare/explosive ordnance disposal

                (EOD) Lesson Training Guide DZSO administered by a current jumpmaster.
          • Designated in writing by the commander as a DZSO:

                 To be DZSO current, the DZSO must have performed the duties of a DZSO within the preceding
                     180 days.

                 If noncurrent, the DZSO received refresher training from a current jumpmaster or DZSO and
                     ran a DZ while under instruction.

             Note. For combination airdrop operations, the DZSO and DZSTL must follow the procedures for
             heavy drop operations but observe the jumpers as they exit the aircraft.

     7-12. A DZSO refresher course can be conducted by an individual who is a current and qualified jumpmaster
     and DZSO. Noncurrent DZSOs need only complete the DZSO requirements of the jumpmaster refresher
     training curriculum found in appendix A. In addition:

          • The individual being refreshed on the duties of the DZSO must be a current jumpmaster.
          • At the completion of DZSO refresher training:

                 The jumpmaster must perform duties of the DZSO within 180 days to be a current DZSO.
                 The jumpmaster must perform one DZSO duty every 180 days from the initial duty to remain

                     current.
          • If the individual has never performed the duties of DZSO, they must assist once before performing

                DZSO duties.

     7-13. Individuals must meet the following prerequisites to be appointed as an assistant drop zone safety
     officer (ADZSO):

          • Be a commissioned officer, warrant officer, or NCO (USA and USN: E-5s or above; USMC and
                USAF: E-4s or above).

          • Be a current and qualified jumpmaster for personnel or heavy equipment drop.
          • Be a certified ADZSO by having attended one of the following:

                 USAIS Jumpmaster Course (for computed air release point [CARP] DZs only).
                 The U.S. Army Advanced Airborne School Jumpmaster Course (for CARP DZs only).
                 United States Army Special Operations Command (USASOC) Jumpmaster Course.
          • Must have the additional skill identifier 5W for warrant officers and enlisted personnel, and
                commissioned officers must have the skill identifier of jumpmaster (USA).
          • Be ADZSO current by—
                 Performing the duties of a DZSO or assistant DZSO within the preceding 180 days.
                 Graduating jumpmaster school within the last 180 days.
                 Completing a jumpmaster refresher course within the preceding 180 days.

             Note. For combination airdrop operations, the DZSO and ADZSO must follow the procedures for
             heavy drop operations but observe the jumpers as they exit the aircraft.

     7-14. Individuals must meet the following prerequisites to be appointed as a DZSTL:
          • Be a commissioned officer, warrant officer, or NCO (USA and USN: E-5 or above; USMC and
                USAF: E-4 or above).
          • Be a current and qualified jumpmaster for personnel or heavy equipment.
          • Be certified as a DZSTL by having attended one of the following:
                 Unit taught DZSTL Course, Lesson Plans on the United States Army Training Development
                     Capability (also called TDC) website.
                 USAIS Jumpmaster Course (for CARP DZs only).
                 The U.S. Army Advanced Airborne School Jumpmaster Course (for CARP DZs only).
                 USASOC Jumpmaster Course.
                 Must have the additional skill identifier 5W for warrant officers and enlisted personnel, and
                     commissioned officers the skill identifier of jumpmaster (USA).
                 Warrior Training Brigade Jumpmaster Course (for CARP DZ’s only).
                 Warrior Training Brigade Pathfinder Course.
                 Sabalauski Air Assault School; Pathfinder.
          • Be observer and assistant of a current and qualified DZSTL performing their duties during an airdrop
                operation involving personnel or heavy equipment.
          • Be DZSTL current by performing the duties of a DZSTL or assistant DZSTL:
                 Within the preceding 180 days.
                 Completed a DZSTL refresher course taught by current DZSTL personnel within the preceding
                     180 days.

             Note. DZSTLs and ADZSOs in support of CDS airdrops are not required to be airborne qualified,
             on jump status, or jumpmaster qualified and current, but they must have attended an authorized
             pathfinder course or DZSTL course. For combination airdrop operations, the DZSO and DZSTL
             must follow the procedures for heavy drop operations but observe the jumpers as they exit the
             aircraft.

     7-15. Individuals must meet the following prerequisites to be appointed as a MALFO:
          • The individual must be a commissioned officer, warrant officer, or NCO (USA and USN: E-5 or
                above; USMC and USAF: E-4 or above).
          • The individual must be a qualified parachute rigger from the unit providing the air items used during
                the operation according to AR 59-4/OPNAVINST 4630.24E/AFMAN 13-210 Volume 1/MCO
                13480.1E Volume 1.

                                     Chapter 8

             Departure Airfield Control Officer

The DACO is appointed by the airborne commander and is responsible for coordination and
control loading personnel, equipment, and supplies into the aircraft. The DACO is located at
the departure airfield.

       Note. Personnel conducting DACO duties must be a current and qualified jumpmaster.

DEPARTURE AIRFIELD CONTROL OFFICER INITIAL
COORDINATION

8-1. When advised of an appointment, the DACO receives the following information:                parachute
     • The units that are jumping.

                                                 Chapter 9

                    Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

    This chapter covers jumpmaster and safety duties performed in the unit area or at the departure
    airfield. Appendix B (Collisions, Entanglements, and Center Panel Strike) covers mock door
    training and prejump for both the T-11 ATPS and the MC-6 series parachute.

    A key factor in jumpmaster duties is the mission briefing. H-hour (time on target [TOT]) is
    established and the backward planning process begins.

             Note. Jumpmaster duties begin immediately upon notification.

ESSENTIAL INFORMATION

     9-1. Upon notification that an individual has been designated as a PJM, the individual obtains or is provided
     the information that is described in paragraphs 9-2 and 9-3.

     9-2. Specific plan information is needed by the PJM. This information includes the following:
          • Mission and ground tactical plan.
          • Air movement plan to include time of flight, formations, route, direction of flight over DZ, drop
                altitude, location and design of code letters, racetracks, and emergency call signs/frequencies.
          • Names of AJMs and safety personnel, and time and place to brief them.
          • Transportation (movement to marshaling area, and departure airfield plan and times).
          • Tactical cross load plan.
          • Weather decision times.
          • Type of aircraft for the operation and special items of equipment being worn by jumpers:
                 AIRPAC.
                 Antitank 84-mm unguided, SMJP.
                 A-series containers aboard aircraft (door bundles).
          • Aircraft tail numbers, chalk numbers, and parking spots.
          • Landing plan to include:
                 DZs, drop times, delivery sequence, number/type of loads (personal parachute, CDS, and free
                     drop).
                 Types of drops (CARP, GMRS, wind streamer vector count [WSVC], VIRS, or jumpmaster
                     spotted and jumpmaster released [JSJR]).
          • Air item turn-in plan.
          • Medical support plan.

     9-3. Times and places concerning various aspects of the operation are important. These include the following:
          • Time and place of initial manifest call.
          • Time and place of final manifest call.
          • Time and place to conduct operations briefing.
          • Time and place to conduct SAT.
          • Time and place to check and inspect jumpers’ uniforms and equipment.
          • Time and place of parachute issue, including types of parachutes.
          • Time and place of troop safety briefing.
          • Load time—time agreed upon by jumping unit and air wing commanders.
          • Time and place of aircrew and jumpmaster briefing.
          • Station time—critical time: all jumpers must be seated onboard the aircraft.
          • Takeoff time.
          • TOT.

ASSISTANT’S BRIEFING (UNIT AREA)

     9-4. After receiving the initial operation briefing, the PJM returns to the unit and briefs the AJM and safety
     personnel. The PJM assigns duties to them for the remainder of the operation. The PJM then determines who
     assumes responsibility for jumpers remaining onboard. The manifest of personnel (DA Form 1306 [Statement
     of Jump and Loading Manifest]) scheduled to jump is prepared. The PJM schedules a full rehearsal with the
     jumpmaster team before the PJM team assembles the chalk (planeload). The rehearsal includes the following:

          • After the briefing—
                 The PJM organizes the chalk according to the tactical cross-load plan and then conducts the
                     initial manifest call.
                 AJMs and safety personnel check the identification card and tags of each jumper.

          • Once the DA Form 1306 is completed, verified, and signed by the PJM, the safety makes seven
                copies of the manifest to be distributed.

          • Items of equipment and personnel are cross loaded based on the ground tactical plan and the planned
                dispersion of personnel across a DZ.

          • The PJM ensures the chalk is manifested according to the tactical cross load and the unit SOP.
          • The PJM, aided by the AJMs and safety personnel:

                 Inspect each jumper’s equipment for serviceability and to ensure proper rigging.
                 Jumpers should have their equipment and containers packed and properly rigged prior to the

                     initial manifest call.

             Note. The PJM can delegate authority, but not responsibility. The PJM is solely responsible for
             the signed DA Form 1306 for the aircraft.

JUMPMASTER/SAFETY KIT BAG

     9-5. The PJM ensures UPRBs for use onboard the aircraft have been prepared to contain extra items that may
     be needed during any phase of the airborne operation. These bags are commonly referred to as the safety kit
     and are used by the PJM, AJM, and safety personnel. Items to consider for use onboard the aircraft (depending
     on the type of airborne operation and according to the unit SOP) include the following:

          • Flashlight (night operations).
          • Masking tape.
          • 100-mph tape, which is scrim-backed, pressure-sensitive tape.
          • Roll of 1/4-inch cotton webbing.
          • Type-3 retainer bands (T-11 stow bars).
          • Type-64 retainer bands (rigging CE).
          • 1/4-inch x 3/8-inch heavy-duty retainer bands (static line slack retainer bands).
          • HSPR complete.
          • HPTLL.
          • Modified HPTLL for special items.
          • Helmet components, such as suspension pads and chinstraps (including hardware).
          • Trash bags.
          • Earplugs and airsickness bags.
          • Two extra reserve parachutes and extra UPRBs (for USLMs and deployment bags); utilize one

                UPRB for every 30 deployment bags.
          • Knife, which is carried by the PJM, AJM, and safety personnel but should not be carried on a point

                of contact.
          • Four sets of extra T-11 reserve inserts.

MARSHALLING AREA CONTROL OFFICER BRIEF

     9-6. As soon as practical after the initial manifest call, the airborne commander should ensure a marshalling
     area control officer briefing is conducted. The briefing should include the following:

          • Introducing key leaders (airborne commander, jumpmaster teams, and others).

          • Chalk number(s).

          • Weather decision time (for GO, NO-GO decision).

                 AIRPAC.
                 Parachute drop bag.
                 Parachutist jump pack.
                 ALICE pack.
                 SMJP.
                 MAWC.

          • Length of flight.
          • TOT.
          • Drop altitude.
          • Predicted winds on the DZ and direction.
          • Route checkpoints.
          • DZ assembly aids and area.
          • Parachute turn in point(s).
          • Medical support plan.

     9-7. If the unit jumps nonstandard equipment or equipment containers, the rigging must be approved
     according to individual service regulations. New equipment testing and recommended rigging procedures
     must be forwarded for testing to U.S. Army Airborne Special Operations Test Directorate at Fort Bragg.
     JMPI and rigging procedures can be developed at the 82nd Advanced Airborne School at Fort Bragg, then
     for validation and approval to Commander, 1st Battalion, 507th Parachute Infantry Regiment at Fort Benning.

SUSTAINED AIRBORNE TRAINING

             Note. The jumpmaster version of mock door training and prejump for both the T-11 ATPS and
             MC-6 series parachute can be found in appendix B.

     9-8. SAT is conducted in the unit area or at the departure airfield. SAT is scheduled and conducted within
     24 hours before takeoff. If more than 24 hours, a colonel/O-6 must give approval. All personnel (jumpmaster
     teams/jumpers) require SAT. The PJM usually does not know the proficiency of all jumpers for which they
     are responsible; therefore, basic airborne jump techniques are rehearsed so each jumper can demonstrate their
     ability to perform them. Jumpmasters, safeties, and key leaders make on-the-spot corrections of any jumper
     not properly performing the required training. (See appendix B for a sample SAT narrative.)

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  145
