Chapter 9

     9-9. At a minimum, SAT consists of PLFs and mock door training, a review of the five points of performance,
     towed jumpers, collisions and entanglements, center panel strike, malfunctions, activation of the reserve, and
     emergency landings (MC-6 video for new MC-6 jumpers). Mock door training includes rehearsal of every
     detail involved with the airborne operation to include static line control, accidental activation of the reserve
     onboard the aircraft, red light procedures, jump refusals, exiting procedures, towed jumper procedures, and
     emergencies onboard the aircraft. The jumpmaster team must run all jumpers through both paratroop doors,
     in case a paratroop door becomes inoperable during the airborne operation. Jumpers must make a minimum
     of two exits, with the last exit as planned for the airborne operation, at the airborne commander’s discretion.
     All topics must be covered and tailored to the aircraft used for the operation.

     9-10. SAT is performance-oriented training. The PJM should introduce the jumpmaster team to all jumpers
     on their aircraft. During SAT, the jumpmaster performing the training needs to be heard by all jumpers
     (a bullhorn should be used, if necessary). All jumpmasters and leaders must make aggressive and positive
     on-the-spot corrections.

             Note. The jumpmaster team performing duties on the airborne operation conducts mock door
             training with their jumpers.

     9-11. Airborne personnel use aircraft fuselage or mockups to rehearse preflight and in-flight actions. Aircraft
     fuselage mockups can be complete airframes or may be field expedient training devices, as simple as rope
     strung to simulate an anchor line cable and helmets on the ground to mark the jump door. The use of field
     expedient training devices is not the preferred method for conducting SAT.

     9-12. Actions in the aircraft training remind jumpers of what occurs in flight before jumping. The PJM can
     use the mock door apparatus to show jumpers where their relative positions are in the aircraft. If in-flight
     rigging is to be performed, the rigging station locations can be indicated also. The PJM reviews and leads a
     rehearsal of all actions related to in-flight procedures so the jump mission is smooth and safe.

     9-13. If time and facilities are available, it is recommended to conduct SAT in the following order:
          • Mock door training.
          • Prejump.
          • PLF (side, front, and rear).

             Note. Training discussed in paragraphs 9-14 through 9-22 is conducted by the jumpmaster team
             inside the mock door with the jumpers observing from outside the mock door.

STATIC LINE CONTROL

     9-14. After the jumpmaster issues the jumper the command HOOK UP, they remove the USL snap hook
     from the carrying handle of the reserve parachute. They hook up to the appropriate anchor line cable with the
     spring opening gate facing toward the skin of the aircraft. The jumper then forms a bight in the USLM,
     making sure they have a good four in the hand and two below bight. Do not touch the double sewn portion
     (the double sewn portion is for safety).

     9-15. Trace the USLM over the appropriate shoulder. The jumper behind then traces the USLM from the
     shoulder to the first stow. They ensure that the USLM has not been misrouted through the riser assembly and
     is properly routed to the first stow. The jumper then covers their ripcord handle with the nonstatic-line hand.
     The first three jumpers have their arm in the elbow-lock position. This creates a proper 1-second interval.
     The remaining jumpers have their arm up high with the elbow bent and stagger inboard and outboard.

EXITING PROCEDURES

     9-16. As the jumpers move to the paratroop door, they lock their arm out to the elbow-lock position. As they
     near the paratroop door, they make eye-to-eye contact with the safety.

     9-17. The safety takes control of the USLM, the jumper places both hands on the ends of the reserve (ensuring
     that they DO NOT swim the static line), turns at a 90-degree angle into the paratroop door, and makes a
     vigorous exit (up 6 inches and out 36 inches) and counts to 6,000.

146  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                           Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

RED LIGHT PROCEDURES

     9-18. There are multiple reasons a red light could come on during flight. Out of the DZ, obstacles on the DZ,
     low-flying aircraft, rotary-wing aircraft, or other reasons. If a red light comes on during exit, the jumpmaster
     places their hand in the jumpers’ face and gives the command RED LIGHT, RED LIGHT, RED LIGHT, and
     pushes the stick away from the paratroop door. If the jumper has already handed off their USLM, and
     committed to the paratroop door, no one stops them. The jumper should continue and get a good vigorous
     exit out of the aircraft, preparing to avoid any obstacle that caused the red light to come on.

JUMP REFUSALS

     9-19. If there is a jump refusal inside the aircraft, the jumpmaster gives the command GREEN LIGHT GO
     (three times physically and verbally). If the jumper fails to exit after the third command, the safety secures
     the jumper by the pack tray, and tells them: YOU ARE A JUMP REFUSAL, I AM REMOVING YOU
     FROM THE PARATROOP DOOR and removes the jump refusal from the paratroop door. The safety seats
     the jump refusal out of the way (on the ramp) and gives the jump refusal a lawful order to not touch their
     equipment. The jumpmaster team then continues to exit jumpers if green light permits.

     9-20. Once the paratroop doors are closed, the safety unhooks the jump refusal’s USL snap hook and moves
     the jump refusal towards the forward portion of the aircraft. The safety then seats the jump refusal and secures
     the jumper’s seat belt. The safety again issues the jump refusal a lawful order of DO NOT TOUCH YOUR
     EQUIPMENT. Upon landing, the safety takes positive control of the jump refusal and turns them over to the
     DACO. The DACO then conducts a JMPI on the jump refusal, and a parachute rigger conducts a T.I. of the
     jump refusal’s equipment. If something is found wrong with the jump refusal’s equipment, no action against
     the jump refusal is taken. If no deficiencies are found, the jump refusal is turned over to the chain of command
     for appropriate actions according to the unit SOP.

TOWED JUMPER PROCEDURES

     9-21. If there is an unconscious jumper being towed by their USLM, the jumper is retrieved back inside the
     aircraft. If conscious, the jumper should make every effort to maintain a good, tight body position with both
     hands covering the ripcord handle. An attempt is made to retrieve the towed jumper inside the aircraft. As
     the towed jumper nears the paratroop door, they do not reach for the jumpmaster team, and they continue to
     protect their ripcord handle.

     9-22. If the jumper cannot be retrieved inside the aircraft, their USLM is cut. Once jumpers feel themselves
     falling free from the aircraft, they start a 6,000 count with T-11 ATPS or the 4,000 count with MC-6 series
     parachute. If no opening shock is felt, they immediately activate their reserve parachute using the pull drop
     method. If jumpers are being towed by an item of equipment, regardless of whether they are conscious or
     unconscious, that item of equipment is cut or jogged free, and the jumpers’ main canopy deploy.

             Note. Training discussed in paragraphs 9-23 through 9-29 is conducted by the jumpmaster team
             with the jumpers inside the mock door.

EMERGENCY PROCEDURES

     9-23. Ground evacuation/continuous ringing of the alarm bell: While inside the aircraft, the jumper hears one
     continuous ring of the alarm bell. That indicates a crash-landing during takeoff. The jumpers remain seated
     and extend their legs out to a 45-degree angle. The jumpers wrap their arms around their legs and place their
     head on their knees until the aircraft stops moving. The jumpers then exit the aircraft under the direction of
     the jumpmasters or loadmaster.

     9-24. Crash landing/ditching/six short rings of the alarm bell or oral warning: While inside the aircraft, the
     jumper hears six short rings of the alarm bell, or an oral warning. That indicates a crash-landing during flight
     without enough time or altitude to bail out. The jumpers remain seated and extend their legs out to a 45-degree
     angle. The jumpers wrap their arms around their legs and place their head on their knees. One long continuous
     ring sounds just prior to impact. Once the aircraft stops moving, the jumpers exit under the direction of the
     jumpmasters or loadmaster.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  147


---

Chapter 9

     9-25. Accidental activation of reserve inside the aircraft with doors closed. While inside the aircraft with the
     doors closed, a reserve parachute is activated; the jumpers sound off with RESERVE, RESERVE,
     RESERVE. Once the parachute is contained, one of the jumpers gets the jumpmaster’s attention by placing
     their hand or arm over an anchor line cable. The jumpmaster replaces that reserve with a new one, and the
     airborne operation continues as planned.

     9-26. Accidental activation of the reserve inside aircraft with doors open. There are two scenarios that should
     be discussed. They are as follows:

          • Forward of the wheel well (toward the pilot’s compartment):
                 All jumpers sound off with RESERVE, RESERVE, RESERVE.
                 All jumpers in the vicinity of the activated reserve attempt to smother and contain the parachute.
                 Once the parachute is contained, one of the jumpers gets the jumpmasters’ attention by placing
                     their hand or arm over the anchor line cable.
                 The jumpmasters close the jump doors, replace that reserve with a new one, and the jumper
                     exits the aircraft on the next pass.

          • Aft of the wheel well (C-130), center mass aft (C-17), or center mass (C-27J) (toward the open
                paratroop jump door):
                 Every attempt is made to smother and contain the parachute.
                 If the reserve starts to make its way toward the open jump door, the jumper with the activated
                     reserve must exit the aircraft immediately.
                 The jumper must make every attempt to beat the reserve parachute out of the jump door.
                 The jumpers in front of the activated reserve parachute must clear a path for the jumper with
                     the activated reserve by either exiting the aircraft, standing on their seat, or moving up onto the
                     ramp.

     9-27. Fire during flight: If there is a fire while in flight, an oral warning is issued to the jumpers. The jumpers
     move away from the affected area, and the loadmasters attempt to extinguish the fire. Be prepared to execute
     bailout procedures, if instructed to do so.

     9-28. Bailout, three short rings of alarm bell or an oral warning: While inside the aircraft, the jumper hears
     three short rings of the alarm bell or an oral warning. That indicates an emergency bailout is imminent. The
     jumpmasters issue the jumpers an abbreviated set of jump commands: STAND UP, HOOK UP. When the
     jumpers hear the long continuous ring of the alarm bell, they follow the commands of the jumpmaster team
     and exit the aircraft as quickly and safely as possible.

EXECUTE MOCK DOOR TRAINING

     9-29. Jumpers must make a minimum of two exits, with the last exit as planned for the airborne operation.
     All topics must be covered and tailored to the aircraft used for the operation including door bundle procedures
     if included in the mission.

T-11 ADVANCED TACTICAL PARACHUTE SYSTEM SUSTAINED
AIRBORNE TRAINING REQUIREMENTS

     9-30. SAT must be conducted and performance oriented. All personnel must attend SAT. Jumpers must be
     positioned so their actions can be viewed and heard by the jumpmaster team. SAT is performance oriented
     and should be tailored to fit the mission. All jumpmasters and leaders must make aggressive and positive
     on-the-spot corrections.

             Note. The jumpmaster version of mock door training and prejump for both the T-11 ATPS and
             MC-6 series parachute given to jumpers can be found in appendix B.

     9-31. Training on the five points of performance must be attended by all jumpers and jumpmasters. The
     following are the five points of performance:

          • Proper exit, check body position, and count.
          • Check canopy and gain canopy control and immediately compare the rate of descent with fellow

                jumpers.

148  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                     Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

     • Always keep a sharp look out and constantly compare the rate of descent.
     • Prepare to land.
     • Land.

9-32. The first point of performance is proper exit, check body position, and count. Jumpers must perform
the following actions:

     • Keep chin on their chest.
     • Keep eyes open.
     • Keep elbows into sides.
     • Keep hands over the ends of the reserve parachute and fingers naturally spread.
     • Bend body forward at the waist.
     • Keep feet and knees together.
     • Lock knees to the rear.
     • Count to 6,000 with the T-11 ATPS (fixed-wing aircraft).
     • Count to 8,000 with the T-11 ATPS (rotary-wing aircraft).
     • Activate the reserve parachute immediately using the pull drop method, if an opening shock is not

          felt.

9-33. The second point of performance is check canopy and gain canopy control and immediately compare
the rate of descent with fellow jumpers. Jumpers must perform the following actions:

     • Reach up to the elbow-locked position and secure the front set of risers in each hand.
     • Make a 360-degree check of the canopy, then move immediately into comparing the rate of descent

          with fellow jumpers.
     • If jumpers have twists, they compare the rate of descent with fellow jumpers:

           If falling faster than fellow jumpers, or cannot compare the rate of descent, jumpers activate the
                reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

           If jumpers are not falling faster than fellow jumpers, then they remove the twists.
     • To remove twists:

           Reach up and grasp a set of risers with each hand, thumbs down, knuckles to the rear.
           Pull the risers apart and begin a vigorous bicycling motion.
     • When the last twist comes out, immediately check the canopy and gain canopy control.

9-34. The third point of performance is keep a sharp lookout at all times and constantly compare the rate of
descent. The three rules of the air are the following:

     • Always look before a slip.
     • Always slip in the opposite direction to avoid collisions using a one-riser or diagonal slip.
     • Always give the right of way to the lower jumper.

           Avoid other jumpers all the way to the ground; maintain 25 feet of separation between jumpers
                in the air.

           Compare their rate of descent throughout the third point of performance.
           Release all appropriate equipment tie-downs at the end of the third point of performance.

9-35. The fourth point of performance is prepare to land. When approximately 200 feet above the ground,
the jumper prepares to land by taking the following actions:

     • Looking below and around to ensure there are no fellow jumpers.
     • At no higher than 200 feet with the T-11 ATPS, lowering CE and immediately slipping into the

          wind, keeping the feet and knees together.
     • Keeping knees slightly bent.
     • Balls of the feet hanging naturally towards the ground.
     • Keeping head and eyes on the horizon.
     • Before making contact with the ground, turn the lower portion of the body (below the waist) to a

          45-degree angle (front or rear PLF), exposing the second, third, and fourth points of contact.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  149


---

Chapter 9

     9-36. The fifth point of performance is land. When the balls of the feet contact the ground, the following
     actions take place:

          • Execute a proper PLF using the five points of contact:
                 Balls of the feet.
                 Calf muscle.
                 Thigh muscle.
                 Buttocks.
                 Pull-up muscle.

          • Do not make a standing landing.

RECOVERY OF EQUIPMENT

     9-37. Once the jumper is out of the parachute harness, the jumper removes all air items from the equipment
     rings. unzips and turns the UPRB right side out. Place the parachute harness inside the UPRB with the smooth
     side facing up. Secure the risers and place them under the parachute harness. There are two methods of
     recovery of equipment, nontactical and tactical.

     9-38. To recover equipment using the nontactical method:
          • Elongate the suspension lines and canopy, removing all debris.
          • Once the jumper reaches the bridle line, they secure the drogue parachute and deployment sleeve in
                one hand, and figure-eight roll the canopy and suspension lines all the way to the UPRB.
          • Place the canopy and suspension lines inside the UPRB, leaving the drogue parachute, deployment
                sleeve, and bridle assembly on top of the main canopy.
          • Snap, do not zip, the UPRB.
          • Place the reserve parachute in the reserve parachute stowage pocket.
          • Secure all equipment, conduct a 360-degree check of the area, and move out to the assembly area.

     9-39. To recover equipment using a tactical method:
          • Remain on a knee at the UPRB.
          • Begin pulling the suspension lines and canopy towards the UPRB, stuffing them in as the jumper
                goes.
          • Place the drogue parachute, deployment sleeve, and bridle assembly on top of the main canopy.
          • Snap, do not zip, the UPRB.
          • Place the reserve parachute in the reserve parachute stowage pocket.
          • Maintain noise and light discipline.
          • Secure all equipment, conduct a 360-degree check of the area, and move out to the assembly area.

PARACHUTE LANDING FALLS AND MALFUNCTIONS

     9-40. PLFs must be performed by all manifested jumpers. Each jumper must perform one satisfactory PLF
     in each of the four directions:

          • Front (left or right).
          • Rear (left or right).
          • Left side.
          • Right side.

             Note. To prevent jumpers from colliding or landing on each other, jumpmasters dictate which
             front and rear PLF jumpers execute during PLF training to maintain control and ensure all jumpers
             on the platform are falling in the same direction.

     9-41. Parachute malfunctions during an airborne operation can be catastrophic, therefore unit leaders at every
     level must reinforce to all subordinates to activate the reserve parachute if a problem occurs. Jumpers must
     continually check their canopy for any damage or irregularities and compare their rate of descent throughout
     their entire jump. If at any time, the jumper cannot compare their rate of descent or the jumper is falling faster
     than their fellow jumpers, immediately activate the reserve parachute using the pull drop method. Jumpers
     must receive training on malfunctions and control of the reserve parachute (see chapter 4 for malfunction
     definitions).

150  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                           Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

ACTIVATION OF RESERVE AND RESERVE PARACHUTE CONTROL

     9-42. The jumper utilizes the pull drop method when activating the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute. To
     activate the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute utilizing the pull drop method, the jumper—

          • Maintains a good, tight body position.
          • Keeps feet and knees together.
          • Grasps the ripcord handle with either hand.
          • Throws their head back and to the rear.
          • Pulls the ripcord handle and drops it to the ground; the reserve parachute activates.
          • Ensures neither hand is in front of the reserve parachute as it deploys.

     9-43. While descending under the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute, control the reserve canopy by using a
     one or two riser slip. At approximately 200 feet AGL, the jumper assumes the ‘prepare to land’ attitude by
     pulling a two-riser slip in the opposite direction of drift.

     9-44. Jumpers must receive training on partial malfunctions (see chapter 4 for definitions), which can be
     distinguished by certain characteristics. The following are partial malfunctions:

          • Corner crossover inversion.
          • Hung slider.
          • Sleeve corner vent entanglement.
          • Blown section or gore.
          • Broken suspension lines.
          • Delayed opening.

     9-45. Should any of these partial malfunctions occur and cause the jumper’s rate of descent to increase in
     comparison to other jumpers, the jumper activates the reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

     9-46. When the reserve parachute inflates, and there are two inflated canopies, the jumper has no directional
     control over the parachute. All other jumpers need to slip away. To assume the proper landing attitude, the
     jumper reaches high on front or rear set of risers of the main parachute and maintains this attitude until
     making ground contact. Immediately after conducting a PLF, the jumper releases the main parachute (using
     the canopy release assemblies) and collapses the reserve by detaching the connector snaps from the D-rings
     of the main lift web or by using either the quick recovery method as follows:

          • Immediately after releasing the T-11 main canopy by activating both canopy release assemblies, the
                jumper gets up and runs to the apex of the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute.

          • The jumper secures the pilot chute of the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute and runs the canopy into
                the wind, collapsing the parachute.

          • Once the canopy is collapsed, the jumper can then detach the connector snaps from the D-rings of
                the main lift web.

COLLISIONS AND ENTANGLEMENTS

     9-47. The jumper must always attempt to slip away using a one riser or diagonal slip to avoid other jumpers
     in the air. If unable to avoid a collision, they use the spread-eagle position to bounce off another jumper’s
     canopy or suspension lines. If a jumper enters another jumper’s suspension lines, the entering jumper assumes
     the modified position of attention with either hand protecting (but not grasping) the ripcord handle. The
     entering jumper may use the opposite hand to assist in exiting the other jumper’s canopy and suspension lines
     the same way they entered, attempting to exit the same location.

     9-48. If jumpers become entangled, their reaction techniques are as follows:
          • The higher jumper attempts to move hand-under-hand down to the lower jumper.
          • They attempt to establish eye-to-eye contact and hold onto each other by the left main lift web.
          • They must not touch the other jumper’s canopy release assemblies.
          • Both jumpers discuss which PLF to execute upon contact with the ground; both jumpers execute the
                same PLF away from each other.
          • Neither jumper executes a front PLF.
          • Both jumpers observe both canopies all the way to the ground and if one canopy collapses both
                jumpers ride the one good canopy all the way to the ground.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  151


---

Chapter 9

          • If both canopies collapse, both jumpers immediately turn away, creating a clear path and activating
                their reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

          • Should jumpers find themselves on another jumper’s canopy without rolling, use whatever means
                necessary to get off the canopy and immediately activate the reserve parachute.

          • Jumpers attempt to avoid the bridle line, deployment sleeve, and the four corner vents on the canopy.
          • If the jumper falls through the corner vent and becomes entangled, the jumper should stay there and

                be prepared to execute a proper PLF.

CENTER PANEL STRIKE

     9-49. Actions of the higher jumper: If the higher jumper is drifting toward a fellow jumper, they should look
     and immediately slip away in the opposite direction of the lower jumper, using a one riser diagonal slip.

     9-50. If the higher jumper finds they are drifting over a jumper’s canopy and believes they will land on top
     of the lower jumper’s canopy: Prior to contacting the canopy, the higher jumper begins a vigorous running
     motion in the direction of their slip, attempting to stay on their feet, until they are off the lower jumper’s
     canopy. Continue to slip away until a minimum of 25-feet separation has been achieved.

     9-51. If the higher jumper lands on the lower jumper’s canopy and cannot run off, it is vital to maintain
     momentum. This should allow the higher jumper to remain on their feet and attempt to get off the closest
     edge of the canopy that their momentum allows. If the higher jumper cannot stay on their feet, they should
     employ a crawling technique by reaching as far as possible in the direction of the closest edge of the canopy.
     They grasp the canopy and continue to pull towards them using the hand-over-hand method until they are
     free from the lower jumper’s canopy. Once the higher jumpers feel themselves falling free, they create a clear
     and unobstructed path, then activate their reserve parachute using the pull drop method. The higher jumper
     keeps feet and knees together and is prepared to execute a PLF.

                                                 WARNING

                    The higher jumper does not attempt to roll off the canopy as this
                    could wrap the canopy or suspension lines around their body,
                    preventing the main canopy from re-inflating or preventing the
                    higher jumper from deploying the reserve parachute.

     9-52. Actions of the lower jumper: At the end of the 6,000 count, the lower jumper immediately begins their
     second point of performance, check canopy and gain canopy control. The lower jumper conducts a
     360-degree check of their canopy to ensure the canopy is free of any damage or fellow jumpers and the slider
     is descending.

     9-53. If there is damage to the canopy or a jumper is on top, the lower jumper compares their rate of descent
     with the fellow jumpers. If the lower jumper is falling faster than their fellow jumpers, immediately activate
     the reserve parachute using the pull drop method. If there is a jumper on top of the canopy and the lower
     jumper is not falling faster than fellow jumpers, continue to observe the canopy. If at any time the main
     parachute begins to deflate, the lower jumper immediately activates their reserve parachute using the pull
     drop method. If the higher jumper slides off the lower jumper’s canopy, use a one-riser diagonal slip in the
     opposite direction to avoid fellow jumpers.

                                                 CAUTION

                    When slipping away from fellow jumpers, always use a diagonal slip. If
                    the higher jumper should fall through a corner vent, they should remain
                    where they are and be prepared to conduct a PLF.

152  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026

                                                                                                           Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

EMERGENCY LANDINGS

     9-54. Tree landings can be dangerous and should be avoided. If a tree landing is imminent, the jumper should
     perform the following:

          • The jumper immediately looks and slips away, utilizing a one-riser or diagonal slip when beginning
                to drift towards a tree.

          • If CE is lowered, the jumper looks below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers, then jettisons the
                CE, making a mental note where it lands, maintaining helmet.

          • If CE is not lowered, the jumper keeps it on to provide added protection while passing through the
                trees.

          • The jumper maintains canopy control and a good landing attitude by keeping the feet and knees
                together, knees slightly bent, and eyes open until contact is made with the trees.

          • After making contact with the trees, the jumper places chin on chest, rotates hands in front of the
                face, and keeps elbows high.

          • The jumper should be prepared to execute a PLF if passing all the way through the trees.
          • The jumper considers activating the reserve parachute and climbing down if hung up in trees.
          • If the jumper is hung up in the trees and cannot safely climb to the ground, they should stay there

                and wait for assistance.

     9-55. Wires are extremely dangerous and should be avoided. If a wire landing is imminent, jumpers should
     perform the following (see figure 9-1 on page 154):

          • If drifting towards wires, jumpers immediately try to slip or turn away using a one-riser or diagonal
                slip.

          • If jumpers cannot slip or turn away, they look to ensure there are no fellow jumpers below them and
                jettison their equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.

          • Jumpers ensure that the helmet is maintained.
          • Jumpers assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together, exaggerating the bend in the

                knees, eyes open, chins on chest, and backs arched.
          • Jumpers place the palms of their hands high on the inside of the front set of risers with the elbows

                locked.
          • When making contact with the wires, jumpers begin a hard rocking motion and attempt to pass

                through the wires.

                                                                                                           Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

WATER LANDING

     9-56. Water landings can be dangerous and should be avoided. Immediately look and slip away utilizing a
     one-riser or diagonal slip when beginning to drift towards a water obstacle. If a water landing is imminent,
     and jumpers do not have a life preserver, they should perform the following:

          • Look below to ensure there are no fellow jumpers and lower and jettison their equipment, making a
                mental note of where it lands.

          • Jettison their helmet, again making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Activate the quick release in the waistband, disconnect the left connector snap, and rotate the reserve

                parachute to the right.
          • Seat themselves well into the saddle and activate the quick release in the chest strap, completely

                removing the chest strap from the chest strap friction adapter.
          • Regain canopy control.
          • Prior to entering the water, assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together, knees

                slightly bent and place their hands on the ejector snaps for the leg straps.
          • When the balls of their feet hit the water, activate both ejector snaps for the leg straps, arch their

                backs, throw their arms above their head, and slide out of the parachute harness.
          • Be prepared to execute a PLF if the water is shallow.
          • Swim upwind or upstream away from the canopy.
          • If the canopy comes down on top of jumpers, locate a seam, and follow it to the skirt of the canopy.

     9-57. Sometimes, life preservers are provided for specific missions or training events. The following are
     instances when life preservers may be provided and the actions that should be taken:

          • Emergency water landings could occur on a tactical training mission where the route to the DZ is
                over a large body of water:
                 On such flights, life preservers are issued to jumpers.
                 If the aircraft malfunctions, the jumpers may need to jump over the water.

          • Emergency water landings require jumpers to leave any CE onboard the aircraft, so they do not
                become entangled with the equipment in the water.

          • Jumpers may find themselves over water with attached CE due to drifting off a DZ bordered by
                water, or during emergency bailout after being hooked up onboard the aircraft:
                 The jumper must lower their CE.
                 The jumper must jettison their equipment.

          • Deliberate water landings are executed for training in selected water drop zones (WDZs) and
                jumpers may wear CE only after:
                 It has been waterproofed.
                 It has been float-checked.

          • The jumper wears the inflatable life preserver under their harness with the inflatable portions under
                the armpits.

          • Jumpers wearing an underwater demolition team (UDT) vest routes the chest strap under the UDT
                vest to prevent crushing the chest if inflated.

          • While still in the air, the jumper activates the life preserver prior to assuming a landing attitude.
          • If the life preserver fails to inflate, the jumper inflates the life preserver manually by blowing air

                into the inflation valve hose.
          • The jumper jettisons any or all of their equipment including their helmet.
          • The jumper looks to ensure there are no fellow jumpers below and lowers and jettisons the

                equipment.
          • The jumper assumes a landing attitude and prepares to do a PLF in the event the water is shallow.
          • Once in the water, the jumper activates both canopy release assemblies by using the

                hand-to-shoulder method or the hand-to-assist method, as described previously in the procedures
                for recovering from the drag.
          • Jumpers remove the harness and any remaining equipment.

             Note. See chapter 6 for more information on life preservers.

Chapter 9

MC-6 ADVANCED TACTICAL PARACHUTE SYSTEM SUSTAINED
AIRBORNE TRAINING REQUIREMENTS

     9-58. All first time MC-6 jumpers must watch the MC-6 instructional video when mandated by the airborne
     commander or the unit SOP. All personnel must attend SAT. Jumpers must be positioned so their actions can
     be viewed and heard by the jumpmaster team. SAT is performance-oriented training and should be tailored
     to fit the mission. All jumpmasters and leaders must make aggressive and positive on-the-spot corrections.
     SAT must be taught proficiently.

             Note. The jumpmaster version of mock door training and prejump for the T-11 ATPS and MC-6
             series parachutes can be found in appendix B.

     9-59. Training on the five points of performance must be attended by all jumpers and jumpmasters. The
     following are the five points of performance:

          • Proper exit, check body position, and count.
          • Check canopy and gain canopy control.
          • Keep a sharp look out at all times and constantly compare the rate of descent.
          • Prepare to land.
          • Land.

     9-60. The first point of performance is proper exit, check body position, and count. Jumpers must perform
     the following actions:

          • Keep chin on chest.
          • Keep eyes open.
          • Keep elbows into sides.
          • Keep hands over the ends of the reserve parachute and fingers naturally spread.
          • Bend body forward at the waist.
          • Keep feet and knees together.
          • Lock knees to the rear.
          • Count to 4,000 with the MC-6 parachute (fixed-wing aircraft).
          • Count to 6,000 with the MC-6 parachute (rotary-winged aircraft).
          • Activate the reserve parachute immediately using the pull drop method if the opening shock is not

                felt.

     9-61. Immediately after the 4,000 or 6,000 count, the jumper conducts the second point of performance of
     check canopy and gain canopy control. Jumpers must perform the following actions:

          • Reaches up to the elbow-locked position and secures one toggle in each hand located on the inside
                of the rear set of risers and pulls the toggles down to approximately eye level.

          • Makes a 360-degree check of the canopy.
          • If the jumper has twists, compare the rate of descent with fellow jumpers:

                 If they are falling faster than fellow jumpers or cannot compare the rate of descent, they activate
                     the reserve parachute using the pull drop method.

                 If they are not falling faster than fellow jumpers, then they remove the twists.
          • Remove twists by—

                 Reaching up and grasping a set of risers with each hand, thumbs down, knuckles to the rear.
                 Pulling the risers apart and beginning a vigorous bicycling motion.
          • When the last twist comes out, immediately check canopy and gain canopy control.

     9-62. The third point of performance is keep a sharp lookout at all times and constantly compare the rate of
     descent. The three rules of the air are:

          • Always look before a turn.
          • Always turn in the opposite direction to avoid collisions.
          • The lower jumper always has the right of way.

156  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                                           Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

     9-63. Avoid other jumpers all the way to the ground, maintaining at least 50 feet of separation between
     canopies in the air:

          • The jumper must continue to compare their rate of descent throughout the third point of
                performance.

          • At the end of the third point of performance, the jumper releases all appropriate equipment
                tie-downs.

     9-64. The fourth point of performance is prepare to land. When approximately 250 feet above the ground the
     jumper prepares to land by taking the following actions:

          • The jumper turns into the wind prior to lowering equipment.
          • The jumper brings both toggles in front of their face and transfers control of one toggle to the

                opposite hand so that both toggles are being controlled by one hand.
          • While maintaining both toggles in front of the face, the jumper uses the free hand to lower their CE.
          • Once the jumper has lowered their CE, immediately regain canopy control with both hands and

                continue to keep a sharp lookout for other jumpers.
          • The jumper uses the appropriate brake position according to chapter 3.
          • The jumper keeps knees slightly bent.
          • The jumper has balls of the feet hanging naturally towards the ground.
          • The jumper keeps head and eyes toward the horizon.
          • Before making contact with the ground, the jumper turns the lower portion of the body (below the

                waist) to a 45-degree angle (front or rear PLF), exposing the portion of the body that makes contact
                with the ground first.

     9-65. The fifth point of performance is land. When the balls of the feet make contact with the ground, the
     following actions take place:

          • Execute a proper PLF using the five points of contact:
                 Balls of the feet.
                 Calf muscle.
                 Thigh muscle.
                 Buttocks.
                 Pull-up muscle.

          • Do not make a standing landing.
          • Jumpers remain on their back and activate one canopy release assembly using either the hand-assist

                method, or hand-to-shoulder method.
          • If the canopy fails to deflate, the jumper activates the second canopy release assembly.
          • Jumpers remain on their back, placing the weapon into operation, removing the parachute harness.

RECOVERY OF EQUIPMENT

     9-66. Once the jumper is out of the parachute harness, they remove all air items from the equipment rings.
     unzip and turn the UPRB right side out. Place the parachute harness inside the UPRB with the smooth side
     facing up, leaving the waistband exposed. Secure the risers and place them under the parachute harness.
     There are two methods of recovery of equipment, nontactical and tactical.

     9-67. To recover equipment using the nontactical method—
          • Elongate the suspension lines and canopy removing all debris.
          • Once jumpers reach the apex of the canopy, insert the thumb into the bridle loop and figure-eight
                roll the canopy and suspension lines all the way to the UPRB.
          • Place the canopy and suspension lines inside the UPRB and route the waistband through the bridle
                loop.
          • Secure the waistband to one of the carrying handles of the UPRB with a half-hitch.
          • Snap, do not zip, the UPRB.
          • Place the reserve parachute in the reserve parachute stowage pocket.
          • Secure the equipment, conduct a 360-degree check of the area, and move out to the assembly area.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  157

Chapter 9

     9-68. To recover equipment using a tactical method—
          • Remain on a knee at the UPRB.
          • Begin pulling the suspension lines and canopy towards the UPRB, stuffing them in as the jumper
                goes.
          • Once the jumper reaches the bridle loop, route the waistband through the bridle loop and secure the
                waistband to one of the carrying handles of the UPRB with a half-hitch.
          • Snap, do not zip, the UPRB.
          • Place the reserve parachute in the reserve parachute stowage pocket.
          • Maintain noise and light discipline.
          • Secure the equipment, conduct a 360-degree check of the area, and move out to the assembly area.

PARACHUTE MALFUNCTIONS AND CONTROL OF THE RESERVE PARACHUTE

     9-69. Jumpers must receive training on total malfunctions and control of the reserve parachute
     (see chapter 6). While descending under the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute, control the reserve canopy by
     using a one-or two-riser slip. At approximately 200 feet AGL, the jumper assumes a prepare to land attitude
     by pulling a two-riser slip opposite the direction of drift.

     9-70. Jumpers must receive training on partial malfunctions, which can be distinguished by certain
     characteristics (see chapter 4). The following are indicators of a partial malfunction:

          • Inversion.
          • Blown section or gore.
          • Four consecutive broken suspension lines or a total of six altogether.
          • Holes.
          • Delayed opening.
          • Streamer.
          • Broken or stuck control line(s).

ACTIVATION OF THE RESERVE PARACHUTE

     9-71. Should any of these malfunctions occur and cause the jumper’s rate of descent to increase in
     comparison to other jumpers, activate the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute utilizing the pull drop method.
     This is done by—

          • Snapping back into a tight body position.
          • Grasping the ripcord handle with either hand.
          • Throwing head back to the rear.
          • Pulling out on the ripcord handle and dropping it.
          • Ensuring neither hand is in front of the reserve parachute as it deploys.

     9-72. When the reserve parachute inflates, and there are two inflated canopies, the jumper has no directional
     control over the parachute. All other jumpers need to turn away. To assume the proper landing attitude, the
     jumper reaches high on the front or rear set of risers of the main parachute and maintains this attitude until
     making ground contact. Immediately after conducting a PLF, the jumper releases the main parachute (using
     the canopy release assemblies) and collapses the reserve by detaching the connector snaps from the D-rings
     of the main lift web, or by using the quick recovery method as follows:

          • Immediately after releasing the MC-6 main canopy by activating both canopy release assemblies,
                the jumper gets up and run to the apex of the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute.

          • The jumper secures the pilot chute of the T-11 reserve/single pin parachute and runs the canopy into
                the wind, collapsing the parachute.

          • Once the canopy is collapsed, the jumper can then detach the connector snaps from the D-rings of
                the main lift web.

COLLISIONS AND ENTANGLEMENTS

     9-73. The jumper must always attempt to turn away. If unable to avoid a collision, they use the spread-eagle
     position to bounce off another jumper’s canopy or suspension lines. If a jumper enters another jumper’s
     suspension lines, the entering jumper assumes the modified position of attention with either hand protecting

158  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026

                                                                                                           Jumpmaster and Safety Duties

     (but not grasping) the ripcord handle. The entering jumper may use the opposite hand to assist in exiting the
     other jumper’s canopy and suspension lines the same way they entered, attempting to exit the same location.

     9-74. If jumpers become entangled, both jumpers immediately clear a path and activate their reserve
     parachutes using the pull drop method. Neither jumper attempts to climb to the other jumper. The higher
     jumper should make every attempt to avoid the lower jumper when landing.

EMERGENCY LANDINGS

     9-75. Tree landings can be dangerous and should be avoided. If landing in trees seems imminent, the jumper
     should perform the following:

          • The jumper immediately turns away when beginning to drift toward the trees.
          • If CE is not lowered, the jumper keeps it on to provide added protection while passing through the

                trees.
          • The jumper maintains canopy control and a good landing attitude by keeping the feet and knees

                together, knees slightly bent, and eyes open until contact is made with the trees.
          • Once making contact with the trees, the jumper places chin on chest, rotates hands in front of the

                face, and keeps the elbows high.
          • The jumper should be prepared to execute a PLF, if passing all the way through the trees.
          • If the jumper is hung up in the trees and cannot safely climb to the ground, they should stay there

                and wait for assistance.
          • The jumper should consider activating the reserve parachute and climbing down if hung up in trees.

     9-76. Wire landings are extremely dangerous and should be avoided. Jumpers do the following if unable to
     avoid wires when landing (see figure 9-2 on page 160):

          • If drifting towards wires, jumpers immediately try to turn away.
          • If they cannot turn away, jumpers look to ensure there are no fellow jumpers below them and jettison

                their equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Jumpers ensure that the helmet is maintained.
          • Jumpers assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together, exaggerating the bend in their

                knees, eyes open, chins on chest, and backs arched.
          • Jumpers place the palms of their hands high on the inside of the front set of risers with the elbows

                locked.
          • When making contact with the wires, jumpers begin a hard rocking motion and attempt to pass

                through the wires.
          • Jumpers prepare to do a PLF in the event they pass through the wires.
          • If jumpers are hung up in the wires, they do not attempt to lower themselves to the ground.
          • Jumpers stay where they are and wait for assistance.

WATER LANDING

     9-77. Water landings can be dangerous and should be avoided. If drifting towards water, they immediately
     try to turn away. If a water landing is imminent, jumpers should perform the following:

          • Look below themselves to ensure there are no follow jumpers and lower and jettison their
                equipment, making a mental note of where it lands.

          • Jettison their helmet, again making a mental note of where it lands.
          • Activate the quick release in the waistband, disconnect the left connector snap, and rotate the reserve

                parachute to the right.
          • Seat themselves well into the saddle and activate the quick release in the chest strap, completely

                removing the chest strap from the chest strap friction adapter.
          • Regain canopy control.
          • Prior to entering the water, assume a landing attitude by keeping feet and knees together, knees

                slightly bent, and place their hands on the ejector snaps for the leg straps.
          • When the balls of their feet hit the water, activate both ejector snaps for the leg straps, arch their

                backs, throw arms above their head and slide out of the parachute harness.
          • Are prepared to execute a PLF, if the water is shallow.
          • Swim upwind or upstream, away from the canopy.
          • If the canopy comes down on top of the jumpers, locate a seam and follow it to the skirt of the

                canopy.

     9-78. Sometimes, life preservers are provided for specific missions or training events. The following are
     instances when life preservers may be provided and the actions that should be taken:

          • Emergency water landings could occur on a tactical training mission where the route to the DZ is
                over a large body of water:
                 On such flights, life preservers are issued to jumpers.
                 If the aircraft malfunctions, the jumpers may need to jump over the water.

          • Emergency water landings require jumpers to leave any CE onboard the aircraft, so they do not
                become entangled with the equipment in the water.

          • Jumpers may find themselves over water with attached CE due to drifting off a DZ bordered by
                water, or during emergency bailout after being hooked up onboard the aircraft:
                 The jumper must lower their CE.
                 The jumper must jettison their equipment.

          • Deliberate water landings are executed for training in selected WDZs and jumpers may wear CE but
                only after it has been waterproofed and float-checked.

          • The jumper wears the inflatable life preserver under the harness with the inflatable portions under
                their armpits and those wearing a UDT vest route the chest strap under the UDT vest to prevent
                crushing the chest if inflated.

          • While still in the air, the jumper activates the life preserver prior to assuming a landing attitude.
          • If the life preserver fails to inflate, the jumper inflates the life preserver manually by blowing air

                into the inflation valve hose.
          • The jumper jettisons any or all equipment including their helmet.
          • The jumper looks to ensure there are no fellow jumpers below, lowers and jettisons their equipment.
          • The jumper assumes a landing attitude and prepares to do a PLF in the event the water is shallow.
          • Once in the water, the jumper activates both canopy release assemblies by using the

                hand-to-shoulder method, or the hand-to-assist method as described previously in the procedures
                for recovering from the drag.
          • Jumpers do not remove their harness since the life preserver supports the jumper.

             Note. See chapter 6 for more information about life preservers

                                                Chapter 10

     Jumpmaster and Safety Duties at Departure Airfield

    Time is a critical factor at the departure airfield. The PJM is overall responsible for all personnel
    and equipment on their aircraft. The PJM can delegate authority and duties within the
    jumpmaster team, but not responsibility. All jumpmaster team personnel must draw their own
    parachutes for wear during airdrop operations. The aircrew cannot provide parachutes for the
    jumpmaster team. The following events occur at the same time to allow the unit to meet station
    time:

          • DACO or jumpmaster update briefing.
          • Manifest distribution.
          • Jumpmaster or aircrew initial coordination.
          • Aircraft inspection.
          • Control of parachute issue by jumpmaster team.
          • Rigging or inspection of jumpers.
          • Loading of aircraft.

DEPARTURE AIRFIELD

     10-1. The airborne commander selects the appropriate key personnel to perform the PJM, AJM, safety,
     DACO, and DZSO/DZSTL duties for a unit airdrop operation. Those selected key personnel must correctly
     perform their assigned duties to ensure mission success and jumper safety.

     10-2. The airborne commander may delegate authority, but not responsibility, and authority may be delegated
     to qualified personnel according to individual service component regulations. The airborne commander may
     delegate authority to qualified personnel according to chapter 7 but is overall responsible for the safe
     execution of an airborne operation.

     10-3. Upon arrival at the airfield, a member of the jumpmaster team reports to the DACO for an update
     briefing to include—

          • Changing the station time.
          • Changing the overall operation plan.
          • Updating the current weather forecast and winds on the DZ.
          • Receiving the serious incident briefing and signing the serious incident roster.
          • Receiving the parking plan of aircraft (location and tail number of the assigned aircraft).
          • Coordinating with the USAF guide if wheeled vehicles are used for transport to the aircraft.
          • Receiving any changes caused by aircraft maintenance problems, crew rest, weather delays, or other

                reasons.

     10-4. Normally the manifest (DA Form 1306) is distributed as follows:
          • DACO—two copies (original plus one copy).
          • PJM—one copy.
          • Pilot or their representative—one copy.
          • Officer in charge (OIC) or noncommissioned officer in charge (NCOIC) of the parachute issue
                facility—one copy.
          • Unit suspense file—one copy.

     10-5. After DACO coordination, a member of the jumpmaster team should proceed to the aircraft for initial
     coordination. The aircraft is normally open with a crewmember onboard 1 hour before station time. The first
     item discussed is aircraft configuration, according to the unit mission. If the aircraft is incorrectly configured,
     the requesting unit has the option to accept or reject it. If the mission request asks for both doors to be open
     for a mass exit operation, but one door is inoperative (in flight or on the ground), the requesting unit has the
     option to continue the mission using one door or to abort the mission. For single-door operations, one door

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  163


---

Chapter 10

     may be used for personnel airdrop. However, if the other paratroop door is open, it must be manned by a
     current jumpmaster. If only one door is being used, it must be manned by a current jumpmaster and safety.
     A single-door aircraft operation must be conducted in a military-controlled air space environment. Other
     items to discuss include the following:

          • Control of the jump paratroop doors.
          • Drop altitude, speed, and heading.
          • Racetracks.
          • Towed jumper procedures (in detail).
          • Emergency actions onboard.
          • Time warnings and checkpoints.
          • Type of drop (CARP, GMRS, and VIRS).
          • Load time.
          • Station time.
          • Takeoff time.
          • Number of jumpers exiting per pass.
          • Initial contact time with CCT or DZST for update on DZ conditions (if communications are being

                used).
          • Drop time.
          • Additional details:

                 If a ground abort occurs, designate which key personnel onboard must be advised.
                 Designate which safety is responsible for the troops left onboard in event of an emergency.
                 Emphasize to the aircrew the importance of the accurate direction and velocity of DZ winds

                     (before the 1-minute time warning) and accurate time warnings.
                 The jumpmaster team needs to establish through the loadmaster a predetermined signal that the

                     aircraft has slowed to drop speed before assuming control of the paratroop door.
                 If it is agreed upon by all parties involved, this signal can be ARMY, YOUR DOOR.
                 Jumpmasters should always confirm the aircraft has slowed to drop speed before assuming

                     control of the paratroop door.

             Note. Jumpmasters do not assume control of the aircraft paratroop door until the loadmaster has
             confirmed the aircraft has slowed to 130 knots indicated airspeed.

AIRCRAFT INSPECTION

     10-6. The PJM is responsible for this inspection but may delegate the authority to a member of the
     jumpmaster team. The aircraft should be available for inspection 1 hour prior to station time. A member of
     the jumpmaster team accompanied by a crew member (usually the loadmaster), inspects the aircraft and
     coordinates any activities related to the airborne operation and coordinates with the DACO for which
     individual(s) are sent. Only one jumpmaster or safety is required to complete this inspection.

     10-7. If required, USAF guides escort the individual past the red line to the aircraft. During engine running
     on-load operations, this inspection is conducted on the first lift only. Each subsequent jumpmaster team
     utilizing the aircraft must ensure that it has been reconfigured for the following lift. A member of the
     jumpmaster team inspects the aircraft according to chapter 15. However, the minimum requirements for
     interior, fixed-winged aircraft inspections are as follows:

          • A sufficient number of seats, complete with seal belts for all jumpers, safeties, and air lands are
                available.

          • Seat securing straps or suitable expedient straps are present.
          • Floors are clean and not slippery (nonskid material present).
          • All excess USAF equipment is lashed down properly and does not block the jumper’s path to the

                door.
          • Emergency exits are clearly outlined (yellow boundaries).
          • Protruding sockets by the paratroop door (C-130 series aircraft) are taped.
          • Emergency floor lighting system is operational (C-17 Globemaster III).

164  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                       Jumpmaster and Safety Duties at Departure Airfield

     • U-bolts must be silver or green and not cracked, broken, or corroded; ensure the locking pin is
          present.

     • Anchor line cables should utilize a length of 1/4-inch cotton webbing and should be inspected
          (traced) the entire length of the anchor line cables (must not have any kinks, rust, or corrosion).

     • The anchor line cable should be inspected individually from the forward portion of the aircraft to
          the aft end (the direction a jumper’s USL snap hook travels).

     • The towed parachutist retrieval system (TPRS) and static line retrieval system must—
           Be operational (loadmaster operates during inspection).
           Have both components (sling assembly and securing strap) secured behind the intermediate
                anchor line support bracket or in red pockets along the bulkhead wall.
           Not be routed under anchor line cables.
           Have at least a 4-inch clearance above anchor line cables.

     • The jump platform must—
           Have no cracks or bends.
           Have nonskid material present.
           Have down locks seated properly (C-130 series aircraft).
           Be secured to floor by screws and washers (at two points) or four turns of steel wire (1/32-inch
                diameter) (C-130 series aircraft).
           Have lower troop door clearance faring (skin of door frame) in serviceable condition
                (C-17 Globemaster III).

     • Paratroop doors must have—
           No sharp or protruding edges.
           Push in place pin is present and secured (C-130 series aircraft).
           Operational platform lights.
           A manual lever for the ramp that is secured by a safety strap, if applicable.
           A functional troop door up-lock and paratroop door lifting bar (C-17 Globemaster III).

     • Air deflector:
           C-130 series aircraft extends 15.5 inches.
           C-17 Globemaster III extends 30 degrees (+/- 5 degrees).

     • Jump caution lights must—
           Have operational green and red lights, and if jumping from the C-17 Globemaster III, include
                amber lights.
           Be highly visible during darkness and daylight.
           Have seven sets (C-130 series aircraft)—one at the pilot’s compartment, three along the skin of
                the aircraft, two at the jump doors, and one on the ramp.
           Have 12 sets (C-17 Globemaster III)—4 along the skin of the aircraft, 4 at the jump doors, 2 on
                the ramp, 1 in the pilot’s compartment, and 1 in the forward compartment of the emergency
                exit on the right before the stairs to the pilot’s compartment.

     • Have an operational emergency alarm bell.
     • Emergency equipment includes—

           First-aid kits (four each).
           Fire extinguisher (three each).
           Emergency Passenger Oxygen System, oxygen, or oxygen masks for each passenger.
     • An operational public address system.
     • Airsickness bags and earplugs.
     • Available water.
     • Safety kits should be placed where they are readily available, if needed.
     • Action or sport cameras (are required to be used) are mounted in appropriate locations.

       Note. For the C-27J inspection, see chapter 15.

10-8. While a member of the jumpmaster team is inspecting the aircraft, safety personnel control the chalk,
making sure personnel always remain in their assigned sticks. Personnel must be accounted for at all times.

Chapter 10

PARACHUTE ISSUE

     10-9. It is the responsibility of the PJM to supervise the chalk during parachute and air item issue. Since
     parachutes are configured differently for the C-130 and C-17 aircraft, jumpers may potentially draw the
     incorrect type if not constantly supervised during this process.

     10-10. Safeties draw extra UPRBs (one for every 30 jumpers) and at least two extra T-11 reserve/single pin
     parachutes, and four sets of T-11 reserve inserts for jumpmaster, AJM, and door bundle pusher(s), if needed.
     The extra UPRBs are used to store the static lines and deployment bags after the jump. (The extra UPRBs
     are placed in or with the jumpmaster or safety kit bag.) Jumpmaster team tasks during parachute issue include
     the following:

          • Departure airfield layout inspection—all air items and CE should be displayed for inspection by
                jumpmaster personnel before donning or loading on the aircraft, if not conducted at unit area.

          • Parachutes and equipment—the jumpmaster team ensures that all jumpers use the buddy system
                when donning parachutes and equipment.

          • Final DACO coordination—a member of the jumpmaster team reports to the DACO for any special
                or last-minute instructions.

          • JMPI—all current and qualified jumpmaster personnel assist in rigging, inspecting, and correcting
                deficiencies, as directed by the PJM:
                 Their role during JMPI is to observe and supervise.
                 The PJM should only perform JMPI to facilitate meeting station time.

ADVANCED EMERGENCY BAILOUT PARACHUTE

     10-11. The advanced emergency bailout parachute (AEBP) is a lightweight emergency parachute with a
     26-foot extended skirt canopy. The canopy is made from low-porosity material that is vacuum sealed to
     protect the main canopy from physical and environmental hazards. For parachute component parts, their
     characteristics, and serviceability checks can be found in TM 10-1670-332-23&P.

JUMPMASTER PERSONNEL INSPECTION, T-11 AND MC-6

     10-12. The PJM is responsible for the inspection of the jumpers on the aircraft before an airborne operation.
     Only by a complete and systematic equipment inspection of each jumper can the PJM ensure that personnel
     aboard their aircraft are safe to jump. Jumpmasters must observe all jumpers don the equipment and make
     corrections as needed to prevent deficiencies. Buddy rigging is used:

          • The buddy system is a systematic method of donning and adjusting the main and reserve parachutes
                providing:
                 Additional safety checks.
                 Unnecessary delay prevention during JMPI.
                 The jumper with the maximum amount of comfort while wearing the parachute harness.

          • To increase efficiency and reduce risks, jumpmasters are encouraged to gather the chalk and provide
                a demonstration of the buddy system prior to donning parachutes, which is especially beneficial
                during reintegration jumps.

          • If a jumpmaster rigs a jumper, it is acceptable for the jumpmaster to JMPI that jumper:
                 The rigging procedures and the JMPI sequence are two different systematic checks.
                 If another jumpmaster is available, then that jumpmaster should not inspect the jumper that they
                     rigged.

             Note. All personnel, including the jumpmasters, must utilize the buddy system to don the main
             and reserve parachutes upon their completion of JMPI.

     10-13. The jumpmaster conducts an overall inspection of the jumper prior to placing the jumper into JMPI
     configuration. The jumpmaster conducts an overall inspection of the jumper to ensure the following:

          • Boots—inspect the jumper’s boots for open lacing hooks and if the jumper is wearing open lacing
                hooks, they must be taped prior to the jumpmaster placing the jumper into JMPI configuration.

          • CE—inspect the MAWC to ensure—
                 The bottom of the adjustable nose cone is at least 6-inches above the ground.

166         TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                             Jumpmaster and Safety Duties at Departure Airfield

                 The top of the MAWC rests between the top of the D-ring and the base of the left canopy release
                     assembly.

          • Canopy release assemblies—look at canopy release assemblies to ensure that—
                 They are seated in the hollows of the jumper’s shoulders, below the collarbone at approximately
                     the name tape level.
                 They look at the riser assemblies to ensure that the type of parachute being inspected either has
                     or does not have blue confluence wrap.

     10-14. The only person authorized to place jumpers into JMPI configuration is the jumpmaster who inspects
     them. To place the jumper into JMPI configuration, the following occurs:

          • The jumpmaster moves behind the jumper and opens the main, curved, pin protector flap from the
                tuck flap:
                 Ensure the main curved pin is fully seated.
                 On a T-11 main parachute, ensure that the main curved pin securing tie is present and properly
                     secured.

          • The jumpmaster disconnects the USL snap hook from the right outer static line stow bar and ensures
                the spring opening gate has spring tension:
                 Looks at both sides of the double-sewn portion of the USLM.
                 Feels the stitching to verify that the double-sewn portion is present on both sides of the USLM,
                     there are three stitches sewn over the raw edge, and it is not cut, frayed, or burned.
                 Removes all excess USLM from the static line slack retainer band on the static line slack
                     retainer loop.
                 Removes all twists.
                 Routes the USL snap hook through one of the static line slack retainer bands and over the
                     jumper’s shoulder corresponding with the paratroop door the jumper is to exit.

          • The jumpmaster secures the USL snap hook to the carrying handle of the T-11 reserve/single pin
                parachute, with the spring opening gate facing the jumper:
                 If the jumper is wearing the T-11 reserve, remove the top and bottom tuck tabs, taking care to
                     ensure that both side tuck tabs remain secure.
                 If the side tuck tabs become unsecure, the jumpmaster notifies a rigger.

                                                 WARNING

                    Boots fitted with lacing hooks must have the hooks taped prior to
                    placing the jumper into JMPI configuration. Taping hooked
                    eyelets is an individual responsibility that must be verified and
                    checked by the jumpmaster.

          • The jumpmaster may now begin their inspection:
                 The general principle during JMPI is that the jumpmaster’s head and eyes are always looking
                     where their hands are working.
                 After the jumpmaster has completed the JMPI, the jumpmaster places the jumper into jump
                     configuration.

             Note. If jumping the MC-6 parachute or any other steerable, military, static line parachute, the
             jumpmaster identifies blue confluence wrap on both riser assemblies. Steerable and non-steerable
             canopies cannot be dropped onto the same DZ during the same pass.

FIVE-FOOT UNIVERSAL STATIC LINE EXTENSION

     10-15. For jumps from C-17 aircraft, the USLM is configured with the 5-foot USL extension. Jumpmasters
     must supervise during parachute issue to ensure their jumpers do not draw incorrectly configured parachutes
     for the aircraft that they are jumping.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  167
