Chapter 10

     10-16. The T-11 series parachutes are easily identifiable when configured with 5-foot USL extensions by:
          • Additional stows on the left and right inner static line stow bars.
          • The girth hitch formed by the upper looped portion of the USLM.
          • The cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL extension, which is centered between the two inner static line
                stows.

     10-17. Jumpmasters must inspect the 5-foot USL extension prior to detaching the USL snap hook from the
     right outer static line stow bar. When the 5-foot USL is present, ensure the green ID marking thread on the
     USLM and the USL extension is on top and outside the loop. With the index finger and thumb of both hands
     pinch off the double sewn portion of both the end of the cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL and the end upper
     looped portion of the USLM.

     10-18. Ensure the 5-foot USL extension is properly girth hitched to the USLM: Push in on the girth hitch at
     the upper looped portion of the USLM and the cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL extension to ensure that the
     girth hitch is completely separated. Then visually inspect both the upper looped portion of the USLM and
     the cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL extension for any burns, cuts, or frays. Ensure the double sewn portion
     of the 5-foot USL extension is routed through the upper looped portion of the USLM, and the double sewn
     portion of the USLM is routed through the cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL extension. Redress the girth hitch,
     ensuring it is centered between two inner static line stows. Then, route the USL snap hook over the jumper’s
     appropriate shoulder and connect it to the carrying handle of the reserve parachute with the spring opening
     gate facing towards the jumper.

     10-19. During the JMPI sequence, when the jumpmaster comes in contact with the girth hitch formed by the
     end of the cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL extension and the end upper looped portion of the USLM, it is
     inspected again by taking the following actions:

          • When the index finger or thumb of the working hand makes contact with the girth hitch formed by
                the 5-foot USL extension and the USLM:
                 Leave the working hand in place and conduct a visual inspection.
                 Ensure the green I.D. marking thread on the USLM and the 5-foot USL extension is on top and
                     outside the loop.

          • Remove the control hand from the top of the pack tray and the working hand from behind the USLM:
                 With the index finger and thumb of both hands pinch off the double sewn portion of both the
                     end of the cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL and the end upper looped portion of the USLM.
                 Ensure the 5-foot USL is properly girth hitched to the USLM.
                 Push in on the girth hitch at the upper looped portion of the USLM and the cotton buffer of the
                     5-foot USL, ensuring that the girth hitch is completely separated.

          • Visually inspect both the upper looped portion of the USLM and the cotton buffer of the 5-foot USL
                for any burns, cuts, or frays.

          • Ensure the double-sewn portion of the 5-foot USL is routed through the upper looped portion of the
                USLM, and the double sewn portion of the USLM is routed through the cotton buffer of the 5-foot
                USL.

          • Redress the girth hitch, then ensure the girth hitch is centered between two inner static line stows.
          • With either hand regrasp the excess USLM and control it on top of the pack tray:

                 This hand becomes the control hand.
                 The opposite hand becomes the working hand.
          • Insert the index finger or thumb of the working hand from bottom to top behind the strand of USL
                at the end of the 5-foot USL:
                 Make contact with the girth hitch formed by the 5-foot USL and the upper looped portion of

                     the USLM.
                 Continue to trace the USLM in the same manner, bypassing the girth hitch to the main curved

                     pin cover.

ADVANCED COMBAT HELMET (FRONT)

     10-20. To inspect the front of the ACH, the jumpmaster places both hands, fingers and thumbs extended and
     joined, fingertips pointing skyward, palms facing the jumper, on the right side of the ACH. The right hand is
     the working hand; the left hand is the control hand. The working hand traces across the rim of the ACH

168  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

             Jumpmaster and Safety Duties at Departure Airfield

     feeling for any sharp or protruding edges that may cut or damage the jumper’s USLM upon exiting the
     aircraft. Once both hands are parallel, place the thumbs on the rim of the ACH and tilt the jumper’s head to
     the rear. Conduct a visual inspection to ensure the three suspension pads are present, are flush with the outer
     rim, and the oval pads are covering the bolt ends.

     10-21. If the jumper is wearing a modified chinstrap assembly, the jumpmaster places the right index finger
     on the front left adjustable buckle, ensuring it is free of all cracked components, is serviceable, the front left
     adjustable strap is properly routed through it, and the free running end is secured in the webbing retainer.
     Trace the front left adjustable strap down, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed to the chinstrap fastener.
     Ensure the chinstrap fastener is free of all cracked components and properly secured. Trace the long portion
     chinstrap under the jumper’s chin to ensure it is not twisted, cut, or frayed to the place where it is sewn into
     the front right adjustable strap. Trace the front right adjustable strap up, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or
     frayed to the front right adjustable buckle. Ensure it is free of all cracked components, is serviceable, the
     front right adjustable strap is properly routed through it, and the free running end is secured in the webbing
     retainer. Place the right index finger on the right side of the short portion chinstrap, trace it across the front
     of the jumper’s chin, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, and drop both hands.

     10-22. If the jumper is wearing the H-Nape Retention System:
          • Place the right index finger on the front left adjustable strap from where it emerges from the helmet
                shell.
          • Trace the front left adjustable strap down ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed until contact is
                made with the front left slider, ensuring it is free of all cracked components and is serviceable:
                 Continue to trace the front left adjustable strap down ensuring that it is not twisted, cut, or
                     frayed until contact is made with the chinstrap buckle.
                 Ensure that it is free of all cracked components, it is serviceable and is properly secured.
          • Trace the long portion chinstrap under the jumper’s chin, ensuring that it is not twisted, cut, or frayed
                to where it is sewn into the front right adjustable strap.
          • Trace the front right adjustable strap up ensuring that it is not twisted, cut, or frayed until contact is
                made with the front right slider, ensuring that it is free of all cracked components and is serviceable:
                 Continue to trace the front right adjustable strap up ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed to
                     wear it disappears into the helmet shell.
                 Place the right index finger on the right side of the short portion chinstrap and trace it across
                     the front of the jumper’s chin, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, then drop both hands.

CANOPY RELEASE ASSEMBLIES

     10-23. The next items of equipment for inspection are the canopy release assemblies. The inspection begins
     with the canopy release assembly opposite the jumper’s USLM. For this example, the jumper is exiting the
     right paratroop door. Since the USLM is routed over the jumper’s right shoulder, begin the inspection with
     the jumper’s left canopy release assembly:

          • Look at the left canopy release assembly and tap it with the knuckles of the right hand one time to
                ensure that it sounds solid.

             Note. This is the cue for jumpers to place both hands on top of their helmet.

          • With the right hand, form a knife-cutting edge, fingers extended and joined, palm facing towards
                the jumpmaster:
                 Insert it from outside to inside behind the main lift web just below the canopy release assembly.
                 Place the right thumb on the outside corner of the canopy release assembly and rotate it a quarter
                     turn to the outside.

          • With head and eyes approximately 6-to-8-inches away, conduct a visual inspection to ensure the
                male fitting canopy release assembly is properly secured by the female fitting canopy release
                assembly, and is properly secured by the latch.

          • Ensure the cable loop is properly secured by the safety clip and the canopy release assembly is free
                of all dirt or foreign material that keeps it from seating completely:
                 Let the canopy release assembly return back to its normal position.
                 Keep the right hand in place.

     • With the left hand, secure the USLM and rotate it over to the right thumb and secure it in place:
           Look at the right canopy release assembly.
           Tap it with the knuckles of the left hand one time to ensure that it sounds solid.

     • With the left hand:
           Form a knife-cutting edge, fingers extended and joined palm facing towards the jumpmaster.
           Insert it from outside to inside behind the main lift web just below the canopy release
               assemblies.

     • Place the left thumb on the outside corner of the canopy release assembly and rotate it a quarter turn
          to the outside and conduct the same inspection.

     • Let the canopy release assembly return to its normal position.

MAIN LIFT WEB, CHEST STRAP, AND WAISTBAND

     10-24.  The jumpmaster inspects the main lift web next by taking the following actions:
          •
               Leaves the right hand in place and looks at the left hand and the right main lift web:
          •     Makes note of which of the three sizes the main lift web is configured.
          •     Keeps this in mind and ensures the main lift web tuck tab assembly is properly assembled and

                    the snap fastener is secure.

               With the left hand, traces down the main lift web, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, until
               making contact with the main lift web adjuster.

               Leaves the left hand in place and looks at the right hand and conducts the same inspection:
                Ensures the left main lift web tuck tab assembly is in the same location as the right main lift

                    web tuck tab assembly.
                Leaves the right hand in place.

     10-25.  The jumpmaster inspects the chest strap by taking the following actions:
          •
          •    Looks at the chest strap to ensure that it is not misrouted around the left main lift web and with the
               left-hand palm facing the reserve parachute, grasps the carrying handle and lifts up and out.
          •
          •    Inserts the right hand:
                Fingers and thumb extended and joined.
          •     Fingertips pointing down, palm facing towards the jumpmaster, from top to bottom behind the

                    chest strap, next to where it is sewn into the left main lift web.

               Traces the chest strap, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, until contact is made with the chest
               strap friction adapter.

               Visually inspect to ensure—
                It has a two-to-three finger quick release that is secured in its webbing retainer.
                The free running end has been S-folded or accordion folded, not rolled.
                It is secured in its webbing retainer with the tab portion on top and facing towards the chest

                    strap friction adapter.

               Continues to trace the chest strap, ensure it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, until contact is made with
               the right main lift web and leave the right hand in place.

     10-26. The jumpmaster begins inspecting the waistband by leaning to the right side of the jumper and taking
     the following actions:

          • Removes the left hand and inserts it:

          • Looks at the waistband where it is sewn to the pack tray to ensure it is secured to the pack tray by a
               box X stitch, with at least 50 percent of the stitching present.

          • Traces the waistband forward, ensures it is not twisted, cut, frayed, or misrouted behind the
               horizontal backstrap or the right main lift web:
                Continues tracing the waistband forward until the right waistband retainer rests in the palm of
                     the left hand.
                Leaves the left hand in place.

T-11 RESERVE PARACHUTE

     10-27. The next item that the jumpmaster inspects is the reserve parachute in its entirety. To do so, take the
     following actions:

          • Look at the left connector snap:
                 With the index finger of the right hand, finger the opening gate one time to ensure it is properly
                     secured to the left D-ring.
                 Ensure it has spring tension, has not been safetied, and the opening gate is facing towards the
                     jumper with the butterfly portion to the outside.

             Note. Jumpers can now place their hands back down to their sides.

          • With the left hand, lift up and out on the carrying handle.
          • Conduct a visual inspection of the left connector snap retaining tie to ensure it is serviceable and

                secured.
          • Visually inspect the left spreader bar tie to ensure it is properly routed through both grommets and

                is secured with a surgeon’s knot, locking the knot with overhand knots.
          • Insert the right index finger from top to bottom into the Army parachute log record stow pocket:

                 Conduct a physical and visual inspection to ensure a DA Form 3912 (Army Parachute Log
                     Record) is present.

                 Transfer control of the carrying handle from the left hand to the right hand, palm facing the
                     reserve parachute and continue to lift up and out.

UNIVERSAL STATIC LINE MODIFIED

10-30.  Inspect the USLM by taking the following actions:
     •
     •    With the right hand, grasp the USL snap hook, ensuring the spring opening gate is facing towards
          the jumper, open the right hand and let the USL snap hook rest in the palm.
     •
     •    Place the index finger of the left hand on the girth hitch of the USLM:
           Ensure the green identification marking thread is present and the girth hitch has not been
     •
     •         reversed.
     •     Place the index finger of the left hand in the vicinity of the rivet pin (do not cover the rivet pin)

     •         to ensure it is present and free of rust and corrosion.

     •    With the right hand, regrasp the USL snap hook and hold it perpendicular to the reserve parachute
          with the spring opening gate facing towards the jumper.

          With the index finger and thumb of the left hand, index finger on top, thumb on bottom, palm facing
          the jumper—
           Grasp the USLM at the end of the double-sewn portion.
           Rotate the USLM down and to the jumper’s right and push it toward the USL snap hook.
           Visually inspect inside the girth hitch to ensure it is free of all cuts, frays, and burns.

          With the index finger or thumb of the right hand, push the girth hitch back towards the USL snap
          hook and again visually inspect inside the girth hitch for any cuts, frays, or burns.

          Redress the girth hitch down around the narrow portion of the USL snap hook and release the USLM
          with the left hand.

          Since the USLM is routed over the right shoulder:
           With the index finger and thumb of the right hand, form an O around the USLM just above the

               USL snap hook.
           The jumpmaster should see metal through the O.

          If the USLM were routed over the jumper’s left shoulder, after redressing the girth hitch down and
          around the narrow portion of the USL snap hook:
           With the index finger and thumb of the left hand forming an O around the USLM just above

               the USL snap hook, you still see metal.
           Now drop the right hand.
           Raise the left hand up and tilt the O towards you, simultaneously inspecting the USLM as it

               passes through the O to ensure it is free of all cuts, frays, or burns.

          Raise the left hand as high as it can go, or until you feel resistance and issue the jumper the command
          TURN.

     10-31. Raise the right hand up, simultaneously inspecting the USLM as it passes through the O to ensure it
     is free of all cuts, frays, or burns:

          • Raise the right hand as high as it can go or until resistance is felt, and issue the jumper the command,
                TURN.

          • Once the jumper has completed the turn, the right hand should be raised high enough to keep the
                USLM tight between the control hand and the first stow.

          • Place the index finger or index and middle finger of the left hand behind the USLM below the right
                hand, making skin-to-skin contact:
                 Trace the USLM down, ensuring it is free of all cuts, frays, and burns, and it has not been
                     misrouted under or through either riser assembly to the static line slack retainer band.
                 Withdraw the index finger or index and middle finger and place below the static line slack
                     retainer band and continue to trace the USLM to the first stow.

          • With either hand, form a bight in the USLM and look at the static line slack retainer loop, ensuring
                it is present, serviceable, and two serviceable static line slack retainer bands are attached.

          • Place the bight on top of the pack tray and control it with either hand which becomes the control
                hand while the opposite hand becomes the working hand.

          • With the index finger and thumb of the working hand, pinch off the first stow and pull it
                1-to-2 inches towards the center of the pack tray:
                 Look behind the first stow, and ensure the USLM is free of cuts, frays, or burns, and has not
                     been misrouted around the static line stow bar.
                 Release the first stow and let it pop back into place.

             Note. When jumpmasters trace the USLM toward themselves, only the index finger is used. When
             tracing away, only the thumb may be used.

          • Insert the index finger or thumb of the working hand from bottom to top behind the first strand of
                USLM, as close as possible to the first stow.

          • Trace the first strand of USLM, ensuring that the second stow is free of all—
                 Cuts.
                 Frays.
                 Burns.

          • With the index finger and thumb of the working hand, pinch it off and pull 1-to-2 inches towards
                the center of the pack tray, and conduct the same inspection.

          • Place the index finger or thumb of the working hand from bottom to top behind the second strand
                of USLM and trace it to ensure it is not cut, frayed, or burned.

          • Continue to inspect the USLM in the same manner to the main curved pin cover, ensuring the last
                strand of USLM is routed from the right outer static line stow bar.

          • With the index finger of the working hand, gently lift the main curved pin cover and inspect the
                main curved pin attaching loop to ensure that it is properly attached to both the USLM and the main
                curved pin.

                or corroded, and is properly routed from left to right through the main closing loop:
                 If the jumper is wearing a T-11 main parachute visually inspect to ensure the main curved pin
                     securing tie is present and made of only one turn of “Orange” ticket 3-inch thread.
                 Ensure the main curved pin is secured by a surgeon’s knot locking knot with the ends trimmed
                     to approximately 2 inches.

          • Visually inspect the main closing loop to ensure it is not cut, frayed, or burned, and the main curved
                pin is not puncturing it in any manner; checking the grommet to ensure it is not bent, cracked, or
                corroded.

          • With the index finger and thumb of the working hand, gently lift the main curved pin protector flap
                and conduct a visual inspection of the main closing loop, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, frayed, or
                burned, and the grommet is not bent, cracked, or corroded.

          • Stand behind the jumper.

                                                                             Jumpmaster and Safety Duties at Departure Airfield

             Notes. Broken securing ties: If a tie breaks any time after the original packer makes the tie, prior
             to getting on the aircraft, it can be replaced by a qualified parachute rigger skill level 1 or higher,
             after a routine inspection of the parachute. If the parachute passes the routine inspection, the tie
             can be replaced, and the parachute returned to service without being repacked. Once the tie is
             made, a qualified parachute rigger inspector skill level 2 or higher must inspect the tie. Both the
             individual replacing the tie and the inspector must sign the DA Form 3912. If the parachute does
             not pass the routine inspection, it must be returned to the parachute pack facility for repack.

             If a securing tie breaks on the aircraft and the main curved pin is still seated in the closing loop,
             the parachute is still serviceable and can be jumped.

ADVANCED COMBAT HELMET (BACK)

     10-32. The jumpmaster inspects the rear of the ACH by placing both hands, fingers and thumbs extended
     and joined, fingertips pointing skyward, palms facing towards the jumper, on the left side of the ACH. The
     left hand is the control hand, and the right hand is the working hand. With the working hand, trace across the
     rim of the ACH feeling for any sharp or protruding edges that may cut or damage the jumper’s USLM upon
     exiting the aircraft.

     10-33. Once both hands are parallel, place the thumbs on the rim of the ACH and gently tilt the jumper’s
     head forward. Conduct a visual inspection to ensure the oval pads are covering the bolt ends, they are flush
     with the rim of the ACH, and the rear trapezoid pad is flush or protruding slightly past the rim of the ACH,
     no more than 1/2-inch.

     10-34. If the jumper is wearing a modified chinstrap assembly, place the right index finger on the rear right
     adjustable buckle. Ensure it is free of all cracked components and is serviceable, the rear right adjustable
     strap is properly routed through it, and the free running end is secured in the webbing retainer.

     10-35. Trace the rear right adjustable strap down, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed until contact is
     made with the long portion chin strap. Leave the right index finger in place.

     10-36. Place the left index finger on the rear left adjustable buckle and conduct the same inspection all the
     way down to the chinstrap fastener. Leave the left index finger in place.

     10-37. Conducts a visual inspection of the nape pad to ensure it is present, secure, serviceable, and has not
     been reversed. If the jumper is wearing the H-Nape Retention System:

          • Place the right index finger on the rear right attaching strap—
                 From where it emerges from the rim of the ACH.
                 Trace the attaching strap down ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed.
                 Route the strap through the nape pad retaining strap until contact is made with the rear right
                     plastic oval link.
                 Ensure it is free of all cracked components and is serviceable.

          • Continue to trace down, picking up the inspection of the rear right adjustable strap until contact is
                made with the rear right slider, ensuring it is free of all cracked components and is serviceable.

          • Continue to trace the rear right adjustable strap down, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed to
                where it is sewn into the long portion chinstrap:
                 Leave the right index finger in place.
                 Place the left index finger on the rear left attaching strap from where it emerges from the rim
                     of the ACH.

          • Conduct the same inspection all the way until contact is made with the chinstrap buckle and keep
                both hands in place.

          • Conduct a visual inspection of the nape pad to ensure that it is present and serviceable.
          • Inspect the H-Nape Pad slider and ensure that it is present, serviceable, and free of all cracked

                components.

INSPECTING RISER ASSEMBLIES AND PACK TRAYS

     10-38.  The jumpmaster performs the inspection of the riser assemblies by taking the following actions:
          •
          •    Reach over the jumper’s shoulders and grasp a riser assembly in each hand, thumbs down, knuckles
               pointing skyward, just above the canopy release assemblies:
          •     Since these are like items of equipment, either riser assembly can be inspected first.
                For this example, begin the inspection with the left riser assembly.

               Give the left riser assembly a sharp tug to the rear and opens the left hand to form a
               distinguishable L:
                Apply upward pressure with the left thumb and trace the riser assembly rearward.
                Conduct a physical and visual inspection to ensure that a DA Form 3912 is present, and that the

                    riser assembly is not twisted, cut, or frayed to where it disappears into the main pack tray.
                Leave the left hand in place.

               Conduct the same inspection on the right riser assembly with the right hand, ensuring that only one
               riser assembly contains a DA Form 3912.

     10-39. An overall inspection of the pack tray is conducted to ensure the pack tray is free of grease, oil, dirt,
     mud, or tears. Jumpmasters inspect the pack tray by taking the following actions:

          • Place both hands, fingers and thumbs extended and joined palms facing towards the pack tray, on
               the top left corner of the pack tray:
                The left hand is the control hand.
                The right hand is the working hand.

          • With the head and eyes 6-to-8 inches away from the working hand:
                Trace across the top pack closing flap, down the right pack closing flap.
                Jumpmasters bend over to see what they are doing and trace across the bottom pack closing
                     flap.

          • Turn the working hand over so the pinkie finger leads the way and trace up the left pack closing flap
               until skin-to-skin contact is made with the control hand.

          • They raise the control hand up out of the way and trace where the control hand has been.

          • Form knife edges with both hands, palms facing towards themselves, and issue the command,
               ARCH YOUR BACK.

INSPECTING BACKSTRAPS

     10-40. Jumpmasters inspect both diagonal and horizontal backstraps.

Diagonal Backstraps

     10-41. Insert both hands behind the diagonal backstraps where the natural pocket is formed. Ensure that
     thumbs rest just below the X formed by the diagonal backstrap retainers. Look at the diagonal backstraps to
     ensure they are properly routed over the appropriate shoulder, and the top diagonal backstrap has one more
     row of exposed stitching than the bottom. Look at the diagonal backstrap retainers to ensure they are routed
     through the sizing channels on the diagonal backstraps, the diagonal backstrap retainers are routed around
     the diagonal backstrap keepers, and the directional snap fasteners are secure.

     10-42. Ensuring the directional snap fasteners are secure, jumpmasters use both thumbs to pluck the tab
     portion of the diagonal backstrap retainers upward from bottom to top. They look at the left hand, and with
     that hand, trace down the diagonal backstrap to ensure it is not twisted, cut, or frayed to the backstrap adjuster.

     10-43. Grasp the backstrap adjuster with the left hand and look at the right hand and the right diagonal
     backstrap. With the right hand, trace down the diagonal backstrap, ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed.

Horizontal Backstraps

     10-44. Bypass the backstrap adjuster and resume inspection of the horizontal backstrap. Trace down,
     ensuring it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, and the free running end is secured in the webbing retainer until it
     disappears into the right main lift web.

     10-45. Withdraw the right hand from under the horizontal backstrap, and reinsert it, fingers and thumb
     extended and joined, fingertips pointing skyward, palms facing towards themselves. Trace from bottom to
     top behind the horizontal backstrap where it re-emerges from the right main lift web. Issue the jumper the
     command, BEND.

     10-46. Place the left shoulder on the bottom pack closing flap and push up on the bottom of the pack tray,
     simultaneously with the left hand, pulling down on the backstrap adjuster. With head and eyes approximately
     6-to-8 inches away, trace the horizontal backstrap across the small of the jumper’s back until the right pinkie
     finger makes contact with the main lift web on the jumper’s left side.

     10-47. Inspect the horizontal backstrap to ensure:
          • It is not twisted, cut, or frayed.
          • That the horizontal backstrap retainers are properly routed over the horizontal backstrap.
          • That the horizontal backstrap retainers are properly routed under and back over the horizontal
                backstrap keepers and secured with directional snap fasteners.
          • Nothing is misrouted behind the horizontal backstrap.

     10-48. Withdraw the right hand from behind the horizontal backstrap and reinsert it from top to bottom
     behind the horizontal backstrap and behind the WAP, where it re-emerges from the left main lift web. Trace
     up until making skin-to-skin contact with the left hand, ensuring that it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, the free
     running end is secured in the webbing retainer, and nothing has been misrouted behind it. Remove the right
     hand and get left hip-to-head with the jumper.

SADDLE

     10-49. The jumpmaster inspects the saddle by taking the following actions:
          • Places the fingertips of the right hand, fingers and thumb extended and joined, palm facing towards
                the jumper, on the lower portion of the left main lift web adjuster:
                 Traces down the lower portion of the main lift web, transitioning to the saddle to ensure it is
                     not twisted, cut, or frayed, and neither leg strap has been misrouted around the saddle.
                 Continues to trace until making contact with the lower portion of the right main lift web
                     adjuster.
          • Keeping the left hand in place, reaches back and gets a handful of air and issues the good seal of
                approval by tapping the jumper on the buttocks while issuing the command, RECOVER.

             Note. Once the jumpmaster has completed the inspection, they place the jumper into jump
             configuration.

     10-50. After the jumpmaster has completed their JMPI, they place the jumper into jump configuration
     (the only person authorized to place the jumper into jump configuration is the jumpmaster who inspected that
     jumper) and take the following actions:

          • The jumpmaster traces the USLM from the USL snap hook to ensure that the USLM is routed over
                the shoulder corresponding with the door the jumper is to exit.

          • Once behind the jumper, the jumpmaster removes all slack from the USLM:
                 USL slack is removed by pulling the USLM through the static line slack retainer band, creating
                     another stow if there is enough slack.
                 Otherwise let the USLM hang free.

INSPECTION OF COMBAT EQUIPMENT (MODULAR AIRBORNE WEAPONS CASE)

     10-52. When jumping a MAWC, the inspection sequence for a combat-equipped jumper is the same as a
     noncombat-equipped rigged jumper all the way down to the waistband. Inspect ACH, canopy release
     assemblies, main lift webs, and the chest strap, as prescribed in paragraphs 10-20 thru 10-26, then take the
     following actions:

          • Insert the right hand behind the chest strap as close as possible to where it is sewn into the right
                main lift web and lean to the right side of the jumper.

          • Insert the left hand:
                 Fingers and thumb extended and joined.
                 Fingertips pointing skyward.
                 Palm facing towards the jumpmaster, from bottom to the top behind the waistband next to where
                     it is sewn to the pack tray.

          • Look at the waistband where it is sewn to the pack tray to ensure it is secured to the pack tray by a
                box X stitch, with at least 50 percent of the stitching present.

          • Trace the waistband forward:
                 Ensure it is not twisted, cut, frayed, or misrouted behind the horizontal backstrap.
                 Ensure it is routed over the right main lift web and under the right equipment ring.
                 Continue tracing the waistband forward until the right waistband retainer rests in the palm of
                     the left hand and leave the left hand in place.

          • Remove the right hand from behind the chest strap:
                 Insert it, fingers and thumb extended and joined, fingertips pointing skyward.
                 Palm facing the jumpmaster, from bottom to top behind the reserve parachute outside of the left
                     adjustable D-ring attaching strap.
                 The left waistband retainer rests in the palm of the right hand.
                 Make fingertip-to-fingertip contact and conduct a physical inspection to ensure the waistband
                     is not twisted and has been routed through both waistband retainers.

                closing flap of the reserve parachute, palm facing the reserve parachute.

          • Remove the right hand from behind the waistband retainer and with the right forearm push out on
                the lead edge of the MAWC for the first time.
                 Look at the waistband to ensure it is not twisted, cut, or frayed.
                 Ensure the waistband has been properly routed over the left main lift web and under the left
                     equipment ring.

          • With the right hand, grasp the trail edge of the MAWC and pull it forward.
          • With the right hand, fingers and thumb extended and joined, fingertips pointing skyward, palm

                facing the jumpmaster, insert it from bottom to top behind the metal adjuster.

                 Ensure that it is no more than three fingers, no less than two and it is not a false quick release.

                 With the index finger and thumb of the left hand, pinch off the free running end of the waistband
                     where it re-emerges from the metal adjuster.

                 Trace the free running end of the waistband, ensure it is not cut, torn, or frayed, and is easily
                     accessible to the jumper until the fingers fall off the end.

          • Place the left hand on the left pack closing flap of the reserve parachute, palm facing the reserve
                parachute and look at the right hand and the WAP:
                 With the right hand, trace the WAP back.
                 Ensure the WAP is not twisted, cut, or frayed, and has not been misrouted behind the horizontal
                     backstrap to where it is sewn to the pack tray.
                 Ensure the WAP is properly secured to the pack tray by a box X stitch, with at least 50 percent
                     of the stitching present.

          • Remove the right hand and move in front of the jumper; using the right forearm, push out on the
                lead edge of the MAWC for the second time.

10-53. The MAWC is inspected in its entirety prior to inspecting the reserve parachute. The inspection of the
MAWC begins with its point of attachment, the snap shackle:

     • Look at the snap shackle, ensuring it is the outermost item of equipment on the left equipment ring,
          and the opening gate is facing the jumper.

     • With the right thumb and index finger, rotate the snap shackle one quarter of a turn so the opening
          gate is facing towards the jumper:
           Conduct a visual inspection of the locking pin to ensure it is seated.
           Conduct a visual inspection to ensure the yellow safety lanyard is present and is secured to the
                appropriate snap fastener.

     • With the right hand:
           Form a fist, leaving the index finger exposed, and trace down the adjusting strap.
           Ensure the adjusting strap is properly routed through the pouch attachment ladder system
                webbing until coming into contact with the friction adapter.

     • Leave the right index finger in place and—
           Visually inspect for proper routing.
           Ensure the adjusting strap is routed through the friction adapter from top to bottom.
           Route the adjusting strap up over the bottom bar and under the top bar to keep the adjusting
                strap from slipping.
           Visually inspect to ensure as much of the excess webbing of the adjusting strap is stowed under
                the pouch attachment ladder system webbing as possible.

       Note. The jumpmaster must ensure the excess webbing of the adjusting strap is not routed over
       the snap shackle.

     • Once satisfied with the inspection, continue tracing down the inside of the MAWC until the right
          index finger naturally falls off the end.

     • With the right hand—
           Form a knife-cutting edge with the fingers extended and joined, palm facing skyward.
           Trace from front to rear along the bottom of the MAWC until the hand falls off the rear, ensuring
                the muzzle of the weapon is not protruding.
           With the palm of the right hand, gently lift up on the base of the adjustable nose cone to ensure
                that the nose cone securing straps are tightened, and the HPT is properly secured.

     • Place the index finger of the right hand on the quick-release buckle at the bottom of the closing flap.
     • Visually inspect to ensure—

           The compression strap has been properly routed through the vertical nylon equipment hanger.
           The quick-release buckle is free of all cracked components and is properly secured.
     • Visually inspect to ensure the free running end of the compression strap has been routed back
          through the vertical nylon equipment hanger and is secured in the webbing retainer:
           Continue to trace up the slide fastener to ensure it is secured with all teeth engaged until making

                contact with the second quick-release buckle and then conduct the same visual inspection.
           Visually inspect to ensure the free running end of the compression strap has been secured in the

                webbing retainer.
           Continue tracing the slide fastener until making contact with the slide fastener and tabbed thong.
     • Leave the right index finger in place and conduct a visual inspection of the upper spring stop to
          ensure the spring portion is present and serviceable:
           Using the index finger of the right hand, form a hook, and insert it from back to front into the

                window created in the tabbed thong portion of the slide fastener and tabbed thong.
           Gently pull up on the slide fastener and tabbed thong to ensure it is secured by the snap fastener,

                and the upper tie down tape is properly routed through it.
     • With the right hand, form a knife-cutting edge, fingers and thumb extended and joined, palm facing

          the MAWC, and trace down approximately 10-to-12 inches from the top of the MAWC.
     • Give the MAWC a sharp slap, feeling for the forward assist of the M4/M16 series rifle or the

          charging handle of the M249 squad automatic weapon (also called SAW).

                on the lead edge of the MAWC:
                 Visually inspect to ensure that the upper tie-down tape is properly routed behind the vertical
                     nylon equipment hanger.
                 Routed through the small window in the tabbed portion of the slide fastener and tabbed thong.

MODULAR LIGHTWEIGHT LOAD-CARRYING EQUIPMENT II RUCKSACK

     10-54. After completing the overall inspection of the reserve parachute, the jumpmaster then inspects the
     MOLLE II rucksack in the following manner:

          • The inspection of the HSPR begins with the adjustable D-ring attaching straps:
                 These are like items of equipment so either one can be inspected first.
                 For this purpose, begin with the right adjustable D-ring attaching strap.

          • Simultaneously—
                 Form fists with index fingers exposed with both hands.
                 Place index fingers on the snap hooks of the adjustable D-ring attaching straps.
                 Focus attention on the left hand.
                 Conduct a visual inspection to ensure that the snap hook is not bent, cracked, corroded, or
                     distorted out of shape, and that the opening gate is facing towards the jumper.

          • With the index finger of the left hand, finger the opening gate one time to ensure that it is properly
                secured to the right equipment ring, and it has spring tension and has not been reversed.

          • With the left thumb, flip the free running end of the right adjustable D-ring attaching strap out of
                the way.

          • Place the left index finger on the black intermittent stitching on the front of the right adjustable
                D-ring attaching strap just below the snap hook.

          • Trace down the right adjustable D-ring attaching strap ensuring that it is not twisted, cut, or frayed
                until contact is made with the triangle link.

          • Bypass the triangle link and pick up the inspection of the attaching loops:
                 Ensure that the white attaching loop is routed from bottom to top through the triangle link.
                 Ensure the green attaching loop is routed from bottom to top through the white attaching loop.
                 Ensure the red attaching loop is routed from bottom to top through the green attaching loop
                     and from bottom to top through the grommet in the female portion leg strap release assembly.
                 Place the index finger of the left hand on the single box X stitch on the release handle cross
                     strap.

          • Look at the release handle cable where it emerges from the release handle cross strap.
          • Ensure the release handle cable is properly routed through the red attaching loop and secured by the

                cable loop retainer.
          • Leave the left index finger in place and with the right hand, conduct the same inspection on the left

                adjustable D-ring attaching strap until the right index finger rests on the single box X stitch.
          • Focus attention on the release handle:

                 With the right index finger on top and thumb on the bottom, lift up gently on the release handle.
                 Ensure the release handle and release handle cable is properly routed between the two piles of

                     the release handle cross strap.
                 Ensure the release handle is secured by the hook-pile tabs and has not been reversed or is upside

                     down.

          • Form a hook with the right index finger and insert it from outside to inside and lift the release handle
                lanyard to ensure it is not twisted, cut, frayed, or misrouted around the equipment retainer strap or
                the release handle cross strap.

          • Place the right index finger back on the single box X stitch.
          • Trace the equipment retainer straps down the outside of the pouch on the MOLLE rucksack until

                making contact with the box X stitches on either side of the adjustable cross strap.
          • Leave the left index finger in place, and with the index finger and thumb of the right hand—

                 Grasp the free running end of the adjustable cross strap and give it a tug to the jumper’s left,
                     ensuring that all the slack has been removed from the adjustable cross strap.

                 Place the right index finger back on the single box X stitch and continue to trace the equipment
                     retainer straps down until fingers fall off.

          • Secure the sides of the MOLLE rucksack and raise it to eye level:
                 Look at the equipment retainer straps to ensure they are routed through the slots at the top
                     corners of the MOLLE rucksack frame and have not been twisted, cut, or frayed.
                 Raise the MOLLE rucksack to the jumper and issue the command, HOLD.

             Note. Jumpers secure the top of the MOLLE rucksack and hold it up high.

          • Continue the inspection of the equipment retainer straps as they route through the adjustable
                shoulder carrying straps from outside to inside:
                 Ensure the equipment retainer straps are routed over the comfort pad and form an X
                     configuration on the rear of the MOLLE rucksack and are not twisted, cut, or frayed.
                 Bypass the girth hitch of the HPTLL and continue the inspection until fingers rest on the friction
                     adaptors and behind the two-to-three finger quick releases in the equipment retainer straps.

          • Simultaneously, inspect the two-to-three finger quick releases by placing the index and middle
                finger of each hand, palms toward the face, on the outside of the quick releases:
                 Visually inspect the free running ends of the equipment retainer straps to ensure they are
                     S-folded or accordion folded, never rolled.
                 Secured with either one turn of masking tape or two turns of retainer bands (one or the other,
                     never both) and not secured to the quick releases.
                 Conduct a visual inspection of the friction adapters to ensure they are routed through the oval
                     cutouts at the base of the MOLLE rucksack frame.
                 Use the index finger of each hand and lightly tap the friction adapters to ensure they are secure.

          • With the thumb and index fingers of each hand, form an O around the base of the adjustable shoulder
                carrying straps:
                 Whenever possible, the free running ends should be on top of both hands.
                 Simultaneously, pull out to ensure they are properly secured to the MOLLE rucksack frame.

          • Visually inspect the free running ends of the adjustable shoulder carrying straps ensuring they are—
                 S-folded or accordion folded, never rolled.
                 Secured with either one turn of masking tape or two turns of retainer bands (one or the other,
                     never both).
                 With the index fingers of each hand, lightly tap the free running ends of the adjustable shoulder
                     carrying straps ensuring they are secure.

                 Conduct the same inspection on the left adjustable equipment ring attaching strap until the right
                     index finger rests on the single box X stitch on the release handle cross strap.

          • Focus attention on the release handle:
                 With the right index finger and thumb, index finger on top, thumb on the bottom lift gently on
                     the release handle.
                 Ensure the release handle and release handle cable is properly routed between the two piles of
                     the release handle cross strap.
                 Ensure the release handle is secured by the hook-pile tabs, is not reversed, or upside down.

          • Form a hook with the right index finger and insert it from outside to inside and gently lift up on the
                release handle lanyard:
                 Ensure it is not twisted more than one half twist, cut, frayed, or misrouted around the equipment
                     retainer strap or the release handle cross strap.
                 Place your right index finger back on the single box X stitch on the release handle cross strap.
                 Visually inspect to ensure that the equipment retainer straps are properly routed through the air
                     item routing channels inside the air items stowage pocket.

          • With both hands, simultaneously—
                 Trace the equipment retainer straps down ensuring they are not twisted, cut, or frayed.
                 Route both equipment retainer straps through the same number of air item routing channels
                     until fingers rest on top of the friction adapters (behind the two to three finger quick releases of
                     the equipment retainer straps).

          • Simultaneously, inspect the 2 to 3 finger quick releases of the equipment retainer straps by placing
                the index and middle finger of each hand, palm facing you, on the outside of the quick releases:
                 Inspect the free running ends of the equipment retainer straps.
                 Ensure that they are S-folded or accordion folded, never rolled.
                 Ensure they are secured with one turn of masking tape or two turns of retainer band, one or the
                     other never both.
                 With the index fingers of each hand, lightly tap the free running ends of the equipment retainer
                     straps to ensure that they are secure.

          • Secure the sides of the MOLLE 4000 and raise it to eye level:
                 Conduct a visual inspection ensuring the equipment retainer straps are routed through the
                     friction adapter stowage pockets.
                 Ensure the V-shaped load lifters are on top of the pack, and behind the MOLLE 4000 frame.

          • Raise the MOLLE 4000 to the jumper and issue the command HOLD. (Jumpers secure the top of
                the MOLLE 4000 and hold it up high.)

          • Simultaneously, place the index fingers of both hands on the equipment retainer straps where they
                re-emerge from under the MOLLE 4000:
                 With both hands, trace down the equipment retainer straps ensuring they are not twisted, cut or
                     frayed and form an X configuration on the back of the MOLLE 4000 pack.
                 Bypass the girth hitch of the HPTLL and continue the inspection until fingers rest on the frame
                     of the MOLLE 4000 frame.
                 Leave index fingers in place and conduct a visual inspection of the equipment retainer straps to
                     ensure they are properly routed through the air item routing channels.

          • With the thumb and index fingers of each hand, form an O around the base of the adjustable shoulder
                carrying straps:
                 Whenever possible the shoulder carrying straps’ free running ends should be on top of the
                     hands.
                 Simultaneously, pull out to ensure they are properly secured to the MOLLE 4000.
                 Inspect the free running ends of the adjustable shoulder carrying straps.
                 Ensure they are S-folded or accordion folded, never rolled.
                 Ensure they are secured with either one turn of masking tape or two turns of retainer bands (one
                     or the other never both).

MEDIUM MODULAR LIGHTWEIGHT LOAD-CARRYING EQUIPMENT PACK

     10-57. After completing an overall inspection of the reserve parachute, the jumpmaster then inspects medium
     MOLLE. To inspect this pack—

          • The HSPR inspection begins with the adjustable D-ring attaching straps:
                 These are like items of equipment so either one can be inspected first.
                 Begin with the right adjustable D-ring attaching strap for this example.

          • With both hands, simultaneously form fists with the index fingers exposed:
                 Place index fingers on top of the snap hooks of the adjustable D-ring attaching straps, focusing
                     attention on the left hand.
                 Conduct a visual inspection to ensure that the snap hook is not bent, cracked, corroded, or
                     distorted out of shape and that the opening gate is facing the jumper.

          • With the index finger of the left hand, finger the opening gate one time to ensure that it is properly
                secured to the right equipment ring, it has spring tension and has not been reversed.

          • With the left thumb flip the free running end of the right adjustable D-ring attaching strap out of the
                way.

          • Place the left index finger on the black intermittent stitching on the front of the right adjustable
                D-ring attaching strap just below the snap hook:
                 Trace down the right adjustable D-ring attaching strap.
                 Ensure that it is not twisted, cut, or frayed until contact is made with the triangle link.

          • Bypass the triangle link and pick up the inspection of the attaching loops and trace down to ensure—
                 The white attaching loop is routed from bottom to top through the triangle link.
                 The green attaching loop is routed from bottom to top through the white attaching loop.
                 The red attaching loop is routed from bottom to top through the green attaching loop.
                 The red attaching loop is routed from bottom to top through the grommet in the female portion
                     leg strap release assembly.

          • Continue tracing until the left index finger rests on the single box X stitch on the release handle
                cross strap.

          • Look at the release handle cable where it emerges from the release handle cross strap, ensuring it is
                properly routed through the red attaching loop and secured by the cable loop retainer.

          • Leaving the left index finger in place, with your right hand conduct the same inspection on the left
                adjustable D-ring attaching strap until the right index finger rests on the single box X stitch on the
                release handle cross strap.

          • Focus attention on the release handle:
                 With the right index finger on top and thumb on the bottom, lift gently on the release handle.
                 Ensure the release handle and release handle cable are properly routed between the two piles of
                     the release handle cross straps.
                 Ensure the release handle is secured by the hook-pile tabs and has not been reversed or upside
                     down.

          • Form a hook with the right index finger and insert it from outside to inside:
                 Gently lift the release handle lanyard, to ensure it is not twisted, cut, frayed, or misrouted around
                     the equipment retainer strap or the release handle cross strap.
                 Place the right index finger back on the single box X stitch on the release handle cross strap.

          • Simultaneously, trace the equipment retainer straps down until you contact the box X stitches on
                either side of the adjustable cross strap.

          • Leave the left index finger in place and with the right index finger and thumb—
                 Grasp the free running end of the adjustable cross strap and give it a tug to the jumper’s left.
                 Ensure that all the slack has been removed from the adjustable cross strap.

          • Place the right index finger back on the single box X stitch and continue to trace the equipment
                retainer straps down until fingers fall off it.

                secured to the right equipment ring, it has spring tension and has not been reversed.

     10-59.  Inspect the HPTLL—when rigged with a MAWC—by taking the following actions:

               from the end of the retainer flap.

               by two sets of girth hitched retainer bands on either end of the retainer flap.

UNIVERSAL PARACHUTIST RECOVERY BAG AND AVIATOR’S KIT BAG

10-60.  Inspect the UPRB by taking the following actions:
     •
          Insert the index and middle finger of each hand:
     •     From outside to inside.
     •     Behind the leg straps and below the UPRB where the natural pocket is formed.
           Simultaneously, slide both hands back towards the saddle to ensure the leg straps are not
     •
               crossed.
     •     Leave the right hand in place.
     •
     •    With the left hand trace the right leg strap up, ensure it is not twisted, cut, or frayed, until contact is
          made with the right leg strap retainer.
     •
          Now remove the index finger and middle finger of the left hand and reinsert them just above the
     •    right leg strap retainer and trace up the right leg strap to ensure that it is—
           Not twisted, cut, or frayed.
           Properly routed so the excess webbing is behind the leg strap retainer.
           Secured in the webbing retainer until contact is made with the quick-fit V-ring.

          With the thumb, press in on the activating lever of the ejector snap to ensure that it is—
           Properly seated over the ball detent.
           Free of foreign matter that would keep it from seating completely.
           Leave the left hand and thumb in place and look at the left leg strap.

          With the right hand, conduct the same inspection of the left leg strap.

          Once skin to metal contact is made, you may remove the right hand and use the right forearm to lift
          up and out on the MAWC.

          With the right thumb, press down on the activating lever to ensure that it is—
           Properly seated over the ball detent.
           Free of any foreign material that keeps it from seating completely and leave both hands and

               thumbs in place.

          Rock back on heels and conduct a visual inspection to ensure that—
           The UPRB is present.
           Neither leg strap retainer is cut or frayed more than 50 percent.
           The folded portions are facing skyward.

          Once satisfied with the inspection, stand up in front of the jumper, secure the sides of the MOLLE
          rucksack, and issue the command of RECOVER.

Note. Jumpers pick up on the reserve parachute and jumpmasters simply allow the MOLLE
rucksack or ALICE pack to rotate between the jumpmaster’s body and the jumper’s body.

TECHNICAL INSPECTION AND HANG OF COMBAT EQUIPMENT

     10-61. The jumpmaster is responsible for inspecting each jumper and item of equipment. Long flights, heavy
     loads, extreme heat, tactical updates, and special items of equipment (AT4JP, SMJP, and other items) may
     warrant delaying the attachment of equipment until a predesignated time later in the mission timeline. Under
     such conditions, the airborne commander may decide to conduct the JMPI without equipment. The
     commander must consider individual and unit proficiency when conducting the command risk assessment.

Chapter 10

     10-62. There are two methods to attach equipment after JMPI is complete: T.I. and hang of CE, and late hang
     and JMPI of CE. When the commander decides to T.I. and hang after JMPI has been conducted, the T.I. is
     conducted on the MOLLE rucksack, ALICE pack, MOLLE 4000 Medium, Assault Pack, MAWC (rigged
     for a tandem load), the HPTLL (MAWC), and leg strap assemblies.

     10-63. The items to be technically inspected are the MAWC, upper tie down tape, the jumpable pack, and
     the HPTLL. The T.I. of all CE is conducted in the prescribed manner according to that equipment’s JMPI
     inspection sequence. No portion of the inspection sequence is omitted. It may be required to manipulate the
     equipment in different ways to perform the inspection properly because it is not hung on the individual
     jumper. After the jumpmaster has completed the T.I. they hang the equipment on the individual jumper.

POSTHANG INSPECTION

     10-64. Once the jumpmaster has completed hanging the equipment on the jumper, they complete a posthang
     inspection verifying all the attachments are properly attached and secured. At a minimum, the following are
     conducted:

          • The snap hooks of the adjustable D-ring attaching straps are:
                 Properly attached to the equipment rings with the opening gates facing the jumper.
                 The adjustable D-ring attaching strap is not twisted.

          • (MAWC) The snap shackle is the outermost item of equipment on the left equipment ring; if rigged
                as part of a tandem load:
                 Ensure that the locking pin is fully seated.
                 Ensure that the yellow safety lanyard is secured to the appropriate snap fastener (whichever
                     creates the least amount of tension).

          • (MAWC) The jumpmaster should ensure that the upper tie-down tape is—
                 Properly routed through the window on the slide fastener and tab thong.
                 Routed around the body of the MAWC, from back to front through the small cutaway portion
                     of the equipment ring.
                 Secured with a single or double loop bowknot on the lead edge of the MAWC and is easily
                     accessible to the jumper.

          • (MAWC) The jumpmaster should ensure that the HPTLL is properly routed through the attachment
                strap:
                 Its ejector snap is attached to the left triangle link with the opening gate facing the jumper.
                 The activating lever is fully seated.

          • The jumpmaster should ensure that the leg strap release assemblies are routed appropriately.
          • If the jumper is exiting from the left paratroop door, the right adjustable leg strap is routed around

                the right leg, and the left adjustable leg strap is placed around the MAWC on the jumper’s left side.
          • If the jumper is exiting from the right paratroop door, the left adjustable leg strap is routed around

                the jumper’s left leg and MAWC, and the right adjustable leg strap is not used.

LATE HANG AND JUMPMASTER PERSONNEL INSPECTION OF COMBAT EQUIPMENT

     10-65. When the airborne commander has decided to conduct late hang and JMPI, jumpers attach equipment
     using the buddy system. After the equipment is properly attached, it must be inspected using the late hang
     JMPI sequence.

     10-66. The only items to be inspected are the MAWC, upper tie down tape, the jumpable pack, and the
     HPTLL. The late hang JMPI sequence is conducted in the same manner as prescribed in the talk through for
     that equipment. The late hang JMPI sequence begins with the snap shackle of the modular airborne weapon’s
     case and ends with the ejector snap of the HPTL. The jumpmaster also inspects the upper tie down tape for
     proper attachment to the horizontal back strap

ADJUSTABLE LEG STRAPS

     10-67. After the jumper is fully rigged, the jumpmaster routes the male portion leg strap release assemblies
     around the jumper’s appropriate leg and attaches it to the female portion leg strap release assembly.

JUMPMASTER PERSONNEL INSPECTION SEQUENCE FOR AIRBORNE PACK

             Note. This JMPI sequence is for the front mounted AIRPAC when jumped with a MAWC.

10-68.  The jumpmaster inspects the AIRPAC as follows:
     •
          Place the left hand on the snap hook for the right D-ring attaching strap and the right hand on the
     •    snap hook for the left D-ring attaching strap:
     •     Leave the right hand in place.
           Focus attention on the left hand and the right D-ring attaching strap.
     •
          With the index finger of the left hand, finger the opening gate to ensure it has spring tension and is
     •    properly attached to the right D-ring to the outside of the connector snap.
     •
     •    Place the index and middle finger of the left hand from outside to inside behind the nylon portion
     •    of the D-ring attaching strap:
           Trace down until the middle finger makes contact with the circular ring.
     •     Ensure the strap is not twisted, cut, or frayed.
     •
     •    Bypass the circular ring and place the index finger on the red attaching loop:
     •     Visually inspect the circular release ring to ensure it has been routed through the circular ring

     •         and folded back against the nylon portion of the D-ring attaching strap.
     •     Ensure the red attaching loop has been routed bottom to top through the circular release ring
     •
     •         and then through the grommet on the female portion of the leg strap release assembly.
     •     With the thumb and index finger, peel back on either the top or bottom corner of the female

               portion of the leg strap release assembly to ensure the red attaching loop has been properly
               routed.

          Place the left index finger on the single boxed X stitch just below the circular ring.

          Conduct a visual inspection of the release handle cable to ensure it is properly routed under both
          piles of the release handle cross strap and through the red attaching loop.

          Conduct the same inspection on the left D-ring attaching strap.

          Leave the left index finger in place, and with the right hand gently lift the release handle to ensure
          that it—
           Has been properly routed under both piles of the release handle cross strap.
           Has been secured by the hook-pile tabs.

          Form a knife edge with both hands, palms facing each other, and place them on the outer edge of
          the equipment retainer straps.

          Simultaneously, trace down the equipment retainer straps until contact is made with the friction
          adapters.

          Leaving both hands in place, look at the friction adapters, ensuring that the—
           Equipment retainer straps have been properly routed through them.
           Free running ends are secured by means of the webbing retainers.

          With either hand, carefully open the circular closing flap and hold it up and out of the way:
           This hand is now the control hand.
           Place the index finger of the working hand on the single boxed X stitch on the 6 o’clock set of

               equipment retainer straps.
           Visually inspect both friction adapters to ensure the free running ends of the equipment retainer

               straps are properly routed through them and are secured by means of the webbing retainers.

          Conduct the same inspection for the 9 o’clock and 3 o’clock set of friction adapters, placing the
          index finger of the working hand on the eyelet of the cotter pin.

          Ensure the white grommet securing loop has been routed through all three grommets, is not cut or

                                                Chapter 11

              Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

    This chapter provides an overview of the duties of the jumpmaster team during flight. For
    aircraft-specific personnel duties, see chapter 14.

PRIMARY AND ASSISTANT JUMPMASTER AND SAFETY DUTIES

     11-1. After the aircraft takes off, the jumpmaster team must remain oriented to the aircraft’s location at all
     times, and keep the jumpers informed of any deviations from the flight plan. The jumpmaster may coordinate
     with the navigator or use a Global Positioning System (also called GPS). The jumpmaster also remains in
     communication with the pilot. To do this, the jumpmaster relays messages through the loadmaster.

     11-2. On Army aircraft, the jumpmaster or safety personnel always wear a flight helmet or headset for direct
     communication with the pilot and to monitor the ground control element.

     11-3. In general, the jumpmaster team—
          • Never sacrifices safety, for any reason.
          • Rehearses jumpmaster procedures on the ground with the complete jumpmaster team for that
                aircraft.
          • Hooks up before opening the paratroop door(s) or ramp.
          • Does not allow anyone in or near the open paratroop door without a helmet, safety harness, AEBP,
                or static line parachute that is hooked up to an anchor line cable.
          • Ensures T-11 reserve inserts are in place and checked by the safety prior to taking the paratroop
                door.

JUMPMASTER DUTIES

     11-4. The jumpmaster gives a sequence of jump commands to ensure positive control of jumpers inside the
     aircraft and immediately before exiting. Every command requires specific actions by each jumper. When
     commands are executed properly, they ensure a safe and systematic exit from the aircraft. The commands are
     given verbally, but to compensate for engine noise, the jumpmaster also uses hand and arm signals. The
     signals must be smooth, coordinated, and precise. The commands listed, with variations explained in chapters
     15 through 19, are employed on a multitude of aircraft. (Jumpmasters ensure that the correct sequence is used
     for each particular aircraft.) The correct commands are explained and demonstrated to jumpers during SAT.

     11-5. The PJM and AJM must—
          • Enforce flight rules and regulations.
          • Perform in-flight rigging missions.
          • Issue time warnings.
          • Issue proper jump commands.
          • Perform proper door safety checks.
          • Perform proper outside air safety checks.
          • Perform door bundle exiting procedures.
          • Control the flow and spacing of all jumpers.

SAFETY PERSONNEL

     11-6. Safety personnel have one of the most important duties during an airborne operation; properly and
     safely handling USLMs during exit. Properly handling USLMs can prevent serious injury or death and is
     vital to mission accomplishment. During in-flight rigging missions, safety personnel assist in parachute issue,
     monitor buddy rigging, JMPI, and operate correction stations as directed by the PJM.

     11-7. The safety must—
          • Enforce flight rules and regulations.
          • Check on the condition of all jumpers and relocate personnel who are too sick to jump.

          • Watch for any unsafe acts.

          • Reinforce the proper static line control and ripcord handle awareness.
          • Ensure jumpers extend their arm once moving towards the paratroop door.
          • Safely control each jumper’s USLM upon exit.
          • Conduct jump-refusal procedures.

C-130, PRACTICAL WORK INSIDE THE AIRCRAFT

     11-8. Time warnings, paratroop door safety checks, and door bundle ejection are events that commonly occur
     during each airdrop operation. Time warnings and door procedures are completed during each airdrop
     operation, but door bundles are not always ejected.

     11-9. The time warnings and door procedures are considered critical aspects of jumpmaster operations during
     all airdrop procedures. When the 20-minute time warning is given, jumpmasters unbuckle their seat belts and
     stand up. They move to the rear of the aircraft, turn, and face the jumpers. (All time warnings begin and end
     at the shoulders with closed fists.) They extend both arms straight forward, extending and spreading the
     fingers and thumb of each hand. This is repeated twice while the verbal command is given.

     11-10. All special items of equipment are attached to designated jumpers and then are inspected. Safety
     personnel assist the jumpmasters with attaching equipment and ensuring the tie-downs are secure and the
     lowering lines are attached and secured. At the 20-minute time warning, if door bundles are used for the
     airborne operation, the door bundle is moved in front of the paratroop door and attached to the outboard
     anchor line cable. From this position, it is then inspected.

     11-11. Conduct the following inspection for G-14 door bundles:
          • Static line cargo only and clevis with cotter pin (bent at a 45-degree angle) or safety wire and lanyard
                (bent 180 degrees until metal-to-metal contact is made).
          • Pack closing tie.
          • Drogue device (one for the C-130; two for the C-17).
          • Point of attachment to the bundles (risers).
          • Tie-down tapes (one on each corner).
          • Pack tray and bundle (for any loose or excess webbing).
          • When the inspection is completed, the jumpmaster slaps the smooth side of the bundle and ensures
                it is facing the trail edge of the door.

     11-12. Conduct the following inspection for T-10 cargo parachute door bundles. Prior to hooking up the
     cargo parachute’s static line to the outboard anchor line cable, the jumpmaster inspects the cargo parachute
     and door bundle in its entirety beginning at the point of attachment, making sure that the following is
     completed:

          • Ensure risers are properly attached and the safety wires are bent around so that they have metal to
                metal contact, or the cotter pins are bent to a 45-degree angle.

          • Ensure the connector link tie is constructed of one turn of 1/4-inch cotton webbing and routed—
                 Through the suspension line protective flap tie loops.
                 Through the first set of connector link tie loops.
                 Through the L-bar connector links.
                 Through the second set of connector link tie loops, secured with a surgeon’s knot, locking knot.

          • Ensure the securing tie is constructed of 1/4-inch cotton webbing and is securing the parachute tight
                to the load and is routed underneath the USL.

          • When satisfied with their inspection, the jumpmaster slaps the smooth side of the door bundle,

     11-13. Once the container has been inspected, hook up the cargo parachute’s static line to the outboard anchor
     line cable and place the container on its end with the parachute towards the inside of the aircraft as close to

     11-16. Jumpmasters should be positioned forward of the paratroop door when conducting jump commands.

11-33. Safeties check each jumper’s USLM. Ensure the USL snap hook is properly secured to the proper
anchor line cable with the opening gate facing towards the skin of the aircraft. Safeties trace down the USLM
to the jumper’s four in the hand two below bight, ensuring it is held at eye level, and they are not covering
the double sewn portion.

11-34. Safeties trace the USLM over the jumper’s shoulder, ensuring it is not misrouted. Continue to trace
the USLM to the first stow.

11-35. Safeties visually inspect the remainder of the USLM to ensure it is properly stowed to the pack tray
and the main curved pin protector flap is properly stowed in the tuck flap and not routed over any portion of
the USLM.

11-36. Safeties stow any excess static line in the static line slack retainer band so that each static line is taut
from the jumper’s bight to the pack tray but not to the point where the excess static line loop hangs below
the main curved pin protector flap.

11-37. Jumpers do not exit the aircraft if a member of the jumpmaster team determines that a jumper’s USLM
is not stowed in the proper manner.

11-38. Safeties remind all jumpers to make eye-to-eye contact and hand their static line to the safety.

PARATROOP DOOR SAFETY CHECK

     11-46. Once the safety and T.I. of the paratroop door is complete, the loadmaster informs the jumpmasters,
     ARMY, YOUR DOOR:

          • The jumpmaster confirms through the loadmaster, the aircraft has slowed to drop speed before

                STATIC LINE.

                following manner:

                     USLM taut between their hands, ensuring no excessive slack is impeding the jumpmaster or
                     causing a safety hazard.
                 The trail hand should be held high near the USL snap hook and the lead hand held low in the
                     vicinity of the jumpmaster’s pack tray.
                 Both hands should be formed in knife-cutting edges, palms facing outward, fingertips pointed
                     skyward, with the USLM secured between their palm and thumb.
                 Securing the USLM in this manner allows the safety to release the jumpmaster’s USLM easily
                     in the event the jumpmaster prematurely exits the paratroop door.

     11-47. The jumpmaster conducts a proper door safety check (see figures 11-8 and 11-9) in the following

                safety.

                having any part of their feet on the jump platform.

          • Using only the lead hand, they ensure the push in place pin is in place, securing the jump door in
                the open position on the C-130.
