Chapter 11

JUMP PLATFORM AND TRAIL EDGE OF THE DOOR

     11-48.  The jumpmaster checks the jump platform in the following manner:
          •    First, kick the lead-down lock one time with the lead foot while visually inspecting to ensure the
               down lock is engaged.
          •    Bring the lead foot back behind the yellow caution line and firmly plant that foot.
          •    The jumpmaster uses the trail foot to kick the trail-down lock one time and visually inspects to
               ensure the down-lock is engaged.
          •    Then, without bringing the trail foot back inside the aircraft, the jumpmaster places the trail foot in
               the center of the jump platform and transfers their weight to the platform.
          •    This ensures that the platform can support the weight of a jumper.
          •    The trail foot remains in place because if the jumpmaster removes their foot from the platform, they
               must again check the down locks and ensure the platform can support their body weight.
          •    Once the trail foot has been planted on the jump platform and the jumpmaster’s weight has been
               shifted, this is the door relaxed position.

     11-49. With the trail hand, the jumpmaster starts at the top of the trail edge of the paratroop door, tracing all
     the way down to the trail-down lock, then tracing back to the top to ensure no sharp or protruding edges exist.
     If for any reason the jumpmaster’s hand breaks contact with the trail edge of the door, the jumpmaster must
     begin the trace of the door over at the top of the door.

                                             CAUTION

             All jumpmasters performing duties on a C-130 aircraft must be able to
             conduct a paratroop door check while maintaining three points of contact
             with the aircraft deck. This check requires the jumpmaster to attain an
             80-inch reach. Jumpmasters must be evaluated by their unit prior to
             performing any duties on this airframe.

     11-50. The jumpmaster leans towards the trail edge of the door, while looking in the direction of flight while
     ensuring the air deflector is properly deployed.

INITIAL OUTSIDE SAFETY CHECK

     11-51. The jumpmaster must make outside air safety checks to ensure there are no unsafe conditions outside
     the aircraft, including trail aircraft in the formation that are below drop altitude or other low-flying aircraft.
     From the same stable door position, the jumpmaster leans forward to the elbow-locked position while keeping
     both heels flat on the floor of the cargo compartment and visually conducts a down-and-behind air-safety
     check.

             Note. Jumpmasters are encouraged to conduct checks in all cardinal directions to maintain the best
             situational awareness, but at a minimum they check below and behind the aircraft.

     11-52. The jumpmaster then comes to the door in a relaxed position, continues observing outside the aircraft
     spotting for reference points enroute to the DZ. In the absence of reference points and checkpoints, they use
     additional time advisories from the aircrew, which was identified during the air mission briefing. A
     checkpoint is a predetermined point on the ground used to control movement, tactical maneuver, and
     orientation (FM 3-90). Jumpmasters relay time warnings to the jumpers by leaning back inside the aircraft,
     keeping their foot centered on the platform, facing the jumpers, and calling off the 1-minute and 30-second
     time warning, as well as giving the proper arm-and-hand signal for each time warning.

     11-53. Once the doors are open and the jumpmasters are conducting their door checks, safeties have all the
     jumpers close in tight, reducing the interval between the No. 1 jumper and the paratroop door. Jumpers
     maintain the proper interval.

208          TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010                                       30 May 2026

                                                                                              Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

     11-54. The jumpmaster locks out their elbows to conduct outside air safety checks properly. The safety also
     locks their elbows while checking for towed jumpers after each pass.

     11-55. The loadmaster should relay time warnings to the jumpmaster or safety by using hand signals. The
     exact hand signals that must be coordinated between the jumpmaster and loadmaster during the aircrew brief
     are:

          • A 1-minute time warning—with the elbow locked out, the index finger extended vertically.
          • A 30-second time warning—with the elbow locked out, the index finger and thumb held closely

                together.

ONE-MINUTE WARNING

     11-56. Once the jumpmaster spots their 1-minute reference point and is about 1 minute from the green light,
     or the safety passes along the loadmaster time warning to the jumpmaster:

          • The jumpmaster relays the 1-minute time warning to the jumpers by leaning back, keeping their foot
                centered on the platform, facing the jumpers, extending the index finger of their lead hand, and
                announces, ONE MINUTE.

          • The jumpers relay the time warning by looking over their shoulder closest to the skin of the aircraft
                and shouting, ONE MINUTE.

          • The jumpmaster continues observing outside for the 30-second reference point, or until the
                30-second time warning is relayed from the loadmaster.

THIRTY-SECOND TIME WARNING AND FINAL CLEAR TO THE REAR

     11-57. Once the jumpmaster spots the 30-second reference point and is about 30 seconds from the green
     light, or the safety passes along the loadmaster time warning to the jumpmaster:

          • The jumpmaster relays the THIRTY SECONDS warning to the jumpers by leaning back, keeping
                their foot centered on the platform, facing the jumpers, and extending the index finger of their lead
                hand and announcing, THIRTY SECONDS.

          • The jumpers relay the time warning by looking over their shoulder closest to the skin of the aircraft
                and shouting, THIRTY SECONDS.

     11-58. After the jumpmaster has called off the 30-second reference point, they immediately conduct their
     final clear to the rear outside safety check. The jumpmaster leans forward to the elbow-locked position while
     keeping both heels flat on the floor of the cargo compartment and visually conducts a down-and-behind air
     safety check.

             Note. For a CARP VIRS DZ, the jumpmaster is not responsible for positively identifying the DZ,
             code letter, or color of smoke. The USAF and other service aircraft personnel are responsible for
             positively identifying the DZ, code letter, or color of smoke.

     11-59. If the jumpmaster observes any unsafe conditions outside the aircraft, they notify the loadmaster by a
     preplanned arm-and-hand signal (for example, a cutting motion across the throat) that a NO DROP situation
     exists for this pass.

                                                 CAUTION

                    Jumpmasters or safeties can call a NO DROP anytime they determine
                    something is wrong or unsafe.

Chapter 11

     11-60. Once jumpmasters make their final clear to the rear air safety check:
          • The jumpmaster removes the trail foot from the jump platform and plants the foot inside the cargo
                compartment.
          • The jumpmaster then releases the paratroop door with the lead hand.
          • The jumpmaster rotates into the aircraft facing the jumpers.
          • The PJM and AJM make eye-to-eye contact and give each other a thumbs-up signal indicating there
                are no unsafe conditions outside the aircraft and they are ready to exit personnel.
          • The jumpmaster stays in place and issues the eighth jump command STANDBY.

             Note. If the first suspended object is an A-series container or door bundle, see door bundle
             procedures in this chapter.

EIGHTH JUMP COMMAND

     11-61. Once the jumpmasters give the thumbs-up signal to each other, they immediately issue the eighth
     jump command of STANDBY (see figure 11-10). Starting at the shoulders with the elbows bent, the
     jumpmaster extends and joins their index and middle fingers, curling the remaining fingers and thumb of
     each hand toward the palm. As they give the command STANDBY, they extend their arms up and out to
     their sides, ending at a 45-degree angle.

     11-62. The jumpmaster takes a step forward with the inboard foot and rotates their body so that both
     jumpmasters are facing the skin of the aircraft, with the body bisecting the lead edge of the paratroop door.
     Jumpmasters must ensure they are not impeding either anchor line cable. Each jumpmaster reaches out with
     the trail hand and secures a proper bight in their USLM. The safety returns control of the jumpmaster’s USLM
     to the jumpmaster by forming it into a small bight, then assumes a position bisecting the trail edge of the
     paratroop door ensuring the flow of jumpers are not impeded.

     11-63. Whenever possible the jumpmaster should protect their ripcord handle with the nonstatic-line hand.
     The AJM must ensure they have eyes on the PJM and No. 1 jumper by looking over or under either shoulder.
     The safety receives the first jumper’s USLM with their lead hand and secures it with their trail hand by
     pinning it against the intermediate anchor line support bracket while preparing to control the next jumper’s
     USLM with the lead hand.

     Figure 11-10. STANDBY

                                                                                              Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

NINTH JUMP COMMAND

     11-64. Once the green light comes on, the PJM issues the ninth jump command, GO. Both jumpmasters give
     the physical and verbal command of GO. This is executed by bending forward at the waist and giving a sharp
     tap on the thigh or buttocks of the No. 1 jumper.

     11-65. The AJM observes the PJM and the No. 1 jumper. When the PJM issues the ninth jump command to
     their No. 1 jumper and the jumper begins to exit, the AJM immediately turns, acknowledges the green light
     is on, and then issues the physical and oral command of GO to the jumper. This action needs to occur in half
     a second to establish the proper interval between paratroop doors.

     11-66. Both jumpmasters ensure they are positioned to best control the flow of jumpers without impeding
     the paratroop door or the safeties controlling USLMs. The safety grasps each USLM with their lead hand,
     and passes it back to their trail hand, ensuring the USLM is firmly seated against the intermediate anchor line
     cable support.

     11-67. The jumpmaster team must have situational awareness of their jumpers once the green light comes
     on. Jumpmasters—

          • Control the flow and spacing and intervals between jumpers without impeding the flow of jumpers.
          • Ensure jumpers’ static line arms are extended once they begin moving.
          • Remind jumpers to make eye-to-eye contact with the safety.
          • Pause or stop the stick for any unsafe act or condition, fix the issue, and continue to exit jumpers if

                the green light is on.
          • Monitor the jump caution lights for the red light.

     11-68. Safeties control the flow of jumpers and USLMs without impeding the flow of jumpers. They also—
          • Ensure that there is a positive transfer of the static line between themselves and the jumpers as they
                exit.
          • Pause or stop the stick for any unsafe act or condition, fix the issue, and continue to exit jumpers.
          • Watch for towed jumpers.

                                                 CAUTION

                    Both the jumpmaster and the safety must be prepared to initiate red-light
                    procedures at any time after the green light has been illuminated.

     11-69. After the last jumper exits, the AJM transfers control of the USLM to the safety. The AJM takes up a
     good door position, reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green, and exits on green.

     11-70. The PJM transfers control of the USLM to the safety and takes up a good door position. Upon seeing
     the AJM exit, the PJM reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green and exits on green.

     11-71. Both safeties immediately conduct a clear to the rear for towed jumpers and give each other a thumbs-
     up. They also give a thumbs-up to the loadmaster(s) and help retrieve deployment bags.

             Note. If the first suspended object is an A-series container or door bundle, see door bundle
             procedures in this chapter.

GROUND MARKING RELEASE SYSTEM

     11-72. After issuing the eighth jump command, the safety receives the first jumper’s USLM with the lead
     hand and passes it to the trail hand, securing the line by pinning it against the intermediate anchor line support
     bracket while preparing to receive the next jumpers USLM. The jumpmaster continues to spot for the DZ
     and DZ markings over the No. 1 jumper’s shoulder. When the panels come into view, the jumpmaster issues
     the ninth jump command, ensuring the jumper is clear of the aircraft when the panels bisect the jump door.

Chapter 11

     11-73. For USAF operations, a safety is not used and either the jumpmaster or loadmaster fulfills the duties.
     Coordination is made during the air movement brief.

            Note. For GMRS operations, jumpmasters are not certified to throw exiting jumpers using GMRS
            unless they are a USASOC jumpmaster graduate, are assigned to a USASOC unit, and have been
            certified by a USASOC jumpmaster.

RED LIGHT PROCEDURES AND JUMP REFUSALS

     11-74. If a jumpmaster sees the jump caution light turn red, they raise their hand towards the jumpers and
     sound off with, RED LIGHT, RED LIGHT, RED LIGHT. No one touches or physically tries to stop a jumper
     who has transferred the USLM and is committed to the paratroop door. Jumpers are stopped only by an oral
     command; this reduces the risk of an incident. If any jumper tries to exit on the red light, they are allowed to
     exit, except in the case of an unsafe jumper.

     11-75.  The procedure for handling a jump refusal is as follows:
          •
          •    When removing a jump refusal from the door, the jumpmaster tells the refusal, GREEN LIGHT,
               GO; GREEN LIGHT, GO; GREEN LIGHT, GO.
          •
          •    If the jumper does not exit after the third command, the safety grasps the sides of their pack tray and
          •    tells the refusal, YOU ARE A JUMP REFUSAL, I AM REMOVING YOU FROM THE
          •    PARATROOP DOOR.

               Under no condition should the safety reach around in front of the refusal to pull them back into the
               aircraft; the safety could accidentally hit or grab the T-11 reserve ripcord handle.

               After the jump refusal is removed from the paratroop door, they are guided and seated on the ramp
               of the aircraft away from the paratroop door and directed to not touch their equipment.

               The jumpmaster team then continues to exit jumpers if any green light remains.
               The safety assists the USAF personnel in retrieving all deployment bags and once the door is
               closed—
                They move the jump refusal as far forward as possible inside the aircraft and buckle them in.
                They unhook their USLM from the anchor line cable, and once again direct them not to touch

                    any of their equipment.

TOWED JUMPER PROCEDURES

     11-76. In the event of a suspected towed jumper, the priority should always be to retrieve the jumper if
     possible and only cut a jumper free as the last resort. The jumpmaster or safety prevents any other jumpers
     from exiting the paratroop door and notifies the remainder of the jumpmaster team and the loadmaster. The
     loadmaster informs the aircraft commander of the situation.

     11-77. The safety conducts a clear to the rear to confirm—
          • If a jumper is being towed or not.
          • How the jumper is being towed, such as by the USLM or equipment.
          • If the jumper appears to be conscious or unconscious.

     11-78. The jumpmaster team moves all remaining jumpers on that door towards the forward portion of the
     aircraft. Only the loadmaster and the jumpmaster team perform towed-jumper retrieval procedures. The
     jumpmaster team on the opposite door assists in moving all jumpers away from the TPRS, creating a clear
     space to work.

     11-79. If the jumper is being towed by the USLM, the jumpmaster or safety may make a retrieve or cut-free
     recommendation to the aircraft commander through the loadmaster. If the jumper is to be retrieved, the
     jumpmaster team assists the loadmaster in the retrieval process. Once the jumper nears the paratroop door,
     the jumpmaster and safety gain physical control of the jumper without grasping the reserve parachute.

     11-80. If the jumper cannot be retrieved, they are cut free over the DZ. The loadmaster cuts the USLM on
     the command of the aircraft commander. This is only considered if the jumper is conscious. If the jumper is
     being towed by anything other than the USLM, the jumpmaster or safety tries to jog them free from the
     aircraft.

212          TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010                              30 May 2026


---

                                                                                              Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

     11-81. Once free from the aircraft, jumpers do not need to activate their reserve since their main parachute
     deploys as normal. If the jumper cannot be freed, they are retrieved using the TPRS. Once inside, the jumper
     is brought to the forward portion of the aircraft where medical assessment and aid is administered. If the
     retrieval is unsuccessful and the jumper must be cut free, the jumpmaster or loadmaster cuts free the item of
     equipment that is towing the jumper.

     11-82. The jumper stays in a tight body position and protects the ripcord handle with both hands in
     preparation of being cut free, in order to activate the reserve parachute. Once they feel themselves fall free
     from the aircraft, they immediately start a 6,000 count with T-11 ATPS or the 4,000 count with MC-6 series
     parachute. If no opening shock is felt, they immediately activate their reserve parachute using the pull drop
     method. If the jumper is being towed by anything other than the USLM, once cut or jogged free, they do not
     need to activate the reserve parachute since the main parachute deploys as normal.

     11-83. The loadmaster attaches and operates the TPRS with the assistance of the jumpmaster and safety.
     They retract the jump platform and draw in the TPRS while it is securing all USLMs, including the towed
     jumper’s USLM. Once near the paratroop door, the jumpmaster and safety gain physical control of the jumper
     without grasping the reserve parachute. The loadmaster then relieves slight tension on the TPRS so that the
     jumper can be brought inside the aircraft. The loadmaster cuts the USLM on the command of the aircraft
     commander, if directed.

     11-84. Once informed of a towed jumper, the aircraft commander maintains the same drop airspeed and at
     least maintains the same drop attitude. The pilot flying lowers the landing gear and sets flaps to 100 percent
     to reduce parachute buffeting. If possible, avoid turning the airplane in the direction of the towed jumper as
     this could cause the jumper to swing violently, increasing the possibility of injury. The aircraft commander
     makes the final decision about cutting the towed jumper free. If the decision is to cut the jumper free, the
     loadmaster cuts the USLM on the aircraft commander’s command.

             Note. It is a general rule that the jumpmaster or safety cuts away anything green (indicating
             equipment) and the loadmaster cuts away anything yellow (indicating a static line). A towed
             jumper may not always be identified by a USLM positioned low on the trail edge of the paratroop
             door; therefore, it is key that a proper clear to the rear check is conducted.

OVER-THE-RAMP OPERATIONS

     11-85. Tailgate drops are those where parachutists exit from the aircraft ramp. The maximum rigged weight
     of the parachutist is 325 pounds. Tailgate drops are approved for special tactics teams, PJs, USAF survival
     evasion resistance escape specialists, U.S. Army Special Forces, USN (sea-air-land) SEAL teams,
     paratroopers equipped for arctic airdrop, other U.S. and allied special operations personnel, U.S. Army
     Quartermaster School (USAQMS), U.S. Army Airborne School, Yuma Proving Ground Airborne Test Force,
     and units for which a combination drop is their normal method of deployment.

     11-86. If a jumper is towed following a ramp exit and is to be cut free, the loadmaster partly retrieves the
     static lines to reach the towed jumper’s static line to cut it. If the jumper is to be retrieved, the loadmaster
     uses the TPRS or installs a CGU-1/B cargo strap (C-130-NSN: 1670-00-725-1437) about 5 and 1/2 feet above
     the ramp. The static lines are retrieved over the CGU-1/B strap. As the jumper is retrieved to the ramp area,
     the jumpmaster and safety personnel gain physical control of the jumper. The jumper is pulled into the aircraft
     (under the strap) as the loadmaster relieves tension from the static line retriever cable. The jumper is moved
     all the way forward and is seated; they do not jump again.

                                                 WARNING

                    The TPRS shall not be used during parachutist retrieval through
                    the ramp and door.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  213

Chapter 11

     11-87. Thread the hook end of the 5,000-pound tie-down strap, front to rear, around the right/left vertical
     support member at framework support (FS) 840, approximately 5 and 1/2 feet above the ramp in the joint
     precision airdrop system position. Attach the hook end into the strap and draw taut. Run the ratchet end of
     the strap across the ramp and thread it, front to rear, around the opposite vertical support member at FS 840.
     Remove all slack from the strap and attach the ratchet end to any convenient tie down ring forward of FS 840.
     Ratchet the strap until taut.

             Note. For aircraft with tie down rings installed at FS 847 (waterline 208), the 5,000-pound
             tie-down strap may be installed by attaching the hook end of the strap to the sidewall ring at FS 847
             on the same side as the towed parachutist with the hook facing forward.

     11-88. Hook the ratchet end of the strap to the opposite sidewall ring at FS 847, remove all the slack from
     the strap, and ratchet the strap until taut. The strap is premeasured prior to pre-slowdown and excess strap is
     taped. Using the static line retriever, retrieve the static lines over the strap and as the parachutist is pulled up
     to the ramp, bring the parachutist into the aircraft by hand underneath the strap.

                                                 WARNING

                    The last 5 feet are the most crucial for the towed parachutist. An
                    oscillating parachutist usually strikes the aircraft headfirst. If the
                    parachutist is oscillating violently, stop the retrieval momentarily
                    to allow stabilization, and then continue with retrieval. Repeat
                    these steps as required.

             Note. After the parachutist is pulled up to the ramp and is being controlled by the jumpmaster, the
             safety observer or loadmaster slightly unwinds the static line retriever to relieve tension on the
             line so the parachutist can be brought into the aircraft.

                                                 WARNING

                    The towed jumper must remain in a tight body position and
                    protect the ripcord handle with both hands. Inadvertent activation
                    of the reserve while being towed may be fatal or cause serious
                    injury to the jumper.

MODIFICATIONS TO TOWED JUMPER PROCEDURES

     11-89. If the towed jumper procedures in paragraphs 10-75 through 10-87 must be modified, jumpmasters
     are responsible for the safety and deployment of all jumpers as long as they are onboard the aircraft. No
     additional jumpmasters or safeties are required to remain onboard the aircraft unless specified in the jumping
     unit’s airborne SOPs.
     11-90. If all jumpers have exited, those actions described as jumpmaster responsibilities are accomplished
     by the loadmaster(s). The aircrew is responsible for all equipment left onboard the aircraft by the jump unit
     until it can be retrieved or turned over to the unit concerned.

                                                                                              Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

C-17A GLOBEMASTER III (PRACTICAL WORK INSIDE THE AIRCRAFT)

     11-91. The universal static line (USL) 5-foot extension is required when jumping the C-17A.
     (See TM 10-1670-272-23&P/NAVSEA-SS400-AS-MMI-010&P for more information.) Time warnings
     include the following:

          • TWO-HOUR, TWENTY-MINUTE TIME WARNING—this is used only on in-flight rigging
                missions.

          • TWENTY-MINUTE TIME WARNING—at the 20-minute time warning, all in-flight rigging is
                complete:
                 All jumpers are alert with helmets fastened.
                 Door bundles are positioned in front of the paratroop doors, inspected, and hooked up to the
                     outboard anchor line cable.
                 Special items of equipment are attached to their respective jumpers and inspected.

             Note. The 20-minute time warning may be increased to 30 minutes aboard the C-17A if the
             jumpmasters need more time to accomplish their duties.

          • TEN-MINUTE TIME WARNING—the aircrew turns on the jump caution lights and then notifies
                the jumpmaster that the inspections are complete:
                 The jumpmasters hook up to their respective inboard anchor line cable and position themselves
                     in front of the wind deflector control panel before beginning to issue jump commands.
                 If both doors are used on one pass, then both jumpmasters issue the commands at the same time.

             Note. The 10-minute time warning may be increased to 15 minutes aboard the C-17A if the
             jumpmasters need more time to accomplish their duties.

JUMP COMMANDS

     11-92. Jump commands are given in the following sequence:
          • GET READY—jumpers undo their seatbelts.
          • OUTBOARD PERSONNEL, STAND UP—all outboard jumpers stand, place their seatbelts in their
                seats, and push in the seats to retract them to the raised position.

             Note. This allows the jumpers to use the handhold straps on the cargo wall, if needed and assists
             in keeping the seatbelts off the floor, reducing tripping hazards.

          • INBOARD PERSONNEL, STAND UP—all inboard jumpers stand and place their seatbelts in their
                seats (the inboard seats do not fold).

     11-93. If time permits, it is recommended after the jumpers stand that safety personnel inspect the following
     items for each jumper while moving forward (toward the cockpit) in the aircraft:

          • Stow the troop cargo seating, if necessary.
          • Assist jumpers in tightening down the appropriate adjustable leg straps and securing them in the

                appropriate webbing retainer.

             Note. Safeties must be alert for any excess webbing that is loose or misrouted and correct the
             situation.

          • HOOK UP:
                 C-17—27 jumpers per outboard anchor line cable.
                 C-17—24 jumpers per inboard anchor line cable.

Chapter 11

             Note. The outboard anchor cable can be utilized for 27 jumpers on each side. Once the centerline
             seats are added, the inboard cable is also installed (which accommodates 24 jumpers, up to
             51 jumpers, and two bundles can be dropped from each paratroop door).

                                                 CAUTION

                    All jumpers on the aircraft must enforce ripcord handle awareness at all
                    times. Once the USLM is hooked up to the anchor line cable, the
                    nonstatic-line hand protects or cover the ripcord handle.

          • CHECK STATIC LINES—the last two jumpers turn toward the skin of the aircraft:
                 The second to last jumper checks the last jumper’s USLM.
                 Each jumper checks the USLM of the jumper to their front.

     11-94. Once the safety has reached the last jumper and after the command, CHECK STATIC LINES, they
     begin their return to the aft end of the aircraft. While moving towards the paratroop door, the safety checks
     and inspects with both hands and eyes:

          • Safeties check each jumper’s USLM and ensure the USL snap hook is properly secured to the proper
                anchor line cable with the opening gate facing towards the skin of the aircraft.

          • Safeties trace down the USLM to the jumper’s four in the hand two below bight, ensuring it is held
                at eye level, and they are not covering the double-sewn portion.

          • Safeties trace the USLM over the jumper’s shoulder, ensuring it is not misrouted, then continue to
                trace the USLM to the first stow.

          • Safeties visually inspect the remainder of the USLM:
                 Ensure it is properly stowed to the pack tray.
                 Ensure the main curved pin protector flap is properly stowed in the tuck flap and not routed
                     over any portion of the USLM.

          • Safeties stow any excess static line in the static line slack retainer band so that each static line is—
                 Taut from the jumper’s bight to the pack tray.
                 Not taut to the point where the excess static line loop hangs below the main curved pin protector
                     flap.

          • If a safety or any member of the jumpmaster team determines that a jumper’s USLM is not stowed
                in the proper manner, that jumper does not exit the aircraft.

          • Safeties remind all jumpers to make eye-to-eye contact and hand their static line to the safety.

                                                 CAUTION

                    All jumpers on the aircraft must enforce ripcord handle awareness at all
                    times. Once the USLM is hooked up to the anchor line cable, the
                    nonstatic-line hand protects or covers the ripcord handle.

          • CHECK EQUIPMENT—jumpmasters lean left then lean right and observe the stick of jumpers as
                they check their equipment:
                 Once all movement has ceased, both jumpmasters give each other a thumbs-up.
                 This tells the other jumpmaster that their jumper’s equipment is good, and they are ready to
                     proceed.
                 After the thumbs-up has been issued, both jumpmasters check their own equipment.

          • SOUND OFF FOR EQUIPMENT CHECK—this command is passed from the forward to the aft
                portion of the aircraft by each jumper.

             Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

11-95.  The aircrew completes its 6-minute slowdown checklist:
     •    Aircraft deck is set between 6 and 7 degrees.
     •    Aircraft slows to a drop speed of 130 knots (+/- 3 knots indicated airspeed).
     •    Air deflectors are deployed and troop doors are opened.
     •    The loadmasters give control of the doors to the jumpmasters and take a position between both jump
          doors.
     •    Once the safety and T.I. of the paratroop door is complete, the loadmaster informs the jumpmasters,
          ARMY, YOUR DOOR.
     •    The jumpmaster needs to confirm through the loadmaster, the aircraft has slowed to drop speed
          before assuming control of the paratroop door.
     •    This signal can be predetermined during the air mission briefing or aircrew and jumpmaster briefing
          before flight.

Note. Jumpmasters do not assume control of the aircraft paratroop door until the loadmaster has
confirmed the aircraft has slowed to 130 knots indicated airspeed.

DOOR SAFETY CHECK

     11-96. After both jumpmasters receive, ALL OKAY, JUMPMASTER, from the No. 1 jumper, the AJM gives
     the PJM a thumbs-up or verbally informs (or both) the PJM by saying ALL OKAY, JUMPMASTER. Both
     jumpmasters back up and regain control of their USLM using the hand respective to the door they are jumping
     from, (right door, right hand, left door, left hand) ensuring that the USLM is not misrouted under their
     shoulder. The safety can assist the jumpmaster in securing their USLM. The jumpmasters then turn towards
     the skin of the aircraft, remove the incorporated twist, and reestablish a proper bight. The jumpmaster
     assumes the No. 1 position and inspects their USLM from the USL snap hook until it disappears over their
     shoulder and then sounds off with NUMBER ONE JUMPER CHECK MY STATIC LINE. After completing
     the No. 1 jumper’s USLM check, the safety inspects the jumpmaster’s USLM. Once the safety or T.I. of the
     paratroop door is complete, the loadmaster informs the jumpmasters by saying ARMY, YOUR DOOR, and
     the following occurs:

          • The safety inspects the jumpmaster’s ripcord assembly to ensure the tuck tabs are in place and the
                T-11 reserve inserts are installed properly, before the jumpmaster assumes control of the jump door.

          • The safety then prepares to take control of the jumpmaster’s USLM.
          • Safety personnel position themselves near the trail edge of the paratroop door, and the jumpmaster

                secures the lead edge of the paratroop door with the nonstatic-line hand.
          • The jumpmaster hands the safety their USLM and sounds off with SAFETY CONTROL MY

                STATIC LINE.
          • The safety controls the USLM for the jumpmaster as they perform the door safety check in the

                following manner:
                 The safety controls the jumpmaster’s USLM by grasping it with one hand above and one hand

                     below their bight.
                 They keep the USLM taut between their hands, ensuring no excessive slack is impeding the

                     jumpmaster or causing a safety hazard.
                 The trail hand should be held high near the USL snap hook and the lead hand held low in the

                     vicinity of the jumpmaster’s pack tray.
                 Both hands should be formed in knife cutting edges, palms facing outward, fingertips pointed

                     skyward, with the USLM secured between their palm and thumb.
                 Securing the USLM in this manner allows the safety to release the jumpmaster’s USLM easily

                     in the event the jumpmaster prematurely exits the paratroop door.

             Note. The jumpmaster must ensure the safety has positive control of the USLM before moving
             toward the paratroop door.

Chapter 11

TROOP DOOR UP LOCK, TRAIL EDGE OF THE TROOP DOOR, AND AIR DEFLECTOR

     11-97. With the trail hand, the jumpmaster grasps the troop door lifting bar and then pulls it down to ensure
     it is seated on the door up lock. Once the physical check has been completed, a visual inspection of the door
     up lock gauge verifies that it is in the locked position. Then place the trail hand on the trail edge of the
     paratroop door.

                                                CAUTIONS

                    All jumpmasters performing duties on a C-17A Globemaster III aircraft
                    must be able to conduct a paratroop door check while maintaining three
                    points of contact with the aircraft deck. This check requires the
                    jumpmaster to attain an 84-inch reach. Jumpmasters must be evaluated
                    by their unit prior to performing any duties on this airframe.
                    All jumpers on the aircraft must enforce ripcord handle awareness at all
                    times. Once the USLM is hooked up to the anchor line cable, the
                    nonstatic-line hand protects or covers the ripcord handle.

     11-98. With the lead hand, the jumpmaster starts at the 12 o’clock position and traces across the top down
     the trail edge of the paratroop door and across to the 6 o’clock position (middle of the jump platform), then
     back up to the 12 o’clock of the door to ensure no sharp or protruding edges exist. Then they secure a
     handhold with their lead hand by grasping the troop door guide or the handhold provided on the lead edge of
     the door. If for any reason the jumpmaster’s hand breaks contact with the trail edge of the door, the
     jumpmaster must begin the trace of the door over at the top of the door.

     11-99. The jumpmaster leans towards the trail edge of the door while looking in the direction of flight and
     ensures the air deflector is properly deployed.

             Note. To check the air deflector, the jumpmaster can visually inspect the interior angle gauge and
             verify the wind deflector is at 35 degrees (+/- 5 degrees), then rotate into the paratroop door.

INITIAL OUTSIDE AIR SAFETY CHECK

     11-100. The jumpmaster places their lead hand inside the handle and secures the trail edge of the paratroop
     door with their trail hand. They walk out onto the jump platform, with both feet on the jump platform, and
     stand outside the aircraft locking both elbows out. From this stable position, the jumpmaster visually conducts
     a down-and-behind air-safety check. Once the initial clear to the rear is complete, the jumpmaster returns to
     the relaxed door position and looks at the jumpers, then the safety, comes to a rest position, and waits for the
     1-minute reference point.

             Note. Jumpmasters are encouraged to conduct checks in all cardinal directions to maintain the best
             situational awareness.

     11-101. Once the doors are open and the jumpmasters are conducting their door checks, safeties have all the
     jumpers close in tight, reducing all the jumper interval between the No. 1 jumper and the paratroop door.
     Once room permits, all jumpers extend their arms before moving. Jumpers maintain the proper interval.

     11-102. The jumpmaster locks out their elbows to conduct outside air safety checks properly, and the safety
     also locks out their elbows while checking for towed jumpers after each pass.

11-103. The loadmaster should relay time warnings (see table 11-1) to the jumpmaster or safety by using
hand signals. The exact hand signals that must be coordinated between the jumpmaster and loadmaster during
the aircrew brief are as follows:

     • A 1-minute time warning—with the elbow locked out, the index finger extended vertically.
     • A 30-second time warning—with the elbow locked out, the index finger and thumb held closely

          together.

                                             WARNING

             Do not sacrifice safety for time. Complete the full inspection of
             each jumper’s USLM. If the inspection cannot be completed in
             time, the pass is aborted. An improperly routed USLM can cause
             death or serious injury.

  Note. Jumpmasters do not issue the command of STANDBY until the amber light is on.

• STANDBY—once the jumpmasters rotate back into the aircraft and cover their ripcord handles with
     their trail hand, they give the thumbs-up signal to each other:
      The jumpmasters look at the jump caution lights to ensure the amber light is on, which
          illuminates at 30 seconds prior to the green light, based off the CARP.
      Once the amber light is on, the jumpmaster then issues the command of STANDBY.
      Starting at the shoulders with the elbows bent, the jumpmaster extends and joins their index and
          middle fingers, curling the remaining fingers and thumb of each hand toward the palm.
      As they give the command, STANDBY, they extend their arms up and out to their sides, ending
          at a 45-degree angle.
      Jumpmasters then take a step forward with the inboard foot and rotate their body so that both
          jumpmasters are facing the skin of the aircraft, with the body bisecting the lead edge of the
          paratroop door.
      Jumpmasters must ensure they are not impeding either anchor line cable, then each reaches out
          with the trail hand and secure a proper bight in their USLM.
      The safety returns control of the jumpmaster’s USLM to the jumpmaster by forming it into a
          small bight, then assumes a position bisecting the trail edge of the paratroop door, ensuring they
          do not impede the flow of jumpers.

     11-104. Once the green light comes on, the PJM issues the ninth jump command, GO. Both jumpmasters
     give the physical and oral command of GO. This is executed by bending forward at the waist giving a sharp
     tap on the thigh or buttocks of the No. 1 jumper.

     11-105. The AJM observes the PJM and the No. 1 jumper. When the PJM issues the ninth jump command
     to their No. 1 jumper and the jumper begins to exit, the AJM immediately turns, acknowledges the green
     light is on, and then issues the physical and oral command of GO to their No. 1 jumper. This action needs to
     occur in 1/2-second to establish the proper interval between paratroop doors. Both jumpmasters ensure they
     are positioned to best control the flow of jumpers without impeding the paratroop door or the safeties
     controlling USLMs. The safety grasps each USLM with their lead hand, and passes it back to their trail hand,
     ensuring the USLM is firmly seated against the intermediate anchor line cable support.

     11-106. The jumpmaster team must have situational awareness of their jumpers once the green light comes
     on. Jumpmasters—

          • Control the flow, spacing, and interval between jumpers without impeding the flow of jumpers.
          • Ensure jumpers’ static line arms are extended once they begin moving.
          • Remind jumpers to make eye-to-eye contact with the safety.
          • Pause or stop the stick for any unsafe act or condition, fix the issue and continue to exit jumpers, if

                the green light is on.
          • Monitor the jump caution lights for the red light.

     11-107. Safeties are responsible for—
          • Controlling the flow of jumpers and USLMs without impeding the flow of jumpers.
          • Ensuring that there is a positive transfer of the static line between themselves and the jumpers as
                they exit.
          • Pausing or stopping the stick for any unsafe act or condition, fixing the issue and continuing to exit
                jumpers.
          • Watching for towed jumpers.

     11-108. After the last jumper exits the aircraft, the AJM transfers control of the USLM to the safety. The
     AJM takes up a good door position, reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green, and exits if the light
     is still green.

     11-109. The PJM transfers control of the USLM to the safety and takes up a good door position. Upon seeing
     the AJM exit, reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green, and exits if the light is still green.

11-110. Both safeties immediately conduct a clear to the rear for towed jumpers and give each other a
thumbs-up. They give a thumbs-up to the loadmaster(s) and help retrieve deployment bags. After all jumpers
have exited the aircraft—

     • The AJM transfers control of USLM to the safety.
     • The AJM takes up a good door position.
     • The AJM reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green.
     • The AJM exits if the light is still green.
     • The PJM transfers control of the USLM to the safety, upon seeing the AJM exit.
     • The PJM takes up a good door position.
     • The PJM reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green.
     • The PJM exits if the light is still green.

11-111. Both safeties immediately conduct a clear to the rear for towed jumpers and give each other a
thumbs-up. They give a thumbs-up to the loadmaster(s) and help retrieve deployment bags.

                                            WARNING

               At no time during airborne operations should the cargo ramp
               door be open when the troop doors are open. If this situation
               exists, all jumpers, including jumpmasters and safety personnel
               must be seated and strapped in, guarding the ripcord handle of
               their reserve parachutes. If Army personnel must work around the
               open troop doors, caution must be taken to prevent personnel
               from being swept out of the aircraft. Inadvertent reserve
               activation with troop doors and the cargo door open can cause
               serious injury or death.

             Jumpmasters must be prepared to initiate red-light procedures at any

DOOR BUNDLE PROCEDURES

     11-112. There are two different and viable door bundle procedures. The airborne commander decides which
     procedure they want to use and best support their ground tactical plan.

     11-113. The commander ensures that the jumpmaster team has rehearsed the door bundle procedure that they
     have directed to be used.

             Note. If the No. 1 jumper pushes a door bundle, the No. 1 jumper must be a jumpmaster (does not
             have to be current) and must have T-11 reserve inserts.

Method 1: Jumpmaster and Number 1 Jumper Pushing Door Bundle

11-114.      At the 20-minute time warning—
     •       Jumpmasters and safeties unlash door bundles and move them near the jump door.
     •       Once positioned, the jumpmaster attaches the static line of each cargo parachute to the outboard
             anchor line cable and inspects the bundle in accordance with chapters 6, 8, and 11.
     •       Once the safeties have checked the last parachutist, they return to the aft end of the aircraft and
             control the jumpmaster’s static line during their door safety check.
     •       After the final clear to the rear, the jumpmasters exchange thumbs-up and issue the command
             STANDBY.

Chapter 11

NIGHT OPERATIONS

     11-116. The PJM must remember that jumpers’ eyes require 20 minutes to adjust to lower light levels before
     night operations. Therefore, only red compartment lights or night vision imaging systems lighting are used
     20 minutes before drop time.

     11-117. This allows for physical adjustment and minimizes the impairment of a jumper’s night vision during
     the critical first seconds of a night drop. If the white light is substituted for the red light before drop time, the
     jumper’s eyes must readjust by turning on the red compartment lights for 20 minutes.

INCIDENT ON AN AIRCRAFT OR DROP ZONE

     11-118. Any incident involving life-threatening injuries or death, or incidents based on severity by the
     airborne commander and the drop ceases. Any medical treatment of injured personnel takes priority over
     preserving the jumper’s equipment or the aircraft. The jumpmaster team—

          • Ceases exiting jumpers.
          • Retrieves all deployment bags but do not unhook them from the anchor line cable.
          • Treats any injured personnel.
          • Does not tamper with any equipment or allow any jumper to de-rig, making every effort to preserve

                the aircraft.
          • Ensures everyone is belted into their seat and the aircraft immediately returns to the departure

                airfield.
          • Does not allow anyone to get off the aircraft until released by investigative authorities.

             Note. See chapter 24 for investigation procedures.

ACTIONS DURING RETURN TO DEPARTURE AIRFIELD

     11-119. Safety personnel assist the loadmaster in retrieving the USLMs and deployment bags. Once the
     USLMs and deployment bags are inside the aircraft, safety personnel detach the USLMs and store them with
     the deployment bags in extra UPRBs, 30 deployment bags per UPRB.

     11-120. While en route to the departure airfield, safety personnel get the name, rank, service number, unit,
     and reason for any alibi jumpers left onboard the aircraft. They also check the aircraft for any jumping unit
     equipment that was left onboard for turn-in to the DACO, collect trash and airsickness bags.

     11-121. Before leaving, assist the aircrew in reconfiguring the aircraft by reinstalling all necessary seats and
     seat belts if subsequent lifts are planned. This assists the USAF to be ready for any additional training or
     follow on missions they may have to support.

     11-122. At the departure airfield, safety personnel escort all personnel left aboard the aircraft, including jump
     refusals, to the DACO according to the unit SOP. Safety personnel also turn over any unit or personal
     equipment left aboard the aircraft and complete any necessary paperwork to the DACO according to the unit
     SOP.

C-27J SPARTAN (PRACTICAL WORK INSIDE THE AIRCRAFT)

     11-123. Time warnings include the following:                                                    rigging

          • TWO-HOUR TWENTY-MINUTE TIME WARNING—this is used only on in-flight
               missions.

          • TWENTY-MINUTE TIME WARNING—at the 20-minute time warning:
                All in-flight rigging is complete.
                All jumpers are alert with helmets fastened.
                Special items of equipment are attached to their respective jumpers and inspected.

     Note. The 20-minute time warning may be increased to 30 minutes aboard the C-27J if the
     jumpmasters need more time to accomplish their duties.

               Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

• TEN-MINUTE TIME WARNING—the aircrew turns on the jump caution lights and then notifies
     the jumpmaster that the inspections are complete:
      The jumpmasters hook up to their respective anchor line cables.
      They position themselves in the vicinity of the paratroop door before beginning to issue jump
          commands.
      If both doors are used on one pass, then both jumpmasters issue the commands at the same time.

  Notes. All jump commands and arm-and-hand signals conducted by the jumpmaster team are the
  same as outlined earlier in this chapter.

  The 10-minute time warning may be increased to 15 minutes aboard the C-27J if the jumpmasters
  need more time to accomplish their duties.

JUMP COMMANDS

11-124.  Jump commands are given in the following sequence:
     •
     •   GET READY—jumpers undo their seatbelts.

     •   PORTSIDE PERSONNEL, STAND UP—only the jumpers for that pass stand up, securing seats is

         optional based upon the unit SOP and mission:
          Seats should be raised and secured.
          Seats can be left secured down, causing all jumpers to execute a 90-degree turn around the last

               cargo seat at the paratroop door (this method of exiting must be rehearsed).
          A 90-degree exit is vital due to the absence of an air deflector.
          Immediately after putting the seats up (if applicable), the jumpers must tighten down their

               appropriate adjustable leg straps.
          They secure the excess webbing in the webbing retainer when jumping with CE.

         STARBOARD SIDE PERSONNEL, STAND UP—only the jumpers for that pass stand up, securing

         seats (in the up position) is optional based upon the unit SOP and mission:
          Seats should be raised and secured.
          Seats can be left secured down, causing all jumpers to execute a 90-degree turn around the last

               cargo seat at the paratroop door (this method of exiting must be rehearsed).
          A 90-degree exit is vital due to the absence of an air deflector.
          Immediately after putting the seats up (if applicable), the jumpers must tighten down their

               appropriate adjustable leg straps.
          They secure the excess webbing in the webbing retainer when jumping with CE.

Note. When the jumpmaster and safety stand up, their seats remain down and locked. This
configuration helps ensure jumpers exit at a 90-degree angle perpendicular to the paratroop door.

11-125. After the jumpers are standing it is recommended (if time permits) that the safety personnel inspect
the following items on each jumper or complete the following while moving forward (toward the cockpit) in
the aircraft:

     • Inspect the waistband for proper quick release.
     • Inspect the ejector snap on the HPTLL for proper attachment.
     • Ensure the weapons case is properly attached.
     • Stow the troop cargo seating, if necessary.
     • Assist jumpers in tightening down the appropriate adjustable leg straps and securing them in the

          appropriate webbing retainer.

       Note. Safeties must be alert for and correct any excess webbing and loose or misrouted equipment.

• HOOK UP—for the C-27J: 13 jumpers per outboard anchor line cable (jumpmaster included).

          • CHECK STATIC LINES—the last two jumpers turn towards the skin of the aircraft:
                The second to the last jumper checks the last jumper’s USLM.

     11-126. Once the safeties have reached the last jumper, and after the command, CHECK STATIC LINES,

     checks or inspects with both hands and eyes:

                That it is attached to the anchor line cable.

                                                 WARNING

                    Do not sacrifice safety for time but complete the full inspection of
                    each jumper’s USLM. If the inspection cannot be completed in
                    time, the pass is aborted. An improperly routed USLM can cause
                    death or serious injury.

          • CHECK EQUIPMENT—jumpmasters lean left, then lean right and observe the stick of jumpers as
               they check their equipment:
                Once all movement has ceased, both jumpmasters give each other a thumbs-up, which tells the
                     other jumpmaster that their jumper’s equipment is good, and they are ready to proceed.
                After the thumbs-up has been issued, both jumpmasters check their own equipment.

          • SOUND OFF FOR EQUIPMENT CHECK—this command is passed from the forward to the aft
               portion of the aircraft by each jumper.

     11-127. The aircrew completes its 3-minute slowdown checklist:
          • The aircraft slows to a drop speed of 130 knots (+/- 3 knots indicated airspeed).
          • Paratroop doors are opened (if applicable).
          • The loadmaster or flight engineer gives control of the doors to the jumpmasters and takes a position
               between both jump doors.
          • Once the safety or T.I. of the paratroop door is complete, the loadmaster informs the jumpmasters

          • The jumpmaster needs to confirm through the loadmaster that the aircraft has slowed to drop speed

          • This signal can be predetermined during the air movement brief, aircrew, or jumpmaster briefing

             Note. Jumpmasters do not assume control of the aircraft paratroop door until the loadmaster has

                    The anchor line cable stop is in line with the trail edge of the jump door.
                    This is different from the C-130, in which the anchor line cable runs
                    further to the aft of the aircraft. The placement of the anchor line cable
                    stop decreases the amount of workspace for the jumpmaster, safety,

DOOR SAFETY CHECK

     11-128. After both jumpmasters receive, ALL OKAY, JUMPMASTER, from the No. 1 jumper, the AJM
     gives the PJM a thumbs-up or informs the PJM by saying ALL OKAY, JUMPMASTER. Both jumpmasters
     back up and regain control of their USLMs using the hand respective to the door they are jumping from,
     (right door, right hand, left door, left hand) ensuring that the USLM is not misrouted under their shoulder.
     The safety can assist the jumpmasters in securing their USLM.

     11-129. The jumpmasters then turn towards the skin of the aircraft, remove the incorporated twist, and
     reestablish a proper bight. The jumpmaster assumes the No. 1 position and inspects their USLM from the
     USL snap hook until it disappears over their shoulder and then sounds off with NUMBER ONE JUMPER
     CHECK MY STATIC LINE. After completing the No. 1 jumper’s USLM check, the safety then inspects the
     jumpmaster’s USLM. Once the safety or T.I. of the paratroop door is complete, the loadmaster informs the
     jumpmasters by saying ARMY, YOUR DOOR, and the following occurs:

          • The safety inspects the jumpmaster’s ripcord assembly to ensure—
                 The tuck tabs are in place.
                 The T-11 reserve parachute inserts are installed properly before the jumpmaster assumes control
                     of the jump door.
                 The safety then prepares to take control of the jumpmaster’s USLM.

          • Safety personnel position themselves near the trail edge of the paratroop door.
          • The jumpmaster secures the lead edge of the paratroop door by only grasping the metal upper or

                lower medical evacuation (MEDEVAC) litter support bracket:
                 Jumpmasters hand the safety their USLM and sound off with SAFETY CONTROL MY

                     STATIC LINE.
                 Then the jumpmaster grasps the trail seat back support rail on the trail edge of the paratroop

                     door.
          • The safety controls the USLM for the jumpmaster as they perform the door safety check in the

                following manner:
                 The safety grasps the jumpmaster’s USLM with one hand above and one hand below their bight,

                     keeping the USLM taut, ensuring no excessive slack is impeding the jumpmaster or causing a
                     safety hazard.
                 The trail hand should be held high near the USL snap hook and the lead hand held low in the
                     vicinity of the jumpmaster’s pack tray.
                 Both hands should be formed in knife cutting edges, palms facing outward, fingertips pointed
                     skyward, with the USLM secured between the thumb and palm.
                 Securing the USLM in this manner allows the safety to release the jumpmaster’s USLM easily,
                     in the event the jumpmaster prematurely exits the paratroop door.

                                            CAUTION

            All jumpers on the aircraft must enforce ripcord handle awareness at all

             Prior to the airborne operation, the platform locking handle should be secured with HPT or

TRAIL EDGE OF THE TROOP DOOR

     11-130. The jumpmaster does not stomp on the platform at any time when conducting door safety checks
     and applies firm downward pressure to the middle of the platform with the trail foot to ensure proper seating
     of the platform. Place the trail foot on the center of the platform with the lead foot a comfortable distance
     behind the trail foot.

                                                 CAUTION

                    All jumpmasters performing duties on a C-27J Spartan aircraft must be
                    able to conduct a paratroop door check while maintaining three points
                    of contact with the aircraft deck. This check requires the jumpmaster to
                    attain an 80-inch reach. Jumpmasters must be evaluated by their unit
                    prior to performing any duties on this airframe.

     11-131. With the lead hand, trace the paratroop door starting at the middle portion of the top edge of the
     paratroop door and trace to the top of the trail edge, down to the jump platform, then back up to the middle
     of the top edge of the door. Once completed, secure a handhold with the lead hand by grasping the upper and
     lower litter support block.

                                                 CAUTION

                    The jumpmaster must be aware that without a wind deflector, the T-11
                    reserve ripcord handle is exposed to higher winds than with other
                    fixed-wing aircraft and could cause inadvertent reserve parachute
                    deployment. Minimize unnecessary exposure of the reserve parachute
                    to relative wind for extended lengths of time.

INITIAL OUTSIDE AIR SAFETY CHECK

     11-132. The jumpmaster leans out by bending forward at the waist 90 degrees, keeping both heels flat, elbows
     bent, and maintaining a firm grasp on the seat back support rail and upper and lower litter support bracket
     with both hands. The jumpmaster performs an initial outside air safety check down and to the rear of the
     aircraft for any unsafe conditions. Jumpmasters are encouraged to conduct checks in all cardinal directions
     to maintain the best situational awareness.

     11-133. Once the initial clear to the rear is complete, the jumpmaster returns to a relaxed door position and
     looks at the jumpers, then the safety, comes to a rest position, and waits for the 1-minute reference point. In
     the absence of reference points or checkpoints, the jumpmaster uses additional time advisories from the

228         TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010                                       30 May 2026

                                                                                              Jumpmaster and Safety Duties in Flight

     aircrew, which must have been identified during the air mission briefing. The jumpmaster relays time
     warnings to the jumpers by leaning back inside the aircraft, keeping their foot centered on the platform, facing
     the jumpers. The 1-minute and 30-second time warnings are called while giving the proper arm-and-hand
     signals for each.

                                                 WARNING

                    At no time does the jumpmaster lock their elbows out during the
                    outside air safety check. Doing so could cause an inadvertent
                    reserve parachute deployment.

ONE-MINUTE WARNING

     11-134. Once the jumpmaster spots their 1-minute reference point and is about 1 minute from the green light,
     or the safety passes along the loadmaster time warning to the jumpmaster:

          • The jumpmaster relays the 1-minute time warning to the jumpers by—
                 Leaning back and keeping their foot centered on the platform.
                 Facing the jumpers, extending the index finger of their lead hand and announcing, ONE
                     MINUTE.

          • The jumpers relay the time warning by looking over their shoulder closest to the skin of the aircraft,
                shouting ONE MINUTE.

          • The jumpmaster continues observing outside for the 30-second reference point, or until the
                30-second time warning is relayed from the loadmaster.

THIRTY-SECOND TIME WARNING AND FINAL CLEAR TO THE REAR

     11-135. Once the jumpmaster spots the 30-second reference point and is about 30 seconds from the green
     light, or the safety passes along the loadmaster time warning to the jumpmaster:

          • The jumpmaster relays the THIRTY SECONDS, warning to the jumpers by—
                 Leaning back, keeping their foot centered on the platform.
                 Facing the jumpers, extending the index finger of their lead hand, and announcing,
                     ONE MINUTE.

          • The jumpers relay the time warning by looking over their shoulder closest to the skin of the aircraft
                shouting, THIRTY SECONDS.

          • After the jumpmaster has called off the 30-second reference point, they immediately conduct their
                final clear to the rear outside safety check:
                 The jumpmaster leans forward 90 degrees at the waist, keeping both heels flat, elbows bent,
                     while keeping both heels flat on the floor of the cargo compartment.
                 The jumpmaster visually conducts a down-and-behind air-safety check.

                                                 WARNING

                    Door bundles are not authorized to exit the paratroop doors on a
                    C-27J.

                                                 CAUTION

                    The jumpmaster or the safety can call a NO DROP anytime they
                    determine something is wrong or unsafe.

Chapter 11

UNSAFE CONDITIONS OUTSIDE THE AIRCRAFT

     11-136. If the jumpmaster observes any unsafe conditions outside the aircraft, they notify the loadmaster by
     a preplanned hand-and-arm signal (for example, a cutting motion across the throat) that a NO DROP situation
     exists for this pass.

     11-137. Once the jumpmaster makes the final clear to the rear outside safety check:
          • The jumpmaster removes the trail foot from the jump platform and plants the foot inside the cargo
                compartment; releasing the paratroop door with the lead hand.
          • The jumpmaster rotates into the aircraft facing the jumpers and covers the ripcord handle with their
                trail hand.
          • The PJM and AJM make eye-to-eye contact and give each other a thumbs-up signal, indicating there
                are no unsafe conditions outside the aircraft, and they are ready to exit personnel.
          • The jumpmasters then release the trail edge of the door, take a step forward to the lead edge of the
                door, and the PJM issues the eighth jump command of STANDBY to their stick of jumpers.

             Note. The AJM waits and observes the actions in the PJM’s door. When they spot the last three
             jumpers in the vicinity of the paratroop door of the PJM’s stick, they face their jumpers and issue
             the jump command of STANDBY.

     • Each jumpmaster then reaches out with the trail hand and secure a proper bight in their USLM,
          protecting their ripcord handle with the nonstatic-line hand.

     • The AJM ensures their eyes are on the PJM before taking control of their USLM by looking over or
          under either shoulder.

     • The safety—
           Returns control of the jumpmaster’s USLM to the jumpmaster by forming it into a small bight.
           Assumes a position bisecting the trail edge of the paratroop door, ensuring they do not impede
               the flow of jumpers.
           Receives the first jumper’s USLM with their lead hand and secures it with their trail hand by
               pinning it against the intermediate anchor line support bracket.
           Prepares to control the next jumper’s USLM with the lead hand.

       Note. The placement of the jump caution lights on the trail-edge or aft of the paratroop doors may
       be difficult to spot and can cause the jumpmaster to take their eyes off the jumpers exiting the
       aircraft.

     11-138.  The jumpmasters and safety personnel take the following action:
          •
          •   Once the green light comes on, the PJM issues the ninth jump command of GO.
          •
              Both jumpmasters give the physical and verbal command of GO, executed by bending forward at
          •   the waist and giving the No. 1 jumper a sharp tap on the thigh.
          •
              The AJM observes the actions in the PJM’s door:
               When the AJM spots the last three jumpers in the vicinity of the paratroop door of the PJM’s

                    stick, they face their jumpers and issue the jump command of STANDBY.
               When the AJM sees the last jumper clear the jump platform in the PJMs door, they turn and

                    recheck their jump caution lights.
               The PJM is now observing the actions in the AJMs paratroop door.

              Both jumpmasters ensure they are positioned to best control the flow of jumpers without impeding
              the paratroop door or the safeties controlling USLMs.

              The safety grasps each USLM with their lead hand, and passes it back to their trail hand, ensuring
              the USLM is firmly seated against the intermediate anchor line cable support.

     11-139. The jumpmaster team must have situational awareness of their jumpers once the green light comes
     on. Jumpmasters:

          • Control the flow and spacing or interval between jumpers without impeding the flow of jumpers.
          • Ensure jumpers’ static line arms are extended once they begin moving.

          • Remind jumpers to make eye-to-eye contact with the safety.
          • Pause or stop the stick for any unsafe act or condition, fix the issue, and continue to exit jumpers, if

          • Monitor the jump caution lights for the red light.

     11-140. Safeties take the following actions:
          • They control the flow and spacing or interval between jumpers without impeding the flow of
                jumpers.
          • They ensure that there is a positive transfer of the static line between themselves and the jumpers as
                they exit.
          • They pause or stop the stick for any unsafe act or condition, fix the issue, and continue to exit

          • They watch for towed jumpers.

                                                CAUTIONS

                    Both the jumpmaster and the safety must be prepared to initiate red-light
                    procedures at any time after the green light has been illuminated.

                    Mass exit is not authorized for this aircraft. It is recommended that all
                    first-time jumpers be briefed planeside regarding the narrow size of the
                    paratroop door and the undisturbed high-velocity airflow immediately
                    outside of the paratroop door prior to their first jump on the C-27J.

     11-141. After the last jumper exits the aircraft, the AJM transfers control of USLM to the safety. The AJM
     takes up a good door position, reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green, and exits if the light is still
     green.

     11-142. Upon seeing the AJM exit, the PJM transfers control of the USLM to the safety. The PJM takes up
     a good door position, reconfirms that the jump caution light is still green, and exits if the light is still green.

     11-143. Both safeties immediately conduct a clear to the rear for towed jumpers and give each other a
     thumbs-up. They give a thumbs-up to the loadmaster or flight engineer(s) and help retrieve deployment bags.

OTHER PROCEDURES

     11-144. If a jumpmaster sees the jump caution light turn red, they raise their hand towards the jumpers and
     sound off with, RED LIGHT, RED LIGHT, RED LIGHT. No one touches or physically tries to stop a jumper
     who has transferred the USLM and is committed to the paratroop door. Jumpers are stopped only by an oral
     command; this reduces the risk an incident. If any jumpers try to exit on the red light, they are allowed to
     exit, except in the case of an unsafe jumper.

     11-145. The procedure for handling a jump refusal is outlined in this chapter. The C-27J is equipped with a
     TPRS and towed-jumper procedures are also outlined in this chapter.

             Note. It is a general rule that the jumpmaster or safety cuts away anything green (indicating
             equipment) and the flight engineer cuts away anything yellow (indicating static line). Towed
             jumpers indicate consciousness and that the reserve parachute is ready by maintaining a tight body
             position with both hands on the reserve parachute. This indicates the jumper is prepared to be cut
             away.

ARMY EMERGENCY BAILOUT PARACHUTE

     11-146. The AEBP is a lightweight emergency parachute with a 26-foot extended skirt canopy. The canopy
     is made from low-porosity material that is vacuum sealed to protect the main canopy from physical and
     environmental hazards. For parachute component parts and characteristics of each part, and serviceability
     checks can be found in TM 10-1670-332-23&P.

Chapter 11

PLANNED AND UNPLANNED EXITS

     11-147. There exists a likely probability of death or permanent total disability if the AEBP is used by an
     inadequately trained Soldier during an unplanned aircraft exit. At a minimum, AEBP instruction should
     include new equipment training before first use and a rehearsal of system use and emergency procedures as
     part of SAT prior to each operational airdrop mission.

     11-148. AEBP training should focus on body position after an unplanned exit, ripcord activation, actions
     under the canopy, emergency procedures, and landing procedures. The following are also recommended
     procedures for AEBP training and rehearsal:

          • Proper method to pull the ripcord.
          • Deployment sequence.
          • Body position.
          • Actions under the canopy.
          • Emergency procedures for collisions.
          • Emergency procedures for entanglements.
          • Emergency procedures for canopy activation inside the aircraft.

     11-149.  To properly pull the ripcord, personnel must take the following actions:
          •
              To activate, the jumper should grasp the ripcord grip (located over the left breast pocket)—
          •    With one or both hands.
          •    Pulling the ripcord downward (hard and fast) toward their feet and away from their body.
          •
              The jumper should pull the ripcord to arm’s length, ensuring it clears the housing, then, immediately
              bring arms close to the body.

              Jumpers scheduled to wear the AEBP should rehearse ripcord activation in conjunction with proper
              body position during SAT mock aircraft rehearsal.

              Immediately after donning the system, jumpers should identify the ripcord grip location and
              simulate ripcord activation.

     11-150. After an emergency bailout, the jumper manually pulls the ripcord handle, which removes the ripcord
     from the closing loop and initiates the parachute deployment process, allowing the spring-loaded pilot
     parachute to open the flaps and spring out into the air current. As the jumper falls away from the inflated
     pilot chute, the pilot parachute bridle cord pulls on the sealed canopy bridle cords. This opens the vacuum
     sealed bag, extracting the suspension lines, followed by the main canopy. Upon the deployment of the main
     canopy, a slider attached to the suspension lines slides down the suspension lines towards the jumper,
     reducing canopy-opening shock. The main canopy inflates.

     11-151. To assume the correct body position during an unplanned exit, place chin on chest, elbows into sides,
     feet and knees together, visually locate and place hand(s) on the ripcord grip, and then pull the ripcord.
     However, when bailing out of an aircraft at extremely low altitude (below 1,000 feet AGL), the most
     important factor is to pull the ripcord as soon as the jumper clears the aircraft, regardless of body position.

     Note. When bailing out of an aircraft at extremely low levels, the most important factor is to pull
     the ripcord immediately upon clearing the aircraft, regardless of body position. The minimum
     recommended altitude use of the AEBP during combat operations is 565 feet AGL. For airborne
     combat operations below 565 feet AGL, the jumpmaster and safety personnel should wear a safety
     harness anchored to the aircraft or a static line parachute attached to the anchor line cable in lieu
     of an AEBP.

     11-152. During descent, the jumper can use the steering handles located on the back side of the rear risers to
     maneuver the parachute in the desired direction of travel, to maneuver the canopy, and to avoid obstacles and
     other jumpers in the air. Jumpers scheduled to wear the AEBP should rehearse actions under canopy during
     SAT. After exiting the aircraft, jumpers complete the remaining four points of performance:

          • Check canopy and gain canopy control.
          • Always keep a sharp lookout and constantly compare rates of descent.

232           TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026
