TIME WARNINGS AND JUMP COMMANDS

     17-5. The 6-minute and 1-minute time warnings are given by the pilot to the crew chief, who in turn relays
     them verbally and by hand signals to the PJM.

     17-6. The PJM gives the following commands:
          • GET READY—all jumpers remove seat belts.
          • STAND UP—all jumpers stand up and secure their seats in the up position.
          • HOOK UP—with the assistance of the AJM, the jumper connects the USLM snap hook to the anchor
                line cable and takes a reverse bight.

                                                WARNINGS

                    The jumpmaster must ensure the jumper has T-11 reserve inserts
                    in place and a 5-foot USL extension attached to the USLM. Failure
                    to use a USL extension may cause personal injury from
                    deployment bag strikes.

                    The jumpmaster must ensure the jumper has a proper reverse
                    bight. If an improper reverse bight is taken, the USLM could
                    become misrouted under the arm and cause a towed jumper or
                    severe injury.

          • CHECK STATIC LINES—all jumpers check the routing of the USLM of the jumper to their front
                to ensure that it is not misrouted.

          • Jumpers Nos. 19 and 20 turn so that the USLM of the last jumper can be checked by No. 19.
          • CHECK EQUIPMENT—all jumpers check their equipment.
          • SOUND OFF FOR EQUIPMENT CHECK.
          • STANDBY—the No. 1 jumper assumes a standing position at the ramp hinge and the remaining

                personnel close intervals behind the first jumper.
          • GO—the No. 1 jumper walks off the center of the ramp and the remaining jumpers follow at

                1-second intervals.

     17-7. Upon exit of all jumpers, the crew chief or static jumpmaster recovers all USLMs.

                                                 WARNING

                    Jumpers deliberately walk off the ramp, which is lowered a
                    minimum of 11-degrees below centerline gauge. Jumpers do not
                    make a vigorous exit by jumping off the ramp.

                    Less than a 1-second interval between jumpers may result in
                    entanglement of jumpers and USLMs.

SAFETY PRECAUTIONS

     17-8. The static jumpmaster or safety personnel ensure that jumpers are hooked up consecutively
     (1 through 20), and that all seats are secured out of the way of the jumpers. The speed of the aircraft during
     jumps is 90 to 110 knots. The minimum drop altitude for aircraft with a 90- to 110-knot drop speed is 1,250
     feet AGL. Either the jumpmaster or AJM must remain with the aircraft to handle the deployment bags and
     towed jumpers.

     17-9. The jumpmaster spots the aircraft using the WSVC, VIRS, GMRS, or JSJR methods. The jumpmaster
     may spot from the crew chief door or the ramp if a safety is controlling the jumpers. If spotting from the ramp
     and jumping, the jumpmaster leads the stick and the AJM stays with the aircraft.

V-22 OSPREY AIRCRAFT

     17-10. The V-22 Osprey (see figure 17-4) is a tilt-rotor aircraft that consists of a twin-engine, twin-prop rotor,
     high wing, and twin-tail design with retractable landing gear. The airframe and prop rotor systems are
     primarily constructed of lightweight composite materials. The fuselage is designed to seat two pilots
     operationally, two crew members, and 24 non-airborne troops.

     17-11. The three-bladed prop rotors are mounted on gimbaled hubs on the ends of the wing. The
     counter-rotating prop rotors are 38-feet in diameter and powered by two turbo-shaft engines. The tilt-rotor
     design combines the vertical flight capabilities of a helicopter with the speed and range of a turboprop
     airplane, to allow aerial refueling and worldwide self-deployment.

PROCEDURES

     17-12. This section outlines the procedures regarding the conduct of airborne operations by USMC units
     from the V-22 Osprey. The PJM ensures that all jumpers have T-11 reserve inserts in place. The primary exit
     point for jump personnel and cargo is the rear cargo loading ramp.

             Note. Only over-the-ramp procedures are authorized for static line personnel parachute operations.

     17-13. The V-22 aircraft can fly in three modes: helicopter, conversion, and airplane modes.
     (See figures 17-5 through 17-7 through page 332.) Transitioning from helicopter to airplane mode takes
     about 12 seconds.

             Figure 17-5. V-22 Osprey helicopter mode

            Figure 17-6. V-22 Osprey conversion mode

     17-14. For static line operations, the V-22 is limited to airplane mode only, with a maximum drop speed of
     125 knots (+/- 5 knots) with a minimum drop altitude of 1,000 feet AGL. A total of 24 passengers can be
     transported to conduct parachute operations. All jump operations are over-the-ramp operations, which is the
     only egress point available to the jumper. A staggered offset file exit formation is used for static line
     operations with CE.

     17-15. Ensure that the pilot is briefed to expect rapid shifts in the aircraft’s center of gravity during stand up,
     hook up, and exit of jumpers. The PJM ensures that all jumpers have T-11 reserve inserts in place. Crowded
     conditions inside the cargo compartment could allow for the accidental activation of a reserve parachute,
     creating an extremely hazardous situation. During movement within the aircraft, the ripcord grip of the
     reserve parachute is protected by placing the right hand and forearm over the front of the reserve. This method
     allows the jumper to control the pilot chute and canopy in case of accidental activation.

SPACE LIMITATIONS

     17-16. The space limitations for the V-22 Osprey aircraft are described in paragraphs 17-17 through 17-20.
     A total of 24 passengers can be transported to conduct parachute operations.

     17-17. Multiple CDSs maximum gross weight is 4,950 pounds. Individual CDSs maximum rigged weight
     does not exceed 2,328 pounds gross rigged weight. The container footprint is limited to double A-22 or
     smaller. A single A-22-sized container height is limited to 60 inches as measured from the bottom of the
     platform to the highest point on the load, including the parachutes. Double A-22-sized container height is
     limited to 50 inches as measured from the bottom of the platform to the highest point on the load including
     the parachutes. Ensure the ramp is level and the upper ramp door is completely open to maintain adequate
     clearance between the load and aircraft when the load exits.

     17-18. When the MV-22 cargo release system releases the cargo load, it falls to the deck of the aircraft,
     presenting a tripping hazard to follow-on jumpers as they move towards the ramp to exit the aircraft. When
     conducting combination personnel and cargo airdrops in which the personnel follow the cargo out of the
     aircraft, unit commanders are required to implement controls designed specifically to mitigate the risks
     associated with this hazard.

     17-19. USLMs and deployment bags are manually retrieved by the crew chief with assistance from the
     jumpmaster immediately after the last jumper is clear. The USLMs and deployment bags are secured as soon
     as they are retrieved inside the aircraft. If the ramp is up, the USLMs can be removed from the anchor cable;
     otherwise, the static lines are not detached until the aircraft is on the ground.

     17-20. Crowded conditions inside the aircraft dictate that caution be used to prevent entanglement or
     misrouting of USLMs during the jumper’s exit. Each jumper is cautioned to watch the USLM of the
     preceding jumper and to observe all the USLMs trailing from the upper corner of the ramp opening. This
     precaution ensures that succeeding jumpers do not jump until the parachute of the preceding jumper has
     deployed, and that the deployment bag has trailed to the rear of the aircraft.

TOWED JUMPER PROCEDURES

     17-21. In the event of a towed jumper, the jumpmaster prevents any other jumpers from exiting and notifies
     the pilot. The jumper stays in a tight position and protects the ripcord handle. The jumpmaster ensures the
     jumper is securely attached to the aircraft and does not break free during descent. If the jumper is not securely
     attached, the jumpmaster attempts to shake or cut them free.

     17-22. If the jumper cannot be safely freed, the aircraft converts to helicopter mode and slowly descends to
     the DZ. A jumper can be lowered and landed safely on the ground while suspended from the MV-22. In the
     event the jumper cannot be lowered to the ground, once the hung jumper is at 10 feet or less above the ground,
     the jumpmaster cuts the jumper free.

STATIC LINE OPERATIONS AND SEATING CONFIGURATION

     17-23. The aircraft speed is 125 +/- 5 knots for static line operations. The jumpmaster controls the ramp level,
     but it is recommended to be placed at the seventh light setting, which is controlled by the aircrew. When
     utilizing the MC-6, jumpers use a 4-second count when conducting the first point of performance.

             Note. Airplane and conversion modes can only be used for military free-fall operations.

     17-24. Jumpers in troop seats should have the seat back webbing in the lower position (see figure 17-8 on
     page 334) and use only the lap belt. Jumpers may also be floor loaded (see figure 17-9 on page 334). In-flight
     rigging of paratroopers is authorized. Safety- and mission-essential equipment dictates the number of
     paratroopers to be airdropped in compliance with the MV-22. Jumpers can be seated on the floor facing the
     rear of the aircraft at a 45-degree angle split between the port and starboard sides of the aircraft. The jumpers
     are restrained by individual safety belts routed around each jumper.

JUMPMASTER AND SAFETY

     17-25. The jumpmaster can be either a static or a jumping jumpmaster. If static, the jumpmaster has
     communications with the pilot at all times. If jumping, the safety is required to have communications with
     the pilot at all times.

     17-26. The safety then relays all time warnings to the jumpmaster in addition to typical safety functions. All
     standard time warnings are observed. There are no jump lights located anywhere on this aircraft. All
     commands are the responsibility of the jumpmaster. The V-22 aircraft has unique connections for onboard
     communications. The jumpmaster or safety have to wear one of the V-22 helmets or have a modified helmet
     connection.

JUMP COMMANDS AND PROCEDURES

     17-27. Jump commands and procedures for the V-22 are as follows:
          • GET READY—jumpers respond in the same manner as for other fixed-wing aircraft; seat belts are
                also removed, reconnected, and stowed.
          • PORT SIDE PERSONNEL, STAND UP—the odd-numbered jumpers seated on the port (left) side
                of the aircraft stand up:
                 Jumper No. 1 on the port side is assisted to their feet by the AJM or safety.
                 Jumper No. 1 in turn assists the No. 3 jumper port side and so on.

                                                                                                                 Sister Service Aircraft

     • STARBOARD SIDE PERSONNEL, STAND UP—the even-numbered jumpers seated on the right
          side of the aircraft stand up, using the port side method for assisting jumpers to their feet.

     • HOOK UP—the open portion of the USL snap hook is oriented towards the skin of the aircraft,
          regardless of which cable is used:
           All jumpers hook up to the same anchor line cable, regardless of which cable is used and
                regardless of the seating arrangement.
           The elbow of the arm holding the static line is kept close to the body.
           The USLM is controlled by each jumper in a reverse bight at waist level in the outboard hand.
           The odd-numbered jumpers hook up first, then the even-numbered jumpers hook up between
                the odd-numbered jumpers forming a staggered stick of jumpers.

     • CHECK STATIC LINES—each jumper checks their own USLM from the anchor line cable through
          their reverse bight and traces the USLM until it disappears behind their back.

     • The jumper inspects the USLM of the jumper in front of them from the shoulder to the pack-closing
          tie.

     • CHECK EQUIPMENT—at a minimum, each jumper checks their—
           Helmet, lowering line, chest strap, ejector snap, both leg strap ejector snaps, and reserve
                parachute.
           If the jumper is jumping any special items of equipment, they inspect those items as well.

     • SOUND OFF FOR EQUIPMENT CHECK—jumpers respond in the same manner as with other
          fixed-wing aircraft.

                                            WARNING

               To ensure safety of jumpers, the aircraft ramp remains closed
               until all jumpers have sounded off for equipment check.

     • STANDBY—the static jumpmaster or safety gives this command and moves the No. 1 jumper to
          the centerline of the ramp.

     • GO or FOLLOW ME—personnel exit the aircraft at 1-second intervals walking off the centerline
          of the ramp:
           Jumpers do not execute an up and out exit off the ramp because the jumper’s head will strike
                the top of the clamshell door creating a safety hazard.
           Instead, jumpers walk off the ramp without jumping up.
           Jumpers bring their feet and knees together and place their chin on their chest to form a tight
                body position upon exit from the aircraft.

       Note. Jumpers in troop seats should have the seat back webbing in the lower position
       (see figure 17-8 on page 334) and use only the lap belt. Jumpers may also be floor loaded using
       the multiaircraft tether. In-flight rigging of paratroopers is authorized. Safety and
       mission-essential equipment dictates the number of paratroopers to be airdropped.

17-28. Jumpers hook up using a reverse bight, with the elbow of the arm holding the USLM close to the
body. They use caution when exiting the aircraft in relation to the aircraft’s upper ramp door, which could
pose a hazard to taller jumpers upon exit and use mandatory hearing protection during V-22 operations.

17-29. The safety must ensure the aircraft floor and ramp area are suitable for jumpers. Prior to takeoff, the
safety ensures all jumpers are secured and prepared for takeoff. If the jumpmaster is jumping, the safety
moves to the aft end of the aircraft and physically controls the jumpmaster’s static line. The AJM or safety
maintains communications with the pilots through the intercom system located in the aft of the aircraft and
relays all information to the jumpmaster.

     jumpmaster looks at the No. 2 jumper and gives the command, FOLLOW ME, and then they exit the aircraft.

     17-31. For jumpmaster-directed release, the jumpmaster may spot from either the ramp or from the front of
     the aircraft by positioning themselves between the pilots and looking through the windshield. The crew
     chief’s window cannot be used for spotting during static line parachute operations. Both techniques present
     challenges and advantages in their use; the jumpmasters decide which technique they use.

            operations prior to being assigned as the PJM on any V-22 parachute operations.

     17-32. The V-22 only supports over-the-ramp operations. The V-22’s interior is manufactured with a nonskid
     coating, which provides nonslip footing. The vehicle ramp extensions are removed.

     17-33. As soon as all jumpers are seated, the crew chief briefs them on aircraft safety, emergency procedures,

TIME WARNINGS

     17-34.  Time warnings include the following:
          •
               TWENTY-MINUTE TIME WARNING—jumpmasters check personnel and equipment:
          •     If CE is not already attached to the jumper, it is attached to the jumper at this time.
          •     Final onboard JMPIs are initiated, HSPR and leg straps are secured, and door bundles are given

          •         a final inspection.
          •     The ramp remains closed.

               TEN-MINUTE TIME WARNING—final onboard JMPI of all jumpers is complete:
                A verbal and visual 10-minute time warning is given to the jumpmasters by the crew chief.
                The PJM begins jump commands.
                The ramp remains closed.

               SIX-MINUTE TIME WARNING—all JMPIs are to be completed by this time warning:
                Jump commands through SOUND OFF FOR EQUIPMENT CHECK, are completed with the

                    ramp closed.
                Door bundles are moved to the hinge of the ramp.
                The ramp is then opened to allow the PJM to perform air safety checks and verify approach into

                    the intended DZ.

               SLOWDOWN WARNING—about 3 minutes from drop time:
                Jumpers are moved to the hinge of the ramp.
                The AJM or safety makes the final inspection of the routing and grip of the USLMs by the

                    jumpers.

               ONE-MINUTE TIME WARNING—the crew chief gives the jumpmasters a visual 1-minute time
               warning; the PJM alerts the jumpers and performs safety checks from ramp.

                                                Chapter 18

                           Nonstandard Aircraft

    This chapter contains aircraft descriptions, jumpmaster procedures, and aircraft preparation
    techniques for nonstandard rotary-wing and fixed-wing aircraft. The aviation supporting unit
    prepares the aircraft for equipment and personnel drops to include seat and door removal or
    installation and rearrangement of seat belts. Installing a field expedient anchor line cable is the
    jumpmaster’s responsibility. Aircraft preparation is usually accomplished jointly by the
    loadmaster or crew chief and jumpmaster. These aircraft are service tested and approved for
    personnel airdrop operations.

PROCEDURE MODIFICATIONS IN NONSTANDARD AIRCRAFT

     18-1. On some nonstandard aircraft, jumpers are required to utilize a control movement technique in the
     aircraft and assume a STAND IN THE DOOR position. The standard jump commands are modified by
     substituting the command, STAND IN THE DOOR for STANDBY.

     18-2. The control movement technique is a method of moving to the paratroop door without losing balance
     or tripping. As each jumper begins moving, they utilize a controlled movement technique (slow deliberate
     walk) and assume an elbow-locked position with the arm that is controlling the USLM. Jumpers place the
     static line control hand so that it is nearly touching the back of the pack tray of the jumper directly in front,
     which establishes the proper interval between jumpers. They do not place the static line control hand in a
     position so that it extends past the pack tray of the jumper in front of them.

     18-3. At the command, STAND IN THE DOOR, the jumpers use the control movement technique towards
     the paratroop door, and the safety takes control of the No. 1 jumper’s USLM. The No. 1 jumper ensures their
     arm is not entangled with the USLM and moves into the paratroop door so that the toe of their outboard foot
     is extended about 2 inches over the edge of the doorsill or jump platform, and their trail foot is about 6 inches
     to the rear.

     18-4. The No. 1 jumper keeps their feet shoulder-width apart. Their weight is equally distributed on both
     feet, knees are bent, upper body is straight, head and eyes are to the front, and hands are outside the aircraft,
     with fingers extended and joined. They are in a position of ‘coiled alertness’ and are ready to exit the aircraft
     without further weight adjustment. Their hands are not grasping the aircraft but are used to maintain balance.

     18-5. The No. 2 jumper is in the control movement technique position, roughly even with the leading edge
     of the jump door and facing the rear of the aircraft. Follow-on jumpers close behind the preceding jumper,
     using the control movement technique position to maintain balance.

     18-6. At the command, GO, the No. 1 jumper makes a vigorous jump up 6 inches and out 36 inches to exit,
     depending on aircraft requirements. The exit action is gained from the legs alone, and the hands are used only
     to guide the jumper. On some aircraft, the vigorous exit is essential to avoid hitting the aircraft or coming in
     contact with another jumper.

     18-7. The No. 2 jumper and all following jumpers use a control movement technique towards the paratroop
     door. The safety takes control of the jumper’s USLM and the jumper ensures their arm is not entangled with
     the USLM. The No. 2 jumper moves into the paratroop door, takes up a proper door position, and exits the
     aircraft without command, maintaining a 1-second interval between jumpers.

C-212

     18-8. The C-212 is a twin-engine, high-wing, multipurpose light transport designed for operations involving
     short, rough airfields. (See figure 18-1 on page 340.) The aircraft can transport 15 combat-equipped jumpers
     in the airdrop mode using the port door. Troops are loaded over the ramp.

JUMP COMMANDS AND SAFETY PRECAUTIONS

18-12.  The following jump commands are used with the C-212 aircraft:
     •    GET READY.
     •    STARBOARD SIDE PERSONNEL, STAND UP.
     •    PORT SIDE PERSONNEL, STAND UP.
     •    HOOK UP—on this command, the odd-numbered personnel hook up between the even-numbered
          personnel to form a continuous stick of jumpers:
     •     They hook the open portion of the USL snap hook facing inboard over the left shoulder.
           All jumpers take up a reverse bight.
     •    CHECK STATIC LINES, CHECK EQUIPMENT, and SOUND OFF FOR EQUIPMENT
          CHECK—these commands are executed in same manner as other fixed-wing aircraft.
     •    STAND IN THE DOOR (if a paratroop door exit) or STANDBY (if an over-the-ramp exit)—a
          proper exit position is taken by the jumper.
          GO—personnel exit the aircraft at 1-second intervals.

18-13. Safety precautions for the C-212 include the actions described:
     • Jumpers ensure that all seats are secured in the raised position when they stand to hook up.
     • During extreme air turbulence, jumpers take a short bight on the USLM to steady themselves.
     • Jumpers remain off the ramp while it is being lowered for over-the-ramp operations.

Note. To assist the jumpmaster in looking for the DZ, the troop door may be removed before the
airborne operation begins. The safety restraint harness is attached to the 500-pound tie-down
positions on the floor of the aircraft, out of the way of the jumpers.

18-14. The jumpmaster or safety ensures all personnel hook up properly. If the jumpmaster jumps last, they
must hook up to the center anchor line cable and exercise caution to control their own USLM and ensure it
does not become fouled.

       Note. On aircraft that do not have a working communication system with the cargo area of the
       aircraft, the following safety measure is recommended: one ring on the alarm bell signals the
       jumpmaster to look at the jump light or communicate with the cockpit.

18-15. When weapons cases are jumped from the paratroop door, they must be reduced to 36-inches in length.
When accompanying supplies and equipment are dropped from the paratroop door, the bundles must be
standard air delivery containers no larger than 40 by 24 by 36 inches.

18-16. When ramp bundles are dropped, either the 15-foot static line with drogue or the breakaway static line
may be used. When door bundles are dropped, the 15-foot static line with drogue is used with cargo
parachutes. When ramp bundles are dropped, troops may follow out the paratroop door. The jumpmaster and
safety or loadmaster push the bundles out.

18-17. Aircraft speed during the jump is 90 to 110 knots. When jumpers are jumping from the paratroop
door, the paratroop door may be opened or removed and set into the door recess provided on the ramp.

18-18. When conducting bundle operations from the ramp, the jumpmaster must close the paratroop door.
The paratroop door may be opened or removed before the ramp is lowered. The antenna, located beneath the
tail section, must be removed prior to ramp bundle operations.

18-19. Towed jumper procedures outlined in chapter 11 are followed for the C-212.

                       Chapter 19

             Airdrop Procedures

This chapter explains drop altitudes, airdrop methods, airdrop release methods, and personnel.

DROP ALTITUDES AND AIRDROP PROCEDURES

19-1. The DZSTL measures drop altitude in feet AGL from the highest point on the DZ (the highest field
elevation) to the aircraft. (See table 19-1.) In the case of combat (wartime) operations, airborne and airlift
commanders jointly determine drop altitudes.

             Table 19-1. Calculation of drop altitude in feet, example

             to the desired altitude of the aircraft, in feet.           +550 feet field
                                                                         elevation

             rounded up to the next 50 (for example, round 505 to
             550).

             Legend: AGL—above ground level; MSL—mean sea level

19-2. For airdrop altitudes by load and aircraft type for different types of training missions, see table 19-2 on
page 346. For minimum aerial delivery altitudes personnel, A-series containers, and heavy equipment drops,
see table 19-3 on pages 346 and 347.

19-3. The aircraft altimeter displays altitude in feet MSL, not in AGL (feet above the highest point on the
ground). The pilot might request the drop altitude in feet MSL. Calculate this by simply following this
example:

     • Obtain the drop altitude, which is the distance in feet from the highest point on the DZ (field
          elevation) to the desired altitude of the aircraft, for example, drop altitude equals 1,000 feet.

     • Obtain the highest field elevation in feet above sea level:
           Round this number up to the nearest multiple of 50 (for example, round 537 up to 550).
           For purposes of obtaining the drop altitude in feet indicated, use this number for field elevation.

     • Total the two numbers obtained to yield drop altitude in feet indicated.

Chapter 19

TYPES AND METHODS OF AIRDROPS

     19-4. The type of load determines the type of airdrop. The three airdrop types are low velocity, high velocity,
     and free drop. The type of airdrop normally determines the location of the control center. The airdrops are
     explained as follows:

          • High velocity—a drogue chute stabilizes and keeps equipment upright but does not slow the descent
                (for example, a 12-foot, high-velocity parachute on a door bundle).

          • Low velocity—a parachute slows the rate of descent for a soft landing (for example, personnel and
                cargo parachutes).

          • Free drop—cargo that has no device to stabilize or slow the rate of descent (for example, durable
                items such as clothing bundles).

     19-5. The three methods of airdrops are—
          • Personnel and door bundles—personnel self-exit, door bundles are pushed from the paratroop door,
                or aircraft ramp and door.
          • Gravity—the aircraft maintains a nose-high attitude (if required) and in-flight release of load
                restraints:
                 Allowing the load to roll out of the aircraft.
                 A rigging system may be used to initiate and accelerate load movement.
          • Extraction—an extraction parachute pulls the load from the cargo compartment.

                                                 CAUTION

                    During over-the-ramp combination airdrops (CDS and/or high velocity
                    followed by personnel), there must be a 3-second interval between the
                    exit of equipment and the exit of jumpers to avoid possible jumper
                    entanglement during over-the-ramp operations. The DZSO or DZSTL
                    must follow the procedures for heavy-drop operations but observe the
                    jumpers as they exit the aircraft.

     19-6. To ensure that the airdrop is safe, and that equipment and personnel can be recovered or employed to
     accomplish the mission, the DZ and adjacent areas should be free of obstacles. Examples of obstacles are—

          • Trees 35 feet or higher impeding recovery of personnel or equipment.
          • Water 4-feet deep and 40-feet wide within 1,000 meters from any portion of the surveyed DZ.
          • A high-tension wire that is carrying an active current of 50 volts or greater (which should be turned

                off prior to the drop).
          • Any other conditions that may injure jumpers or damage equipment, such as inactive electric wires,

                barbed wire fences, swamps, ditches, and gullies.

     19-7. The DZ should be sited at least 1,000 meters from a power line. If this is impractical and a power line
     is within 1,000 meters of any boundary of the DZ, then the DZSO must coordinate with the local power
     company to shut off the power to that line NLT 15 minutes prior to TOT. If this is impossible, then the flying
     mission commander, aircrew, and jumpmaster must assess the risk and consider at least the following:

          • Type of jump.
          • Jumpers’ experience.
          • Aircrew’s experience.
          • Ceiling.
          • Surface and altitude wind limits are required to approve, suspend, or cancel.

     19-8. To minimize risks further, the DZSO and jumpmaster should consider how they might alter the mission
     profile to raise or lower drop altitudes, change the DZ run-in or escape headings, or remove inexperienced
     jumpers from the stick. If possible, they should clearly mark power lines with lights, high visual panel
     markers or any other conspicuous marking.

DROP ZONES

     19-9. The unit must have access to and from the DZ to recover personnel, equipment, or both, or to conduct
     troop movement. DZs with no roads leading to them or those next to a river with no bridges are examples of
     impeded access to areas.

     19-10. Air routes to and from the DZ should not conflict with other air operations or restrictive terrain, or
     with man-made objects such as television or radio towers. Other considerations are—

          • No-fly areas (restricted operations zones).
          • Obstacles to the aircraft (man-made items).
          • The terrain above the DZ.
          • The enemy situation.

     19-11. The following information provides minimum peacetime DZ sizes when using fixed-wing and
     rotary-wing aircraft and must be adhered to unless a waiver is issued in writing according to service
     regulations. During contingency or wartime missions, DZ sizes may also be waived. However, size
     requirements remain a joint responsibility of the airlift commander and the airborne commander.

             Note. To convert yards to meters, multiply yards times .9144 (yards x .9144). To convert meters
             to yards, divide meters by .9144 (meters ÷ .9144).

formula D=RT. The minimum size is 275 meters by 275 meters for a single shipment for USASOC and other
service missions. See table 19-4 through page 352 for the CARP to determine size requirements for all CARP
DZs and GMRS/VIRS equipment drops.

AIRDROP RELEASE METHODS AND PERSONNEL

     19-13. The number and type of aircraft that delivers personnel and equipment usually dictates the type and
     composition of the DZ support party, which can be tailored for a mission.

             Note. The unit mission request for aircraft specifies the type of drop method to be used, such as
             CARP, GMRS, VIRS, or WSVC, and the composition of the ground support party (CCT and
             DZSO, DZST and DZSO).

     19-14. To ensure accurate delivery on the DZ, jumpmasters use four different airdrop methods. Each method
     uses various input from the ground and air in the calculation formula.

     19-15. The CARP is the method most often used in aerial delivery for conventional airborne operations. The
     CARP is computed by the aircrew (navigator) and it determines the release point (RP) from the air. The
     GMRS is computed by the DZSTL and it determines the RP from the ground.

352  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                  Airdrop Procedures

     19-16. The VIRS is one of the two methods used by services (USA and USMC) having rotary-wing and
     fixed-wing aircraft for small DZs, for dropping a specified number of personnel. VIRS is computed by the
     DZSTL; the RP is indicated by an oral command to the aircraft.

     19-17. The WSVC is one of two methods used by services having rotary-wing and fixed-wing aircraft for
     DZs for dropping a specified number of personnel. The RP is jumpmaster-directed and is the only method
     not requiring markings on the DZ.

     19-18. JSJR is used by USMC, USN, USAF Special Warfare, and U.S. Special Operations Command units
     only. The JSJR RP computation or ‘spotting’ may be used from all types of aircraft.

     19-19. To become operational, DZs require key personnel to be located on the DZ for controlling, marking,
     medical evacuating, wind readings, and malfunctions.

     19-20. The CCT and DZSO personnel are normally used in joint airborne operations when more than four
     USAF aircraft are used. (See DAFMAN 13-217.)

     19-21. The DZST consists of trained military personnel. It is normally used in small joint airborne operations
     involving four or fewer troop carrier aircraft. CARP, GMRS, JSJR, WSVC, or VIRS are used.

     19-22. Acting alone, without CCT support, the DZSTL operates DZs with a small number of aircraft and
     dropping a limited number of personnel. The airdrop release method used is CARP or GMRS, or, if
     rotary-wing and small fixed-wing aircraft are employed, VIRS or WSVC.

DROP ZONE SAFETY OFFICER AND SUPPORT PERSONNEL REQUIREMENTS

     19-23. When the USAF CCT is supporting an airborne operation, the DZSO is the airborne commander’s
     direct representative on the DZ and is responsible for the safe operation of the DZ. No personnel or equipment
     is dropped if the DZSO is not physically on the DZ. The USAF CCT and USA DZSO have specific duties,
     which are discussed in paragraphs 19-24 to 19-26.

             Note. The prerequisites to perform the duties of the DZSO are outlined in chapter 7.

19-24.  When advised of the appointment as DZSO by the airborne commander or their representative, the
DZSO    should attend an air briefing for coordination and should be furnished with the following information:

     •    Type of jump.
     •    Number of lifts, including any heavy drop, CDS, or door bundles.
     •    Type of aircraft and sequence of aircraft if multiple aircraft are used.
     •    DZ requirements (personnel and equipment).
     •    Unit SOP.
     •    Current AF Form 3823 (Drop Zone Survey), for the DZ being used.
     •    Airborne timeline.
     •    Number of personnel, heavy drops, CDS, and door bundles for each pass.
     •    Establish time and place for the DZSO party to linkup and convoy to DZ.

19-25.  The duties of the DZSO are as follows:
     •    Coordinate with the USAF CCT.
     •    Ensure the appropriate personnel and equipment are in place to support the airborne operation.
     •    Ensure the DZ is fully operational 1 hour before drop time.
     •    Ensure the DZ is opened through range control.
     •    Ensure the DZ is closed when accountability of personnel, air items, and equipment is completed.
     •    Before the drop, conduct ground or aerial reconnaissance of the DZ for obstacles or safety hazards.
     •    Collocate with the USAF CCT and take initial wind readings 1 hour before the scheduled drop time.
     •    Establish communications with the DACO NLT 1 hour before drop time.
     •    Conduct continuous surface wind readings NLT 12 minutes before the scheduled drop.
     •    Give the CLEAR TO DROP or NO DROP to the CCT (if present to relay to aircraft) 2 minutes
          before the scheduled drop.
     •    Monitor surface winds from the jumpers’ PI and at the highest point of elevation on the DZ.

          • A NO DROP situation exists when surface winds exceed the maximum allowable limits (13 knots)
                within 10 minutes of the actual drop.

          • Control all ground and air MEDEVACs.
                 Priority for airspace must be given to MEDEVACs.
                 This is particularly important when rescue or medical aircraft are involved, since they may be
                     delayed if follow-on airborne operations continue.

          • Ensure that any water obstacle is covered by a boat detail. A boat detail is required if—
                 The water obstacle is more than 4-feet deep.
                 The water obstacle is more than 40-feet wide.
                 The water obstacle is within 1,000 meters of any portion of the surveyed DZ.

          • Submit postmission reports, for example, DD Form 1748-2 (Airdrop Malfunction Report
                [Personnel-Cargo]); or AF IMT Form 4304 (Drop Zone/Landing Zone Control Log) to the
                appropriate agency.

          • Notify the airborne commander or DACO immediately upon notification of a parachute malfunction
                from the MALFO. The DACO immediately notifies the ALCE of a parachute malfunction.

                                                 CAUTION

                    Both the DZSO and the CCT have the authority and responsibility to
                    declare a no drop if they believe an unsafe condition exists. A no-drop
                    decision by either one is acted upon by the other without fail. It cannot
                    be overruled.

             Note. The CLEAR TO DROP or NO DROP that is relayed at 2 minutes does not indicate the
             final wind reading. If surface winds increase beyond authorized limits, a NO DROP can be
             relayed at any time during the drop. If readings exceed the limits, the DZSO must reestablish a
             10-minute window.

     19-26. A complete control group is required for airdrop operations involving multiple fixed-wing aircraft,
     for single aircraft operations on DZs more than 2,100 meters in length, or if there is at least 20 seconds of
     exit time (green light). If any three of these conditions apply, the following is required:

          • The DZSO ensures the ground support team is in place on the DZ 1 hour before the drop.
          • The assistant DZSO (not required for USN or USAF operations, however if present, must be a

                current and qualified DZSTL).
          • Two field litter ambulances or emergency medical service vehicles with appropriate supplies and

                medical support personnel; USMC, USN, and USAF require one qualified support person.
          • A senior medic, who should be positioned on the DZ for the best supervision of medical operations

                and must always have communications with the DZSO.
          • A MALFO with still and video cameras (see chapter 24 for MALFO requirements).
          • A parachute recovery detail with wood saw and tree climbing equipment.
          • Parachute turn-in detail with vehicles.

DROP ZONE SAFETY OFFICER EQUIPMENT REQUIREMENTS

     19-27. The following equipment requirements may vary depending on the airborne operation being
     conducted, including equipment for daytime and nighttime operations:

          • Radios:
                 One for the DZSO and one for the assistant DZSO (minimum).
                 The DZSO should have communications with the DACO, the aircraft, range control (if needed),
                     and internally with the DZSO control group (party).
                 Senior medic.
                 MALFO.

          • Two compasses—one each for the DZSO and the assistant DZSO.

                                                                                                                           Airdrop Procedures

          • Vehicles.
          • Military map of the DZ and protractor.
          • Road guards, if required.
          • Military police, if needed to control vehicles and spectators, or appropriate crowd control.
          • Equipment for daytime airdrop operations:

                 Nine panel markers (at a minimum).
                 One raised angle marker (RAM).
                 Red smoke grenades or identified means of nonverbal communication with the aircraft.
                 Signal mirror or other acquisition aids (only if prebriefed during aircrew mission briefing).
          • Equipment for nighttime airdrop operations:
                 Eleven white omnidirectional white lights (at a minimum).
                 One colored filter to fit one of the omnidirectional lights, ensuring the color and light position

                     is briefed on the DZSO or aircrew mission briefing.
                 One amber rotating beacon (if used, it must be briefed in the DZSO or air movement brief)

                     placed along the surveyed DZ centerline 1,000 meters from the PI or the trail edge of the DZ,
                     whichever is closer to the PI (see DAFMAN 13-217).
                 White flanker lights—if used must be briefed in the DZSO or air mission brief and placed 250
                     meters to the left and right abeam to the PI unless precluded by obstacles or obstructions.
                 If 250 meters is not used, the aircrew is briefed.
                 One red star cluster for every planned pass or other precoordinated no-drop signal.
                 NVD (DZSO, ADZSO, and MALFO).
                 Strobe light or other acquisition aid (only if prebriefed on the DZSO or aircrew mission
                     briefing).
          • Anemometers—services only use approved anemometers to measure surface winds during all
                personnel and cargo parachute operations:
                 The approved anemometers are the DIC-3 and the Turbometer.
                 The DIC-3 and Turbometer cannot be calibrated; they must be given an expedient check before
                     use.
          • Ensure fresh batteries are installed in the anemometer:
                 Check the anemometer in a no-wind condition such as in a vehicle cab or a building.
                 Turn on the anemometer and if any reading other than zero registers, the anemometer is not fit
                     for use and must be discarded.
                 Use a three-anemometer check by comparing the reading on three anemometers in identical
                     conditions and discard the one anemometer that does not read the same as the other two.

Types of Anemometers

     19-28. The DIC-3 anemometer (NSN: 6660-01-699-8944) is a handheld, compact, lightweight,
     factory-calibrated device approved for use during airborne operations. The DIC-3 uses folding cups to catch
     the wind and electronically display wind speed, but not direction. During use, it is critical that the cups are
     fully extended to ensure an accurate reading, and all component parts must be present and serviceable. The
     device is omnidirectional and does not need to be oriented with wind direction to provide accurate readings.
     Post-manufacture calibration methods are not available. The DIC-3 can depict wind data in knots, mph,
     kilometers per hour, or meters per second. The additional features of the DIC-3 are the ability to display peak
     wind velocity over a given period, and average wind speed over two time periods. The DIC-3 utilizes a
     nine-volt battery.

     19-29. The Turbometer anemometer is a small, lightweight, electronic wind speed indicator. It can also be
     commercially purchased. It does not display direction, but when turned into the wind, it depicts wind data in
     knots, mph, meters per second, and feet per second. For the most accurate results, the Turbometer must be
     oriented within 20 degrees of the wind direction, with the wind entering the rear of the meter. Because the
     Turbometer cannot be calibrated, conduct the same pre-operation and three-anemometer check as when using
     the DIC-3 anemometer.

             Note. The unidirectional anemometers must be held in the wind line with the wind entering the
             rear of the meter to ensure accurate readings.

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  355

Chapter 19

     19-30. Other anemometers not tested and recommended for use should be employed only after a deliberate
     risk assessment is completed. Regardless of the method or device used to measure DZ winds, the airborne
     commander is responsible for ensuring winds on the DZ do not exceed 13 knots during static line personnel
     airdrops.

Boat Detail Equipment (If Required, Unintentional Water Landing)

     19-31. A deliberate risk assessment conducted by the airborne commander dictates the required equipment
     needed for the airborne operation. For best results, equipment can be altered to accomplish the mission. The
     following personnel and equipment should be considered for boat detail:

          • One OIC or NCOIC and assistant boat operator.
          • Two boat operators for each boat—one primary and one assistant.
          • Recovery personnel for each boat—two (one can be a lifeguard and combat lifesaver certified) and

                all boat detail personnel should be strong swimmers.
          • Spotlight or NVDs for nighttime operations.
          • Recovery boat teams—each may need the following equipment:

                 Boat (combat rubber raiding craft or solid-bodied boat of comparable size) with operable
                     outboard motor.

                 Enough fuel or oil to complete the mission.
                 Life vest or flotation device for each boat detail member, and enough flotation devices for

                     jumpers (not to exceed the maximum capacity of the boat).
                 One life ring with an attached rope.
                 One radio with a spare battery.
                 One shepherd’s crook.
                 One grappling hook.
                 One long backboard to facilitate cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
                 One aid bag with resuscitation equipment.
                 One rope, 120-feet long.

Tree Recovery Detail Equipment (If Required)

     19-32. A deliberate risk assessment conducted by the airborne commander dictates the required equipment
     needed for the airborne operation. For best results, equipment can be altered to accomplish the mission. The
     following personnel and equipment should be considered for the tree recovery detail:

          • Ladder (12-feet minimum).
          • One wood saw capable of cutting through at least a 4-inch branch.
          • Nylon rope, 120 feet.
          • Two snap links.
          • Pole climbing equipment.
          • Safety belt and approved helmet.
          • Chainsaw.

                                                 CAUTION

                    Any personnel climbing trees with pole climbing equipment should be
                    familiar or trained with the equipment prior to execution of the tree
                    recovery. Personnel operating with unfamiliar pole climbing equipment
                    can seriously injure themselves from a fall, unsecured equipment, or
                    tree limbs falling on personnel on the ground.

             Note. These requirements may be supplemented based on the type of drop, size of operation,
             number of aircraft, number of jumpers, and obstacles on or within 1,000 meters of the DZ.

356  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026

                                                                                                                           Airdrop Procedures

     19-33. A partial control group can be used for airdrop operations involving single aircraft if less than a
     20-second exit time exists or if there is less than 2,100 meters of usable DZ. The composition of a partial
     control group includes the following:

          • DZSO (DZSTL qualification is not required).
          • Personnel to conduct wind reading from a single location on the DZ.
          • One medic (with field litter ambulance or emergency medical service vehicle with appropriate

                supplies and medical support personnel); USMC and USN require one qualified Navy corpsman.
          • MALFO with still and video cameras, binoculars, and NVDs for night operations.
          • Parachute recovery detail.

     19-34. The DZSO has operational responsibility for the DZ. In addition to the DZSO’s duties for DZs, the
     DZSO must also—

          • Be positioned at the personnel PI 15 minutes before drop time:
                 The assistant DZSO is at the highest point of the DZ or at a location determined by the DZSO
                     if the DZSO is at the highest point of the DZ.
                 For combination airdrop operations, the DZSO or DZSTL must follow the procedures for heavy
                     drop operations.
                 The DZSO or DZSTL relocate to the personnel PI to conduct personnel drops after the heavy
                     equipment drops have landed.

             Note. For heavy drop operations, the DZSO or DZSTL should be no closer than 300 meters from
             the heavy equipment PI and should not be positioned under the direction of flight.

          • Relay a ground weather decision and CLEAR TO DROP or NO DROP signal to the lead aircraft
                2 minutes before the drop for each pass.

          • During night drops—
                 Ensure all lights that are on or next to the DZ and are not a part of the DZ marking system are
                     turned off 5 minutes before drop time.
                 Ensure lights remain off during the drop, except those lights that mark obstacles.

          • Contact the pilot of the aircraft immediately after the drop:
                 Ask if any personnel or equipment did not drop.
                 The DZSO or DZSTL relays this information to the airborne commander or DACO for
                     accountable purposes.

DROP ZONE SUPPORT TEAM LEADER DUTIES

     19-35. In operations in which the CCT is not present, the DZSTL has overall responsibility for the conduct
     of operations on the DZ and represents the airborne and airlift commanders. The DZSTL assumes all the
     responsibilities normally associated with the USAF CCT and DZSO. The following are the DZST
     responsibilities:

          • DZSTs have the primary mission of supporting wartime CDS airdrops for battalion-size units and
                below:
                 The DZSTs mission during peacetime includes airdrops of personnel, CDS, and heavy
                     equipment for one to four aircraft operations.
                 With some exceptions, these primary mission airdrops are limited to day and night visual
                     conditions.

          • DZSTs also maintain the secondary mission of supporting other types of airdrops:
                 Wartime force projection and sustainment of personnel, equipment, and CDS.
                 Peacetime airdrops under IMC and visual meteorological conditions formation drops with four
                     or more aircraft.

                                               PART FOUR

DROP ZONE SUPPORT TEAM LEADER FORMULAS
           FOR GMRS AND VIRS DROP ZONES

This part discusses parachute techniques and drop zone activity.

                                                Chapter 20

                      Formulas and Computations

    Once the composition of the ground party and the selection of a DZ have been established,
    several technical aspects must be considered and planned for marking the DZ. These technical
    aspects are critical because of the data that must be used (ground, winds, drift distance formula,
    forward throw, and RP).

GROUND MARKING AND VERBALLY INITIATED RELEASE
SYSTEMS

     20-1. To apply the distance and time formulas to GMRS and VIRS, compute the DZ length for a specific
     mission by using the D = RT formula. (D is the required length of the DZ in meters; R is the ground speed
     of the aircraft in meters per second; and T is the time required for the aircraft to release its cargo.) To use this
     formula, some conversions and mathematics are required.

     20-2. To find the aircraft ground speed, convert aircraft airspeed (expressed in knots) to ground speed (meters
     per second). Do this by multiplying knots times 0.51 (knots by 0.51) (1 knot equals 0.51 meters per second).

     20-3. To determine the time over the DZ that is needed to release a jumper or equipment, use the following
     factors:

          • Allow 1 second for each jumper to exit the aircraft; do not include the first jumper (10 jumpers
                require 9 seconds). Mathematically, this is represented as 9 x 1 second.

          • Allow 3 seconds per bundle to exit the aircraft; do not include the first bundle (three bundles would
                require 6 seconds); mathematically, this is represented as 2 x 3 seconds.

          • Personnel jumping T-11 ATPS parachutes may exit both doors simultaneously. The door with the
                most jumpers is used to calculate the time required.

     20-4. For example, what length DZ would eight jumpers require when jumping from an aircraft flying at a
     drop speed of 90 knots? To solve this question, apply the following steps:

          • Step 1—solve for R (answer is expressed in meters per second): airspeed by 0.51 (90 knots by 0.51)
                = 45.90 meters per second.

          • Step 2—solve for T (answer is expressed in seconds): number of jumpers by 1 second (8 by 1) =
                7 seconds.

          • Step 3—solve for D (answer is expressed in meters): 45.90 meters per second by 7 seconds =
                321.30 meters:
                 Always round up to the nearest whole number.
                 Therefore, D = a length of 322 meters.

          • Step 4—always add a 200-meter buffer:
                 100 meters to lead ledge and 100 meters to trail edge for any drop involving personnel.
                 Therefore, 322 meters + 200 meters = 522 meters, the required DZ length.

     20-5. Solving the time formula (T = D/R) provides the seconds available to exit the jumpers over the DZ
     (time = meters divided by meters per second rounded up). If a DZ less than the required length must be used,

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  361


---

Chapter 20

     compute the flight time over the DZ to determine how much of the load can be released in one pass. Use the
     T = D/R formula: T is the time the aircraft is over the DZ in seconds, D is the length of the DZ in meters, and
     R is the ground speed (rate) of the aircraft in meters per second.

     20-6. Convert the aircraft’s airspeed (expressed in knots) to its ground speed (expressed in meters per second)
     as in the D = RT formula (knots by 0.51). Round up the answer to the next whole number.

     20-7. Divide the ground speed conversion number into D (the DZ length minus the 200-meter buffer for all
     drops involving personnel); this determines T. Any fractional answer is rounded down to the next whole
     number.

     20-8. For example, how many jumpers from a CH-47 (drop speed of 90 knots) can land on a 750-meter DZ
     in each pass? To figure it out, use the following:

          • T = Number of jumpers.
          • D = DZ length is 750 meters (given).
          • R = Airspeed is 46 meters per second (90 knots x .51 = 45.9; round up to 46).
          • Solution: T = D/R (D divided by R).
          • D/R = 750 meters - 200 meters = 550 divided by 46 meters per second = 11.9 seconds.
          • T = 11 seconds (round down).
          • 11 seconds over DZ by one jumper per second + 1 jumper (the first jumper exiting the aircraft does

                not affect the number of seconds spent over the DZ) = 12 jumpers, thus, 12 jumpers per pass can
                land on the 750-meter DZ.

WIND DRIFT

     20-9. Two means of determining wind drift are the WSVC method and the distance x constant x velocity
     (D = KAV) formula. The WSVC method (see figure 20-1) is used when the RP is determined from the air. It
     is normally jumpmaster executed and does not require markings to be placed on the DZ. Below are the
     procedures for WSVC:

          • Streamer drop—on the first aircraft pass over the desired PI, a streamer is dropped from the aircraft:
                 The aircraft then turns to allow the jumpmaster to keep the streamer in sight.
                 The pilot adjusts the route so that the flight path is over the streamer on the ground and the
                     desired impact point (in a straight line).

          • Count—as the aircraft passes over the streamer, the jumpmaster begins a count, stopping the count
                directly over the impact point:
                 They immediately begin a new count.
                 When that count equals the first count, the aircraft is over the RP for the first jumper.

          • Aircraft flight adjustment—the pilot then maneuvers the aircraft to fly along the axis of the DZ and
                over the RP:
                 Slight adjustments may be made by observing the jumpers as they land on the DZ.
                 Table 20-1 on page 365 shows airdrop altitudes for different types of training missions.

             Note. Avoid using this method for tactical employment, since the aircraft must make multiple
             passes over the DZ.

362  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                  Formulas and Computations

                      Figure 20-1. Determination of the release point by WSVC

20-10. The D = KAV formula is another method for determining the effects of wind on a parachute: D = drift
of parachute (in meters) from a given altitude; K = constant that represents the typical drift characteristic for
a type of parachute. These constants are—

     • 1.5 meters for cargo parachutes and heavy equipment.
     • 3.0 meters for personnel parachutes.
     • 2.4 meters for standardized airborne training bundles.
     • 0 meters for high velocity and free drop items.

20-11. A = drop altitude (expressed in hundreds of feet AGL); and V = velocity of wind. The MEW must be
used.

       Note. If an aircraft must be shut down for a long period, a wind drift indicator should be thrown
       at the last RP to ensure the RP is still valid.

20-12. For example, an aircraft drops cargo from 500 feet AGL with a surface wind of 10 knots. What is the
calculated parachute drift? (The parachute drift is calculated using the D = KAV formula.):

     • D = wind induced drift in meters.
     • K = wind drift constant for type of parachute.
     • A = drop altitude expressed in hundreds of feet (500 feet would be expressed as 5).
     • V = velocity of wind in knots (either MEW or surface wind measurement).
     • Step 1: K = 1.5 (cargo parachute or heavy-equipment constant).
     • Step 2: A = 5 (500 feet).
     • Step 3: V = 10 (10 knots).
     • Step 4: D = 1.5 by 5 = 75.0, or 75 meters of drift (any fractional answer is rounded up to the nearest

          whole number).

30 May 2026  TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  363


---

Chapter 20

WIND VELOCITY

     20-13. There are two types of winds that must be accounted for: MEW and surface winds. The MEW is a
     constant wind speed average from drop altitude to the ground. The PIBAL system determines the MEW. For
     surface wind measurements, see anemometer usage in chapter 19.

     20-14. The equipment needed to compute the MEW by the PIBAL method is as follows:
          • Helium source.
          • PIBALs (10 or 30 grams).
          • Clinometers or other devices for measuring from 0 to 90 degrees.
          • Balloon measuring tape to measure balloon circumference:
                10 grams—57 inches day, 74 inches night.
                30 grams—75 inches day, 94 inches night.
          • PIBAL lighting units (type 5) for night use (liquid activated lights).
          • Compass.
          • Conversion charts:
                10 and 30 grams.
                See table 20-1 and table 20-2 through page 366.
          • Watch with a second hand.

     20-15.  The procedures for measuring MEW using the PIBAL are as follows:
          •    Fill the 10-gram or 30-gram balloon with helium to the required size.
          •    Check the conversion chart for drift time to drop altitude (see table 20-1 and table 20-2 through
               page 366).
          •    Release the balloon and begin timing.
          •    Keep the balloon in sight.
          •    Once the required time has elapsed, determine the azimuth to the balloon with the compass and read
               the degrees from the drift scale.
          •    See the conversion chart and read down the angle column to the number closest to the angle on the
               scale.
          •    Read across the top of the chart (altitude in feet) to the drop altitude in use and read down this
               column until the two lines (6 and 7) intersect.
          •    Where the two lines intersect is the MEW at drop altitude, in knots. The direction of the MEW is
               the back azimuth of the compass reading that was taken at the same time as the angle measurement.
          •    MEW becomes the variable V in the D = KAV formula to determine the amount of drift in meters.

FORWARD THROW

     20-16. Forward throw is the effect that inertia has on a falling object. When an object leaves an aircraft, it
     travels at a speed equal to the speed of the aircraft. The jumper (or bundle) continues to move in the direction
     of flight until the dynamics of drag and parachuting takes effect.

     20-17. To determine the amount of forward throw for rotary-wing aircraft, divide the drop speed of the
     aircraft in half. This yields the forward throw in meters. (For example, an aircraft flying at 70 knots would
     have a forward throw of 35 meters.) To determine the forward throw for fixed-wing aircraft, the distances in
     table 20-3 apply.

DROP HEADINGS, POINT OF IMPACT, WIND DRIFT
COMPENSATION, AND FORWARD THROW COMPENSATION

20-18. For CARP operations, the navigator onboard the aircraft determines when the load is to be released
from the aircraft (when the green light is turned on and off). For GMRS and VIRS operations, ground
personnel determine the RP. (See figure 20-2 on page 368.)

20-19. Drop heading on all DZs depends on three factors—the long axis, prevailing winds, and obstacles on
approach and departure ends. The DZSO or DZSTL uses all three when the situation permits; however, the
long axis is the primary concern. With a GMRS, WSVC, or CARP DZ, drop heading can be obtained from
AF Form 3823. A circular or random approach DZ does not have a set drop heading. The mission commander
notifies the aircrew and the DZ commander of the drop heading to be used NLT 24 hours in advance of the
airdrop operation.

Note. On some DZs, predetermined drop headings must be used.

20-20. The location selected where the first bundle or parachutist should land is the PI. The PI should be
located along the DZ centerline. However, due to the tactical situation, the PI may need to be located near a
wood line. The DZSO or DZSTL uses a buffer zone of 100 meters on each side of the DZ during personnel
drops for safety reasons. The PI location for GMRS, VIRS, and WSVC is 100 meters in from the leading
edge centerline for personnel. The CARP PI is designated on AF Form 3823.

20-21. To compensate for wind drift, the DZSO or DZSTL moves from the desired PI into the wind the
number of meters calculated using the D = KAV formula. (For example, if drift equals 350 meters from the
PI, the DZSO or DZSTL faces into the wind and walks 350 meters in a straight line.)

20-22. To compensate for aircraft forward throw, the DZSO or DZSTL faces the back azimuth of the drop
heading and walks the appropriate forward throw distance to the RP.

       Note. A parachute’s K factor is based on the parachute’s flight characteristics, not on its mode of
       use. According to TM 4-48.04 (FM 4-20.142)/MCRP 4-11.3P/NAVSEA SS400-AD-MMO-
       010/TO 13C7-51-21, the K factor for the T-10 series parachute used in the cargo mode is the same
       (3.0) as for personnel drops using the T-11 ATPS parachute.

                                                Chapter 21

             Drop Zone Establishment and Operation

    Five methods may be used to establish or operate a DZ. Three of these require markings to be
    placed on the DZ through the employment of the CARP, GMRS, and VIRS. The WSVC and
    jumpmaster spotted jumpmaster directed methods do not require RP markings on the DZ.

COMPUTED AIR RELEASE POINT

     21-1. The CARP is used only by fixed-wing aircraft in conjunction with a CCT or qualified DZSTL. CARP
     minimum points of impact are shown in figure 21-1 on page 370 and figure 21-2 on page 372, and are as
     follows:

          • Personnel drops at the PI are—
                 300 yards (C-130 day, C-17 day or night, IMC).
                 350 yards (C-130 night or C-17 night pilot-directed airdrop) from the leading edge.

          • CDS drops:
                 From a C-130, drops at the PI are 200 yards (day) or 250 yards (night) from the leading edge.
                 From a C-17, the PI is 225 yards (day or night, IMC) and 275 yards (night pilot-directed
                     airdrop).

          • Heavy equipment drops at the PI are—
                 500 yards (C-130 day, C-17 day or night, IMC).
                 550 yards (C-130 night or C-17 night pilot-directed airdrop) from the leading edge.

             Note. On surveyed DZs, the PI for a particular type of load is predetermined. Its surveyed location
             can be found on AF Form 3823.

     21-2. The conditions for NO DROP are relayed directly to the aircraft in the following ways: red smoke, red
     flares, scrambling the code letter, removing the RAM, the absence of a planned signal, or verbal radio
     communications.

             Note. The type of marking used for NO DROP conditions is coordinated in the pre-mission
             briefing.

     21-3. Control center locations (location of the DZSTL) are the following:
          • Personnel and door bundle drops are normally located at the PI.
          • CDS drops are located 200 yards to the 6 o’clock position of the PI.
          • Heavy equipment drops are located 300 yards from the 6 o’clock position of the PI.
          • High-Altitude Airdrop Resupply System IMC, free drops, high velocity, IMC, or a ceiling of
                600 feet or less are all off the DZ.
          • For any non-personnel operation, the DZSTL uses the best vantage point off the DZ to observe the
                airdrop if it cannot be accomplished from the 6 o’clock position.

MARKINGS

     21-4. A marked DZ has a PI or RP marked with a precoordinated visual or electronic signal. Standard DZ
     markings consist of RAMs (the RAM is required for all Army conventional units and daytime CARP
     airdrops), panel markers, visible lighting systems, and light beacons. Virtually any type of lighting or visual
     marking system is acceptable if all participating units are briefed and concur. Night markings or visual
     acquisition aids may include a light gun, flares, fire pots, railroad fuses, flashlights, chemical lights, and IR
     lighting systems. Electronic navigation aids markings may be used for day or night operations and are placed
     as directed by mission requirements.

     21-5. During daytime CARP operations, the PI is marked with a RAM or block letter. All conventional Army
     units use the RAM as the minimum and required markings. If authentication is required, a block letter is used
     in conjunction with the RAM. Authorized letters for PI markings are A, C, J, R, and S. The block letters H
     and O are authorized for random or circular approach DZs. The block letters should be aligned with the
     surveyed DZ axis or with the aircraft line-of-flight, if different from the survey. The minimum size for block
     letters is 35 feet by 35 feet and consists of at least nine marker panels.

     21-6. During night operations, the PI is marked with a block letter. The minimum size is 35 feet by 35 feet
     and consists of at least nine omnidirectional white lights with a recommended minimum output rating of
     15 candela. The apex of the block letter is located on the PI. If used, flanker lights are omnidirectional white
     lights, located 250 meters left and right abeam the PI. When used, the amber trailing edge beacon is placed
     along the surveyed DZ centerline 1,000 meters from the PI, or at the DZ trailing edge, whichever is closer to
     the PI. During pre-mission coordination for personnel drops, aircrews identify their trailing edge beacon
     requirements to CCT or DZSO. For all airdrops, the DZ identification is coordinated and briefed to the ground
     party and aircrews.

370         TC 3-21.220/NAVAIR AS-400TC-TRN-010  30 May 2026


---

                                                                                             Drop Zone Establishment and Operation

             Note. Flanker lights and the amber rotating beacon are optional and can be used when coordinated
             with aircrews.

     21-7. When mission requirements dictate and aircrews are qualified and equipped, IR lights may be
     substituted for overt lights using the DZ marking patterns specified earlier in this chapter.

GROUND MARKING RELEASE SYSTEM

     21-8. The GMRS uses markings known as the four-panel inverted L, six-panel T, or seven panel H. The T or
     H pattern is recommended for C-17 airdrops due to the aircraft's side angle vision limitations. When the drop
     aircraft is 100 meters directly to the right of the corner panel (inverted L marking), the drop is executed.
     Markings (four panels) for the inverted L are placed as follows (see figure 21-2 on page 372):

          • From the RP:
                 Move 100 meters to the left (90 degrees) of drop heading for the location of the corner panel.
                 Emplace a panel marker with the long axis of the panel parallel with the drop heading.
                 Elevate the panel at a 45-degree angle toward the approaching aircraft; this aids the aircrew and
                     the jumpmaster in visual identification of the DZ.

          • From the corner panel—
                 Move in the same direction as above (from the RP) for 50 meters for the location of the
                     alignment panel.
                 Emplace a panel marker with the long axis of the panel perpendicular to the drop heading.
                 Elevate the panel at a 45-degree angle toward the approaching aircraft.

          • From the alignment panel—
                 Move 150 meters (or edge of the DZ) in the same direction as above (from the RP) for the
                     location of the flanker panel.
                 Emplace a panel marker with the long axis of the panel perpendicular to the drop heading.
                 Elevate the panel at a 45-degree angle toward the approaching aircraft.

          • From the corner panel—
                 Move 50 meters on a back azimuth of the drop heading for the location of the approach panel.
                 Emplace a panel marker with the long axis of the panel parallel with the drop heading.
                 Elevate the panel at a 45-degree angle toward the approaching aircraft.

          • At night, replace all panels with a directional light; lights are shielded on three sides or placed in
                pits.

          • The RP/control center must be distinguishably marked from all other markings on the DZ.
          • NO DROP may be signaled to the aircraft by red smoke, red flares, scrambled panels, or the absence

                of a planned signal.

MASK CLEARANCE AND CODE LETTERS

     21-9. Since the aircraft is required to fly along the DZ markings, these markings must be visible to the
     aircrew. The markings are placed where obstacles do not mask the pilot's line of sight. As a guide, a mask
     clearance ratio of 1 to 15 (1:15) is used, which is one unit of vertical clearance for every 15 units of horizontal
     clearance. For example, if a DZ marker must be positioned near a terrain mask, such as the edge of a forest
     that is on the DZ track, and the trees are 10-meters high (33 feet), the markings would require 150 meters
     (492 feet) of horizontal clearance from the trees. (See figure 21-2 on page 376.) If the panels are in the
     masking ratio due to usable DZ size restrictions, a far marker must be placed in line with the corner panel on
     the drop heading where it can best be observed by aircraft. This only applies to static line jumps.

     21-10. If any portion of the inverted L falls within a 15-to-1 (15:1) mask clearance ratio of obstacles on the
     approach end of the DZ, a far panel or a code letter (H, E, A, T) is required on the departure end of the DZ
     or where it can best be seen for a CDS or bundle drop and should be coordinated during the DZST or aircrew
     mission briefing. This far marking is online with the corner panel to allow the aircrew to begin alignment on
     the RP until the inverted L comes into view. If a code letter is used, it can be used to distinguish the DZ from
     other DZs in the area.

     21-12. VIRS is used to execute a drop over the RP by ground-to-air (GTA) verbal command. This method
     allows the conduct of the operation with a minimum amount of prior DZ information and coordination. The
     aircraft flies in the given direction until spotted by the DZSTL. Only one aircraft is on any one given leg at
     any one given time. A code letter (H, E, A, T) marks the RP. Once the crew identifies the DZ, the radio
     operator directs the aircraft over the drop heading RP. When the aircraft is directly over the RP, the command
     EXECUTE, EXECUTE, EXECUTE initiates the drop. (See figure 21-5.)

DAY AND NIGHT DROP ZONE MARKINGS

     21-13. The following actions are required for a day VIRS DZ. The DZSTL places the code letter on the drop
     heading, with the base panel of the letter at the RP. The code letter is formed by panel markers placed
     together. Each letter is two panels high and one panel wide.

     21-14. The flank panel is placed parallel to the code letter oriented lengthwise on drop heading and aligned
     with the base panel and elevated 45 degrees towards the RP. It is placed 200 meters to the left of the code
     letter (or at the edge of the DZ, whichever is closer). The far panel is placed 500 meters from the base panel
     (or at the edge of the DZ, whichever is closer) and online with the drop heading oriented lengthwise on drop
     heading and elevated 45 degrees towards the RP. Both the far and flank panels consist of a single panel
     marker. These panels must also be elevated at a 45-degree angle towards the RP to improve visibility.

     21-15. The procedures for establishing the DZ are the same for night operations except that white lights are
     used for the code letter and far and flank markings. Each code letter is four lights high and three lights wide
     with five meters between each light. The far and flank lights are signal lights. A white-and-red lens ATC (SE
     11) light should also be located at the RP. Lights must be shielded on three sides or placed in pits to prevent
     enemy ground observation.

GUIDANCE PROCEDURES

     21-16. During Army DZ operations, the GTA operator is responsible for guiding the jump aircraft to the DZ,
     over the DZ on the proper drop heading, and at the proper altitude and drop speed. They ensure the jumpers
     exit the aircraft at the proper RP.
